PostgreSQL Practice

10 phases, 92 sessions. Open a phase, then a session: topics to read, then questions to solve on the practice database.

Phase 0 Setup Load the practice database, set up psql, warm up. Session 1 · 1 of 1 ready Phase 1 Joins Write any join correctly the first time and predict its row count. Sessions 2–12 · 11 of 11 ready Phase 2 Subqueries + Date/Time Use subqueries on purpose, and handle dates and time zones without bugs. Sessions 13–18 · 6 of 6 ready Phase 3 CTEs + Window functions Solve ranking, running totals, gaps and islands, hierarchies and cohorts in one readable query. Sessions 19–36 · 18 of 18 ready Phase 4 JSONB, arrays + modelling Know when to use columns, arrays or JSONB, and design schemas that keep data correct. Sessions 37–43 · 7 of 7 ready Phase 5 Indexes + EXPLAIN Read any query plan, choose the right index, and prove the speed-up. Sessions 44–54 · 11 of 11 ready Phase 6 Transactions + locking Prevent lost updates, races and deadlocks, and change big tables without downtime. Sessions 55–63 · 9 of 9 ready Phase 7 Functions, triggers + RLS Write safe functions, procedures and triggers, and secure data with roles and row-level security. Sessions 64–74 · 11 of 11 ready Phase 8 Internals + operations Understand how Postgres stores and versions data, and run backups, replicas and pooling yourself. Sessions 75–86 · not written yet Phase 9 Final project: Visitly Review and tune the database of your Visitly restaurant app like a senior engineer. Sessions 87–92 · not written yet

Phase 1 · Sessions 2–12

Joins

Write any join correctly the first time and predict its row count.

Session 2 INNER JOIN and the join mental model Understand what a join actually does to rows, predict how many rows any inner join returns, and join three or four tables along their foreign keys. 15 questions Session 3 Outer joins: LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and NULLs Keep rows that have no match, count correctly after an outer join, and use FULL OUTER JOIN to compare two data sets. 15 questions Session 4 Semi-joins and anti-joins: EXISTS, NOT EXISTS and the NOT IN trap Answer "has at least one…" and "has none…" questions correctly, without duplicates, and never fall into the NOT IN + NULL trap. 15 questions Session 5 ON vs WHERE in outer joins, and the chain trap Know exactly where a filter belongs in an outer join, and stop a later join from silently undoing your LEFT JOIN. 15 questions Session 6 Self joins, CROSS JOIN and non-equi joins Join a table to itself (hierarchies, pairs, comparisons), generate combinations with CROSS JOIN, and join on ranges instead of equal keys. 15 questions Session 7 Review + Apply: joins week 1 Pull Sessions 2–6 back out of memory without notes, then build the first real query of your Phase 1 project. 15 questions Session 8 Fan-out: why your SUM is wrong after a join Recognise when a join multiplies rows, know the grain of every result, and aggregate several one-to-many relationships without double counting. 15 questions Session 9 Joins inside UPDATE, DELETE and INSERT Change data based on other tables safely: UPDATE … FROM, DELETE … USING, INSERT … SELECT, always inside a transaction you can inspect and roll back. 15 questions Session 10 Latest row per group: DISTINCT ON and LATERAL Answer "the latest / first / top-N per group" questions deterministically, with DISTINCT ON for top-1 and LATERAL for anything per-row. 15 questions Session 11 How Postgres executes a join (EXPLAIN) Know the three join algorithms, read the join part of an EXPLAIN plan, and understand why foreign keys need indexes. 15 questions Session 12 Exit test + Apply: Joins Prove you own joins: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct. Then finish the joins dashboard. 15 questions

Phase 3 · Sessions 19–36

CTEs + Window functions

Solve ranking, running totals, gaps and islands, hierarchies and cohorts in one readable query.

Session 19 CTEs: name your steps Write complex queries as a readable chain of named steps with WITH, reuse a step several times, and know when Postgres inlines or materializes it. 15 questions Session 20 CTEs for cleaning, aggregation and changing data Build clean-validate-load pipelines as CTE steps, and use data-modifying CTEs to delete, insert and update in one statement. 15 questions Session 21 Review: set operations, dates, spines and CTEs Pull Sessions 15–20 back out of memory, mixed together, without notes. 15 questions Session 22 How window functions work Compute group values next to every row without collapsing rows, and know exactly when window functions run. 15 questions Session 23 ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK Number and rank rows overall or per group, and choose the right function for ties. 15 questions Session 24 Top-N per group and removing duplicates Solve "the top N of each group" and "keep one row per key" the standard way, and know when DISTINCT ON or LATERAL is the better tool. 15 questions Session 25 Running totals, moving averages and frames Control exactly which rows a window adds up with ROWS, RANGE and GROUPS frames, for running totals, moving averages and time-based rolling windows. 15 questions Session 26 LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE Compare each row with the row before or after it, and pick the first, last or Nth value of a Phase 6 · Sessions 55–63

Transactions + locking

Session 55 Transactions and savepoints Group changes into all-or-nothing units, recover from errors inside a transaction with savepoints, and know what a rollback does and does not undo. 15 questions Session 56 Review: performance and transactions Pull Sessions 50–55 back out of memory: sorting, pagination, statistics, settings and transactions, mixed on the big tables. 15 questions Session 57 Isolation levels and anomalies Know exactly what one transaction can see of another at each isolation level, recognise lost updates and write skew, and handle serialization failures with retries. 15 questions Session 58 Row locks and job queues Lock exactly the rows you need with FOR UPDATE and its variants, build a job queue that many workers can share, and find, avoid and survive lock waits and deadlocks. 14 questions Session 59 Race-free creation and advisory locks Create rows exactly once under concurrency (constraints, ON CONFLICT, exclusion constraints, idempotency keys), and serialise work that has no row to lock with advisory locks. 15 questions Session 60 Views and materialized views Name and reuse queries with views, write through simple views safely, and serve expensive reports from materialized views refreshed without blocking readers. 15 questions Session 61 Zero-downtime migrations Change the schema of a busy database without blocking the application: know which DDL takes which lock, avoid the lock queue, and use NOT VALID, CONCURRENTLY and expand/contract. 14 questions Session 62 Exit test + Apply: Concurrency Prove you can keep data correct when many sessions work at once: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct. 15 questions Session 63 Review: isolation, locks and migrations Pull Sessions 57–62 back out of memory, mixed with earlier phases, before moving on to functions and triggers. 15 questions

← Phase 0: SetupAll phasesSchema

Phase 0 · Session 1

Set up your lab and warm up

Load the practice database, set up psql the way professionals use it, learn how a query is really executed, and warm up with single-table questions.

Topics

What you are setting up

Every session from now on uses one database called practice. It is a small online shop: customers, orders, order items, products, payments, reviews, employees and a few lookup tables. It is small on purpose (20 customers, 36 orders) so you can read the data with your own eyes and check every answer. It is also full of the mess real data has: customers who never ordered, an order with no items, payments for orders that do not exist, NULL cities and a duplicate customer. Those edge cases are exactly where joins go wrong, so they are where you will learn.

Step 1 · Create and load the database

Download practice.sql (also in this repo at docs/data/practice.sql). Then in a terminal:

psql -U postgres -c "CREATE DATABASE practice"
psql -U postgres -d practice -f practice.sql

The file starts with DROP TABLE IF EXISTS …, so you can run it again any time to reset the data, for example after practising UPDATEs and DELETEs.

Step 2 · Configure psql once

psql reads a start-up file every time it opens. On Windows it is %APPDATA%\postgresql\psqlrc.conf (create the folder if it does not exist); on Mac/Linux it is ~/.psqlrc. Put this in it:

\set QUIET 1
\pset null '∅'
\timing on
\x auto
\set ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK interactive
\set HISTSIZE 5000
\set QUIET 0
  • \pset null '∅' prints NULL as ∅. Without it a NULL and an empty string look identical, and you will misread join results. The expected outputs on this site also show NULL as ∅.
  • \timing on prints how long every query took. You will start caring about this in Phase 5.
  • \x auto switches to vertical output when a row is too wide for the screen.
  • ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK interactive means a typo inside a transaction does not throw away everything you did before it.

Step 3 · Look around the schema

Connect with psql -U postgres -d practice, then try \dt (list tables) and \d orders (describe one table). The relationships you will join on all session long:

customers ──< orders ──< order_items >── products >── categories
    │            │                            │
    │            ├── payments (no FK!)        └──< product_suppliers >── suppliers
    │            └── deliveries (one per shipped order)
    ├── referred_by → customers (self)
    ├──< page_views (website clicks)
    └──< reviews >── products

departments ──< employees ── manager_id → employees (self)

routes: one-way shipping routes between cities
lookups: discount_tiers, shipping_zones, sizes, colors

Phase 4 (arrays, JSONB, modelling):
products ──  product_details (tags[], specs JSONB)
         ──< product_attributes, price_history, inventory (per warehouse)
customers ──< events (JSONB payload)
stock_feed: incoming stock counts (no FK!)

Phase 6 (transactions and locking): accounts, jobs (a work queue), table_bookings

Phase 5 (load big.sql): big_customers ──< big_orders (200,000 rows); big_events (JSONB)

──<  means "one to many": one customer has many orders

How Postgres really runs a query

You write a query top to bottom, but Postgres evaluates it in a different order. Learn this order now; almost every confusing join result later is explained by it.

1. FROM / JOIN    build the rows (this is where joins happen)
2. WHERE          throw away rows that fail the condition
3. GROUP BY       collapse rows into groups
4. HAVING         throw away groups
5. SELECT         compute the output columns (aliases are born here)
6. DISTINCT       remove duplicate output rows
7. ORDER BY       sort (can use SELECT aliases)
8. LIMIT/OFFSET   cut

That is why WHERE total > 100 fails when total is an alias defined in SELECT (WHERE runs before SELECT), while ORDER BY total works (ORDER BY runs after).

SELECT order_id, quantity * unit_price AS line_total
FROM order_items
WHERE quantity * unit_price > 100000   -- repeat the expression: the alias does not exist yet
ORDER BY line_total DESC;             -- the alias works here
order_idline_total
11120000.00
20120000.00
25119000.00
1118000.00

(4 rows)

NULL is not a value, it is "unknown"

Any comparison with NULL gives NULL (unknown), and WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is true. So city = NULL never matches anything, and neither does city <> 'Mumbai' for a row whose city is NULL. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, and IS DISTINCT FROM when you want NULL to count as "different".

SELECT
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE city <> 'Mumbai')                  AS not_mumbai_with_equals,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE city IS DISTINCT FROM 'Mumbai')    AS not_mumbai_null_safe
FROM customers;
not_mumbai_with_equalsnot_mumbai_null_safe
1517

(1 row)

The second number is 2 higher: the two customers with an unknown city. Remember this. In joins, NULL keys never match anything, which is the root of half the bugs in this phase.

How to work through every session

  • Read the topics and type every example yourself.
  • Create one file per session in psql/ (for example psql/s01.sql) and write each answer there.
  • Before running a query, guess how many rows it will return. Then run it and compare with Expected.
  • Open Answer only after a real attempt, then retype the answer yourself.
  • Got one wrong? Write it in mistakes.md and redo it at the start of the next session.

Questions say how to order the output, so your rows should match the expected output exactly, row for row.

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s01.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. How many customers are there? Return one number.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    SELECT count(*) AS customers
FROM customers;
    customers
    20

    (1 row)

    count(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs. There are 20.

  2. List the customer_id and full_name of customers who live in Mumbai, ordered by customer_id.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    SELECT customer_id, full_name
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Mumbai'
ORDER BY customer_id;
    customer_idfull_name
    1Aarav Shah
    8Myra Chawla
    17Arnav Desai

    (3 rows)

    A simple equality filter. Text comparison is case-sensitive.

  3. Which customers have an unknown city? Show customer_id and full_name.

    Expected: 2 rows

    Answer
    SELECT customer_id, full_name
FROM customers
WHERE city IS NULL
ORDER BY customer_id;
    customer_idfull_name

  15. Challenge: This one runs on your track1 database (from psql/track1.sql), not on practice. Fix track1 Q31: one UPDATE that gives Engineering +12%, Finance +8%, HR +6%, Sales +10% and everyone else +3%, capped at 150,000. Every employee with a salary must be raised, including Nisha Shah, whose department_id (99) matches no department. Employees with a NULL salary must stay NULL. Run it inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK and RETURN employee_id, full_name and the new salary.

    Runs on your track1 database

    Answer
    BEGIN;

UPDATE employees e
SET salary = LEAST(
      e.salary * CASE (SELECT d.name FROM departments d WHERE d.department_id = e.department_id)
                   WHEN 'Engineering' THEN 1.12
                   WHEN 'Finance'     THEN 1.08
                   WHEN 'HR'          THEN 1.06
                   WHEN 'Sales'       THEN 1.10
                   ELSE 1.03                 -- also covers department 99 (subquery returns NULL)
                 END,
      150000)
WHERE e.salary IS NOT NULL                    -- LEAST ignores NULLs: LEAST(NULL, 150000) = 150000!
RETURNING e.employee_id, e.full_name, e.salary;

ROLLBACK;

    Two bugs hide in the original. 1) UPDATE … FROM is an inner join, so Nisha (department 99) never matched and was never updated. A scalar subquery returns NULL when nothing matches, which falls through to ELSE. 2) LEAST and GREATEST ignore NULL arguments, so without the WHERE clause a NULL salary would become 150,000.

Phase 1 · Session 2

INNER JOIN and the join mental model

Understand what a join actually does to rows, predict how many rows any inner join returns, and join three or four tables along their foreign keys.

Topics

Why joins exist

The orders table does not store the customer's name. It stores customer_id, a pointer to one row in customers. Storing each fact once (normalisation) keeps data consistent: change a customer's email in one place and every order "sees" it. The price is that answering almost any business question means putting rows from several tables back together. That is a join.

The mental model: pairs of rows

Think of A JOIN B ON condition like this: take every possible pair of one row from A and one row from B, and keep the pairs where the condition is true. Postgres never literally builds every pair (Session 11 shows the clever algorithms it uses), but the result is always the same as if it had. Here are customers 1 and 9 joined to their orders:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.status
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IN (1, 9)
ORDER BY o.order_id;
customer_idfull_nameorder_idorder_datestatus
1Aarav Shah12025-01-05delivered
1Aarav Shah32025-01-20delivered
1Aarav Shah132025-04-18delivered
1Aarav Shah272025-10-03pending

(4 rows)

Two things to notice. Customer 1 appears four times, once per matching order: a join repeats the "one" side for every match on the "many" side. Customer 9 does not appear at all: they have no orders, so no pair satisfies the condition. An inner join drops unmatched rows from both sides. Keeping them is what outer joins (next session) are for.

Syntax you will use every day

SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, c.full_name
FROM orders AS o                      -- AS is optional: "orders o" is the same
INNER JOIN customers AS c             -- INNER is optional: JOIN means INNER JOIN
        ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
order_idorder_datefull_name
12025-01-05Aarav Shah
22025-01-09Diya Menon
32025-01-20Aarav Shah
42025-02-03Kabir Khan
52025-02-11Ananya Gupta

(36 rows, first 5 shown)

  • Aliases (o, c) keep queries short. Once you alias a table you must use the alias.
  • Qualify every column (o.order_id, not order_id) once two tables are involved. If both tables have a column with the same name, an unqualified reference is an error ("column reference is ambiguous"); if not, it still makes the query easier to read.
  • ON holds the join condition. It is usually "foreign key = primary key", but it can be any boolean expression (Session 6 joins on ranges).
  • USING (col) is a shortcut when both columns have the same name: orders JOIN order_items USING (order_id). The joined column then appears once and is referenced without a table prefix.
  • NATURAL JOIN joins on every column with the same name, silently. Add a created_at column to both tables next year and your query changes meaning. Never use it in real code.

Predict the row count before you run

This is the single most valuable habit in this phase. For an inner join along a foreign key from a "many" table to a "one" table, the result has one row per row of the many side that has a match.

  • orders JOIN customers: every order has exactly one customer (customer_id is NOT NULL with a foreign key), so the result has exactly as many rows as orders: 36.
  • order_items JOIN products: one row per order item: 59.
  • products JOIN categories: 15 products, but the Gift Card has a NULL category_id. NULL never equals anything, so it has no match and disappears: 14.
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id) AS orders_x_customers,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM products p JOIN categories k ON k.category_id = p.category_id) AS products_x_categories,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM products) AS all_products;
orders_x_customersproducts_x_categoriesall_products
361415

(1 row)

When your count is lower than you predicted, an inner join dropped rows (unmatched or NULL keys). When it is higher, a join multiplied rows (you joined to something with several matches per row). Both are bugs until you can explain them.

Joining three or more tables

Each JOIN adds one table to the rows built so far. Follow the foreign keys like a path: orders → order_items → products → categories. Order 9 had three lines:

SELECT o.order_id, c.full_name, p.name AS product, k.name AS category,
       oi.quantity, oi.unit_price, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS line_total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers   c  ON c.customer_id  = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id    = o.order_id
JOIN products    p  ON p.product_id   = oi.product_id
JOIN categories  k  ON k.category_id  = p.category_id
WHERE o.order_id = 9
ORDER BY line_total DESC;
order_idfull_nameproductcategoryquantityunit_priceline_total
9Diya MenonLaptop Air 13Computers184000.0084000.00
9Diya MenonUSB-C HubAccessories13500.003500.00
9Diya MenonWireless MouseAccessories11500.001500.00

(3 rows)

The grain (what one row represents) of this result is "one order line", because order_items is the finest table in the chain. Always know the grain of your result; Session 8 is entirely about what happens when you forget it.

Where filters go (for INNER joins)

Remember the execution order: FROM/JOIN first, then WHERE. For an inner join, a condition in ON and the same condition in WHERE give identical results. By convention, put the relationship (keys) in ON and the business filters in WHERE. This stops being true for outer joins, which is the whole topic of Session 5.

Classic mistakes

  • Joining on the wrong columns, for example ON o.order_id = c.customer_id. It runs, returns plausible-looking rows, and is completely wrong. Read every ON clause as a sentence: "the order's customer_id equals the customer's customer_id".
  • Forgetting the condition with old comma syntax: FROM orders, customers with no WHERE produces 36 × 20 = 720 rows. Use explicit JOIN … ON and this cannot happen silently.
  • SELECT * across joins returns duplicate column names (two customer_id columns) and breaks when tables change. List the columns you need.

Phase 1 · Session 3

Outer joins: LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and NULLs

Keep rows that have no match, count correctly after an outer join, and use FULL OUTER JOIN to compare two data sets.

Topics

The problem inner joins cannot solve

"Show every customer with their number of orders" sounds simple. With an inner join, the 4 customers who never ordered vanish, and a report that silently drops customers is wrong. An outer join keeps rows that have no match and fills the missing side with NULLs.

LEFT JOIN

A LEFT JOIN B ON … returns every inner-join pair, plus every row of A that matched nothing, with all of B's columns set to NULL. A is the "preserved" side; B is the "optional" side.

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, o.order_id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IN (1, 9)
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;
customer_idfull_nameorder_idstatus
1Aarav Shah1delivered
1Aarav Shah3delivered
1Aarav Shah13delivered
1Aarav Shah27pending
9Reyansh Jain∅∅

(5 rows)

Customer 1 still appears four times. Customer 9 now appears once, with ∅ (NULL) in every order column. Row count rule: LEFT JOIN rows = inner-join rows + unmatched left rows. For all customers: 36 + 4 = 40.

Counting after a LEFT JOIN: COUNT(*) lies

The NULL-filled row is still a row. count(*) counts it, so customers with no orders get 1 instead of 0. Count a column from the optional side instead: count(o.order_id) skips NULLs. Use the optional table's primary key, because it is never NULL on a real match.

SELECT c.customer_id,
       count(*)          AS wrong_count,
       count(o.order_id) AS right_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IN (1, 9, 13)
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idwrong_countright_count

(3 rows)

The same applies to sums: sum(x) over only NULLs is NULL, not 0. Wrap it: COALESCE(sum(x), 0).

COALESCE for display

COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL argument. Use it to label missing data (COALESCE(k.name, 'Uncategorised')) or to turn missing totals into 0. Use it in SELECT for display; be careful using it in ON or WHERE, because wrapping a column in a function usually stops Postgres from using an index on it.

RIGHT JOIN

A RIGHT JOIN B is exactly B LEFT JOIN A: it preserves the right side. Most teams never use RIGHT JOIN because reading a query is easier when the "main" table comes first and everything else hangs off it with LEFT JOINs. Recognise it; prefer writing LEFT.

FULL OUTER JOIN

FULL JOIN preserves both sides: matched pairs, unmatched left rows (right side NULL) and unmatched right rows (left side NULL). Its natural use is comparing or reconciling two data sets, for example our orders against the payment provider's file:

SELECT o.order_id AS order_in_shop, p.order_id AS order_in_payments, p.amount
FROM orders o
FULL JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL OR p.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY COALESCE(o.order_id, p.order_id);
order_in_shoporder_in_paymentsamount
12∅∅
20∅∅
27∅∅
29∅∅
30∅∅
32∅∅
34∅∅
35∅∅
36∅∅
∅401200.00
∅99994999.00

(11 rows)

Rows with ∅ on the left are payments for orders the shop does not have (9999 and 40). Rows with ∅ on the right are orders with no payment. One query finds both kinds of mismatch.

NULL and join keys

  • A NULL key never matches anything, not even another NULL. NULL = NULL is NULL, not true.
  • So a row with a NULL foreign key is always "unmatched": dropped by an inner join, NULL-extended by an outer join.
  • To test "did this row find a match?", check the optional side's primary key: WHERE o.order_id IS NULL. Checking a nullable column (like o.shipping_city IS NULL) mixes up "no match" with "matched, but the value is NULL" (order 24!). Next session builds on this.

Rule of thumb for reports: start FROM the table whose rows must all appear (customers, products, departments), then LEFT JOIN everything else to it.

    SELECT COALESCE(o.order_id, pay.order_id) AS order_id,
       it.items_total,
       pay.paid,
       CASE
         WHEN o.order_id IS NULL          THEN 'payment without order'
         WHEN pay.paid IS NULL            THEN 'unpaid'
         WHEN pay.paid = 0                THEN 'refunded'
         WHEN pay.paid = it.items_total   THEN 'paid'
         WHEN pay.paid > it.items_total   THEN 'overpaid'
         ELSE 'underpaid'

FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS items_total
           FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) it ON it.order_id = o.order_id
FULL JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(amount) AS paid
           FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER BY 1;

Phase 1 · Session 4

Semi-joins and anti-joins: EXISTS, NOT EXISTS and the NOT IN trap

Answer "has at least one…" and "has none…" questions correctly, without duplicates, and never fall into the NOT IN + NULL trap.

Topics

Two questions that are not really joins

Many questions do not need any columns from the second table. They only ask whether a match exists:

  • Semi-join: rows of A that have at least one match in B. "Customers who have ordered."
  • Anti-join: rows of A that have no match in B. "Customers who have never ordered."

You can force these into ordinary joins, but each has a cleaner, safer form, and Postgres has special plan nodes for both (Hash Semi Join, Hash Anti Join) that stop looking as soon as the answer is known.

Semi-join with EXISTS

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id   -- correlated: refers to the outer row
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idfull_name
1Aarav Shah
2Diya Menon
3Kabir Khan
4Ananya Gupta
5Ishaan Reddy

(16 rows, first 5 shown)

The subquery is correlated: for each customer it asks "is there any order with this customer_id?". What it SELECTs does not matter (SELECT 1 is the convention); EXISTS only checks whether at least one row comes back. Each customer appears once, no matter how many orders they have. Compare with a plain join, which repeats customer 1 four times and needs DISTINCT to undo the damage:

SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id)  AS join_rows,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)) AS exists_rows;
join_rowsexists_rows
3616

(1 row)

WHERE c.customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) also works for semi-joins and Postgres usually plans it the same way. Prefer EXISTS when the matching condition has more than one column or extra filters.

Anti-join: three ways to write "has no match"

-- 1. NOT EXISTS (recommended)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idfull_name
9Reyansh Jain
13Liam Wong
15Noah Fernandes
16Tara Singh

(4 rows)

-- 2. LEFT JOIN … IS NULL
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL                -- test the PRIMARY KEY of the optional side
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idfull_name
9Reyansh Jain
13Liam Wong
15Noah Fernandes
16Tara Singh

(4 rows)

Both return the same 4 customers. The LEFT JOIN version works because unmatched rows are NULL-extended, and WHERE keeps only those. Always test a column that cannot be NULL in a real match (the primary key); testing a nullable column like o.shipping_city would also return customers whose order merely has no city.

The NOT IN trap

The third way, NOT IN (subquery), looks the most natural and is the most dangerous. "Customers who never referred anyone":

-- Looks right, returns NOTHING
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.customer_id NOT IN (SELECT referred_by FROM customers);
customer_idfull_name

(0 rows)

Zero rows, although most customers never referred anyone. Why? referred_by contains NULLs. x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL. The last comparison is NULL (unknown), so the whole condition can never be true. One NULL in the subquery wipes out the entire result, and nothing warns you.

-- Correct: NOT EXISTS is not affected by NULLs
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers r WHERE r.referred_by = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idfull_name
5Ishaan Reddy
7Vivaan Bose
9Reyansh Jain
10Kiara Sethi
11Aditya Rao

(12 rows, first 5 shown)

Never use NOT IN with a subquery unless the column is declared NOT NULL, and even then prefer NOT EXISTS, because columns change. NOT IN with a literal list you typed yourself (status NOT IN ('cancelled', 'pending')) is fine.

Multi-condition existence

EXISTS shines when "a match" means more than one condition, for example "customers who have a delivered order to a different city". You put every condition inside the subquery:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND o.status = 'delivered'
    AND o.shipping_city <> c.city
);
customer_idfull_name
1Aarav Shah

(1 row)

"For all" questions: double NOT EXISTS

SQL has no FOR ALL keyword. "Customers who bought every product in a category" is rewritten as "customers for whom there is no product in the category that they have not bought". That is two nested NOT EXISTS, a pattern called relational division. You will build it in the hard problem.

Choosing

  • Need columns from B? Use a JOIN.
  • Only need to know whether a match exists? Use EXISTS / NOT EXISTS.
  • Anti-join? NOT EXISTS by default; LEFT JOIN … IS NULL is fine (test the PK). Avoid NOT IN (subquery).

Phase 1 · Session 5

ON vs WHERE in outer joins, and the chain trap

Know exactly where a filter belongs in an outer join, and stop a later join from silently undoing your LEFT JOIN.

Topics

The bug that ships to production

Business question: "every customer with their number of delivered orders, zero included". Here is the version most people write first:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, count(o.order_id) AS delivered_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.full_name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idfull_namedelivered_orders
1Aarav Shah3
2Diya Menon3
3Kabir Khan1
4Ananya Gupta1

(14 rows, first 4 shown)

14 rows, not 20. Customers with no orders and customers with no delivered orders are gone, even though we wrote LEFT JOIN. Walk through the execution order: the LEFT JOIN runs first and correctly produces NULL-filled rows for customer 9. Then WHERE runs: NULL = 'delivered' is NULL, not true, so the row is thrown away. A WHERE condition on the optional side of a LEFT JOIN turns it back into an inner join.

The fix: put optional-side filters in ON

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, count(o.order_id) AS delivered_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND o.status = 'delivered'          -- decides which orders MATCH
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.full_name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idfull_namedelivered_orders
1Aarav Shah3
2Diya Menon3
3Kabir Khan1
4Ananya Gupta1

(20 rows, first 4 shown)

20 rows. Now the status test is part of the matching rule: only delivered orders match, and customers with no matching order are still kept (NULL-extended) because that is what LEFT JOIN does with unmatched rows.

The rule

Filter on the PRESERVED table (left side of LEFT JOIN)  →  WHERE
Filter on the OPTIONAL table  (right side of LEFT JOIN) →  ON

Exception: WHERE optional.pk IS NULL is deliberate. It is the anti-join
from Session 4 ("keep only the rows that found no match").

And the mirror image, which surprises people: a condition on the preserved side placed in ON does not filter the preserved rows. Rows that fail it are simply unmatched, and LEFT JOIN keeps them anyway:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.city, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                  AND c.city = 'Mumbai'      -- wrong place: does not remove non-Mumbai customers
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.city
ORDER BY c.customer_id
LIMIT 4;
customer_idcityorders
1Mumbai4
2Bengaluru0
3Delhi0
4Pune0

(4 rows)

Every customer is still listed; non-Mumbai customers just show 0 orders, which is a lie. "Only Mumbai customers" belongs in WHERE.

For INNER joins it does not matter

An inner join keeps only matched pairs, so "fails the ON condition" and "removed by WHERE" end the same way. Postgres treats both placements identically for inner joins. The rule above only matters for outer joins, and that is exactly why it gets forgotten.

The chain trap

You LEFT JOIN orders to keep customers without orders, then add order items with a plain JOIN:

SELECT count(*) AS rows_returned, count(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS customers_kept
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi      ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id;
rows_returnedcustomers_kept
5916

(1 row)

Only 16 customers survive. For customer 9 the LEFT JOIN produced a row with o.order_id = NULL; the next INNER JOIN needs oi.order_id = NULL, which is never true, so the row is dropped. Order 30 (no items) disappears the same way. Once a table is joined with LEFT JOIN, every join that hangs off it must also be LEFT, or it cancels the LEFT.

SELECT count(*) AS rows_returned, count(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS customers_kept
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id;
rows_returnedcustomers_kept
6420

(1 row)

When the inner part must stay inner: nested joins

Sometimes the optional part is itself an inner join. "Every order, with its Kitchen items if it has any" needs order_items JOIN products filtered to Kitchen, and that whole combination is optional. Put it in parentheses and LEFT JOIN the result:

SELECT o.order_id, p.name AS kitchen_item
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (order_items oi
           JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
                          AND p.category_id = 5)        -- 5 = Kitchen
       ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id BETWEEN 4 AND 7
ORDER BY o.order_id, p.name;
order_idkitchen_item
4∅
5Chef Knife
5Coffee Maker
6∅
7Air Fryer

(5 rows)

Order 4 and 6 have no kitchen items and still appear once with ∅. If you wrote LEFT JOIN order_items … LEFT JOIN products … AND p.category_id = 5 instead, every non-kitchen line would appear as a row with a NULL product: wrong grain.

Checklist for every outer join you write

  • Which table must keep all its rows? Put it first.
  • Every filter on a LEFT-joined table: is it in ON?
  • Every table joined after a LEFT-joined table: is it also LEFT (or nested in parentheses)?
  • Counts use the optional side's PK; sums are wrapped in COALESCE.
  • Predict the row count; if it is lower than the preserved table, something cancelled your LEFT JOIN.

Phase 1 · Session 6

Self joins, CROSS JOIN and non-equi joins

Join a table to itself (hierarchies, pairs, comparisons), generate combinations with CROSS JOIN, and join on ranges instead of equal keys.

Topics

Self joins: one table, two roles

employees.manager_id points to another row in employees. To show each employee next to their manager's name, you use the table twice with different aliases, one per role. Postgres treats the two aliases as if they were separate tables.

SELECT e.employee_id, e.full_name AS employee, m.full_name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
employee_idemployeemanager
1Asha Rao∅
2Vikram MehtaAsha Rao
3Neha KulkarniVikram Mehta
4Rahul VermaNeha Kulkarni
5Priya NairNeha Kulkarni
6Arjun SinghNeha Kulkarni

(12 rows, first 6 shown)

Read the ON clause carefully: the manager row's id equals the employee row's manager_id. Swapping the sides (m.manager_id = e.employee_id) gives you each employee's reports instead, a completely different question. LEFT JOIN keeps the CEO, who has no manager. Name the aliases after the role (e, m), never a / b.

Going up more than one level

Each extra level is one more self join: LEFT JOIN employees mm ON mm.employee_id = m.manager_id gives the manager's manager. That works for a fixed depth. For "the whole chain, however deep", you need a recursive CTE (Phase 3).

Pairs without duplicates

"Pairs of employees in the same department" joins employees to employees on department. Without care you get every pair twice (A–B and B–A) plus everyone paired with themselves. The fix is an inequality on the key: a.employee_id < b.employee_id keeps each unordered pair exactly once.

SELECT a.full_name AS person_a, b.full_name AS person_b, a.department_id
FROM employees a
JOIN employees b ON b.department_id = a.department_id
                AND a.employee_id < b.employee_id
WHERE a.department_id = 2
ORDER BY a.employee_id, b.employee_id;
person_aperson_bdepartment_id
Sneha IyerKaran Malhotra2
Sneha IyerMeera Joshi2
Karan MalhotraMeera Joshi2

(3 rows)

Sales has 3 people, so 3 pairs (3 choose 2). With <> instead of < you would get 6; with no condition at all, 9.

CROSS JOIN: every combination

A CROSS JOIN B pairs every row of A with every row of B, with no condition. Rows = |A| × |B|. It is the right tool when you want all combinations: every size in every colour, every customer for every month (to fill gaps with zeros), every product in every store.

SELECT s.size || '-' || c.color AS variant
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c
ORDER BY s.sort_order, c.color;
variant
S-Black
S-Blue
S-White
M-Black
M-Blue
M-White

(12 rows, first 6 shown)

An accidental CROSS JOIN is a classic production incident: a missing join condition between two 100,000-row tables produces 10 billion rows. If a query is unexpectedly slow and returns far too many rows, look for a table with no ON condition.

Non-equi joins: joining on ranges

Nothing says ON must use =. Any boolean condition works. The discount_tiers table defines amount ranges; to find each product's tier, join on "price is inside the range":

SELECT p.name, p.price, t.tier, t.discount_pct
FROM products p
JOIN discount_tiers t
  ON p.price >= t.min_amount
 AND (t.max_amount IS NULL OR p.price <= t.max_amount)
ORDER BY p.price DESC
LIMIT 6;
namepricetierdiscount_pct
Laptop Pro 14120000.00Platinum10.0
Laptop Air 1385000.00Gold8.0
4K Monitor42000.00Silver5.0
Standing Desk32000.00Silver5.0
Noise-Cancel Headphones18000.00Silver5.0
Air Fryer11000.00Silver5.0

(6 rows)

  • The max_amount IS NULL branch handles the open-ended top tier ("100,000 and above").
  • Make sure ranges do not overlap, or a row matches two tiers and gets duplicated. Ours use 9,999.99 / 10,000 boundaries for exactly that reason. (Postgres range types and exclusion constraints, Phase 8, can enforce this.)
  • Range joins cannot use a hash join (hashing needs equality), so Postgres uses a nested loop. That is fine for small lookup tables; Session 11 shows why it matters for big ones.

Comparing rows with other rows

Self joins with inequalities answer "compared with others" questions, such as "for each product, how many products in the same category are cheaper?" The join condition combines an equality (same category) and an inequality (cheaper):

SELECT p.name, p.price, count(q.product_id) AS cheaper_in_category
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN products q ON q.category_id = p.category_id
                    AND q.price < p.price
WHERE p.category_id = 3
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.name, p.price
ORDER BY p.price;
namepricecheaper_in_category
Earbuds Lite2500.000
Bluetooth Speaker7000.001
Noise-Cancel Headphones18000.002

(3 rows)

Phase 3 replaces many of these with window functions, which are faster on large tables. But the self-join form is how you reason about them, and it still wins for some range comparisons.

FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 12) AS m(month)

       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND o.order_date >= DATE '2025-01-01'
      AND o.order_date <  DATE '2026-01-01'

ORDER BY c.customer_id, m.month;

    Expected: 8 rows

    SELECT r.full_name AS referrer,
       count(*)                      AS referred,
       count(rev.customer_id)        AS referred_with_delivery,
       COALESCE(sum(rev.revenue), 0) AS referred_revenue
FROM customers r
JOIN customers c ON c.referred_by = r.customer_id
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT o.customer_id, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
) rev ON rev.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY r.customer_id, r.full_name
ORDER BY referred_revenue DESC, r.full_name;

Phase 1 · Session 7

Review + Apply: joins week 1

Pull Sessions 2–6 back out of memory without notes, then build the first real query of your Phase 1 project.

Topics

How to run a review session

  • First 20 minutes: open mistakes.md and redo every question you got wrong in S2–S6, cold. No peeking at your old answers.
  • Then the 14 questions below. They mix every join type from the week, in random order, on purpose. Deciding which technique a question needs is the skill being trained, and blocked practice ("all LEFT JOIN questions in a row") never trains it.
  • Then the Apply project (the hard problem). It is the first piece of your Phase 1 dashboard.

One-page cheat sheet

Question shape                                  Tool
----------------------------------------------  -----------------------------------------
Need columns from both tables, matches only     JOIN … ON
Keep every row of A, B optional                 A LEFT JOIN B ON …
Keep both sides, compare two data sets          FULL JOIN … ON …  (WHERE a.pk IS NULL OR b.pk IS NULL)
A has at least one match in B                   WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE …)
A has no match in B                             WHERE NOT EXISTS (…)   never NOT IN (subquery)
B for all X (division)                          NOT EXISTS ( … NOT EXISTS ( … ))
Rows compared with other rows of same table     self join with role aliases (e, m)
Each pair once                                  a.id < b.id
Every combination / build a grid                CROSS JOIN
Match on a range                                ON x >= lo AND (hi IS NULL OR x <= hi)
Rules
1. Predict the row count before running.
2. Filters on a LEFT-joined table go in ON; filters on the preserved table go in WHERE.
3. After a LEFT JOIN, every join hanging off it is LEFT too (or nested in parentheses).
4. Count the optional side's PK; COALESCE sums.
5. Test "no match" with the optional side's PK IS NULL.
6. NULL never equals anything. Use IS NULL / IS DISTINCT FROM.

← Phase 1: JoinsAll phasesSchema

Phase 1 · Session 8

Fan-out: why your SUM is wrong after a join

Recognise when a join multiplies rows, know the grain of every result, and aggregate several one-to-many relationships without double counting.

Topics

The most expensive join bug

A join repeats the "one" side once per matching row on the "many" side. That is harmless when you only display rows, and dangerous the moment you aggregate. Finance reports, dashboards and invoices are wrong in production every day because of it, and nothing errors. This session makes you immune.

Grain: what does one row mean?

Every table has a grain: one row of orders is one order; one row of order_items is one line of an order; one row of payments is one payment. After a join, the grain of the result is the finest grain involved, and when you join two independent "many" tables to the same parent, the grain becomes "every combination of them".

Order 9 has 3 items and 2 payments. Join both to the order:

SELECT o.order_id, oi.product_id, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS line_value,
       p.payment_id, p.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN payments p     ON p.order_id  = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id = 9
ORDER BY oi.product_id, p.payment_id;
order_idproduct_idline_valuepayment_idamount
9284000.001050000.00
9284000.001139000.00
931500.001050000.00
931500.001139000.00
953500.001050000.00
953500.001139000.00

(6 rows)

3 × 2 = 6 rows. Each line value appears twice (once per payment) and each payment appears three times (once per line). Now aggregate it:

SELECT sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS items_total,
       sum(p.amount)                    AS paid
FROM order_items oi
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE oi.order_id = 9;
items_totalpaid
178000.00267000.00

(1 row)

The real item total is 89,000 and the real amount paid is 89,000. The query reports double and triple. This is fan-out (also called a "chasm trap"). Note that the totals still look like plausible money amounts, which is why nobody notices.

Fix 1 (default): aggregate each side first, then join

Reduce each "many" table to one row per key before joining. Each derived table then joins 1:1 and nothing can multiply.

SELECT o.order_id, it.items_total, pay.paid
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS items_total
           FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) it  ON it.order_id  = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(amount) AS paid
           FROM payments GROUP BY order_id)    pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id IN (2, 9, 30)
ORDER BY o.order_id;
order_iditems_totalpaid
223000.0046000.00
989000.0089000.00
30∅∅

(3 rows)

This is the pattern to reach for whenever a report combines measures from two or more child tables. In Phase 3 you will write the same thing with CTEs (WITH items AS (…), pay AS (…)), which reads even better.

Fix 2: COUNT(DISTINCT …), for counts only

count(DISTINCT oi.product_id) and count(DISTINCT p.payment_id) give correct counts even on the multiplied rows, because duplicates collapse. It is quick and fine for counts. It is not a fix for sums: sum(DISTINCT amount) adds each distinct value once, so two genuinely different payments of the same amount become one:

SELECT sum(amount)          AS real_paid,
       sum(DISTINCT amount) AS sum_distinct_is_wrong
FROM payments
WHERE order_id = 2;     -- the customer was charged 23,000 twice
real_paidsum_distinct_is_wrong
46000.0023000.00

(1 row)

SUM(DISTINCT) hides exactly the problems a finance report exists to find (here, a double charge). Never use it to "fix" fan-out.

Fix 3: scalar subqueries in SELECT

For a small number of measures per row, a correlated subquery per measure is clear and safe:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS orders,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM reviews r WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS reviews
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.customer_id
LIMIT 5;
customer_idfull_nameordersreviews
1Aarav Shah42
2Diya Menon43
3Kabir Khan30
4Ananya Gupta21
5Ishaan Reddy32

(5 rows)

It runs one subquery per output row, which is fine for 20 customers and usually fine with an index. For millions of rows the derived-table version is generally faster. Session 11 and Phase 5 show how to check with EXPLAIN.

Detecting fan-out

  • Before aggregating, run the join with count(*) and count(DISTINCT parent_key). If they differ, every parent row is repeated and parent-level sums will be multiplied.
  • Sanity-check one total against a direct calculation: the revenue for one customer computed from order_items alone must equal the number in your report.
  • Ask for every table in a join: "how many rows can match one row of the table I am grouping by?" If two different tables answer "many", you have fan-out.

Group by the primary key

When you group by a table's primary key, Postgres lets you select any other column of that table without listing it in GROUP BY, because one key means one value (functional dependency). GROUP BY c.customer_id lets you select c.full_name, c.city and so on. It is shorter, and it makes the grain explicit.

Challenge: Customer value table for all 20 customers: customer_id, full_name, orders, delivered_orders, units (delivered), revenue (delivered), paid (all payments on their orders), reviews and avg_rating (2 decimals, ∅ if none). Order by revenue descending, then customer_id. Then prove there is no fan-out: the sum of your revenue column must equal total delivered revenue computed directly from orders + order_items.

    Expected: 20 rows

    Answer
    SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name,
       COALESCE(o.orders, 0)    AS orders,
       COALESCE(o.delivered, 0) AS delivered_orders,
       COALESCE(d.units, 0)     AS units,
       COALESCE(d.revenue, 0)   AS revenue,
       COALESCE(pay.paid, 0)    AS paid,
       COALESCE(r.reviews, 0)   AS reviews,
       r.avg_rating
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders,
                  count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') AS delivered
           FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT o.customer_id, sum(oi.quantity) AS units,
                  sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
           FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
           WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
           GROUP BY o.customer_id) d ON d.customer_id = c.customer_id

Phase 1 · Session 9

Joins inside UPDATE, DELETE and INSERT

Change data based on other tables safely: UPDATE … FROM, DELETE … USING, INSERT … SELECT, always inside a transaction you can inspect and roll back.

Topics

Every question today changes data: work inside a transaction

Every solution below starts with BEGIN and ends with ROLLBACK, and uses RETURNING to show exactly which rows changed. That is not just for practice: it is how professionals run data fixes in production. Write the change, look at what RETURNING (or a follow-up SELECT) shows, and only then decide between COMMIT and ROLLBACK. If you ever do commit something by mistake, reload practice.sql to reset the database.

BEGIN;
  UPDATE … RETURNING …;     -- look at the rows
  SELECT …;                 -- check the effect
ROLLBACK;                   -- or COMMIT when you are sure

Write the SELECT first

Every data change starts as a SELECT. Write the query that returns exactly the rows you want to change, check the row count, then turn it into UPDATE or DELETE. It is the cheapest insurance there is.

UPDATE … FROM

Postgres lets an UPDATE read other tables in a FROM clause. The join condition between the target table and the FROM tables goes in WHERE:

BEGIN;
UPDATE products p
SET price = round(p.price * 1.10, 2)
FROM categories k
WHERE k.category_id = p.category_id      -- join condition
  AND k.name = 'Audio'                   -- filter
RETURNING p.product_id, p.name, p.price;
ROLLBACK;
product_idnameprice
6Noise-Cancel Headphones19800.00
7Bluetooth Speaker7700.00
8Earbuds Lite2750.00

(3 rows)

  • It is an inner join. Target rows with no match in FROM are not updated at all. That was the Q31 bug in your track1 file: an employee with department 99 matched no department and silently got no raise.
  • Do not repeat the target table in FROM (UPDATE products p … FROM products p2) unless you mean a self join; otherwise you build a cross join of the table with itself.
  • Each target row is updated at most once, even if it matches several FROM rows. Which match wins is not defined. See below.

The silent multiple-match problem

Products appear in many order lines. Try to "set each product's price to the price it was sold at":

BEGIN;
UPDATE products p
SET price = oi.unit_price
FROM order_items oi
WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
RETURNING p.product_id, p.price;
ROLLBACK;
product_idprice
1118000.00
31500.00
618000.00
82500.00
46500.00

(13 rows, first 5 shown)

It "works": 13 rows updated. But Laptop Pro 14 was sold at 118,000, 120,000 (twice) and 119,000, and Postgres picked one of them with no rule you control. Run it on another day, with a different plan, and you may get a different price. The fix is always the same as in Session 8: aggregate to one row per target key first (for example min(unit_price) per product), then join.

DELETE … USING

DELETE uses the keyword USING for the same idea:

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM order_items oi
USING orders o
WHERE o.order_id = oi.order_id
  AND o.status = 'cancelled'
RETURNING oi.order_id, oi.product_id;
ROLLBACK;
order_idproduct_id
42
127
201
342

(4 rows)

For "delete rows that have no match" use NOT EXISTS, exactly like Session 4: DELETE FROM payments p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.order_id = p.order_id).

INSERT … SELECT

Any query, joins included, can feed an INSERT. The column order of the SELECT must match the INSERT column list. Use it for archive tables, summary tables and data migrations. CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT creates and fills a table in one step (without constraints or indexes, so add those yourself if it is permanent).

BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE vip_customers (customer_id int PRIMARY KEY, full_name text, revenue numeric);

INSERT INTO vip_customers (customer_id, full_name, revenue)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.full_name
HAVING sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) > 100000;

SELECT * FROM vip_customers ORDER BY revenue DESC;
ROLLBACK;
customer_idfull_namerevenue
8Myra Chawla150500.00
1Aarav Shah139200.00
10Kiara Sethi126500.00
2Diya Menon117500.00

(4 rows)

When you need every target row: correlated subquery

If a row must be updated even when the lookup finds nothing, do not use FROM (inner join). Use a scalar subquery in SET, which returns NULL when nothing matches, and handle the NULL with COALESCE or CASE. You did exactly this in S1's hard problem.

Check affected row counts every time. psql prints UPDATE 13; RETURNING shows the rows. If the number surprises you, ROLLBACK and find out why before anything else.

  15. Challenge: Merge the duplicate customer safely, in one transaction. Find duplicates by case-insensitive email; the account with the earlier signup_date is canonical. Move the duplicate's orders, reviews and referrals to the canonical account; fill any NULL city, country or referred_by on the canonical account from the duplicate; delete the duplicate; add a unique index on lower(email) so it cannot happen again. Finish by returning the canonical customer (customer_id, full_name, email, orders) and ROLLBACK.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;

-- 1. Which account is the duplicate of which?
CREATE TEMP TABLE merge_map AS
SELECT dup.customer_id AS dup_id, keep.customer_id AS keep_id
FROM customers dup
JOIN customers keep
  ON lower(keep.email) = lower(dup.email)
 AND (keep.signup_date, keep.customer_id) < (dup.signup_date, dup.customer_id);

-- 2. Move everything that points at the duplicate
UPDATE orders o    SET customer_id = m.keep_id FROM merge_map m WHERE o.customer_id = m.dup_id;
UPDATE reviews r   SET customer_id = m.keep_id FROM merge_map m WHERE r.customer_id = m.dup_id;
UPDATE customers c SET referred_by = m.keep_id FROM merge_map m WHERE c.referred_by = m.dup_id;

-- 3. Fill gaps on the canonical row from the duplicate
UPDATE customers k
SET city        = COALESCE(k.city, d.city),
    country     = COALESCE(k.country, d.country),
    referred_by = COALESCE(k.referred_by, d.referred_by)
FROM merge_map m
JOIN customers d ON d.customer_id = m.dup_id
WHERE k.customer_id = m.keep_id;

-- 4. Remove the duplicate and prevent new ones
DELETE FROM customers c USING merge_map m WHERE c.customer_id = m.dup_id;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_ci_uq ON customers (lower(email));

-- 5. Prove it
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.email, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE lower(c.email) = 'diya@mail.test'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.email;

ROLLBACK;
    customer_idfull_nameemailorders
    2Diya Menondiya@mail.test5

    (1 row)

    Diya now has 5 orders and the duplicate is gone. The order of steps matters: you must move every row that references the duplicate before deleting it, or the foreign keys stop you (which is exactly what they are for). The row comparison (signup_date, customer_id) < (…) breaks ties deterministically. The unique index on lower(email) only succeeds after the duplicate is removed.

Phase 1 · Session 10

Latest row per group: DISTINCT ON and LATERAL

Answer "the latest / first / top-N per group" questions deterministically, with DISTINCT ON for top-1 and LATERAL for anything per-row.

Topics

A question GROUP BY cannot answer well

"For each customer, their latest order: id, date and status." GROUP BY gives you max(order_date) per customer, but not the id or status of that order. Selecting o.status next to max(o.order_date) is an error, because a group has many statuses. The old workaround joins the max date back to orders, which breaks when a customer has two orders on the same date (you get both). Postgres has two clean tools for this.

DISTINCT ON: keep the first row of each group

SELECT DISTINCT ON (o.customer_id)
       o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.status
FROM orders o
ORDER BY o.customer_id,           -- 1. must start with the DISTINCT ON expression(s)
         o.order_date DESC,       -- 2. what "first" means: latest date
         o.order_id DESC;         -- 3. tie-breaker: makes the result deterministic
customer_idorder_idorder_datestatus
1272025-10-03pending
2362026-02-14pending
3352026-02-01pending
4232025-08-14shipped
5332026-01-08pending

(16 rows, first 5 shown)

How to read it: sort the rows by the ORDER BY, then for each distinct value of the DISTINCT ON expression keep only the first row. So the ORDER BY decides which row survives.

  • The ORDER BY must begin with the same expressions as DISTINCT ON (Postgres raises an error otherwise).
  • Always add a tie-breaker (usually the primary key). Without it, two orders on the same date make the result depend on physical row order, which can change after an UPDATE or VACUUM.
  • DISTINCT ON is Postgres-only. In other databases (and in Phase 3) you write the same thing with row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …) = 1.

LATERAL: a subquery that runs per row

Normally a subquery in FROM cannot see the other tables in FROM. Adding LATERAL lets it refer to columns of tables listed before it, so it is evaluated once per outer row, like a loop:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, last.order_id, last.order_date
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id        -- refers to the outer row
  ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.order_id DESC
  LIMIT 1
) AS last
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idfull_nameorder_idorder_date
1Aarav Shah272025-10-03
2Diya Menon362026-02-14
3Kabir Khan352026-02-01
4Ananya Gupta232025-08-14
5Ishaan Reddy332026-01-08

(16 rows, first 5 shown)

  • CROSS JOIN LATERAL (…) behaves like an inner join: customers for whom the subquery returns nothing are dropped (16 rows).
  • LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) ON true keeps them with NULLs (20 rows). The ON true is required syntax: the real condition lives inside the subquery.
  • Change LIMIT 1 to LIMIT 3 and you have top-3 per group, which DISTINCT ON cannot do.
  • The subquery can return several columns, aggregates, anything. It is the most flexible "per row" tool in SQL.
SELECT c.customer_id, last.order_id, last.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.status
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.order_id DESC
  LIMIT 1
) AS last ON true
WHERE c.customer_id IN (1, 9)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
customer_idorder_idstatus
127pending
9∅∅

(2 rows)

Which one to use

Need                                   Use
-------------------------------------  ------------------------------------------
One row per group, simple              DISTINCT ON
Top N per group                        LATERAL … ORDER BY … LIMIT N
Keep groups with no rows               LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true
Different "latest" rules per column    one LATERAL per rule
Portable SQL / rank numbers needed     row_number() window function (Phase 3)

Performance preview

LATERAL with ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 is, in effect, a nested loop: for each customer, find their latest order. With an index on orders (customer_id, order_date DESC) each lookup reads one index entry, which makes this one of the fastest ways to get "latest per group" on large tables with few groups. With no index, every lookup scans orders. Session 11 shows how to see this in EXPLAIN.

Phase 1 · Session 11

How Postgres executes a join (EXPLAIN)

Know the three join algorithms, read the join part of an EXPLAIN plan, and understand why foreign keys need indexes.

Topics

SQL says what, the planner decides how

You describe the result; the planner chooses how to compute it: which table to read first, whether to use an index, and which join algorithm to use for every pair of tables. It estimates the cost of many alternative plans from table statistics and picks the cheapest. EXPLAIN shows you the plan it picked. Learning to read plans is Phase 5's main job; today you learn the join part.

The three join algorithms

NESTED LOOP
  for each row r in outer:
      for each row s in inner where s matches r:      ← fast if inner has an index
          emit (r, s)
  + works for ANY condition (=, <, BETWEEN, functions)
  + best when the outer side is small and the inner side is indexed
  - without an index: outer × inner comparisons

HASH JOIN
  build: put every row of the smaller input into a hash table keyed by the join column
  probe: for each row of the bigger input, look up its key in the hash table
  + great for large unsorted inputs, one pass over each
  - equality conditions only (=); needs memory (work_mem) for the hash table

MERGE JOIN
  sort both inputs by the join key (or read them already sorted from an index),
  then walk both lists together like a zipper
  + great when both inputs are already sorted / indexed, and for very large inputs
  - needs sorted input; equality-style conditions

Use The Index, Luke's join chapter (linked in the Guide) explains the same three with diagrams. Read it today.

Reading a plan

In this course we use EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF), which hides the cost numbers so the shape is easy to read. A plan is a tree: each node feeds its parent, and the most indented nodes run first.

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
Hash Join
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o
  ->  Hash
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c

Read it from the innermost nodes outwards. The planner chose a Hash Join: it reads customers (the smaller input) into a hash table (the Hash node), then reads orders sequentially and looks up each order's customer in that hash table (Hash Cond). Each table is read exactly once. Every row is needed anyway, so an index would not help here.

The expected outputs on this site come from Postgres 18 with default settings. On tiny tables the planner's choice is a close call, so another version may pick a different join here. Plans depend on version, table statistics and settings; that is exactly why you always check EXPLAIN on your database with realistic data.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and adds what really happened. TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF hide the timings so the output is stable to read; in real work you keep them on. BUFFERS OFF hides the page counters that Postgres 18 prints by default (Phase 5 uses them). Postgres 18 shows actual rows with two decimals, because it is an average per loop.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
Hash Join (actual rows=36.00 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o (actual rows=36.00 loops=1)
  ->  Hash (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
        Buckets: 1024  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 9kB
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
  • actual rows=36 loops=1 on the join: it produced 36 rows, once.
  • Hash (actual rows=20): all 20 customers went into the hash table.
  • Buckets: 1024 Batches: 1 Memory Usage: …kB: the hash table fitted in memory in one batch. Batches above 1 means it did not fit in work_mem and spilled to disk (Phase 5).
  • In Phase 5 you will also compare estimated rows (hidden here by COSTS OFF) with actual rows. A big mismatch is the number one cause of bad plans.

Making the planner show you the others

You can switch algorithms off for your session to see what the alternatives look like: SET enable_nestloop = off; (also enable_hashjoin, enable_mergejoin, enable_seqscan). These are diagnostic tools only: never leave them off in production. Undo with RESET enable_nestloop; or by ending the transaction. With hash joins and merge joins off:

SET enable_hashjoin = off;
SET enable_mergejoin = off;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
Nested Loop (actual rows=36.00 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o (actual rows=36.00 loops=1)
  ->  Memoize (actual rows=1.00 loops=36)
        Cache Key: o.customer_id
        Cache Mode: logical
        Hits: 20  Misses: 16  Evictions: 0  Overflows: 0  Memory Usage: 2kB
        ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c (actual rows=1.00 loops=16)
              Index Cond: (customer_id = o.customer_id)
              Index Searches: 16

Now a Nested Loop: read orders sequentially (the outer side), and for each order look up its customer through the customers_pkey index (Index Cond: customer_id = o.customer_id). Memoize is a cache in front of the inner side: many orders belong to the same customer, so repeated lookups are answered from memory. loops=36 on Memoize: it was asked once per order. Hits: 20 Misses: 16: only 16 distinct customers were looked up in the index. A small outer side and an indexed inner side is the textbook case for a nested loop.

Why foreign keys need indexes

A primary key always gets an index. The referencing column of a foreign key (orders.customer_id) does not. Postgres does not create one for you. Without it:

  • A nested loop from customers to orders must scan all of orders for every customer.
  • "All orders of customer 42" scans the whole orders table.
  • Deleting a customer forces Postgres to scan orders to check that no order still references it.

On our 36-row table the planner ignores indexes because reading the whole table is cheaper. The difference only shows on realistic sizes, so the questions below build a 200,000-row table.

Outer joins that are not really outer

The planner is smart about the Session 5 traps: when a WHERE clause or a later inner join makes NULL-extended rows impossible to keep, it converts the LEFT JOIN into an inner join, and the plan contains no "Left" join node at all. Looking for "Left" (or "Right") in the plan is a quick way to check whether your outer join is still outer.

One detail that confuses everyone the first time: a plan may say Hash Right Join for a query you wrote as LEFT JOIN. The planner swapped the inputs (it prefers to build the hash table from the smaller side), so "preserve the left table" became "preserve the right input". Same result, different internal order.

The N+1 problem

ORMs often load a list (1 query), then run one more query per item to load its children (N queries): "SELECT * FROM customers", then "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?" twenty times. Each query has network and parsing overhead, and the database can never choose a hash join. One JOIN with GROUP BY replaces all N+1 queries. If you see hundreds of near-identical queries in a log, this is usually why.

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s11.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Run EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) on customers JOIN orders ON customer_id. Which join algorithm does your Postgres choose, and which index (if any) does it use?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
    Hash Join
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o
  ->  Hash
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c

    Postgres 18 picks a Hash Join: customers goes into the hash table, orders is read once and probes it. No index is used, because every row is needed. On 36 rows the choice is a close call, and another version may pick a nested loop.

    Answer

SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
    Hash Join (actual rows=36.00 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o (actual rows=36.00 loops=1)
  ->  Hash (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
        Buckets: 1024  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 9kB
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)

    36: one row per order.

  3. Force a nested loop for the same query (disable hash joins and merge joins) and show the plan. What is on the inner side, and why does it help?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    SET enable_hashjoin = off;
SET enable_mergejoin = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
    Nested Loop
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o
  ->  Memoize
        Cache Key: o.customer_id
        Cache Mode: logical
        ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
              Index Cond: (customer_id = o.customer_id)

    orders is the outer side, read once. For each order, Memoize answers from its cache or does an Index Scan on customers_pkey. The index turns "find this customer" into a direct lookup; the cache saves repeated lookups of the same customer.

  4. Force a merge join (disable hash joins and nested loops), and show the plan. What extra nodes appear?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    SET enable_hashjoin = off;
SET enable_nestloop = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
    Merge Join
  Merge Cond: (c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
  ->  Sort
        Sort Key: c.customer_id
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c
  ->  Sort
        Sort Key: o.customer_id
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o

    Two Sort nodes appear: a merge join needs both inputs sorted by the join key. On tables this small sorting is cheaper than reading them in key order through an index; on big tables an index on the key can supply the order without a sort.

  5. Show the plan for "customers who never ordered" written with NOT EXISTS. What kind of join node does Postgres use?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
    Hash Anti Join
  Hash Cond: (c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on customers c
  ->  Hash
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o

    An anti join (Merge, Hash or Nested Loop Anti Join depending on version): it stops looking at a customer's orders as soon as one is found. NOT EXISTS gets this special node; NOT IN with a nullable subquery cannot.

  ->  Hash
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c

    A semi join: each customer is emitted at most once, however many orders match. (Postgres may instead join against a de-duplicated list of orders; both strategies are valid.)

  10. Show the plan for joining products to discount_tiers on a price range. Which algorithm is used, and why can't it be a hash join?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT p.name, t.tier
FROM products p
JOIN discount_tiers t
  ON p.price >= t.min_amount
 AND (t.max_amount IS NULL OR p.price <= t.max_amount);
    Nested Loop
  Join Filter: ((p.price >= t.min_amount) AND ((t.max_amount IS NULL) OR (p.price <= t.max_amount)))
  ->  Seq Scan on products p
  ->  Materialize
        ->  Seq Scan on discount_tiers t

    A nested loop. Hashing needs an equality to hash on; a range has none.

GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

  12. Build a realistic table: create temp table demo_orders with 200,000 rows (order_id 1…200000, customer_id = (order_id % 2000) + 1, amount = order_id % 1000) and temp table demo_customers with customer_id 1…2000, then ANALYZE both. Show EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for total amount per customer.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TEMP TABLE demo_orders AS
SELECT g AS order_id, (g % 2000) + 1 AS customer_id, g % 1000 AS amount
FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g;
CREATE TEMP TABLE demo_customers AS
SELECT g AS customer_id, 'Customer ' || g AS name
FROM generate_series(1, 2000) g;
ANALYZE demo_orders;
ANALYZE demo_customers;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, sum(o.amount)
FROM demo_customers c
JOIN demo_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id;
    HashAggregate (actual rows=2000.00 loops=1)
  Group Key: c.customer_id
  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 217kB
  ->  Hash Join (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
        Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
        ->  Seq Scan on demo_orders o (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
        ->  Hash (actual rows=2000.00 loops=1)
              Buckets: 2048  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 87kB
              ->  Seq Scan on demo_customers c (actual rows=2000.00 loops=1)

    All 200,000 orders must be read anyway, so both tables are scanned sequentially and an index would not help. Postgres 18 chooses Hash Join + HashAggregate: the 2,000 customers go into a hash table, the 200,000 orders stream through it, and the sums are kept in another hash table, one entry per customer. Batches: 1 on both: everything fitted in memory (work_mem), a Phase 5 topic.

  13. With the same two tables, show the plan for the orders of customer 42 only, first without an index and then after CREATE INDEX on demo_orders(customer_id) + ANALYZE. Return the second plan.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TEMP TABLE demo_orders AS
SELECT g AS order_id, (g % 2000) + 1 AS customer_id, g % 1000 AS amount
FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g;
ANALYZE demo_orders;

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM demo_orders WHERE customer_id = 42;   -- Seq Scan: reads 200,000 rows

CREATE INDEX demo_orders_customer_idx ON demo_orders (customer_id);
ANALYZE demo_orders;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM demo_orders WHERE customer_id = 42;   -- uses the index
    Bitmap Heap Scan on demo_orders
  Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 42)
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on demo_orders_customer_idx
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)

    100 matching rows out of 200,000: the index (Bitmap or Index Scan) reads a tiny fraction of the table. This is the everyday reason FK columns need indexes.

  14. Show the plan of the Session 5 chain-trap query (customers LEFT JOIN orders, then plain JOIN order_items). Does the plan still contain a left join?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, oi.product_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id;
    Hash Join
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
  ->  Hash Join
        Hash Cond: (oi.order_id = o.order_id)
        ->  Seq Scan on order_items oi
        ->  Hash
              ->  Seq Scan on orders o
  ->  Hash
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c

    No "Left" anywhere: the planner proved the inner join discards every NULL-extended row and turned your LEFT JOIN into an inner join. The plan tells you the truth about your query.

  15. Challenge: Make it fast. Build demo_customers (2,000 rows: customer_id, city = one of 10 cities by customer_id % 10) and demo_orders (200,000 rows as in Q12, plus order_date = DATE '2025-01-01' + (order_id % 365)). The slow version uses a correlated subquery per customer: for customers in city 'City 3', their number of orders in March 2025. Rewrite it as a join with GROUP BY, add the index (or indexes) that makes it efficient, check the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and return the final result: customer_id and march_orders for those 200 customers, ordered by customer_id.

    Expected: 200 rows

    Answer
    CREATE TEMP TABLE demo_customers AS
SELECT g AS customer_id, 'City ' || (g % 10) AS city
FROM generate_series(1, 2000) g;
CREATE TEMP TABLE demo_orders AS
SELECT g AS order_id, (g % 2000) + 1 AS customer_id, g % 1000 AS amount,
       DATE '2025-01-01' + (g % 365) AS order_date
FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g;
CREATE INDEX demo_orders_cust_date_idx ON demo_orders (customer_id, order_date);
ANALYZE demo_customers;
ANALYZE demo_orders;

-- Check the plan first (run this line on its own):
-- EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) <the query below>

SELECT c.customer_id, count(o.order_id) AS march_orders
FROM demo_customers c
LEFT JOIN demo_orders o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND o.order_date >= DATE '2025-03-01'
      AND o.order_date <  DATE '2025-04-01'
WHERE c.city = 'City 3'
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

    38
    138
    238
    338
    438
    538
    639
    739
    839
    939
    1038
    1138

    (200 rows, first 12 shown)

    The join version lets the planner choose between one hash join over all orders and an index-driven nested loop per customer. The composite index (customer_id, order_date) serves both the join key and the date range, so each customer's March orders are a single index range read. Compare the two plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and timing on; that before/after habit is the core of Phase 5.
