Phase 1 · Session 12

Exit test + Apply: Joins

Prove you own joins: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct. Then finish the joins dashboard.

Topics

Exit test rules

  • Cold: no notes, no earlier sessions, no answers until you are done.
  • Time box: 75 minutes for all 14 questions. Running out of time on easy questions is itself a signal.
  • Score honestly: a question counts only if the output matches the expected rows exactly (count and values).
  • Pass = 11 of 14 or more. Pass → move on to subqueries and dates. Fail → redo every missed question, re-read the session it belongs to, and take the test again later.

What the test checks

Q1–Q2   anti-join two ways                   (S4)
Q3      LEFT JOIN + filter in ON + COALESCE  (S3, S5)
Q4      latest row per group                 (S10)
Q5      self join                            (S6)
Q6–Q7   anti-joins on two different tables   (S4)
Q8      LEFT JOIN with a missing lookup      (S3)
Q9      join + group + HAVING DISTINCT       (S2, S8)
Q10     pre-aggregate to avoid fan-out       (S8)
Q11     the chain trap                       (S5)
Q12     self join on a link table, pairs     (S6)
Q13     UPDATE … FROM with NULL-safe compare (S9)
Q14     top-N per group with LATERAL         (S10)

Apply project, part 2: the Phase 1 dashboard

After the test, finish psql/projects/p1-dashboard.sql. Each query below should run against practice, have a comment explaining its grain, and state its expected row count:

  • Your S7 Customer 360 query.
  • Revenue per category per month for 2025, with every category × month present (CROSS JOIN a month grid, LEFT JOIN facts).
  • Payment reconciliation from S3's hard problem, filtered to problems only (overpaid, underpaid, refunded, unpaid, payment without order).
  • Supplier exposure: for each supplier, delivered revenue of their products and how many of those products have a second supplier.
  • Data quality report: one row per issue type with a count (orphan payments, orders without items, duplicate customer emails, reviews without purchase, employees without department).

Then, on your track1 database: find the orphans with anti-joins, fix them, and add the foreign keys from track1 Q19, plus an index on each foreign-key column (Session 11 showed why).

Phase 2 · Session 13

Subqueries 1: scalar, correlated and derived tables

Know every place a subquery can go, what it must return there, and when a correlated subquery should become a join.

Topics

A query inside a query

A subquery is a complete SELECT in parentheses, used where a value, a list or a table is expected. You already used two kinds in the joins phase: EXISTS (…) in Session 4 and derived tables (SELECT … GROUP BY …) t in Session 8. This session covers all of them properly, because the place a subquery appears decides what it is allowed to return.

Where it appears              What it must return            Example
----------------------------  -----------------------------  ---------------------------------
SELECT list, WHERE, SET       one row, one column (scalar)   price > (SELECT avg(price) …)
WHERE x IN / = ANY (…)        one column, any rows           customer_id IN (SELECT …)
WHERE EXISTS (…)              anything (only "any rows?")    EXISTS (SELECT 1 …)
FROM (…) alias                a table (any rows and columns) FROM (SELECT … GROUP BY …) t

Scalar subqueries

A scalar subquery returns exactly one value, so you can use it anywhere a value fits. The classic use is comparing with an aggregate, which you cannot do directly in WHERE (aggregates are computed after WHERE):

SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products)
ORDER BY price DESC;
nameprice
Laptop Pro 14120000.00
Laptop Air 1385000.00
4K Monitor42000.00
Standing Desk32000.00

(4 rows)

  • Zero rows → NULL. If the subquery finds nothing, its value is NULL, and any comparison with it is not true. That silently drops rows; wrap with COALESCE(…, 0) when "nothing" should mean zero.
  • More than one row → error: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression. It is a runtime error, so a query can work for months and then fail the day the data gets a duplicate. If you mean "any of them", use IN; if you mean "the latest", add ORDER BY … LIMIT 1.
  • More than one column → error as well. A scalar subquery is one column.

Uncorrelated vs correlated

The subquery above is uncorrelated: it does not mention the outer query, so Postgres runs it once (EXPLAIN shows it as an InitPlan). A correlated subquery refers to the current outer row, so conceptually it runs once per outer row (a SubPlan):

SELECT e.full_name, e.salary,
       (SELECT round(avg(x.salary)) FROM employees x
        WHERE x.department_id = e.department_id) AS dept_avg     -- uses the outer row
FROM employees e
WHERE e.department_id = 2
ORDER BY e.salary DESC;
full_namesalarydept_avg
Sneha Iyer160000.0094000
Meera Joshi62000.0094000
Karan Malhotra60000.0094000

(3 rows)

Correlated subqueries are easy to read and often fine. On big tables "once per row" can be slow, and Postgres cannot always turn it into a join for you. The standard rewrite is: compute the per-group value once in a derived table, then join to it. You will write both versions in the questions.

IN, NOT IN, ANY and ALL

  • x IN (SELECT col …) is true when x equals any returned value. It is the same as x = ANY (SELECT col …).
  • x NOT IN (SELECT …) is the trap from Session 4: one NULL in the list makes it return no rows. Use NOT EXISTS.
  • x > ALL (SELECT …) is true when x is greater than every value. Careful: > ALL of an empty list is true (there is nothing to beat), and if the list contains a NULL the result can never be true.
  • x > ANY (SELECT …) is true when x beats at least one value.
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > ALL (SELECT p.price FROM products p
                   JOIN categories k ON k.category_id = p.category_id
                   WHERE k.name = 'Audio')
ORDER BY price DESC;
nameprice
Laptop Pro 14120000.00
Laptop Air 1385000.00
4K Monitor42000.00
Standing Desk32000.00

(4 rows)

Derived tables (subqueries in FROM)

A subquery in FROM is treated like a table for the rest of the query. It must have an alias. Use it to aggregate first and then filter, join or aggregate again. "Average order value" needs two levels: lines → order totals, then orders → average:

SELECT round(avg(t.total), 2) AS avg_order_value, count(*) AS orders_with_items
FROM (SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS total
      FROM order_items
      GROUP BY order_id) AS t;
avg_order_valueorders_with_items
36894.2935

(1 row)

In Phase 3 you will write the same thing as a CTE (WITH t AS (…) SELECT …), which reads top to bottom. A derived table and a CTE are usually planned the same way in modern Postgres.

Subquery or join?

  • Need columns from the other table in the output → join.
  • Only need "is there a match" → EXISTS / NOT EXISTS.
  • Need one computed value per row (an average, a latest date) → scalar subquery is fine for small data; derived table + join for large data.
  • Need a value at two levels of aggregation → derived table.

When a scalar subquery should return "the latest" or "the first" row, always add ORDER BY with a tie-breaker and LIMIT 1. Otherwise it either errors on ties or picks an arbitrary row.

In Phase 3, dense_rank() solves this in one line; knowing the subquery version is still expected in interviews.

Phase 2 · Session 14

Review: fan-out, data changes, latest-per-group, plans and subqueries

Pull Sessions 8–13 back out of memory, mixed together, without notes.

Topics

How to run this review

  • First 20 minutes: redo every question in mistakes.md from Sessions 8–13, cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below. They are mixed on purpose: deciding which technique a question needs is the skill being trained.
  • Then the challenge, which combines four techniques in one query.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 8–13

Problem                                         Tool
----------------------------------------------  ---------------------------------------------
Two one-to-many tables summed together          aggregate each in a derived table, then join
Counts across a multiplying join                count(DISTINCT key) (counts only, never sums)
Change rows based on another table              UPDATE … FROM / DELETE … USING (inner joins!)
Every target row must be updated                scalar subquery in SET, not FROM
One source row per target row                   aggregate the FROM source first
Latest / first row per group                    DISTINCT ON (… ORDER BY …, tie-breaker)
Top-N per group, or keep groups with no rows    LEFT JOIN LATERAL (… LIMIT n) ON true
Compare with an aggregate                       scalar subquery: x > (SELECT avg(…) …)
Per-group comparison                            correlated subquery, or join to a derived table
See how Postgres runs it                        EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) / EXPLAIN ANALYZE

  14. Show the plan of "products priced above the average price". What node does the uncorrelated subquery become?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products);
    Seq Scan on products
  Filter: (price > (InitPlan 1).col1)
  InitPlan 1
    ->  Aggregate
          ->  Seq Scan on products products_1

    An InitPlan: computed once before the main scan, then used as a constant. A correlated subquery shows as a SubPlan instead, evaluated per row.

LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(amount) AS paid
           FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) pay ON pay.order_id = l.order_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Phase 2 · Session 15

Subqueries 2 and set operations: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT

Stack and compare result sets with UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT, and use inline VALUES tables, row comparisons and subqueries in UPDATE.

Topics

Joins go sideways, set operations go down

A join puts columns from two tables side by side. A set operation puts the rows of two queries on top of each other (UNION), or keeps the rows they have in common (INTERSECT), or the rows of the first that are missing from the second (EXCEPT). The two queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types; the column names come from the first query.

SELECT full_name, 'customer' AS kind FROM customers WHERE city = 'Pune'
UNION ALL
SELECT full_name, 'employee' FROM employees WHERE department_id = 4
ORDER BY full_name;      -- one ORDER BY at the very end sorts the whole result
full_namekind
Ananya Guptacustomer
Isha Kapooremployee
Reyansh Jaincustomer
Riya Kapoorcustomer

(4 rows)

UNION vs UNION ALL

  • UNION ALL simply appends the rows. Fast, keeps duplicates.
  • UNION appends and then removes duplicate rows, which means a sort or hash over everything. Use it only when you actually want duplicates gone.
  • Default to UNION ALL. Writing UNION "just in case" is a common performance bug and can silently merge two rows that were legitimately the same.
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT shipping_city FROM orders) a) AS union_all_rows,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT city FROM customers UNION     SELECT shipping_city FROM orders) u) AS union_rows;
union_all_rowsunion_rows
5612

(1 row)

INTERSECT and EXCEPT

  • A INTERSECT B: rows that appear in both.
  • A EXCEPT B: rows of A that do not appear in B. Order matters: B EXCEPT A is a different answer. Running both directions is the standard way to diff two data sets.
  • Like UNION, both remove duplicates; INTERSECT ALL and EXCEPT ALL keep counts ("A has 3 copies, B has 1, EXCEPT ALL leaves 2").
-- products that were ordered but never reviewed
SELECT product_id FROM order_items
EXCEPT
SELECT product_id FROM reviews
ORDER BY product_id;
product_id
5
10

(2 rows)

Set operations treat NULLs as equal

This surprises everyone once. In a join or WHERE, NULL = NULL is not true. In UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT (and DISTINCT, GROUP BY) two NULLs count as the same row. So "customer cities that never appear as a shipping city" does not return NULL, because NULL appears on both sides:

SELECT city FROM customers
EXCEPT
SELECT shipping_city FROM orders;
city
Singapore
Panaji

(2 rows)

The same question with NOT EXISTS would also return the customers with a NULL city, because there the NULL never matches anything. Neither is wrong; know which semantics you are using.

Precedence and LIMIT inside a branch

INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT, just as multiplication binds tighter than addition. Use parentheses whenever you mix them. ORDER BY and LIMIT at the end apply to the whole result; to limit one branch, wrap it in parentheses: (SELECT … ORDER BY … LIMIT 3) UNION ALL (SELECT …).

Inline tables with VALUES

VALUES (…), (…) is a table you type into the query. Give it an alias with column names and use it anywhere a table fits. It is perfect for small lookup lists and test data:

SELECT v.status, v.label
FROM (VALUES ('pending', 'Waiting'), ('shipped', 'On the way'), ('delivered', 'Done')) AS v(status, label)
ORDER BY v.status;
statuslabel
deliveredDone
pendingWaiting
shippedOn the way

(3 rows)

Row comparisons

You can compare several columns at once with a row constructor: (customer_id, status) IN ((1, 'pending'), (2, 'delivered')) or (a, b) IN (SELECT x, y FROM …). It also works with < and >, comparing left to right like sorting: (order_date, order_id) < (DATE '2025-03-01', 10). That form is the basis of keyset pagination in Phase 5.

Subqueries in UPDATE

A scalar subquery in SET computes the new value per row. Pair it with a WHERE EXISTS so rows without a source keep their value instead of becoming NULL:

BEGIN;
UPDATE products p
SET price = (SELECT round(avg(oi.unit_price), 2) FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id)
WHERE p.category_id = 3
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id)
RETURNING p.name, p.price;
ROLLBACK;
nameprice
Noise-Cancel Headphones17916.67
Bluetooth Speaker7000.00
Earbuds Lite2466.67

(3 rows)

Phase 2 · Session 16

Dates, timestamps and time zones

Pick the right date/time type, do date arithmetic correctly, and never get bitten by time zones.

Topics

Reload the practice database first

This session uses the new deliveries table (when each order shipped and was delivered). Re-run practice.sql to get it: psql -U postgres -d practice -f practice.sql. The file also sets the database time zone to India (Asia/Kolkata), so your output matches this page. Reconnect after loading so the setting applies.

SHOW timezone;
TimeZone
Asia/Kolkata

(1 row)

The five types you need

Type          Stores                                   Example
------------  ---------------------------------------  ------------------------------
date          a calendar day                           2025-03-02
time          a time of day, no date                   18:45:00
timestamp     date + time, NO time zone ("wall clock") 2025-03-02 01:15:00
timestamptz   an exact instant (stored as UTC)         2025-03-02 01:15:00+05:30
interval      a duration                               2 days 08:15:00
  • timestamptz ("timestamp with time zone") does not store a time zone. It stores an exact instant in UTC and displays it in your session's time zone. Use it for anything that happened at a real moment: orders placed, payments, logins, deliveries.
  • timestamp (without time zone) is just a wall-clock reading with no idea where it was taken. payments.paid_at is one: 18:40 where? Use it only for things that are truly local (a store opening hour).
  • date for birthdays, signup days, order days: things with no time of day.

Arithmetic

SELECT DATE '2025-03-01' - DATE '2025-02-01'                     AS days_between,     -- date - date = integer
       DATE '2025-01-31' + 30                                    AS plus_30_days,     -- date + integer = date
       TIMESTAMP '2025-01-08 18:45' - TIMESTAMP '2025-01-06 10:30' AS gap,            -- = interval
       age(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2024-03-29')                 AS age,              -- years/months/days
       round(extract(epoch FROM INTERVAL '2 days 08:15') / 3600, 2) AS hours;
days_betweenplus_30_daysgapagehours
282025-03-022 days 08:15:001 year 9 mons 3 days56.25

(1 row)

extract(epoch FROM interval) gives seconds, the easiest way to turn a duration into hours or minutes. age() gives a human "1 year 9 mons 3 days" result, good for display and bad for maths.

Time zones: one instant, many clocks

Order 7 left the warehouse at 01:15 on 2 March, India time. In UTC that same instant was 19:45 on 1 March. Same row, different date, depending on whose clock you read:

SELECT order_id, shipped_at,
       shipped_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'        AS utc_clock,
       shipped_at::date                     AS india_date,
       (shipped_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS utc_date
FROM deliveries
WHERE order_id IN (7, 14, 15, 16)
ORDER BY order_id;
order_idshipped_atutc_clockindia_dateutc_date
72025-03-02 01:15:00+05:302025-03-01 19:45:002025-03-022025-03-01
142025-05-02 10:30:00+05:302025-05-02 05:00:002025-05-022025-05-02
152025-05-10 12:30:00+05:302025-05-10 07:00:002025-05-102025-05-10
162025-05-21 00:40:00+05:302025-05-20 19:10:002025-05-212025-05-20

(4 rows)

  • timestamptz AT TIME ZONE 'X' answers: "what did a clock in X show at this instant?" The result is a plain timestamp (no zone).
  • timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'X' does the reverse: "this wall-clock time was in X; which instant is that?" The result is a timestamptz.
  • shipped_at::date and date_trunc(…) on a timestamptz use the session time zone. The same query gives different days in Mumbai and London. Be explicit when it matters: (shipped_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date.
  • Order 14 was entered with a Dubai offset (+04) and order 15 with a London offset (+01); Postgres converted both to the same UTC timeline, and they display in India time like everything else.

Changing the session time zone changes only the display, never the stored instant:

SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
SELECT order_id, shipped_at FROM deliveries WHERE order_id = 7;
order_idshipped_at
72025-03-01 19:45:00+00

(1 row)

Use full zone names like 'Asia/Kolkata' or 'Europe/London', not fixed offsets like '+05:30'. Names know about daylight saving time; offsets do not.

Daylight saving time

India has no daylight saving; London does. On 30 March 2025 UK clocks jumped from 01:00 to 02:00. One hour of instants apart, the London clock moves two hours:

SELECT TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-03-30 00:30+00' AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London' AS before_jump,
       TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-03-30 01:30+00' AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London' AS after_jump;
before_jumpafter_jump
2025-03-30 00:30:002025-03-30 02:30:00

(1 row)

This is why "add 24 hours" and "add 1 day" can differ for local times, and why you store timestamptz and convert only for display.

Extracting parts and formatting

SELECT extract(year FROM DATE '2025-03-02')   AS year,
       extract(isodow FROM DATE '2025-03-02') AS iso_weekday,   -- 1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday
       to_char(TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-01-08 18:45+05:30', 'Dy DD Mon YYYY, HH24:MI') AS pretty;
yeariso_weekdaypretty
20257Wed 08 Jan 2025, 18:45

(1 row)

to_char formats, to_date / to_timestamp parse with an explicit pattern. Never rely on '01/12/2020'::date: whether that is 1 December or 12 January depends on the server's DateStyle setting, which is exactly the bug in your track1 Q26.

SELECT to_date('15/02/2021', 'DD/MM/YYYY')                         AS parsed_date,
       to_timestamp('2025-03-02 01:15', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI')        AS parsed_timestamptz;
parsed_dateparsed_timestamptz
2021-02-152025-03-02 01:15:00+05:30

(1 row)

"Now" makes answers change

now(), CURRENT_DATE and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP return the start time of the current transaction. Real reports use them; practice questions here use a fixed "as of" date instead (for example DATE '2026-02-15') so the expected answers never change. Also prefer half-open ranges, order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-04-01', over BETWEEN with an end date: they work the same for dates and timestamps and can use an index.

  15. Challenge: Carrier SLA report. One row per carrier: shipments, delivered, in_transit, late (delivered more than 3 days after shipping), avg_hours (delivered only, 1 decimal), and slowest_order (the order_id with the longest delivery; ties → lower order_id). Order by carrier.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    SELECT d.carrier,
       count(*)                                                                AS shipments,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE d.delivered_at IS NOT NULL)                      AS delivered,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE d.delivered_at IS NULL)                          AS in_transit,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE d.delivered_at - d.shipped_at > INTERVAL '3 days') AS late,
       round(avg(extract(epoch FROM d.delivered_at - d.shipped_at)) / 3600, 1)  AS avg_hours,
       (SELECT x.order_id FROM deliveries x
        WHERE x.carrier = d.carrier AND x.delivered_at IS NOT NULL
        ORDER BY x.delivered_at - x.shipped_at DESC, x.order_id
        LIMIT 1)                                                              AS slowest_order
FROM deliveries d
GROUP BY d.carrier
ORDER BY d.carrier;
    carriershipmentsdeliveredin_transitlateavg_hoursslowest_order

    Delhivery1192482.628
    DHL2111101.014

← Phase 2: Subqueries + Date/TimeAll phasesSchema

Phase 2 · Session 17

date_trunc, intervals and date spines

Group by day, week and month correctly, build a calendar of every period so empty periods show as zero, and handle month-end and overlapping ranges.

Topics

Grouping by period with date_trunc

date_trunc('month', x) rounds a date or timestamp down to the start of its month (also 'year', 'quarter', 'week', 'day', 'hour'). Every row in the same month gets the same value, so it is the natural GROUP BY key for "per month" reports. On a date it returns a timestamp; cast it back with ::date for tidy output.

SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date)::date AS month, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND order_date < DATE '2025-07-01'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
monthorders
2025-01-013
2025-02-014
2025-03-013
2025-04-013
2025-05-013
2025-06-013

(6 rows)

  • 'week' truncates to the Monday of the ISO week.
  • Prefer date_trunc('month', d) over extract(month FROM d) for grouping: extract gives 3 for March of every year, so two years get merged by accident.
  • On a timestamptz, date_trunc uses the session time zone, so "the day" of a shipment depends on whose midnight you use (Session 16). Postgres also accepts the zone explicitly: date_trunc('day', shipped_at, 'Asia/Kolkata').

The missing-rows problem

GROUP BY only produces groups that have rows. If nothing happened on 2 January, there is simply no row for 2 January, and a chart of that query draws a straight line across the gap, which is a lie. The fix is a spine: a list of every period you want, built with generate_series, and the facts LEFT JOINed onto it.

SELECT d::date AS day
FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-01-31', INTERVAL '1 day') AS g(d)
LIMIT 5;
day
2025-01-01
2025-01-02
2025-01-03
2025-01-04
2025-01-05

(5 rows)

Note the ::date. With date arguments and an interval step, generate_series returns timestamps with time zone (midnight in your session zone). Comparing them with a date column works, but cast to date for output, or you will see 2025-01-01 00:00:00+05:30.

Then the facts go on with a LEFT JOIN (everything from the joins phase applies: the spine is the preserved side, count the optional side's key, COALESCE the sums):

SELECT s.day::date AS day, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-01-10', INTERVAL '1 day') AS s(day)
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = s.day
GROUP BY s.day
ORDER BY s.day;
dayorders
2025-01-010
2025-01-020
2025-01-030
2025-01-040
2025-01-051
2025-01-060
2025-01-070
2025-01-080
2025-01-091
2025-01-100

(10 rows)

For monthly or weekly reports, generate the period starts (INTERVAL '1 month', or Mondays with '1 week') and match facts with date_trunc(…) = spine, or better with a half-open range o.order_date >= s.month AND o.order_date < s.month + INTERVAL '1 month', which can use an index on order_date.

Aggregate first, then join to the spine, when the facts are many-to-one with the period. Or LEFT JOIN raw rows and count the key, as above. Both are correct; mixing them with two fact tables reintroduces fan-out.

Month arithmetic and month-end

SELECT (DATE '2025-01-31' + INTERVAL '1 month')::date                          AS jan31_plus_month,
       (DATE '2024-02-29' + INTERVAL '1 year')::date                           AS leap_plus_year,
       (date_trunc('month', DATE '2025-02-10') + INTERVAL '1 month - 1 day')::date AS last_day_of_feb,
       make_date(2025, 12, 1)                                                  AS built_date;
jan31_plus_monthleap_plus_yearlast_day_of_febbuilt_date
2025-02-282025-02-282025-02-282025-12-01

(1 row)

  • Adding a month to 31 January gives 28 February: Postgres clamps to the last valid day. Adding it again gives 28 March, not 31 March. Always compute month-ends from the month start, as in last_day_of_feb.
  • make_date(y, m, d) builds a date from numbers, handy with generate_series over integers.

Relative windows

"Last 30 days" is order_date > as_of - 30 AND order_date <= as_of (with a fixed as-of date in practice, CURRENT_DATE in production). "This month so far" is >= date_trunc('month', as_of). Keep the column bare on one side of the comparison so an index on it can be used.

Overlapping periods

Two periods overlap when each starts before the other ends: a_start < b_end AND b_start < a_end. Postgres also has the OVERLAPS operator, which treats periods as half-open [start, end):

SELECT (DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-03-01') OVERLAPS (DATE '2025-02-15', DATE '2025-04-01') AS overlaps,
       (DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-03-01') OVERLAPS (DATE '2025-03-01', DATE '2025-04-01') AS touching;
overlapstouching
tf

(1 row)

Touching periods (one ends exactly when the next starts) do not overlap. Phase 8 shows range types (daterange) and constraints that forbid overlaps entirely, used for bookings.

  15. Challenge: Monthly revenue report for 2025 (this is the Phase 2 Apply project). One row per month, all 12: month, revenue (delivered), previous month's revenue (January compares with December 2024, which had none), change (revenue − previous) and change_pct (rounded to 1 decimal, ∅ when the previous month is 0). No window functions: build the monthly table once and join it to itself shifted by one month.

    Expected: 12 rows

    Answer
    SELECT cur.month::date AS month,
       cur.revenue,
       prev.revenue                AS prev_revenue,
       cur.revenue - prev.revenue  AS change,
       round(100.0 * (cur.revenue - prev.revenue) / NULLIF(prev.revenue, 0), 1) AS change_pct
FROM (
  SELECT s.month, COALESCE(r.revenue, 0) AS revenue
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-12-01', DATE '2025-12-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS s(month)
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date) AS month, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
             FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
             WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
             GROUP BY 1) r ON r.month = s.month
) cur
JOIN (
  SELECT s.month, COALESCE(r.revenue, 0) AS revenue
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-12-01', DATE '2025-12-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS s(month)
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date) AS month, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
             FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
             WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
             GROUP BY 1) r ON r.month = s.month
) prev ON prev.month = cur.month - INTERVAL '1 month'
WHERE cur.month >= DATE '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY cur.month;

    A spine with one extra month gives January a previous month to compare with. The self-join "shifted by one period" is how month-over-month was done before window functions; in Phase 3, lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) replaces the whole second copy. Writing the same derived table twice is painful, and that pain is exactly why CTEs exist.

Phase 2 · Session 18

Exit test + Apply: Subqueries and dates

Prove you own subqueries, set operations and dates: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct.

Topics

Exit test rules

  • Cold: no notes, no earlier sessions, no answers until you are done.
  • Time box: 75 minutes for all 14 questions.
  • Score honestly: a question counts only if the output matches the expected rows exactly.
  • Pass = 11 of 14 or more. Pass → move on to CTEs and window functions. Fail → redo every missed question, re-read its session, and retake the test later.

What the test checks

Q1, Q8, Q13   scalar and correlated subqueries          (S13)
Q3, Q4        INTERSECT / EXCEPT                        (S15)
Q11           UNION ALL with matching column types      (S15)
Q2, Q6        weekdays, intervals, time zones           (S16)
Q9, Q12       fixed "as of" dates, interval comparisons (S16)
Q5, Q7, Q10, Q14   spines with zero-filled periods      (S17)

Apply project

  • Save the S17 challenge (monthly revenue with month-over-month change) as psql/projects/p2-monthly.sql, with a comment explaining the spine.
  • On your track1 database: finish Q23 (salary cleanup, S15 challenge), fix Q24 and Q26 with explicit date formats (S16 Q12), and complete the second half of Q27 (the ₹10,000 value that makes the type change fail).

Phase 3 · Session 19

CTEs: name your steps

Write complex queries as a readable chain of named steps with WITH, reuse a step several times, and know when Postgres inlines or materializes it.

Topics

The problem CTEs solve

In Phase 2 you wrote the same derived table twice in one query (S13 Q14, the S17 challenge), and you read nested subqueries inside-out. A CTE (common table expression) gives a subquery a name at the top of the statement. The query then reads top to bottom like a recipe, and each named step can be used as many times as you like.

WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS total
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT order_id, total
FROM order_totals
WHERE total > (SELECT avg(total) FROM order_totals)   -- the same step, used twice
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 5;
order_idtotal
25138500.00
11126500.00
20120000.00
1119500.00
989000.00

(5 rows)

Syntax

  • WITH a AS (…), b AS (…), c AS (…) SELECT …: one WITH, steps separated by commas, then one final statement.
  • Each step can use every step defined before it. That is what makes chaining work.
  • Name the output columns in the header when that reads better: WITH m(month, orders) AS (SELECT …).
  • A CTE exists only for that one statement. It is not a view and not a temporary table.
  • The final statement can also be INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE (next session).

Chaining steps

Average order value per customer is "line → order total → customer average". Each arrow is a step:

WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS total
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
),
customer_avg AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, round(avg(t.total), 2) AS avg_order_value, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_totals t ON t.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.full_name, a.avg_order_value, a.orders
FROM customer_avg a
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
ORDER BY a.avg_order_value DESC
LIMIT 5;
full_nameavg_order_valueorders
Om Prakash120000.001
Emma Brown85000.002
Myra Chawla75250.002
Kiara Sethi69750.002
Zara Ali63000.002

(5 rows)

Debug a CTE chain one step at a time: replace the final SELECT with SELECT * FROM order_totals, check it, then move to the next step. Most wrong reports are wrong at one specific step, and this finds it in seconds.

Inlined or materialized?

Since Postgres 12, a CTE that is used once (and does not change data) is usually inlined: the planner merges it into the main query as if you had written a subquery, so filters can be pushed into it and indexes used. A CTE used more than once is materialized: computed once into a temporary result that each use reads.

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH o AS (SELECT * FROM orders)
SELECT * FROM o WHERE order_id = 5;
Seq Scan on orders
  Filter: (order_id = 5)

Inlined: the filter reached the orders table itself (Filter: (order_id = 5) on the scan). On 36 rows a sequential scan is cheapest; on a big table the primary-key index would be used, which a materialized CTE makes impossible. You can force either behaviour with AS MATERIALIZED (…) or AS NOT MATERIALIZED (…). Materializing on purpose is useful when a step is expensive and used several times, or to stop the planner from making a bad choice. Before Postgres 12 every CTE was materialized, which is why old blog posts call CTEs an "optimization fence".

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH o AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM orders)
SELECT * FROM o WHERE order_id = 5;
CTE Scan on o
  Filter: (order_id = 5)
  CTE o
    ->  Seq Scan on orders

CTE, subquery, view or temp table?

  • CTE: steps inside one query; readability first.
  • Derived table: a one-off step inside FROM; fine for short queries.
  • View: a named query saved in the database, reused by many queries (Phase 6).
  • Temporary table: a real table for the session; use when you need an index on an intermediate result or reuse it across several statements.

  11. Segment all 20 customers by delivered revenue: 'high' (over 100,000), 'medium' (over 20,000), 'low' (over 0), 'none'. Return segment and number of customers, ordered by customers descending, then segment.

  FROM customers c
  LEFT JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
  LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
  GROUP BY c.customer_id

segmented AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         CASE WHEN revenue > 100000 THEN 'high'
              WHEN revenue > 20000  THEN 'medium'
              WHEN revenue > 0      THEN 'low'
              ELSE 'none' END AS segment
  FROM revenue
)
SELECT segment, count(*) AS customers
FROM segmented
GROUP BY segment
ORDER BY customers DESC, segment;

  13. Show the plan of WITH o AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM orders) SELECT * FROM o WHERE order_id = 5. Which node shows the CTE was computed separately?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH o AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM orders)
SELECT * FROM o WHERE order_id = 5;
    CTE Scan on o
  Filter: (order_id = 5)
  CTE o
    ->  Seq Scan on orders

    A CTE Scan: all orders are read into the CTE first, and the filter runs afterwards on that result. The index cannot be used.

  14. The same query with NOT MATERIALIZED. Show that the CTE disappears from the plan.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH o AS NOT MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM orders)
SELECT * FROM o WHERE order_id = 5;
    Seq Scan on orders
  Filter: (order_id = 5)

    No CTE Scan: the CTE was inlined and the filter pushed down to orders, where an index could serve it on a big table. This is the default for a CTE used once.

  15. Challenge: Rebuild the S7 Customer 360 as a CTE pipeline and add a segment. For all 20 customers: customer_id, full_name, zone ('Unknown' if none), orders, delivered_revenue, last_order, reviews, and segment ('high' over 100,000 of delivered revenue, 'medium' over 20,000, 'low' over 0, else 'none'). One CTE per source (orders, revenue, reviews), then one final SELECT. Order by customer_id.

    Expected: 20 rows

    Answer
    WITH ord AS (
  SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders, max(order_date) AS last_order
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
),
rev AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
),
rv AS (
  SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS reviews FROM reviews GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name,
       COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown')  AS zone,
       COALESCE(ord.orders, 0)      AS orders,
       COALESCE(rev.revenue, 0)     AS delivered_revenue,
       ord.last_order,
       COALESCE(rv.reviews, 0)      AS reviews,
       CASE WHEN rev.revenue > 100000 THEN 'high'
            WHEN rev.revenue > 20000  THEN 'medium'
            WHEN rev.revenue > 0      THEN 'low'
            ELSE 'none' END         AS segment
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN shipping_zones z ON z.city = c.city
LEFT JOIN ord ON ord.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN rev ON rev.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN rv  ON rv.customer_id  = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Phase 3 · Session 20

CTEs for cleaning, aggregation and changing data

Build clean-validate-load pipelines as CTE steps, and use data-modifying CTEs to delete, insert and update in one statement.

Topics

Pipelines: raw → clean → valid → result

Real data arrives messy. A CTE pipeline gives every cleaning rule its own named step, so a reviewer (or you, next month) can read exactly what happens to a value. A typical shape:

WITH raw AS (…the input…),
     cleaned AS (…trim, lower, strip symbols…),
     parsed AS (…convert types, NULL when invalid…),
     checked AS (…one row per input with a status/reason…)
SELECT … FROM checked;
WITH raw(id, phone) AS (
  VALUES (1, ' +91-98765 43210 '), (2, '022-44556677'), (3, '98765')
),
digits AS (
  SELECT id, phone, regexp_replace(phone, '[^0-9]', '', 'g') AS d FROM raw
)
SELECT id, phone, d,
       CASE WHEN length(d) >= 10 THEN right(d, 10) END AS mobile_10
FROM digits
ORDER BY id;
idphonedmobile_10
1 +91-98765 43210 9198765432109876543210
2022-44556677022445566772244556677
39876598765∅

(3 rows)

Data-modifying CTEs

A WITH step may be an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE with RETURNING. The returned rows become a table that later steps and the final statement can use. The classic example: move rows to an archive in one statement, so they cannot be deleted without also being archived.

BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE payments_archive (LIKE payments);

WITH moved AS (
  DELETE FROM payments p
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.order_id = p.order_id)
  RETURNING p.*
)
INSERT INTO payments_archive
SELECT * FROM moved
RETURNING payment_id, order_id, amount;
ROLLBACK;
payment_idorder_idamount
3099994999.00
31401200.00

(2 rows)

The rules that surprise people

  • All parts run against the same snapshot. The main query and the other CTEs do not see changes made by a data-modifying CTE. The only way to see what it changed is through its RETURNING rows.
  • Data-modifying CTEs always run, even if nothing reads their result.
  • Do not modify the same row twice in one statement (two CTEs updating the same row): the result is unpredictable.
  • Constraint checks (like foreign keys) happen at the end of the whole statement. That is why you can delete an order's items and the order itself in the same WITH.
BEGIN;
WITH upd AS (
  UPDATE products SET price = price * 2 WHERE product_id = 1 RETURNING price
)
SELECT (SELECT price FROM products WHERE product_id = 1) AS seen_by_main_query,
       (SELECT price FROM upd)                             AS returned_by_update;
ROLLBACK;
seen_by_main_queryreturned_by_update
120000.00240000.00

(1 row)

Insert from a pipeline

INSERT INTO target SELECT … FROM last_step and CREATE TABLE t AS WITH … SELECT … both accept a CTE pipeline. This is how summary tables, snapshots and imports are usually built.

Run every pipeline with a plain final SELECT first and check the row counts of each step. Only then change the final statement to INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE, inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK, and look at RETURNING.

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s20.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Find duplicate customer emails after normalising them (trim + lower) in a CTE: email, accounts, ids (array of customer_ids in order).

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    WITH norm AS (
  SELECT customer_id, lower(trim(email)) AS email FROM customers
)
SELECT email, count(*) AS accounts, array_agg(customer_id ORDER BY customer_id) AS ids
FROM norm
GROUP BY email
HAVING count(*) > 1;
    emailaccountsids
    diya@mail.test2{2,18}

    (1 row)

    array_agg collects a group's values into one array: handy for showing which rows are duplicates.

  2. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: delete the order lines of cancelled orders with a data-modifying CTE, and return how many lines were removed and their total value in one row.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
WITH moved AS (
  DELETE FROM order_items oi
  USING orders o
  WHERE o.order_id = oi.order_id AND o.status = 'cancelled'
  RETURNING oi.*
)
SELECT count(*) AS lines_removed, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS value_removed
FROM moved;
ROLLBACK;
    lines_removedvalue_removed
    4304000.00

    (1 row)

    RETURNING rows behave like a table you can aggregate.

  3. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: in one statement, create customer 21 ('Test Buyer', test@mail.test, Pune, India, signed up 2026-02-15) and order 37 for that customer (2026-02-15, pending, shipping to Pune). Return the new order_id and customer_id.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer

WITH c AS (
  INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, full_name, email, city, country, signup_date)
  VALUES (21, 'Test Buyer', 'test@mail.test', 'Pune', 'India', DATE '2026-02-15')
  RETURNING customer_id
)
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, status, shipping_city)
SELECT 37, customer_id, DATE '2026-02-15', 'pending', 'Pune' FROM c
RETURNING order_id, customer_id;
ROLLBACK;

    The order takes its customer_id from the first step's RETURNING, so the two inserts cannot get out of sync. Your track1 Q9 DO block, as one statement.

  4. Clean these phone numbers: '9876543210', '+91-9988776655', '022-44556677', '98765', '(+91) 91234 56789', ''. Keep digits only; when there are at least 10, keep the last 10, otherwise NULL. Return raw and clean in input order.

    Expected: 6 rows

    Answer
    WITH raw(id, phone) AS (
  VALUES (1, '9876543210'), (2, '+91-9988776655'), (3, '022-44556677'),
         (4, '98765'), (5, '(+91) 91234 56789'), (6, '')
),
digits AS (
  SELECT id, phone, regexp_replace(phone, '[^0-9]', '', 'g') AS d FROM raw
)
SELECT phone AS raw, CASE WHEN length(d) >= 10 THEN right(d, 10) END AS clean
FROM digits
ORDER BY id;

    98765432109876543210
    +91-99887766559988776655
    022-445566772244556677
    98765∅
    (+91) 91234 567899123456789
    ∅

    (6 rows)

    Look at the landline: 022-44556677 has 11 digits, so "last 10" silently drops the leading 0 of the area code and produces 2244556677, a number nobody owns. A rule that works for mobiles corrupts landlines. Always check cleaned values against the raw ones before trusting a rule.

  9. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: archive the cancelled orders in one statement. Create a temp table orders_archive (LIKE orders); then one WITH that deletes the cancelled orders' lines, deletes the cancelled orders and inserts them into the archive. Return the archived order_ids.

  RETURNING oi.order_id

  10. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create a temp table customer_stats with CREATE TABLE … AS WITH … SELECT (customer_id, orders, delivered_revenue for all 20 customers), then return the top 3 by delivered_revenue.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer

CREATE TEMP TABLE customer_stats AS
WITH ord AS (
  SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
),
rev AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, COALESCE(ord.orders, 0) AS orders, COALESCE(rev.revenue, 0) AS delivered_revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN ord ON ord.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN rev ON rev.customer_id = c.customer_id;

  11. An import file arrives as (row, email, city): (1, ' AARAV@mail.test ', 'mumbai'), (2, 'newbie@mail.test', 'Goa'), (3, 'Liam@Mail.Test', ' singapore'), (4, '', 'Delhi'), (5, 'kiara@mail.test', NULL). Clean it (trim, lowercase emails, empty → NULL, city in Title Case) and classify each row as 'existing' (email matches a customer, case-insensitively), 'new', or 'reject: no email'. Columns: row, email, city, customer_id, action, ordered by row.

    Expected: 5 rows

    Answer
    WITH raw(rn, email, city) AS (
  VALUES (1, ' AARAV@mail.test ', 'mumbai'), (2, 'newbie@mail.test', 'Goa'),
         (3, 'Liam@Mail.Test', ' singapore'), (4, '', 'Delhi'), (5, 'kiara@mail.test', NULL)
),
clean AS (
  SELECT rn, NULLIF(lower(trim(email)), '') AS email, initcap(trim(city)) AS city FROM raw
)
SELECT cl.rn AS row, cl.email, cl.city, c.customer_id,

            WHEN c.customer_id IS NULL  THEN 'new'

    (5 rows)

    Matching on the normalised value on both sides is what makes " AARAV@mail.test " find customer 1.

  12. A simple funnel from page_views: how many customers viewed home; of those, how many viewed a product; of those, the cart; of those, checkout. Return step number, page and customers.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    WITH home AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM page_views WHERE page = 'home'
),
product AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM page_views
  WHERE page = 'product' AND customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM home)
),
cart AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM page_views
  WHERE page = 'cart' AND customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM product)
),
checkout AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM page_views
  WHERE page = 'checkout' AND customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM cart)
)
SELECT 1 AS step, 'home' AS page, count(*) AS customers FROM home
UNION ALL SELECT 2, 'product',  count(*) FROM product
UNION ALL SELECT 3, 'cart',     count(*) FROM cart
UNION ALL SELECT 4, 'checkout', count(*) FROM checkout
ORDER BY step;
    steppagecustomers
    1home4
    2product4
    3cart3
    4checkout2

    (4 rows)

    4 → 4 → 3 → 2. Each step only counts people who passed the previous one. A stricter funnel would also require the steps in time order, which Session 26 (lag/lead) makes easy.

  13. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create a temp table revenue_snapshot (month date primary key, revenue numeric not null) and fill it from a CTE with delivered revenue per month of 2025. Return the inserted rows.

    Expected: 10 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE revenue_snapshot (month date PRIMARY KEY, revenue numeric NOT NULL);

WITH m AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date)::date AS month, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
    AND o.order_date >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND o.order_date < DATE '2026-01-01'
  GROUP BY 1
)
INSERT INTO revenue_snapshot
SELECT month, revenue FROM m ORDER BY month
RETURNING month, revenue;
ROLLBACK;

    2025-01-01156000.00
    2025-02-0139400.00
    2025-03-01121500.00
    2025-04-01132700.00
    2025-05-0149700.00
    2025-06-0143000.00
    2025-07-0114200.00
    2025-08-0114300.00
    2025-09-01138500.00
    2025-10-0113600.00

    (10 rows)

    Ten months had delivered revenue. A snapshot table like this is how dashboards avoid recomputing history every time (Phase 6: materialized views).

  14. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: prove the snapshot rule. In one statement, double product 1's price in a CTE and, in the main query, read product 1's price both from the table and from the CTE's RETURNING. Return seen_by_main_query and returned_by_update.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
WITH upd AS (
  UPDATE products SET price = price * 2 WHERE product_id = 1 RETURNING price
)
SELECT (SELECT price FROM products WHERE product_id = 1) AS seen_by_main_query,
       (SELECT price FROM upd)                             AS returned_by_update;
ROLLBACK;
    seen_by_main_queryreturned_by_update
    120000.00240000.00

    (1 row)

    120,000 vs 240,000: the main query still sees the old row. If a later step needs the new values, it must read them from RETURNING.

  15. Challenge: A small version of your track1 Q50: validate a legacy employee import. Input rows (id, name, salary, joined, active, dept_code): ('101','Vikram Rao','75000.50','2022-01-15','yes','ENG'), ('102','Ananya Das','₹85,000','15/02/2021','Y','FIN'), ('103','Dev Malhotra','N/A','2020-10-25','no','HR'), ('ABC','Sara Ali','65000','not-a-date','1','SALES'), ('105','Karan Roy','','2023-06-01','FALSE','ENG'), ('106','Neha Kapoor',' 92,500.75 ','01/12/2020','true','UNKNOWN'). Department codes map to names: ENG → Engineering, FIN → Finance, SALES → Sales, MKT → Marketing; then to departments.department_id. A row is rejected if its id is not a whole number, its date cannot be parsed, or its department is unknown (list every reason). A bad salary just becomes NULL. Return employee_id, name, salary, joined_on, is_active, department_id and status ('ok' or 'rejected: …'), in input order.

    Expected: 6 rows

    Answer
    WITH raw(rn, id, name, salary, joined, active, dept_code) AS (
  VALUES (1, '101', 'Vikram Rao',   '75000.50',    '2022-01-15', 'yes',   'ENG'),
         (2, '102', 'Ananya Das',   '₹85,000',     '15/02/2021', 'Y',     'FIN'),
         (3, '103', 'Dev Malhotra', 'N/A',         '2020-10-25', 'no',    'HR'),
         (4, 'ABC', 'Sara Ali',     '65000',       'not-a-date', '1',     'SALES'),
         (5, '105', 'Karan Roy',    '',            '2023-06-01', 'FALSE', 'ENG'),
         (6, '106', 'Neha Kapoor',  ' 92,500.75 ', '01/12/2020', 'true',  'UNKNOWN')
),
parsed AS (
  SELECT rn, name, dept_code,
         CASE WHEN id ~ '^\d+$' THEN id::int END AS employee_id,
         CASE WHEN pg_input_is_valid(NULLIF(regexp_replace(salary, '[^0-9.]', '', 'g'), ''), 'numeric')
              THEN NULLIF(regexp_replace(salary, '[^0-9.]', '', 'g'), '')::numeric(12, 2) END AS salary,
         CASE WHEN joined ~ '^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$' THEN joined::date
              WHEN joined ~ '^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4}$' THEN to_date(joined, 'DD/MM/YYYY') END AS joined_on,
         CASE WHEN lower(trim(active)) IN ('yes', 'y', 'true', '1')  THEN true
              WHEN lower(trim(active)) IN ('no', 'n', 'false', '0') THEN false END AS is_active
  FROM raw
),
mapped AS (
  SELECT p.*, d.department_id
  FROM parsed p
  LEFT JOIN (VALUES ('ENG', 'Engineering'), ('FIN', 'Finance'), ('SALES', 'Sales'), ('MKT', 'Marketing')) AS m(code, dept_name)
         ON m.code = p.dept_code
  LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.name = m.dept_name
)
SELECT employee_id, name, salary, joined_on, is_active, department_id,
       CASE WHEN employee_id IS NULL OR joined_on IS NULL OR department_id IS NULL
            THEN 'rejected: ' || concat_ws(', ',
                   CASE WHEN employee_id IS NULL   THEN 'bad id' END,
                   CASE WHEN joined_on IS NULL     THEN 'bad date' END,
                   CASE WHEN department_id IS NULL THEN 'unknown department' END)
            ELSE 'ok' END AS status
FROM mapped
ORDER BY rn;
    employee_idnamesalaryjoined_onis_activedepartment_idstatus
    101Vikram Rao75000.502022-01-15t1ok
    102Ananya Das85000.002021-02-15t4ok
    103Dev Malhotra∅2020-10-25f∅rejected: unknown department
    ∅Sara Ali65000.00∅t2rejected: bad id, bad date
    105Karan Roy∅2023-06-01f1ok
    106Neha Kapoor92500.752020-12-01t∅rejected: unknown department

    (6 rows)

    Three rows load, three are rejected with every reason listed (Sara has two). concat_ws skips NULL pieces, so only the reasons that apply are joined. The full Q50 adds a rejected table, retry safety and counts, which you will build in Phase 7.

Phase 3 · Session 21

Review: set operations, dates, spines and CTEs

Pull Sessions 15–20 back out of memory, mixed together, without notes.

Topics

How to run this review

  • First 20 minutes: redo every question in mistakes.md from Sessions 15–20, cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below, mixed on purpose.
  • Then the challenge, an RFM-style customer table built as a CTE pipeline.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 15–20

Problem                                     Tool
------------------------------------------  ----------------------------------------------
Stack two result sets                       UNION ALL (UNION only to remove duplicates)
In both / in A but not B                    INTERSECT / EXCEPT (NULLs count as equal here)
Small inline table                          (VALUES (…), (…)) AS v(col1, col2)
Duration between two moments                b - a (interval); extract(epoch …) / 3600 for hours
The day/time in a specific zone             (ts AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date / ::time
Per day / week / month                      date_trunc(…); weeks start on Monday
Show empty periods as zero                  generate_series spine LEFT JOIN facts
Name and reuse steps                        WITH a AS (…), b AS (…) SELECT …
Change data and use what changed            WITH x AS (DELETE/UPDATE/INSERT … RETURNING …)

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s21.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

LEFT JOIN rev ON rev.customer_id = rf.customer_id
ORDER BY rf.customer_id;

Phase 3 · Session 22

How window functions work

Compute group values next to every row without collapsing rows, and know exactly when window functions run.

Topics

Aggregates collapse, windows do not

GROUP BY department_id turns 12 employees into 5 rows. Often you want to keep every employee and see the department average next to each one. In Phase 2 that took a correlated subquery or a join to a derived table. A window function does it directly: it computes over a set of rows related to the current row (its "window") and writes the result onto the current row.

SELECT full_name, department_id, salary,
       round(avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id)) AS dept_avg
FROM employees
ORDER BY department_id, salary DESC;
full_namedepartment_idsalarydept_avg
Vikram Mehta1220000.00136000
Neha Kulkarni1150000.00136000
Rahul Verma1120000.00136000
Arjun Singh195000.00136000
Priya Nair195000.00136000
Sneha Iyer2160000.0094000
Meera Joshi262000.0094000
Karan Malhotra260000.0094000
Rohan Das3110000.00110000
Isha Kapoor485000.0085000
Asha Rao∅300000.00162500
Dev Patel∅25000.00162500

(12 rows)

Anatomy of OVER (…)

function(args) OVER (
  PARTITION BY …     which rows belong together (like GROUP BY, but rows are kept)
  ORDER BY …         order inside each partition (needed for running totals, ranks, lag)
  frame              which rows of the partition count (Session 25)
)
  • OVER (): empty window = all rows of the result. sum(x) OVER () is the grand total on every row.
  • PARTITION BY a: one window per value of a. Unlike a correlated subquery, NULL is its own partition: employees with no department are grouped together.
  • Any aggregate (sum, avg, count, min, max…) can be used as a window function, plus special ones: row_number, rank, lag, lead and others in the next sessions.

ORDER BY inside OVER makes it running

Add ORDER BY inside the window and an aggregate becomes cumulative: by default it covers the rows from the start of the partition up to the current row. Rows that tie on the ORDER BY value are included together (the default frame is RANGE, Session 25), so always add a tie-breaker when you want one row at a time:

SELECT order_id, order_date,
       count(*) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)            AS running_by_date,      -- ties counted together
       count(*) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id)  AS running_by_row
FROM orders
WHERE order_date < DATE '2025-02-15'
ORDER BY order_date, order_id;
order_idorder_daterunning_by_daterunning_by_row
12025-01-0511
22025-01-0922
32025-01-2033
42025-02-0344
52025-02-1155
62025-02-1466

(6 rows)

When windows run, and why WHERE cannot use them

FROM / JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → WINDOW FUNCTIONS → SELECT list → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY. So you cannot filter on a window result in the same query's WHERE (the value does not exist yet); you get window functions are not allowed in WHERE. Compute the window in a CTE or subquery, then filter outside:

WITH e AS (
  SELECT full_name, salary, avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
)
SELECT full_name, salary, round(dept_avg) AS dept_avg
FROM e
WHERE salary > dept_avg
ORDER BY salary DESC;
full_namesalarydept_avg
Asha Rao300000.00162500
Vikram Mehta220000.00136000
Sneha Iyer160000.0094000
Neha Kulkarni150000.00136000

(4 rows)

Four rows, while the correlated-subquery version in S13 Q9 returned three. The difference is Asha (CEO): her department is NULL, and the window puts Asha and Dev (the intern) into one NULL partition, where she is above the average. The correlated subquery compared department_id = NULL, which never matches. Neither is "wrong"; know which rule you are using.

Windows over aggregates

Because windows run after GROUP BY, you can window over the grouped result. sum(sum(x)) OVER () reads as "the total of the group totals", which gives each group's share in one query:

SELECT COALESCE(k.name, 'Uncategorised') AS category,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue,
       round(100 * sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) / sum(sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
LEFT JOIN categories k ON k.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
categoryrevenuepct
Computers441000.0061.0
Audio125200.0017.3
Kitchen81300.0011.2
Accessories52000.007.2
Home15400.002.1
Uncategorised8000.001.1

(6 rows)

The ORDER BY inside OVER only decides the window's order. It does not sort the output. Always add a final ORDER BY to the query.

Phase 3 · Session 23

ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK

Number and rank rows overall or per group, and choose the right function for ties.

Topics

Three ways to count positions

All three number rows in the order given by the window's ORDER BY. They only differ on ties. Priya and Arjun both earn 95,000:

SELECT full_name, salary,
       row_number() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_number,
       rank()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank,
       dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 1
ORDER BY salary DESC, full_name;
full_namesalaryrow_numberrankdense_rank
Vikram Mehta220000.00111
Neha Kulkarni150000.00222
Rahul Verma120000.00333
Arjun Singh95000.00544
Priya Nair95000.00444

(5 rows)

  • row_number(): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Every row gets a different number; ties are split arbitrarily unless you add a tie-breaker to the ORDER BY.
  • rank(): 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, then 6 would come next. Ties share a number and the next number is skipped (like sports: two silver medals, no bronze).
  • dense_rank(): 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, then 5. Ties share a number, no gaps.
Question                                   Use
-----------------------------------------  ------------------------------------------
Exactly one row per position (dedup, top-1) row_number() + a unique tie-breaker
"Top 3 salaries" counting tied people        rank() <= 3
"Top 3 distinct salary values"              dense_rank() <= 3
The Nth highest value                       dense_rank() = N

Per group with PARTITION BY

Add PARTITION BY and numbering restarts at 1 in every group. "Each customer's orders, numbered in date order":

SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS nth_order
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 2)
ORDER BY customer_id, nth_order;
customer_idorder_idorder_datenth_order
112025-01-051
132025-01-202
1132025-04-183
1272025-10-034
222025-01-091
292025-03-152
2222025-08-013
2362026-02-144

(8 rows)

Make row_number deterministic

If two rows tie on the window ORDER BY, row_number may number them differently from one run to the next (it depends on the physical order rows arrive in). For anything you rely on (deduplication, "the latest", pagination) end the ORDER BY with a unique column, usually the primary key.

Filtering on a rank

Same rule as last session: compute the rank in a CTE, filter outside. That is the core of the next session (top-N per group).

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, price, dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY price DESC) AS dr
  FROM products
)
SELECT name, price FROM ranked WHERE dr = 2;     -- the second-highest distinct price
nameprice
Laptop Air 1385000.00

(1 row)

NULLs sort last in ascending order and first in descending order in Postgres. When ranking a column that can be NULL with DESC, write ORDER BY x DESC NULLS LAST, or the NULL rows take rank 1.

Phase 3 · Session 24

Top-N per group and removing duplicates

Solve "the top N of each group" and "keep one row per key" the standard way, and know when DISTINCT ON or LATERAL is the better tool.

Topics

The pattern

Almost every "top / latest / best N per X" question has the same three-line skeleton. Learn it until you can type it without thinking:

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT …, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY <group> ORDER BY <best first>, <tie-breaker>) AS rn
  FROM …
)
SELECT … FROM ranked WHERE rn <= N;
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category_id, name, price,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY price DESC, product_id) AS rn
  FROM products
)
SELECT category_id, name, price, rn
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY category_id, rn;
category_idnamepricern
2Laptop Pro 14120000.001
2Laptop Air 1385000.002
3Noise-Cancel Headphones18000.001
3Bluetooth Speaker7000.002
4Standing Desk32000.001
4Desk Lamp2200.002
5Air Fryer11000.001
5Coffee Maker9000.002
7Mechanical Keyboard6500.001
7USB-C Hub3500.002
∅Gift Card1000.001

(11 rows)

  • row_number gives exactly N rows per group (ties cut by the tie-breaker).
  • rank gives at least N rows when there are ties at the boundary ("top 3 salaries, including everyone tied for 3rd").
  • dense_rank gives the rows with the top N distinct values.

Three tools for the same job

Tool                          Best when
----------------------------  -----------------------------------------------------------------
row_number() in a CTE          portable SQL, any N, ties rules via rank/dense_rank, reads all rows
DISTINCT ON (Session 10)       top-1 only, Postgres only, shortest to write
LATERAL … LIMIT N (Session 10) few groups + an index on (group, sort): reads only N rows per group

For a table with millions of rows and few groups (top 3 orders for each of 20 carriers), LATERAL with an index reads 60 index entries. The window version reads and sorts everything. With many small groups the window version is usually fine, and since Postgres 15 the planner can stop early for row_number() … WHERE rn <= N (shown as a "Run Condition" in EXPLAIN).

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
Subquery Scan on ranked
  Filter: (ranked.rn = 1)
  ->  WindowAgg
        Window: w1 AS (PARTITION BY orders.customer_id ORDER BY orders.order_date, orders.order_id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
        Run Condition: (row_number() OVER w1 <= 1)
        ->  Sort
              Sort Key: orders.customer_id, orders.order_date DESC, orders.order_id DESC
              ->  Seq Scan on orders

Removing duplicates

Deduplication is "keep the top 1 per key, remove the rest". Number the rows within each duplicate group, decide which one survives (lowest id, newest, most complete), and delete everything with rn > 1. Always SELECT the rows you are about to delete first.

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, email,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY lower(email) ORDER BY customer_id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
SELECT customer_id, email FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1;
customer_idemail
18DIYA@mail.test

(1 row)

Then delete by primary key: DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1) (after moving their orders, as in S9). If a table has no primary key, Postgres's hidden row id ctid can identify rows, but a table without a key is the real problem to fix.

Choose the survivor on purpose. "Keep the lowest id" is easy; "keep the most recently updated row" or "keep the row with the most non-NULL fields" may be what the business actually needs.

Challenge: Product of the month: for every month of 2025 with delivered sales, the product with the highest delivered revenue that month (ties → lower product_id), its revenue, and its share of that month's delivered revenue (1 decimal).     Expected: 10 rows

    Answer
    WITH mp AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date)::date AS month, oi.product_id,
         sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id

),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *, sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY month) AS month_total,
            row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id) AS rn
  FROM mp
)
SELECT r.month, p.name, r.revenue, round(100 * r.revenue / r.month_total, 1) AS pct_of_month
FROM ranked r
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = r.product_id
WHERE r.rn = 1
ORDER BY r.month;

Phase 3 · Session 25

Running totals, moving averages and frames

Control exactly which rows a window adds up with ROWS, RANGE and GROUPS frames, for running totals, moving averages and time-based rolling windows.

Topics

The frame: which rows count

Inside each partition, the frame is the subset of rows the function actually looks at for the current row. You have been using defaults:

  • No ORDER BY in OVER → the frame is the whole partition.
  • With ORDER BY → RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW: from the first row up to the current row and every row that ties with it.
{ ROWS | RANGE | GROUPS } BETWEEN <start> AND <end>

start / end:  UNBOUNDED PRECEDING | n PRECEDING | CURRENT ROW | n FOLLOWING | UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING

ROWS    counts physical rows               ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW  = last 3 rows
RANGE   uses the ORDER BY value            RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
GROUPS  counts groups of tied values      GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

ROWS vs RANGE on ties

Priya and Arjun earn the same. A running total ordered by salary treats them differently depending on the frame:

SELECT full_name, salary,
       sum(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary)                                           AS range_default,
       sum(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rows_frame
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 1
ORDER BY salary, full_name;
full_namesalaryrange_defaultrows_frame
Arjun Singh95000.00190000.00190000.00
Priya Nair95000.00190000.0095000.00
Rahul Verma120000.00310000.00310000.00
Neha Kulkarni150000.00460000.00460000.00
Vikram Mehta220000.00680000.00680000.00

(5 rows)

With the default RANGE frame both tied rows get the same total (both include each other). With ROWS each row adds only itself. For running totals you usually want ROWS plus a unique tie-breaker in the ORDER BY.

Moving averages

"Average of this order and the two before it" is a frame of exactly three rows:

WITH t AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.order_id, o.order_date
)
SELECT order_id, order_date, total,
       round(avg(total) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id
                              ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg_3
FROM t
ORDER BY order_date, order_id
LIMIT 6;
order_idorder_datetotalmoving_avg_3

22025-01-0923000.0071250.00
32025-01-2013500.0052000.00
42025-02-0385000.0040500.00
52025-02-1117000.0038500.00
62025-02-1411400.0037800.00

(6 rows)

The first rows average fewer than three values because there are not enough preceding rows; decide whether to show or hide them.

Rolling time windows with RANGE

ROWS counts rows, not days: "the last 7 rows" might cover 3 days or 3 months. When the window must be a span of time, use RANGE with an interval offset on a date or timestamp ORDER BY. It looks at the values, so gaps in the data are handled correctly:

SELECT order_id, order_date,
       count(*) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
                      RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS orders_last_7_days
FROM orders
WHERE order_date < DATE '2025-03-01'
ORDER BY order_date;
order_idorder_dateorders_last_7_days

Running totals that reset

A running total that restarts every month is just a running total partitioned by month: sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', d) ORDER BY d, id). A total that resets on some event (a refund, a status change) needs a group id first; that is Session 32.

Excluding the current row

EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW (also EXCLUDE TIES, EXCLUDE GROUP) removes rows from the frame. "Compare me with the average of everyone else in my group" is avg(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW).

Frame-related bugs are silent. When a running number looks wrong, check: is there a tie-breaker? Is the frame ROWS or the default RANGE? Does the partition reset where you expect?

  12. Customer 2's running balance: every order (item total, owed) and payment (paid) in date order, with balance = owed so far − paid so far. Columns: happened_at, kind, amount, balance, ordered by happened_at, kind.

  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id

       sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY happened_at, kind ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS balance
FROM events
ORDER BY happened_at, kind;

Phase 3 · Session 26

LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE

Compare each row with the row before or after it, and pick the first, last or Nth value of a window without a self-join.

Topics

Looking at neighbouring rows

lag(x) returns x from the previous row of the window, lead(x) from the next one, in the window's ORDER BY. In Phase 2 you needed a self-join for "previous month"; now it is one function:

SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
       lag(order_date)  OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS prev_order,
       order_date - lag(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS days_since_prev,
       lead(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS next_order
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 4)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
customer_idorder_idorder_dateprev_orderdays_since_prevnext_order
112025-01-05∅∅2025-01-20
132025-01-202025-01-05152025-04-18
1132025-04-182025-01-20882025-10-03
1272025-10-032025-04-18168∅
452025-02-11∅∅2025-08-14
4232025-08-142025-02-11184∅

(6 rows)

  • lag(x, n) looks n rows back; lag(x, n, default) returns default instead of NULL when there is no such row.
  • The first row of each partition has no previous row: lag is NULL there. That is usually correct ("no previous order") and should not be hidden with a fake 0.
  • lag and lead ignore the frame: they always count rows in the partition.

Month over month in one line

WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT s.month::date AS month, COALESCE(sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-06-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS s(month)
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.status = 'delivered'
                    AND o.order_date >= s.month AND o.order_date < s.month + INTERVAL '1 month'
  LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY s.month
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)            AS prev_month,
       revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)  AS change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
monthrevenueprev_monthchange

first_value, last_value, nth_value, and the frame trap

These three do use the frame. With an ORDER BY in the window, the default frame ends at the current row, so last_value returns… the current row. That is the most common window-function bug:

SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
       first_value(order_id) OVER w AS first_order,
       last_value(order_id)  OVER w AS last_value_default_frame,   -- wrong: just the current row
       last_value(order_id)  OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id
                                   ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_order
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id)
ORDER BY order_date;
customer_idorder_idorder_datefirst_orderlast_value_default_framelast_order
112025-01-051127
132025-01-201327
1132025-04-1811327
1272025-10-0312727

(4 rows)

Fix it with a full frame (ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING), or avoid it: the last value in ascending order is the first value in descending order. nth_value(x, 2) works the same way and needs the full frame to see the 2nd row from every row.

The WINDOW w AS (…) clause above names a window once and reuses it. Session 27 covers it properly.

Interview PDF #103, solved with lag: given fuel readings (1, '2014-04-25 10:00', 10), (2, '2014-04-25 11:00', 9), (3, '2014-04-25 12:00', 8), (4, '2014-04-25 14:00', 12), (5, '2014-04-25 15:00', 11), (6, '2014-04-25 19:00', 15), (7, '2014-04-25 20:00', 14), (8, '2014-04-25 23:00', 20): when was the car refuelled (fuel went up)? Return reading_time, fuel_before, fuel_after.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    WITH readings(id, reading_time, fuel) AS (
  VALUES (1, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 10:00', 10), (2, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 11:00', 9),
         (3, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 12:00', 8),  (4, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 14:00', 12),
         (5, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 15:00', 11), (6, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 19:00', 15),
         (7, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 20:00', 14), (8, TIMESTAMP '2014-04-25 23:00', 20)
),
w AS (
  SELECT reading_time, fuel, lag(fuel) OVER (ORDER BY reading_time) AS fuel_before FROM readings
)
SELECT reading_time, fuel_before, fuel AS fuel_after
FROM w
WHERE fuel > fuel_before
ORDER BY reading_time;

    WITH g AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
         order_date - lag(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS gap
  FROM orders
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY gap DESC NULLS LAST, order_date, order_id) AS rn
  FROM g
),
summary AS (
  SELECT customer_id, min(order_date) AS first_order, max(order_date) AS last_order,
         round(avg(gap), 1) AS avg_gap_days, max(gap) AS longest_gap_days
  FROM g
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING count(*) >= 2
)
SELECT s.customer_id, s.first_order, s.last_order, s.avg_gap_days, s.longest_gap_days,
       r.order_id AS order_after_longest_gap
FROM summary s
JOIN ranked r ON r.customer_id = s.customer_id AND r.rn = 1
ORDER BY s.customer_id;

Phase 3 · Session 27

NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST and named windows

Bucket rows into quartiles or deciles, express a row's position as a percentile, name windows for reuse, and avoid the window-plus-GROUP BY trap.

Topics

Buckets with ntile(n)

ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY x) splits the ordered rows into 4 groups as equal in size as possible and returns the group number (1–4). With 15 products, the groups have 4, 4, 4 and 3 rows: the remainder goes to the first groups. ntile splits by row count, so tied values can land in different buckets.

SELECT name, price, ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY price DESC, product_id) AS price_quartile
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 6;
namepriceprice_quartile
Laptop Pro 14120000.001
Laptop Air 1385000.001
4K Monitor42000.001
Standing Desk32000.001
Noise-Cancel Headphones18000.002
Air Fryer11000.002

(6 rows)

Relative position: percent_rank and cume_dist

  • percent_rank() = (rank − 1) / (rows − 1): 0 for the first row, 1 for the last. "What fraction of the others are below me?"
  • cume_dist() = (rows up to and including my value) / rows: always above 0, 1 for the last. "What fraction are at or below me?"
  • Both treat ties as equal, unlike ntile.
SELECT full_name, salary,
       round(percent_rank() OVER (ORDER BY salary)::numeric, 2) AS pct_rank,
       round(cume_dist()    OVER (ORDER BY salary)::numeric, 2) AS cume_dist
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary
LIMIT 6;
full_namesalarypct_rankcume_dist

They return double precision, so cast to numeric before round().

Named windows: the WINDOW clause

When several functions share a window, name it once at the end of the query (after HAVING, before ORDER BY) and refer to it by name. A named window can also be extended: OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) adds a frame to w, as long as w has no frame of its own.

SELECT full_name, department_id, salary,
       row_number() OVER w AS rn,
       rank()       OVER w AS rnk,
       sum(salary)  OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running
FROM employees
WHERE department_id IN (1, 2)
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC, employee_id)
ORDER BY department_id, rn;
full_namedepartment_idsalaryrnrnkrunning

The window + GROUP BY trap

Windows run after GROUP BY. So in a grouped query, the window sees one row per group, and every column it uses must be either a GROUP BY column or an aggregate. sum(quantity) OVER () in a query grouped by category fails ("quantity must appear in the GROUP BY clause"), because individual quantities no longer exist at that stage. Wrap the aggregate: sum(sum(quantity)) OVER (). Likewise, count(*) OVER () in a grouped query counts groups, not original rows.

SELECT customer_id,
       count(*)                                         AS orders,
       count(*) OVER ()                                 AS groups_seen_by_window,
       round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_all_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY orders DESC, customer_id
LIMIT 5;
customer_idordersgroups_seen_by_windowpct_of_all_orders
141611.1
241611.1
33168.3
53168.3
42165.6

(5 rows)
