Phase 3 · Session 28

Review: window functions

Pull Sessions 22–27 back out of memory, mixed together, without notes.

Topics

How to run this review

  • First 20 minutes: redo every question in mistakes.md from Sessions 22–27, cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below. For each one, decide first: which function, which PARTITION BY, which ORDER BY, which frame?
  • Then the challenge.

Cheat sheet: window functions

Need                                          Write
--------------------------------------------  -------------------------------------------------------
Group value on every row                      agg(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)
Share of total                                x / sum(x) OVER ()        (grouped: sum(sum(x)) OVER ())
Running total, one row at a time              sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY d, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
Last N rows / moving average                  ROWS BETWEEN N-1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
Last N days with gaps                         RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 'N-1 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
Exactly one row per position                  row_number() … tie-breaker
Ties share a place                            rank() (gaps) / dense_rank() (no gaps)
Top N per group                               CTE with row_number() … WHERE rn <= N
Previous / next row                           lag(x) / lead(x)
Last value of the window                      last_value(x) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
Buckets / percentiles                         ntile(n) / percent_rank() / cume_dist()
Filter on a window result                     compute in a CTE, filter outside

ORDER BY customer_id, order_date, order_id;

Phase 3 · Session 29

Recursive CTEs: trees and hierarchies

Walk a hierarchy of any depth (org charts, category trees) top-down and bottom-up, with depth, paths and subtree totals.

Topics

Why joins are not enough

In S6 you found an employee's manager with one self-join and the manager's manager with two. "Everyone below Vikram, however deep" needs as many joins as there are levels, and you do not know how many there are. A recursive CTE repeats a join until it stops finding new rows.

WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  -- 1. anchor: the starting rows
  SELECT employee_id, full_name, manager_id, 0 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  -- 2. recursive part: join the table to the rows found in the previous round
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.full_name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id
)
SELECT * FROM org;
  • Postgres runs the anchor once. Then it runs the recursive part using only the rows produced by the previous round, adds the results, and repeats until a round returns no rows.
  • The recursive part refers to the CTE itself (org) exactly once.
  • Carry information down the tree in extra columns: depth (+1 per level), a path (an array or text that grows), a running total.
  • UNION ALL keeps every row; UNION would also remove duplicates and can help stop loops, but costs a de-duplication every round.
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT employee_id, full_name, manager_id, 0 AS depth, full_name AS chain
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.full_name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1, o.chain || ' > ' || e.full_name
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id
)
SELECT depth, full_name, chain
FROM org
ORDER BY chain;
depthfull_namechain

Top-down and bottom-up

The direction is decided by the join. Top-down (who is below X): anchor on X, join children where child.manager_id = found.employee_id. Bottom-up (who is above X): anchor on X, join parents where parent.employee_id = found.manager_id:

WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
  SELECT employee_id, full_name, manager_id, 0 AS level
  FROM employees WHERE full_name = 'Dev Patel'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT m.employee_id, m.full_name, m.manager_id, u.level + 1
  FROM employees m
  JOIN up u ON m.employee_id = u.manager_id
)
SELECT level, full_name FROM up ORDER BY level;
levelfull_name
0Dev Patel
1Neha Kulkarni
2Vikram Mehta
3Asha Rao

(4 rows)

Sorting a tree for display

Sorting by a text path works for display but breaks if names contain the separator. An array path of ids (ARRAY[employee_id], then path || e.employee_id) sorts correctly: parents come before their children and siblings stay together. Postgres 14+ also has SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY employee_id SET ordercol, which builds that sort key for you.

Totals over a subtree

You cannot use aggregates inside the recursive part, so to get "team size" or "payroll of everyone below a manager", first produce every (ancestor, descendant) pair recursively, then GROUP BY the ancestor:

WITH RECURSIVE pairs AS (
  SELECT manager_id AS ancestor, employee_id AS descendant
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.ancestor, e.employee_id
  FROM pairs p
  JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = p.descendant
)
SELECT ancestor, count(*) AS people_below
FROM pairs
GROUP BY ancestor
ORDER BY people_below DESC;
ancestorpeople_below
111
25
34
72

(4 rows)

If the data contains a loop (A manages B, B manages A), a recursive CTE never ends. Your check constraint from track1 Q20 stops an employee managing themselves, but not longer loops. Guard with a depth limit (WHERE o.depth < 20) or a path check (WHERE NOT e.employee_id = ANY(o.path)); Session 30 shows the CYCLE clause.

  UNION ALL

product_rev AS (

LEFT JOIN products p   ON p.category_id = cp.descendant
LEFT JOIN product_rev r ON r.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY k.category_id, k.name
ORDER BY rolled_up_revenue DESC, k.name;

  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL

  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id

pairs AS (

  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.ancestor, e.employee_id FROM pairs p JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = p.descendant
),
subtree AS (
  SELECT p.ancestor, count(*) - 1 AS total_reports, sum(d.salary) AS team_payroll
  FROM pairs p JOIN employees d ON d.employee_id = p.descendant
  GROUP BY p.ancestor
)
SELECT o.full_name, o.depth, o.chain,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM employees r WHERE r.manager_id = o.employee_id) AS direct_reports,
       s.total_reports, s.team_payroll
FROM org o
JOIN subtree s ON s.ancestor = o.employee_id
ORDER BY o.path;

Phase 3 · Session 30

Recursive CTEs: graphs, cycles and sequences

Traverse networks that have several paths and loops, find shortest routes, stop infinite recursion safely, and generate sequences.

Topics

Trees vs graphs

In a tree every node has one parent, so there is exactly one way to reach it. In a graph (roads, flights, social networks) a node can be reached by many paths, and paths can loop. The routes table is a small one-way network between warehouses, with one loop: Delhi → Kolkata → Delhi.

Walk all paths, carrying the path

Carry the list of visited cities in an array. It gives you the route for output, and it is how you stop loops: only extend a path to a city that is not already in it.

WITH RECURSIVE paths AS (
  SELECT to_city, km AS total_km, ARRAY[from_city, to_city] AS path, 1 AS hops
  FROM routes WHERE from_city = 'Mumbai'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT r.to_city, p.total_km + r.km, p.path || r.to_city, p.hops + 1
  FROM paths p
  JOIN routes r ON r.from_city = p.to_city
  WHERE NOT r.to_city = ANY (p.path)          -- never revisit a city
)
SELECT array_to_string(path, ' → ') AS route, total_km, hops
FROM paths
WHERE to_city = 'Chennai'
ORDER BY total_km;
routetotal_kmhops
Mumbai → Pune → Bengaluru → Chennai13303
Mumbai → Hyderabad → Chennai13402
Mumbai → Pune → Hyderabad → Chennai13403
Mumbai → Hyderabad → Bengaluru → Chennai16303
Mumbai → Pune → Hyderabad → Bengaluru → Chennai16304

(5 rows)

Five different ways to reach Chennai. The shortest is just the first row (ORDER BY total_km LIMIT 1, or DISTINCT ON per destination). This brute-force approach explores every simple path, which is fine for small networks; for road maps with millions of edges you would use a graph extension such as pgRouting.

The CYCLE clause (Postgres 14+)

Instead of writing the path check yourself, you can let Postgres detect cycles. CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path adds a boolean column and a path column, and stops expanding a row as soon as it revisits a value:

WITH RECURSIVE r AS (
  SELECT from_city, to_city FROM routes WHERE from_city = 'Delhi'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT rt.from_city, rt.to_city FROM routes rt JOIN r ON rt.from_city = r.to_city
) CYCLE to_city SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT from_city, to_city, is_cycle FROM r;
from_cityto_cityis_cycle
DelhiKolkataf
KolkataDelhif
DelhiKolkatat

(3 rows)

There is also SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY col SET ordercol / SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY col SET ordercol, which adds a column you can ORDER BY to list results in depth-first or breadth-first order.

Without a loop guard, a recursive query over a graph with a cycle runs until it fills the disk or memory. Always add one of: a path check, the CYCLE clause, or a hard depth limit (WHERE hops < 10). With UNION instead of UNION ALL, duplicate rows are dropped, which stops some loops, but not when a column like total_km keeps changing.

Sequences

Recursion also generates sequences where each value depends on the previous one: compound growth, Fibonacci, balances. generate_series is simpler for plain counting; recursion is for "the next value is computed from the last".

WITH RECURSIVE fib(n, a, b) AS (
  SELECT 1, 0::numeric, 1::numeric
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1, b, a + b FROM fib WHERE n < 10
)
SELECT n, a AS fibonacci FROM fib;
nfibonacci
10
21
31
42
53
65
78
813
921
1034

(10 rows)

Phase 3 · Session 31

Gaps and islands

Find runs of consecutive values (streaks, outages, ranges) and the gaps between them, with two standard techniques.

Topics

The problem

"Islands" are runs of consecutive values: days in a row a customer was active, months in a row above target, ids without holes. "Gaps" are the missing stretches between them. GROUP BY alone cannot do this, because what makes rows belong together is that they are next to each other, not that they share a value.

Technique 1: value minus row number

Number the rows in order. Within an island, both the value and the row number go up by exactly 1 each step, so value − row_number stays constant. When there is a gap, the value jumps but the row number does not, so the difference changes. That constant is an island id you can GROUP BY:

WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT viewed_at::date AS day FROM page_views WHERE customer_id = 1
)
SELECT day,
       row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)       AS rn,
       day - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)::int AS island_key
FROM days
ORDER BY day;
dayrnisland_key
2025-03-0112025-02-28
2025-03-0222025-02-28
2025-03-0332025-02-28
2025-03-0542025-03-01
2025-03-0652025-03-01
2025-03-1062025-03-04

(6 rows)

WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT viewed_at::date AS day FROM page_views WHERE customer_id = 1
),
keyed AS (
  SELECT day, day - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)::int AS island_key FROM days
)
SELECT min(day) AS streak_start, max(day) AS streak_end, count(*) AS days
FROM keyed
GROUP BY island_key
ORDER BY streak_start;
streak_startstreak_enddays
2025-03-012025-03-033
2025-03-052025-03-062
2025-03-102025-03-101

(3 rows)

  • De-duplicate first (DISTINCT days): two views on the same day must count as one day, or the row numbers drift.
  • For integers, n − row_number(); for dates, date − row_number()::int (date − integer is a date).
  • Per customer: add PARTITION BY customer_id to the row_number and to the GROUP BY.

Technique 2: flag and running sum

More flexible: mark each row that starts a new island (compare with the previous row using lag), then a running sum of those flags numbers the islands. This works for any rule, such as "a gap of more than 1 day", "status changed", or "more than 30 minutes since the last click" (next session).

WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT viewed_at::date AS day FROM page_views WHERE customer_id = 1
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT day,
         CASE WHEN day - lag(day) OVER (ORDER BY day) = 1 THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS starts_island
  FROM days
)
SELECT day, starts_island,
       sum(starts_island) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS island_no
FROM flagged
ORDER BY day;
daystarts_islandisland_no
2025-03-0111
2025-03-0201
2025-03-0301
2025-03-0512
2025-03-0602
2025-03-1013

(6 rows)

Gaps

Gaps are the space between islands: for each row, lead(value) is the next value; if it is more than 1 step away, the values in between are missing. Or build the full range with generate_series and EXCEPT the values you have.

Always ask what "consecutive" means before writing the query: calendar days or business days? Whose time zone decides the date? Does one click at 00:10 count for that day? Customer 5's session across midnight (S32) is exactly this question.

  9. Streaks of consecutive months in 2025 with delivered revenue above 40,000: streak_start, streak_end, months, ordered by streak_start.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT s.month::date AS month, COALESCE(sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-12-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS s(month)
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.status = 'delivered'
                    AND o.order_date >= s.month AND o.order_date < s.month + INTERVAL '1 month'
  LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY s.month
),
good AS (
  SELECT month, extract(month FROM month)::int - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY month)::int AS island_key
  FROM monthly
  WHERE revenue > 40000
)
SELECT min(month) AS streak_start, max(month) AS streak_end, count(*) AS months
FROM good
GROUP BY island_key
ORDER BY streak_start;

Phase 3 · Session 32

Sessionization and running totals that reset

Group click events into sessions with a time-gap rule, and build running totals and streak counters that restart on an event.

Topics

What a session is

Web analytics tools group a visitor's clicks into sessions: a new session starts when the gap since their previous click is longer than some limit (30 minutes is the usual default). It is the flag-and-running-sum technique from Session 31, with a time gap instead of a day gap.

1. lag(viewed_at) per customer          → time since the previous click
2. flag = 1 when there is no previous click or the gap > 30 minutes
3. session_no = running sum of the flag per customer
4. GROUP BY customer, session_no        → one row per session
WITH g AS (
  SELECT customer_id, view_id, viewed_at, page,
         viewed_at - lag(viewed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY viewed_at, view_id) AS gap
  FROM page_views
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN gap IS NULL OR gap > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
  FROM g
)
SELECT customer_id, viewed_at, page, gap, new_session,
       sum(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY viewed_at, view_id) AS session_no
FROM flagged
WHERE customer_id = 1
ORDER BY viewed_at;
customer_idviewed_atpagegapnew_sessionsession_no

(18 rows, first 12 shown)

  • The boundary matters: customer 5 clicked at 12:00 and exactly 12:30. With gap > 30 minutes that is one session; with >= it would be two. Write down which rule you use.
  • Sessions are per person: always PARTITION BY the user.
  • A session can cross midnight (customer 5, 23:50 → 00:10). Grouping clicks by day would split it; grouping by gap does not.

Running totals that reset on an event

The same trick builds any "reset when X happens" calculation: count the X events so far (a running sum of a flag) and use that count as a group id. Then do the running total within each group. For example, payments where every refund starts a new running balance:

WITH p AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, p.payment_id, p.paid_at, p.amount,
         CASE WHEN p.amount < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_refund
  FROM payments p JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
  WHERE o.customer_id = 3
),
grp AS (
  SELECT *, COALESCE(sum(is_refund) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id
                                          ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING), 0) AS reset_group
  FROM p
)
SELECT payment_id, paid_at, amount, reset_group,
       sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, reset_group ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id) AS running_since_reset
FROM grp
ORDER BY paid_at;
payment_idpaid_atamountreset_grouprunning_since_reset
42025-02-03 12:00:0085000.00085000.00
52025-02-05 16:30:00-85000.0000.00
172025-05-20 12:12:008700.0018700.00

(3 rows)

The frame … AND 1 PRECEDING counts refunds before the current row, so the refund itself still belongs to the old group and the next payment starts the new one. Move it to CURRENT ROW and the refund would open the new group instead. Decide which you mean.

Streak counters

"How many delivered orders in a row, up to this one" is a running count that resets whenever an order is not delivered: group id = number of non-delivered orders so far; within the group, count delivered rows.

When a running value must depend on its own previous value in a non-additive way (cap at 100, never below zero, apply a rate to the current balance), windows cannot express it. That needs a recursive CTE stepping row by row, or code outside SQL.

FROM g
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

  FROM page_views
),

              OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY viewed_at, view_id) AS session_no
  FROM g

  9. Payments of customers 2 and 3 in time order with a running total that restarts after every refund (the refund stays in the old group): customer_id, payment_id, amount, reset_group, running_since_reset, ordered by customer_id, paid_at.

    Expected: 8 rows

    Answer
    WITH p AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, p.payment_id, p.paid_at, p.amount,
         CASE WHEN p.amount < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_refund
  FROM payments p JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
  WHERE o.customer_id IN (2, 3)
),
grp AS (
  SELECT *, COALESCE(sum(is_refund) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id
                                          ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING), 0) AS reset_group
  FROM p
)
SELECT customer_id, payment_id, amount, reset_group,
       sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, reset_group ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id) AS running_since_reset
FROM grp
ORDER BY customer_id, paid_at;

  10. Coffee Maker sales in order-date order with a running count of units that restarts every time the unit price changes: order_id, order_date, unit_price, price_run, units_at_this_price, ordered by order_date.

    Expected: 5 rows

    Answer
    WITH s AS (
  SELECT oi.order_id, o.order_date, oi.unit_price, oi.quantity,
         CASE WHEN oi.unit_price IS DISTINCT FROM lag(oi.unit_price) OVER (ORDER BY o.order_date, oi.order_id)
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS changed
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  WHERE p.name = 'Coffee Maker'
),
r AS (
  SELECT *, sum(changed) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS price_run FROM s
)
SELECT order_id, order_date, unit_price, price_run,
       sum(quantity) OVER (PARTITION BY price_run ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS units_at_this_price
FROM r
ORDER BY order_date;

  FROM page_views
),
s AS (
  SELECT *, sum(CASE WHEN gap IS NULL OR gap > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
              OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY viewed_at, view_id) AS session_no
  FROM g
),
per_session AS (
  SELECT customer_id, session_no,
         bool_or(page = 'cart') AS has_cart, bool_or(page = 'checkout') AS has_checkout
  FROM s GROUP BY customer_id, session_no

SELECT count(*) AS sessions,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE has_cart) AS with_cart,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE has_cart AND has_checkout) AS with_cart_and_checkout

ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;

Phase 3 · Session 33

Subtotals and pivots: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE and FILTER

Produce detail rows, subtotals and grand totals in one query, label them correctly, and turn rows into columns with FILTER.

Topics

Several GROUP BYs in one query

A report often needs totals at several levels: per zone and status, per zone, and overall. Without help that is three queries glued with UNION ALL. GROUPING SETS lists the groupings you want, and Postgres computes all of them in one pass:

SELECT COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown') AS zone, o.status, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN shipping_zones z ON z.city = o.shipping_city
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown'), o.status), (COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown')), ())
ORDER BY zone NULLS LAST, status NULLS LAST
LIMIT 8;
zonestatusorders
Eastdelivered1
Eastpending1
East∅2
Northcancelled2
Northdelivered2
Northpending1
Northshipped1
North∅6

(8 rows)

In a row produced by a coarser grouping, the columns that were not grouped come back as NULL: the zone subtotal row has status NULL, the grand total has both NULL.

ROLLUP and CUBE

ROLLUP (a, b, c)  =  GROUPING SETS ((a, b, c), (a, b), (a), ())      hierarchical subtotals
CUBE   (a, b)     =  GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), (b), ())            every combination
  • ROLLUP for hierarchies: year → month, zone → city, category → product.
  • CUBE for cross-tabs where every dimension gets its own subtotal. The number of groupings doubles with each column, so keep CUBE to 2–3 columns.

Telling a subtotal from a real NULL

Problem: an order with a NULL shipping city and a subtotal row both show NULL. GROUPING(col) returns 1 when the column was rolled up in that row (so the NULL means "all") and 0 when it was really grouped. Use it to label rows:

SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(status) = 1 THEN 'ALL STATUSES' ELSE status END AS status,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP (status)
ORDER BY GROUPING(status), status;
statusorders
cancelled4
delivered21
pending7
shipped4
ALL STATUSES36

(5 rows)

FILTER: conditional aggregates and pivots

agg(…) FILTER (WHERE condition) aggregates only the rows that pass the condition. It is the clean way to compute several differently-filtered numbers side by side, and to pivot rows into columns (one column per status, per month, per category). It replaces the older sum(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) idiom.

SELECT COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown') AS zone,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'delivered') AS delivered,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'pending')   AS pending,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
       count(*) AS total
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN shipping_zones z ON z.city = o.shipping_city
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY total DESC;
zonedeliveredshippedpendingcancelledtotal
West822012
South802111
North21126
Unknown21115
East10102

(5 rows)

A pivot with FILTER needs the column list written out. For a truly dynamic list of columns, Postgres has crosstab() in the tablefunc extension, or you generate the SQL in application code. For reports, a fixed list is usually what you want anyway.

Write your answers in psql/s33.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  12. Employees counted by department ('None' if NULL) and salary band ('under 100k' / '100k+'), with every subtotal (CUBE): department, band, employees, ordered by department NULLS LAST, band NULLS LAST.

    Expected: 16 rows

    Answer
    SELECT COALESCE(d.name, 'None') AS department,
       CASE WHEN e.salary < 100000 THEN 'under 100k' ELSE '100k+' END AS band,
       count(*) AS employees
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
GROUP BY CUBE (COALESCE(d.name, 'None'), CASE WHEN e.salary < 100000 THEN 'under 100k' ELSE '100k+' END)
ORDER BY department NULLS LAST, band NULLS LAST;
    departmentbandemployees
    Engineering100k+3
    Engineeringunder 100k2
    Engineering∅5
    Financeunder 100k1
    Finance∅1
    Marketing100k+1
    Marketing∅1
    None100k+1
    Noneunder 100k1
    None∅2
    Sales100k+1
    Salesunder 100k2

    (16 rows, first 12 shown)

    COALESCE turns real NULL departments into 'None', so the remaining NULLs are always subtotal rows. That is the simplest alternative to GROUPING().

  13. One query for a dashboard: delivered revenue in total, per shipping zone ('Unknown' included) and per category ('Uncategorised' included). Columns: level ('total', 'zone' or 'category'), name, revenue, ordered by level, revenue descending.

    Expected: 12 rows

    Answer
    SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown')) = 0 THEN 'zone'
            WHEN GROUPING(COALESCE(k.name, 'Uncategorised')) = 0 THEN 'category'
            ELSE 'total' END AS level,
       COALESCE(COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown'), COALESCE(k.name, 'Uncategorised'), 'All') AS name,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
LEFT JOIN categories k ON k.category_id = p.category_id
LEFT JOIN shipping_zones z ON z.city = o.shipping_city
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown')), (COALESCE(k.name, 'Uncategorised')), ())
ORDER BY level, revenue DESC;

    categoryComputers441000.00
    categoryAudio125200.00
    categoryKitchen81300.00
    categoryAccessories52000.00
    categoryHome15400.00
    categoryUncategorised8000.00
    totalAll722900.00
    zoneWest337400.00
    zoneSouth180000.00
    zoneNorth135200.00
    zoneUnknown49800.00
    zoneEast20500.00

    (12 rows)

    One scan of the data feeds three dashboard tiles. The zone rows and the category rows each add up to the total.

  14. In one row, count customers by whether they have orders and whether they have reviews: both, orders_only, reviews_only, neither.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    WITH f AS (
  SELECT c.customer_id,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)  AS has_orders,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS has_reviews
  FROM customers c
)
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE has_orders AND has_reviews)         AS both,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE has_orders AND NOT has_reviews)     AS orders_only,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT has_orders AND has_reviews)     AS reviews_only,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT has_orders AND NOT has_reviews) AS neither
FROM f;
    bothorders_onlyreviews_onlyneither
    10622

    (1 row)

    A 2×2 table in one row; the four numbers add up to 20.

  15. Challenge: A delivered-revenue report by shipping zone and city with subtotals: one row per (zone, city), a 'Zone total' row after each zone, and a 'Grand total' row at the end. Columns: zone, city, orders, revenue. Unknown zones show 'Unknown' and a missing city 'No city'. Label subtotal rows in the city column using GROUPING(), and sort so each zone's cities come first (by revenue descending), then its total, with the grand total last.

    Expected: 15 rows

    Answer
    WITH t AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, COALESCE(z.zone, 'Unknown') AS zone, COALESCE(o.shipping_city, 'No city') AS city,
         sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  LEFT JOIN shipping_zones z ON z.city = o.shipping_city
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY o.order_id, z.zone, o.shipping_city
)
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(zone) = 1 THEN 'Grand total' ELSE zone END AS zone,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(zone) = 1 THEN ''
            WHEN GROUPING(city) = 1 THEN 'Zone total'
            ELSE city END AS city,
       count(*)   AS orders,
       sum(total) AS revenue
FROM t
GROUP BY ROLLUP (zone, city)
ORDER BY GROUPING(zone), zone, GROUPING(city), sum(total) DESC;
    zonecityordersrevenue
    EastKolkata120500.00
    EastZone total120500.00
    NorthDelhi2135200.00
    NorthZone total2135200.00
    SouthBengaluru5138100.00
    SouthHyderabad230900.00
    SouthChennai111000.00
    SouthZone total8180000.00
    UnknownDubai141000.00
    UnknownNo city18800.00
    UnknownZone total249800.00
    WestMumbai5300000.00

    (15 rows, first 12 shown)

    Pre-aggregating to one row per order keeps the counts honest (orders, not lines). Sorting on GROUPING() places each subtotal directly under its own detail rows, which is what makes a report readable. London does not appear: its only non-cancelled order is still in transit, not delivered.

Phase 3 · Session 34

Medians, percentiles and collecting values: ordered-set and collection aggregates

Compute medians and percentiles, find the most common value, collect values into text, arrays and JSON, and build a cohort retention table.

Topics

Why the average is not enough

The average salary is pulled up by the CEO. The median (the middle value) describes a typical employee better. SQL computes it with an ordered-set aggregate: an aggregate that needs the values sorted, written with WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …).

SELECT round(avg(salary))                                      AS average,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)     AS median_cont,
       percentile_disc(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)     AS median_disc
FROM employees;
averagemedian_contmedian_disc
12350010250095000.00

(1 row)

  • percentile_cont(p) interpolates: with an even number of values the median is halfway between the two middle ones.
  • percentile_disc(p) returns an actual value from the data (the first one at or above the percentile).
  • Pass an array to get several at once: percentile_cont(ARRAY[0.25, 0.5, 0.75]) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x).
  • mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x) returns the most common value.
  • They work with GROUP BY like any aggregate: median per department, per month, …

Collecting values

string_agg(text, ', ' ORDER BY …)   one text value                  'Mouse, Keyboard'
array_agg(x ORDER BY …)               a Postgres array                {3,4,5}
array_agg(DISTINCT x)                 unique values only
jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(…))      a JSON array of objects         [{"id": 1, …}]
bool_and(cond) / bool_or(cond)        all true? / any true?
SELECT o.order_id,
       string_agg(p.name, ', ' ORDER BY p.name) AS products,
       array_agg(oi.product_id ORDER BY oi.product_id) AS product_ids
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_id IN (9, 25)
GROUP BY o.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
order_idproductsproduct_ids
9Laptop Air 13, USB-C Hub, Wireless Mouse{2,3,5}
25Laptop Pro 14, Noise-Cancel Headphones, Wireless Mouse{1,3,6}

(2 rows)

The ORDER BY inside the aggregate decides the order of the collected values; without it the order is whatever the rows happened to arrive in. jsonb_agg is how an API endpoint gets a whole nested response from one query (Phase 4 goes deep into JSON).

SELECT c.customer_id,
       jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('order_id', o.order_id, 'date', o.order_date, 'status', o.status)
                 ORDER BY o.order_date) AS orders
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 4
GROUP BY c.customer_id;
customer_idorders
4[{"date": "2025-02-11", "status": "delivered", "order_id": 5}, {"date": "2025-08-14", "status": "shipped", "order_id": 23}]

(1 row)

Hypothetical-set aggregates

"Where would a new value land?" rank(100000) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary DESC) returns the rank a salary of 100,000 would have among existing salaries, without inserting anything. Also available: dense_rank, percent_rank and cume_dist in the same form.

Cohort retention

A cohort table groups customers by when they started (first order month) and shows what share came back later. It combines almost everything in this phase: first-order month per customer (min or row_number), months since that start for every order (date arithmetic), then counting distinct customers per (cohort, month offset) with FILTER for a pivot.

percentile_cont returns double precision. Cast to numeric and round for display: round(percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)::numeric, 2).

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s34.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id

  15. Challenge: Cohort retention. Group customers by the month of their first order (any status). For every cohort: cohort_month, customers, and how many of them placed another order 1, 2 and 3 or more months after their first month (m1, m2, m3_plus; a customer counts in a column if they ordered in that month offset, so one customer can count in several). Order by cohort_month.

    Expected: 7 rows

    Answer
    WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, date_trunc('month', min(order_date))::date AS cohort_month
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
),
offsets AS (
  SELECT f.customer_id, f.cohort_month,
         (extract(year FROM o.order_date) - extract(year FROM f.cohort_month)) * 12
         + extract(month FROM o.order_date) - extract(month FROM f.cohort_month) AS months_since
  FROM firsts f JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
)
SELECT cohort_month,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id)                                     AS customers,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) FILTER (WHERE months_since = 1)      AS m1,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) FILTER (WHERE months_since = 2)      AS m2,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) FILTER (WHERE months_since >= 3)     AS m3_plus
FROM offsets
GROUP BY cohort_month
ORDER BY cohort_month;
    cohort_monthcustomersm1m2m3_plus
    2025-01-012012
    2025-02-014004
    2025-03-012002
    2025-04-012002
    2025-05-012002
    2025-06-012001
    2025-07-012001

    (7 rows)

    Most cohorts come back only after 3+ months: this shop has slow repeat purchases. In a real product you would show percentages and a full matrix of offsets, which is the same query with more FILTER columns (or a spine of offsets and a pivot).

Phase 3 · Session 35

Review: recursion, islands, sessions, subtotals and percentiles

Pull Sessions 29–34 back out of memory, mixed together, without notes.

Topics

How to run this review

  • First 20 minutes: redo every question in mistakes.md from Sessions 29–34, cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below, mixed on purpose.
  • Then the challenge, which combines recursion with ordered-set aggregates.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 29–34

Problem                                  Tool
---------------------------------------  ------------------------------------------------------------
Walk a hierarchy of unknown depth        WITH RECURSIVE: anchor UNION ALL join-to-previous-round
Totals over a subtree                    recursive (ancestor, descendant) pairs, then GROUP BY ancestor
Graphs with loops                        path array + NOT x = ANY(path), or CYCLE … SET … USING …
Runs of consecutive values               value − row_number()  (or flag + running sum)
Sessions from events                     lag gap > limit → flag → running sum = session number
Running total that resets on an event    group id = running count of events, then sum per group
Subtotals and grand totals               GROUP BY ROLLUP / CUBE / GROUPING SETS, label with GROUPING()
Rows to columns                          agg(…) FILTER (WHERE …) per column
Median / percentiles / most common       percentile_cont / percentile_disc / mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …)
Collect values                           string_agg / array_agg / jsonb_agg (… ORDER BY …)

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s35.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Number of employees at each level of the org chart (CEO = level 0): level, employees, ordered by level.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT employee_id, 0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, o.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id
)
SELECT depth AS level, count(*) AS employees FROM org GROUP BY depth ORDER BY depth;
    levelemployees
    01
    14
    23
    34

    (4 rows)

    1, 4, 3, 4.

  2. The median item total of orders in each status (orders with items): status, orders, median, ordered by status.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    WITH t AS (SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id)

  15. Challenge: For every employee who manages someone: team_size (everyone below them at any depth), team_median_salary (median of that team, excluding the manager) and team_max_salary. Columns: full_name, team_size, team_median_salary, team_max_salary, ordered by team_size descending, full_name.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    WITH RECURSIVE pairs AS (
  SELECT manager_id AS ancestor, employee_id AS descendant FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.ancestor, e.employee_id FROM pairs p JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = p.descendant
)
SELECT m.full_name,
       count(*)                                              AS team_size,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY d.salary) AS team_median_salary,
       max(d.salary)                                         AS team_max_salary
FROM pairs p
JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = p.ancestor
JOIN employees d ON d.employee_id = p.descendant
GROUP BY m.employee_id, m.full_name
ORDER BY team_size DESC, m.full_name;
    full_nameteam_sizeteam_median_salaryteam_max_salary
    Asha Rao1195000220000.00
    Vikram Mehta595000150000.00
    Neha Kulkarni495000120000.00
    Sneha Iyer26100062000.00

    (4 rows)

    Recursion produces the membership; ordered-set aggregates summarise it. Asha, Vikram and Neha all have a team median of 95,000, yet their team maximums are 220,000, 150,000 and 120,000: the median ignores the top earners, the max is set by them.

Phase 3 · Session 36

Exit test + Apply: CTEs and window functions

Prove you own CTEs, window functions, recursion and advanced aggregation: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct.

Topics

Exit test rules

  • Cold: no notes, no earlier sessions, no answers until you are done.
  • Time box: 90 minutes for all 14 questions (these are longer than earlier tests).
  • Score honestly: a question counts only if the output matches the expected rows exactly.
  • Pass = 11 of 14 or more. Pass → Phase 4 (JSONB and data modelling). Fail → redo every missed question, re-read its session, and retake the test later.

What the test checks

Q1, Q4        ranking and top-N per group             (S23, S24)
Q2, Q9        running totals and frames               (S25)
Q3, Q12       lag / lead                              (S26)
Q5            CTE pipeline                            (S19)
Q6, Q14       recursive CTEs: tree and graph          (S29, S30)
Q7            ordered-set aggregates                  (S34)
Q8            ROLLUP subtotals                        (S33)
Q10           gaps and islands                        (S31)
Q11           sessionization                          (S32)
Q13           cumulative share (Pareto)               (S25)

Apply project: the business dashboard

Save the challenge below as psql/projects/p3-dashboard.sql, together with: the customer timeline (S28 challenge), the cohort table (S34 challenge), the session table (S32 challenge) and the org report (S29 challenge). Each query gets a comment saying what one row means. That file is a portfolio piece: it shows you can answer real analytics questions in plain SQL.

Write your answers in psql/s36.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  12. Delivered revenue for every month of 2025 with the change from the previous month, using lag: month, revenue, change, ordered by month.

    Expected: 12 rows

    Answer
    WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT s.month::date AS month, COALESCE(sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-12-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS s(month)
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.status = 'delivered'
                    AND o.order_date >= s.month AND o.order_date < s.month + INTERVAL '1 month'
  LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY s.month
)
SELECT month, revenue, revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly ORDER BY month;

  13. Pareto: the products that make up the first 80% of delivered revenue, including the product that crosses 80%: name, revenue, cumulative_pct (1 decimal), ordered by revenue descending.

    Expected: 5 rows

    Answer
    WITH rev AS (
  SELECT oi.product_id, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
c AS (
  SELECT product_id, revenue,
         100 * sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) / sum(revenue) OVER () AS cum_pct,
         100 * sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) / sum(revenue) OVER () AS prev_cum_pct
  FROM rev
)
SELECT p.name, c.revenue, round(c.cum_pct, 1) AS cumulative_pct
FROM c JOIN products p ON p.product_id = c.product_id
WHERE COALESCE(c.prev_cum_pct, 0) < 80
ORDER BY c.revenue DESC;
    namerevenuecumulative_pct

  14. The shortest route from Mumbai to Kolkata: route (cities joined by ' → '), total_km.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    WITH RECURSIVE paths AS (
  SELECT to_city, km AS total_km, ARRAY[from_city, to_city] AS path FROM routes WHERE from_city = 'Mumbai'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT r.to_city, p.total_km + r.km, p.path || r.to_city
  FROM paths p JOIN routes r ON r.from_city = p.to_city
  WHERE NOT r.to_city = ANY (p.path)
)
SELECT array_to_string(path, ' → ') AS route, total_km
FROM paths WHERE to_city = 'Kolkata'
ORDER BY total_km LIMIT 1;

    S30.

  15. Challenge: Monthly KPI board for 2025, all 12 months: month, revenue (delivered), mom_pct (change vs previous month in %, 1 decimal, ∅ when the previous month is 0 or missing), ytd_revenue (running total), orders (placed that month, any status), median_order_value (orders with items placed that month, 0 decimals), top_product (best product by delivered revenue that month; ties → lower product_id; ∅ if none). Order by month.

    Expected: 12 rows

    Answer
    WITH spine AS (
  SELECT s.month::date AS month FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2025-12-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS s(month)
),
rev AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date)::date AS month, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY 1
),
ord AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date)::date AS month, count(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY 1
),
aov AS (
  SELECT month, round((percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total))::numeric) AS median_order_value
  FROM (SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date)::date AS month, o.order_id, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total
        FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY 1, 2) t
  GROUP BY month
),
top AS (
  SELECT month, product_id FROM (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date)::date AS month, oi.product_id,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', o.order_date)
                              ORDER BY sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) DESC, oi.product_id) AS rn
    FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
    GROUP BY date_trunc('month', o.order_date), oi.product_id
  ) r WHERE rn = 1
),
board AS (
  SELECT s.month, COALESCE(rev.revenue, 0) AS revenue, COALESCE(ord.orders, 0) AS orders,
         aov.median_order_value, p.name AS top_product
  FROM spine s
  LEFT JOIN rev ON rev.month = s.month
  LEFT JOIN ord ON ord.month = s.month
  LEFT JOIN aov ON aov.month = s.month
  LEFT JOIN top ON top.month = s.month
  LEFT JOIN products p ON p.product_id = top.product_id
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       round(100.0 * (revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / NULLIF(lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_pct,
       sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS ytd_revenue,
       orders, median_order_value, top_product
FROM board
ORDER BY month;

Phase 4 · Session 37

Arrays

Store, search, unpack and clean array columns, and know when a child table is the better choice.

Topics

What an array column is

An array column holds an ordered list of values of one type in a single field: TEXT[], INTEGER[] and so on. In the practice database, product_details.tags is a TEXT[]. Postgres arrays start at 1, not 0.

SELECT p.name, d.tags,
       d.tags[1]               AS first_tag,
       cardinality(d.tags)     AS n_tags,
       array_length(d.tags, 1) AS array_length
FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY p.product_id;
nametagsfirst_tagn_tagsarray_length
Laptop Pro 14{laptop,premium,work}laptop33
Laptop Air 13{laptop,portable,work}laptop33
Wireless Mouse{wireless,work,bestseller}wireless33
Mechanical Keyboard{work,gaming}work22
USB-C Hub{work,portable}work22
Noise-Cancel Headphones{wireless,premium,travel,bestseller}wireless44
Bluetooth Speaker{wireless,party}wireless22
Earbuds Lite{Wireless,budget}Wireless22
Coffee Maker{kitchen,premium}kitchen22
Chef Knife{kitchen}kitchen11
Air Fryer{kitchen,bestseller,healthy}kitchen33
Desk Lamp{}∅0∅
4K Monitor{work,premium,gaming}work33

(13 rows)

  • Writing arrays: '{laptop,work}'::text[] (text literal) or ARRAY['laptop', 'work'] (constructor). array_agg(x) builds one from rows.
  • Reading elements: tags[1] is the first element; tags[1:2] is a slice (a smaller array). An index past the end returns NULL, not an error.
  • Counting: cardinality(tags) is the number of elements, 0 for an empty array. array_length(tags, 1) returns NULL for an empty array, which is a common source of bugs (look at Desk Lamp above).

Searching inside arrays

'x' = ANY (tags)              tags contains x
tags @> ARRAY['a', 'b']       tags contains a AND b   (all of)
tags && ARRAY['a', 'b']       tags contains a OR b    (overlap, any of)
tags <@ ARRAY['a', 'b', 'c']  every element of tags is in the list
array_position(tags, 'x')     position of x, NULL if absent
'x' <> ALL (tags)             x is not in tags
SELECT p.name, d.tags
FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE d.tags @> ARRAY['wireless']
ORDER BY p.name;
nametags
Bluetooth Speaker{wireless,party}
Noise-Cancel Headphones{wireless,premium,travel,bestseller}
Wireless Mouse{wireless,work,bestseller}

(3 rows)

Earbuds Lite is wireless, but it is missing above: its tag is Wireless with a capital W. Array comparisons are exact and case-sensitive. Clean tags when you write them (lower-case, no duplicates) and enforce it with a CHECK constraint (Session 41).

'x' <> ANY (tags) does not mean "x is not in tags". It means "x differs from at least one element", which is true for almost every array. Write NOT ('x' = ANY (tags)) or 'x' <> ALL (tags).

unnest: from array to rows, and back

unnest(tags) turns every element into its own row; WITH ORDINALITY adds the element's position. array_agg (or ARRAY(SELECT …)) turns rows back into an array. Between the two you can use all of SQL on the elements: filter, lower-case, deduplicate, sort, join.

SELECT p.name, t.pos, t.tag
FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(d.tags) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(tag, pos)
WHERE p.product_id IN (6, 12)
ORDER BY p.name, t.pos;
namepostag
Noise-Cancel Headphones1wireless
Noise-Cancel Headphones2premium
Noise-Cancel Headphones3travel
Noise-Cancel Headphones4bestseller

(4 rows)

Desk Lamp (product 12) has vanished: unnesting an empty array produces no rows, and CROSS JOIN drops the product. Use LEFT JOIN LATERAL unnest(…) AS t(tag, pos) ON true to keep it with NULLs. This is the same lesson as Session 9.

SELECT array_append(ARRAY['a', 'b'], 'c')                         AS appended,
       array_remove(ARRAY['a', 'b', 'a'], 'a')                    AS removed,
       ARRAY['a'] || ARRAY['b', 'c']                              AS concatenated,
       ARRAY(SELECT DISTINCT lower(x) FROM unnest(ARRAY['B', 'a', 'b']) AS x ORDER BY 1) AS cleaned,
       string_to_array('red, green ,blue', ',')                   AS split_raw,
       array_to_string(ARRAY['red', 'green'], ' / ')              AS joined;
appendedremovedconcatenatedcleanedsplit_rawjoined
{a,b,c}{b}{a,b,c}{a,b}{red," green ",blue}red / green

(1 row)

Notice split_raw: the spaces stay inside the elements (" green "). Split, then trim each element with unnest → trim → array_agg.

Indexing arrays: GIN

A normal (B-tree) index cannot look inside an array. A GIN index stores every element separately, so it can answer @>, && and <@. It cannot help = ANY. The plans below force the index with enable_seqscan = off, because 13 rows are too few for Postgres to want an index (Phase 5 measures this on a big table).

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX product_details_tags_gin ON product_details USING gin (tags);
SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT product_id FROM product_details WHERE tags @> ARRAY['work'];
ROLLBACK;
Bitmap Heap Scan on product_details
  Recheck Cond: (tags @> '{work}'::text[])
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on product_details_tags_gin
        Index Cond: (tags @> '{work}'::text[])
BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX product_details_tags_gin ON product_details USING gin (tags);
SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT product_id FROM product_details WHERE 'work' = ANY (tags);
ROLLBACK;
Seq Scan on product_details
  Disabled: true
  Filter: ('work'::text = ANY (tags))

Same question, two spellings, and only one of them can use the index. The second plan says Disabled: true: Postgres had to use a Seq Scan even though we switched it off, because nothing else can answer = ANY. Prefer tags @> ARRAY['work'] on indexed array columns.

Array or child table?

Use an array when …                          Use a child table when …
-------------------------------------------  ----------------------------------------------
the list is small and read with its row       each item has its own data (qty, price, date)
elements need no foreign key                  elements must reference another table
you search with @> or && (GIN)                you update, count or join single items often
the list is replaced as a whole               items change independently of each other

Rule of thumb: if you ever want to "update element 3" or say "every tag must exist in the tags table", it should be a table. order_items is a table, not an array of product ids, for exactly this reason.

  15. Challenge: Tag-based recommendations for customer 1. Candidates: products that have details, are not discontinued and that customer 1 never ordered (any status). Score = number of distinct tags a candidate shares with all the products customer 1 ordered. Return the top 3: name, shared_tags (sorted), score, ordered by score descending, then product_id.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    WITH mine AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT oi.product_id
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.customer_id = 1
),
my_tags AS (
  SELECT array_agg(DISTINCT t.tag) AS tags
  FROM product_details d
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(d.tags) AS t(tag)
  WHERE d.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM mine)
),
scored AS (
  SELECT p.product_id, p.name,
         ARRAY(SELECT unnest(d.tags) INTERSECT SELECT unnest(m.tags) ORDER BY 1) AS shared_tags
  FROM products p
  JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
  CROSS JOIN my_tags m
  WHERE NOT p.discontinued
    AND p.product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM mine)
)
SELECT name, shared_tags, cardinality(shared_tags) AS score
FROM scored
ORDER BY score DESC, product_id
LIMIT 3;

    Noise-Cancel Headphones{bestseller,premium,wireless}3

Phase 4 · Session 38

JSONB querying

Read values, paths and arrays out of JSONB, tell the three kinds of "nothing" apart, and filter in a way an index can use.

Topics

json vs jsonb

json stores the text exactly as received: spaces, key order and duplicate keys. jsonb parses it into a binary form: keys are sorted and de-duplicated (the last one wins), queries are faster and it can be indexed. Use jsonb unless you must keep the original text byte for byte.

SELECT '{"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}'::json  AS as_json,
       '{"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}'::jsonb AS as_jsonb;
as_jsonas_jsonb
{"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}{"a": 3, "b": 1}

(1 row)

In the practice database, product_details.specs holds each product's specifications (different keys per category), and events.payload holds raw app events. The event type lives inside the JSON.

Getting values out

specs -> 'brand'             jsonb   "Zentro"   (still JSON: note the quotes)
specs ->> 'brand'            text    Zentro
specs -> 'ports' -> 0        jsonb   first element of a JSON array (0-based!)
specs #> '{storage,gb}'      jsonb   value at a path
specs #>> '{storage,gb}'     text    value at a path
jsonb_typeof(specs -> 'x')   'object', 'array', 'string', 'number', 'boolean' or 'null'
SELECT p.name,
       d.specs -> 'brand'             AS brand_json,
       d.specs ->> 'brand'            AS brand_text,
       (d.specs ->> 'ram_gb')::int    AS ram_gb,
       d.specs #>> '{storage,gb}'     AS storage_gb,
       d.specs -> 'ports' -> 0        AS first_port
FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE p.product_id IN (1, 2, 5)
ORDER BY p.product_id;
namebrand_jsonbrand_textram_gbstorage_gbfirst_port
Laptop Pro 14"Zentro"Zentro321024"usb-c"
Laptop Air 13"Zentro"Zentro16512"usb-c"
USB-C Hub"Portly"Portly∅∅"usb-c"

(3 rows)

->> always returns text. As text, '9' > '10' is true. Cast before comparing or summing: (specs ->> 'ram_gb')::int >= 16. And remember: JSON arrays are 0-based, Postgres arrays are 1-based.

Three kinds of "nothing"

SELECT p.name,
       d.specs ? 'warranty_years'                AS has_key,
       d.specs -> 'warranty_years'               AS json_value,
       jsonb_typeof(d.specs -> 'warranty_years') AS json_type,
       d.specs ->> 'warranty_years'              AS text_value
FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE p.product_id IN (1, 3, 12)
ORDER BY p.product_id;
namehas_keyjson_valuejson_typetext_value
Laptop Pro 14t2number2
Wireless Mousef∅∅∅
Desk Lamptnullnull∅

(3 rows)

  • Key missing (Wireless Mouse): -> and ->> both give SQL NULL; ? is false.
  • JSON null (Desk Lamp): the key exists. -> gives the JSON value null, which is not SQL NULL (so IS NULL is false!). ->> gives SQL NULL.
  • A value (Laptop Pro 14): a JSON number.
  • To tell them apart use ? (is the key there?) and jsonb_typeof (what kind of value?).

Filtering: containment and existence

specs @> '{"wireless": true}'            contains this key and value (works for nested objects too)
specs ? 'colors'                         has this top-level key
specs ?| ARRAY['dpi', 'switch']          has any of these keys
specs ?& ARRAY['brand', 'ports']         has all of these keys
SELECT p.name, d.specs -> 'storage' AS storage
FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE d.specs @> '{"storage": {"type": "ssd"}}'
ORDER BY p.name;
namestorage
Laptop Air 13{"gb": 512, "type": "ssd"}
Laptop Pro 14{"gb": 1024, "type": "ssd"}

(2 rows)

A GIN index on the column (CREATE INDEX ON product_details USING gin (specs)) speeds up @>, ?, ?| and ?&, exactly like the array index in Session 37. specs ->> 'brand' = 'Zentro' cannot use it; it needs an expression index on (specs ->> 'brand'). So write filters you want indexed as containment: specs @> '{"brand": "Zentro"}'.

Expanding: from JSON to rows

jsonb_array_elements(arr)          one jsonb row per array element
jsonb_array_elements_text(arr)     one text row per array element
jsonb_each(obj), jsonb_each_text   one (key, value) row per key
jsonb_object_keys(obj)             one row per key
jsonb_to_recordset(arr)            array of objects → typed rows; you name the columns
jsonb_array_length(arr)            number of elements
SELECT e.event_id, e.payload ->> 'order_id' AS order_id, i.*
FROM events e
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_to_recordset(e.payload -> 'items') AS i(product_id int, qty int, price numeric)
WHERE e.payload ->> 'type' = 'checkout'
ORDER BY e.event_id, i.product_id;
event_idorder_idproduct_idqtyprice
427416500
427513500
8292185000
103114101000
1232919000
12321014000
14336118000
2035321500
2035513500
23361222200

(10 rows)

After this step the JSON is gone: you have ordinary typed rows that you can join to products, sum and group.

SQL/JSON path

A jsonpath is a small query language for one document: $ is the whole document, .ports a key, [*] every element, ? (@ == "hdmi") a filter on the current item. @? asks "does the path find anything?"; jsonb_path_query returns every match as a row; jsonb_path_query_array returns them as one JSON array.

SELECT p.name,
       jsonb_path_query_array(d.specs, '$.ports[*] ? (@ == "hdmi")') AS hdmi_ports
FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE d.specs @? '$.ports[*] ? (@ == "hdmi")'
ORDER BY p.name;
namehdmi_ports
4K Monitor["hdmi", "hdmi"]
Laptop Pro 14["hdmi"]
USB-C Hub["hdmi"]

(3 rows)

jsonpath compares types strictly. $.battery_hours ? (@ > 5) silently skips Earbuds Lite, whose battery_hours is the string "6". Question 9 shows the difference.

  GROUP BY order_id

JOIN db ON db.order_id = app.order_id

             AND c.payload ->> 'type' = 'checkout'
             AND c.created_at > e.created_at

  15. Challenge: App quality report per app version. Version = device.app; use web when the device os is web, and unknown when there is no device. Per version: events, searches, carts (add_to_cart), checkouts, errors, checkout_value (sum of qty × price over all checkout items) and error_pct (errors as % of events, 1 decimal). Ordered by version.

    Expected: 6 rows

    Answer
    WITH ev AS (
  SELECT event_id,
         payload ->> 'type' AS type,
         CASE WHEN NOT payload ? 'device'                THEN 'unknown'
              WHEN payload #>> '{device,os}' = 'web'      THEN 'web'
              ELSE payload #>> '{device,app}' END AS version
  FROM events
),
value AS (
  SELECT e.event_id, sum((it.item ->> 'qty')::int * (it.item ->> 'price')::numeric) AS checkout_value
  FROM events e
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(e.payload -> 'items') AS it(item)
  GROUP BY e.event_id
)
SELECT ev.version,
       count(*)                                        AS events,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE ev.type = 'search')      AS searches,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE ev.type = 'add_to_cart') AS carts,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE ev.type = 'checkout')    AS checkouts,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE ev.type = 'app_error')   AS errors,
       COALESCE(sum(v.checkout_value), 0)              AS checkout_value,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE ev.type = 'app_error') / count(*), 1) AS error_pct
FROM ev
LEFT JOIN value v ON v.event_id = ev.event_id
GROUP BY ev.version
ORDER BY ev.version;
    versioneventssearchescartscheckoutserrorscheckout_valueerror_pct
    5.1.0411118500025.0
    5.2.041210100000.0
    5.3.072230375000.0
    5.3.131011440033.3
    unknown1100000.0
    web521111000020.0

    (6 rows)

    Both payment timeouts came from iOS versions 5.1.0 and 5.3.1 (25% and 33.3% of their events); the web error was the out-of-stock. The checkout value is summed per event first, so joining it back cannot multiply the event counts. This is what product analytics on raw JSON events looks like.

← Phase 4: JSONB, arrays + modellingAll phasesSchema

Phase 4 · Session 39

Modifying and aggregating JSONB

Change keys and nested values safely, build JSON documents from rows, and aggregate values that live inside documents.

Topics

Changing a JSONB value

specs || '{"color": "black"}'        merge: add or replace TOP-LEVEL keys
specs - 'dpi'                         remove a key
specs - ARRAY['dpi', 'battery']       remove several keys
specs #- '{battery,type}'             remove a key at a path
jsonb_set(specs, '{storage,gb}', '2048')       replace or add the value at a path
jsonb_insert(specs, '{ports,0}', '"vga"')        insert into an array (before element 0)
jsonb_strip_nulls(specs)              remove keys whose value is JSON null
SELECT specs || '{"color": "black"}'        AS merged,
       specs - 'dpi'                         AS without_dpi,
       jsonb_set(specs, '{battery,count}', '2') AS two_batteries
FROM product_details
WHERE product_id = 3;
mergedwithout_dpitwo_batteries
{"dpi": 1600, "brand": "Clicko", "color": "black", "battery": {"type": "AA", "count": 1}, "wireless": true}{"brand": "Clicko", "battery": {"type": "AA", "count": 1}, "wireless": true}{"dpi": 1600, "brand": "Clicko", "battery": {"type": "AA", "count": 2}, "wireless": true}

(1 row)

None of these change the table. They return a new document; an UPDATE … SET specs = … stores it.

|| is shallow. Merging {"storage": {"gb": 2048}} replaces the whole storage object, and "type": "ssd" is lost. Use jsonb_set with a path for nested changes.

SELECT specs -> 'storage'                                         AS before,
       (specs || '{"storage": {"gb": 2048}}') -> 'storage'          AS merged_shallow,
       jsonb_set(specs, '{storage,gb}', '2048') -> 'storage'       AS set_at_path
FROM product_details
WHERE product_id = 1;
beforemerged_shallowset_at_path
{"gb": 1024, "type": "ssd"}{"gb": 2048}{"gb": 2048, "type": "ssd"}

(1 row)

jsonb_set returns SQL NULL for the whole document when the new value is SQL NULL. An UPDATE would then wipe the column (or fail on NOT NULL). Use jsonb_set_lax(…, 'use_json_null') or 'null'::jsonb when a value may be missing.

SELECT jsonb_set(specs, '{warranty_years}', to_jsonb(NULL::int)) IS NULL       AS whole_document_lost,
       jsonb_set_lax(specs, '{warranty_years}', to_jsonb(NULL::int)) -> 'warranty_years' AS lax_keeps_document
FROM product_details
WHERE product_id = 3;
whole_document_lostlax_keeps_document
tnull

(1 row)

Updating rows

BEGIN;
UPDATE product_details
SET specs = specs || '{"color": "black"}'
WHERE product_id = 3
RETURNING product_id, specs;
ROLLBACK;
product_idspecs
3{"dpi": 1600, "brand": "Clicko", "color": "black", "battery": {"type": "AA", "count": 1}, "wireless": true}

(1 row)

Postgres writes a whole new row version (and a new copy of the document) even when one key changes. A value that changes many times a minute (a counter, a status) deserves its own column. JSONB is for data that is read often and changed rarely.

Building JSON from rows

jsonb_build_object('id', id, 'name', name)   object from key/value pairs
jsonb_build_array(a, b, c)                  array from values
to_jsonb(c)                                 a whole row as an object
jsonb_agg(x ORDER BY …)                     rows → one JSON array
jsonb_object_agg(key, value)                rows → one JSON object
jsonb_pretty(doc)                           indented text, for reading
SELECT k.name AS category,
       jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', p.product_id, 'name', p.name, 'price', p.price)
                 ORDER BY p.price) AS products
FROM categories k
JOIN products p ON p.category_id = k.category_id
WHERE k.name = 'Audio'
GROUP BY k.name;
categoryproducts
Audio[{"id": 8, "name": "Earbuds Lite", "price": 2500.00}, {"id": 7, "name": "Bluetooth Speaker", "price": 7000.00}, {"id": 6, "name": "Noise-Cancel Headphones", "price": 18000.00}]

(1 row)

This is how an API can get nested data in one round trip: the database builds exactly the JSON the client needs. Numbers stay JSON numbers, dates become strings, SQL NULL becomes JSON null.

Aggregating values inside documents

To aggregate what is inside documents, use the pattern from Session 38: expand (jsonb_array_elements, jsonb_each) → aggregate with normal SQL → rebuild JSON if needed.

SELECT c.color, count(*) AS products
FROM product_details d
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(d.specs -> 'colors') AS c(color)
GROUP BY c.color
ORDER BY products DESC, c.color;
colorproducts
black2
blue1
red1
silver1
white1

(5 rows)

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s39.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: set Desk Lamp's (product 12) warranty_years to 1 with jsonb_set. Return product_id and specs.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
UPDATE product_details
SET specs = jsonb_set(specs, '{warranty_years}', '1')
WHERE product_id = 12
RETURNING product_id, specs;
ROLLBACK;
    product_idspecs
    12{"brand": "Lumo", "colors": ["white"], "power_w": 8, "warranty_years": 1}

    (1 row)

    The third argument is a JSON value, so '1' is the JSON number 1. For a string you would write '"1"'.

  2. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: add "color": "black" to Wireless Mouse (product 3) using ||. Return product_id and specs.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
UPDATE product_details
SET specs = specs || '{"color": "black"}'
WHERE product_id = 3
RETURNING product_id, specs;
ROLLBACK;
    product_idspecs
    3{"dpi": 1600, "brand": "Clicko", "color": "black", "battery": {"type": "AA", "count": 1}, "wireless": true}

    (1 row)

    For a new top-level key, || and jsonb_set do the same job. If the key already existed, || would replace its value.

  3. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: remove the dpi and battery keys from Wireless Mouse in one expression. Return specs.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
UPDATE product_details
SET specs = specs - ARRAY['dpi', 'battery']
WHERE product_id = 3
RETURNING specs;
ROLLBACK;
    specs
    {"brand": "Clicko", "wireless": true}

    (1 row)

    The minus operator removes one key (text) or several (text[]). Removing a key that does not exist is not an error.

UPDATE product_details
SET specs = jsonb_insert(jsonb_set(specs, '{storage,gb}', '1024'),
                         '{ports,-1}', '"hdmi"', true)
WHERE product_id = 2
RETURNING specs -> 'storage' AS storage, specs -> 'ports' AS ports;

                   FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id

WHERE o.order_id = 9;

  15. Challenge: Nightly catalog export as one JSON document: {"generated_for": "2026-02-15", "categories": [{"category": …, "products": [{"id", "name", "price", "brand", "tags"}, …]}, …]}. Only products that are not discontinued and have details; categories sorted by name, products by price. Return the document plus two checks computed from it: categories (number of categories) and products (number of products, using a JSON path).

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    WITH prod AS (
  SELECT k.name AS category, p.price, p.product_id,
         jsonb_build_object('id', p.product_id, 'name', p.name, 'price', p.price,
                            'brand', d.specs ->> 'brand', 'tags', to_jsonb(d.tags)) AS obj
  FROM products p
  JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
  JOIN categories k ON k.category_id = p.category_id
  WHERE NOT p.discontinued
),
cat AS (

  FROM prod
  GROUP BY category
),
doc AS (
  SELECT jsonb_build_object(
           'generated_for', DATE '2026-02-15',
           'categories', jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('category', category, 'products', products)
                                   ORDER BY category)) AS doc
  FROM cat
)
SELECT doc,
       jsonb_array_length(doc -> 'categories') AS categories,
       jsonb_array_length(jsonb_path_query_array(doc, '$.categories[*].products[*]')) AS products
FROM doc;

Phase 4 · Session 40

Upsert and MERGE

Load data that may already exist with INSERT … ON CONFLICT and MERGE: atomic, rerunnable, and safe with dirty source data.

Topics

The problem: insert, or update if it is already there

The obvious way is two statements: SELECT to check, then INSERT or UPDATE. Under load this is a race: two sessions both see "not there" and both insert. You then get either a duplicate-key error or, without a unique constraint, two rows. INSERT … ON CONFLICT does the check and the write as one atomic step.

This session uses inventory (stock per warehouse, primary key (warehouse, product_id)) and stock_feed (incoming counts with every kind of problem: a duplicate key, an unknown product, a stale row, a negative quantity and a row that changes nothing).

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO inventory (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at)
VALUES ('Pune', 1, 4, '2026-02-12 09:00+05:30')
ON CONFLICT (warehouse, product_id)
DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
RETURNING *;
ROLLBACK;
warehouseproduct_idqtyupdated_at
Pune142026-02-12 09:00:00+05:30

(1 row)

  • The conflict target (warehouse, product_id) must match a primary key or unique index exactly. (ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT name also works.)
  • EXCLUDED is the row you tried to insert. The table name (inventory.qty) is the row already there.
  • DO NOTHING skips the row silently. Skipped rows are not returned by RETURNING.
  • DO UPDATE … WHERE updates only when a condition holds, for example "the incoming row is newer". Otherwise the existing row is left alone, and it is not returned either.
BEGIN;
-- feed row 8 is older than the stock row: the WHERE stops the update
INSERT INTO inventory (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at)
VALUES ('Delhi', 12, 9, '2026-02-09 08:00+05:30')
ON CONFLICT (warehouse, product_id)
DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > inventory.updated_at
RETURNING *;
ROLLBACK;
warehouseproduct_idqtyupdated_at

(0 rows)

Duplicates in the source

stock_feed contains (Pune, 3) twice. Loading the whole feed in one INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE fails:

ERROR:  ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
HINT:  Ensure that no rows proposed for insertion within the same command have duplicate constrained values.

One statement cannot apply two different values to the same row, because which one would win? Deduplicate first and keep the latest row per key, with DISTINCT ON (Session 10):

SELECT DISTINCT ON (warehouse, product_id) feed_id, warehouse, product_id, qty, received_at
FROM stock_feed
ORDER BY warehouse, product_id, received_at DESC;
feed_idwarehouseproduct_idqtyreceived_at
10Delhi122026-02-14 12:00:00+05:30
4Delhi602026-02-12 10:00:00+05:30
12Delhi7-22026-02-14 12:00:00+05:30
8Delhi1292026-02-09 08:00:00+05:30
5Delhi1532026-02-12 10:00:00+05:30
1Pune142026-02-12 09:00:00+05:30
6Pune3362026-02-13 09:00:00+05:30
11Pune5222026-02-14 12:00:00+05:30
3Pune762026-02-12 09:00:00+05:30
9Pune1322026-02-14 12:00:00+05:30
7Pune9952026-02-13 09:00:00+05:30

(11 rows)

MERGE

MERGE compares a source with a target and runs a different action for each case. Postgres 17 adds WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE (target rows the source does not mention) and RETURNING with merge_action().

MERGE INTO inventory t
USING source s ON t.warehouse = s.warehouse AND t.product_id = s.product_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.qty = 0      THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED                    THEN UPDATE SET qty = s.qty, updated_at = s.received_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED                THEN INSERT (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at)
                                     VALUES (s.warehouse, s.product_id, s.qty, s.received_at)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND … THEN …        -- Postgres 17
RETURNING merge_action(), t.*;                 -- Postgres 17
BEGIN;
MERGE INTO inventory t
USING (VALUES ('Delhi', 6, 0), ('Delhi', 7, 8), ('Delhi', 15, 3)) AS s(warehouse, product_id, qty)
  ON t.warehouse = s.warehouse AND t.product_id = s.product_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.qty = 0 THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET qty = s.qty, updated_at = TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-02-15 10:00+05:30'
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (s.warehouse, s.product_id, s.qty, TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-02-15 10:00+05:30')
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.warehouse, t.product_id, t.qty;
ROLLBACK;
actionwarehouseproduct_idqty
DELETEDelhi65
UPDATEDelhi78
INSERTDelhi153

(3 rows)

  • WHEN clauses are tried top to bottom; the first one whose condition is true wins. Put the narrow cases (AND s.qty = 0) above the general ones.
  • A source row that matches two target rows is an error, and so is a target row matched by two source rows. Deduplicate the source first, exactly as with ON CONFLICT.
  • For a DELETE, RETURNING shows the row as it was before it was deleted.

MERGE is not ON CONFLICT. If another session inserts the same key between MERGE's check and its insert, MERGE fails with a unique violation. ON CONFLICT handles that race. Use ON CONFLICT for "insert or update this row" from an application; use MERGE for batch syncs that also delete, and retry on error (Phase 6).

Idempotent loads

A load is idempotent when running it twice gives the same result as running it once. An upsert load can simply be rerun after a crash halfway through. A plain INSERT load cannot: the rerun duplicates rows or fails.

Upserts need a unique key on what identifies a row in the outside world: an email, a (warehouse, product) pair, an external order number. Give every table you load into such a key, even if it also has a surrogate id.
