  9. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: load the cleaned feed (Q8) with one INSERT … ON CONFLICT. Update only when the feed row is newer than the stock row and the qty actually changes. Return warehouse, product_id, qty and inserted (true for new rows), ordered by warehouse, product_id.

    Expected: 7 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
WITH up AS (
  INSERT INTO inventory (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at)
  SELECT warehouse, product_id, qty, received_at
  FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (warehouse, product_id) *
    FROM stock_feed
    ORDER BY warehouse, product_id, received_at DESC, feed_id DESC
  ) latest
  WHERE qty >= 0
    AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.product_id = latest.product_id)
  ON CONFLICT (warehouse, product_id)
  DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
  WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > inventory.updated_at
    AND EXCLUDED.qty <> inventory.qty
  RETURNING warehouse, product_id, qty, (xmax = 0) AS inserted
)
SELECT * FROM up ORDER BY warehouse, product_id;
ROLLBACK;
    warehouseproduct_idqtyinserted
    Delhi60f
    Delhi153t
    Pune14f
    Pune336f
    Pune522f
    Pune76t
    Pune132t

    (7 rows)

    7 rows: 3 inserted, 4 updated. RETURNING has no ORDER BY, so wrap the statement in WITH and sort outside. The stale row and the no-op row are not returned because the WHERE skipped them. xmax = 0 (no previous version) is a widely used trick to tell inserts from updates; it relies on internals (Phase 8). MERGE's merge_action() is the official way. Note that Delhi's Noise-Cancel Headphones now has qty 0: ON CONFLICT cannot delete.

  10. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: the same sync with MERGE, but delete the stock row when the new qty is 0. Same rules: only newer and changed rows are updated. Return action (merge_action()), warehouse, product_id, qty.

    Expected: 7 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
MERGE INTO inventory t
USING (
  SELECT feed_id, warehouse, product_id, qty, received_at
  FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (warehouse, product_id) *
    FROM stock_feed
    ORDER BY warehouse, product_id, received_at DESC, feed_id DESC
  ) latest
  WHERE qty >= 0
    AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.product_id = latest.product_id)
) s
ON t.warehouse = s.warehouse AND t.product_id = s.product_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.received_at > t.updated_at AND s.qty = 0 THEN
  DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.received_at > t.updated_at AND s.qty <> t.qty THEN
  UPDATE SET qty = s.qty, updated_at = s.received_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at)
  VALUES (s.warehouse, s.product_id, s.qty, s.received_at)
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.warehouse, t.product_id, t.qty;
ROLLBACK;
    actionwarehouseproduct_idqty
    UPDATEPune14
    UPDATEPune336
    UPDATEPune522
    DELETEDelhi65
    INSERTPune76
    INSERTPune132
    INSERTDelhi153

    (7 rows)

    1 delete, 3 updates, 3 inserts. Matched rows that fit no WHEN clause (stale, unchanged) are simply left alone. The deleted row shows its old qty (5).

  11. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: a full stocktake of Delhi says: product 1 → 2, product 3 → 28, product 7 → 10, product 12 → 7, product 15 → 3. Make Delhi's inventory match exactly: update changed quantities, insert new products, delete Delhi rows the count does not mention. Leave Pune alone, and do not touch rows that did not change. Use 2026-02-15 18:00 India time as updated_at. Return action, product_id, qty.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
MERGE INTO inventory t
USING (VALUES ('Delhi', 1, 2), ('Delhi', 3, 28), ('Delhi', 7, 10), ('Delhi', 12, 7), ('Delhi', 15, 3))
      AS s(warehouse, product_id, qty)
ON t.warehouse = s.warehouse AND t.product_id = s.product_id
WHEN MATCHED AND t.qty <> s.qty THEN
  UPDATE SET qty = s.qty, updated_at = TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-02-15 18:00+05:30'
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT VALUES (s.warehouse, s.product_id, s.qty, TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-02-15 18:00+05:30')
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.warehouse = 'Delhi' THEN
  DELETE
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.product_id, t.qty;
ROLLBACK;
    actionproduct_idqty
    UPDATE328
    DELETE65
    DELETE113
    INSERT153

    (4 rows)

    One update (product 3), one insert (15), two deletes (6 and 11). The source only describes Delhi, so to MERGE every Pune row is "not matched by source". Forget the warehouse condition and the stocktake wipes out Pune. Always scope NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE to what the source covers.

  12. Prove idempotency. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create a temp table daily_revenue (day date primary key, revenue numeric not null). Load delivered revenue per order_date with an upsert, then run the exact same statement again. Return days and total from the table.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE daily_revenue (day date PRIMARY KEY, revenue numeric NOT NULL);

INSERT INTO daily_revenue (day, revenue)
SELECT o.order_date, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY o.order_date
ON CONFLICT (day) DO UPDATE SET revenue = EXCLUDED.revenue;

INSERT INTO daily_revenue (day, revenue)
SELECT o.order_date, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY o.order_date
ON CONFLICT (day) DO UPDATE SET revenue = EXCLUDED.revenue;

SELECT count(*) AS days, sum(revenue) AS total FROM daily_revenue;
ROLLBACK;
    daystotal
    21722900.00

    (1 row)

    21 days and 722,900 after two runs, the same as after one. With a plain INSERT the second run fails on the primary key; without the primary key it doubles the revenue. Note SET revenue = EXCLUDED.revenue: replacing makes reruns safe, while adding (+) would not.

  13. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: a newsletter table must treat emails case-insensitively. Create temp table subscribers (email text not null, name text, subscribed_on date not null) with a unique index on lower(email). Insert ('Aarav@Mail.test', 'Aarav', 2026-01-01), then upsert ('AARAV@mail.test', 'Aarav Shah', 2026-02-01) so that the name is updated but the original subscription date is kept. Return the table.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE subscribers (email text NOT NULL, name text, subscribed_on date NOT NULL);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX subscribers_email_lower ON subscribers (lower(email));

INSERT INTO subscribers VALUES ('Aarav@Mail.test', 'Aarav', '2026-01-01');

INSERT INTO subscribers VALUES ('AARAV@mail.test', 'Aarav Shah', '2026-02-01')
ON CONFLICT ((lower(email))) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name;

SELECT * FROM subscribers;
ROLLBACK;
    emailnamesubscribed_on
    Aarav@Mail.testAarav Shah2026-01-01

    (1 row)

    One row: the original email and date, the new name. Columns not in SET keep their old values. A unique index on an expression is how Postgres enforces "unique, ignoring case". This would have prevented the duplicate customer 18.

  14. Get-or-create. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create temp table tags (tag_id int generated always as identity primary key, name text unique) and insert 'work' and 'kitchen'. Then, in one statement, return the tag_id for 'kitchen' and 'travel', creating any that are missing. Columns: tag_id, name.

    Expected: 2 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE tags (tag_id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name text UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO tags (name) VALUES ('work'), ('kitchen');

WITH wanted(name) AS (VALUES ('kitchen'), ('travel')),
ins AS (
  INSERT INTO tags (name)
  SELECT name FROM wanted
  ON CONFLICT (name) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING tag_id, name
)
SELECT tag_id, name FROM ins
UNION ALL
SELECT t.tag_id, t.name FROM tags t JOIN wanted w ON w.name = t.name
ORDER BY tag_id;
ROLLBACK;
    tag_idname
    2kitchen
    4travel

    (2 rows)

    kitchen keeps id 2; travel gets id 4, not 3. The skipped insert of 'kitchen' still used up identity value 3: sequences never go back, so ids always have gaps. The second SELECT cannot see 'travel' (same snapshot, Session 20), so nothing appears twice.

  15. Challenge: The nightly stock sync, with a report. In one statement (inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK): validate and deduplicate the feed, apply it with MERGE (delete at qty 0, update only newer and changed rows, insert new keys), and return one row for every feed row with its outcome: inserted, updated, deleted, skipped: stale, skipped: no change, superseded, rejected: unknown product or rejected: negative qty. Columns: feed_id, warehouse, product_id, qty, outcome, ordered by feed_id.

    Expected: 12 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT f.*,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY warehouse, product_id ORDER BY received_at DESC, feed_id DESC) AS rn,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.product_id = f.product_id) AS known
  FROM stock_feed f
),
valid AS (
  SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 AND known AND qty >= 0
),
m AS (
  MERGE INTO inventory t
  USING valid s ON t.warehouse = s.warehouse AND t.product_id = s.product_id
  WHEN MATCHED AND s.received_at > t.updated_at AND s.qty = 0 THEN
    DELETE
  WHEN MATCHED AND s.received_at > t.updated_at AND s.qty <> t.qty THEN
    UPDATE SET qty = s.qty, updated_at = s.received_at
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at) VALUES (s.warehouse, s.product_id, s.qty, s.received_at)
  RETURNING merge_action() AS action, s.feed_id
)
SELECT r.feed_id, r.warehouse, r.product_id, r.qty,
       CASE WHEN NOT r.known                   THEN 'rejected: unknown product'
            WHEN r.qty < 0                     THEN 'rejected: negative qty'
            WHEN r.rn > 1                      THEN 'superseded'
            WHEN m.action = 'INSERT'           THEN 'inserted'
            WHEN m.action = 'UPDATE'           THEN 'updated'
            WHEN m.action = 'DELETE'           THEN 'deleted'
            WHEN i.updated_at >= r.received_at THEN 'skipped: stale'
            ELSE 'skipped: no change' END AS outcome
FROM ranked r
LEFT JOIN m ON m.feed_id = r.feed_id
LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.warehouse = r.warehouse AND i.product_id = r.product_id
ORDER BY r.feed_id;
ROLLBACK;
    feed_idwarehouseproduct_idqtyoutcome
    1Pune14updated
    2Pune338superseded
    3Pune76inserted
    4Delhi60deleted
    5Delhi153inserted
    6Pune336updated
    7Pune995rejected: unknown product
    8Delhi129skipped: stale
    9Pune132inserted
    10Delhi12skipped: no change
    11Pune522updated
    12Delhi7-2rejected: negative qty

    (12 rows)

    Every input row is accounted for: 3 inserted, 3 updated, 1 deleted, 2 skipped, 1 superseded, 2 rejected. MERGE can sit inside WITH, and its RETURNING can include source columns (s.feed_id), which is what links each action back to its feed row. The final SELECT reads inventory as it was before the MERGE, which is exactly what the "stale" check needs.

← Phase 4: JSONB, arrays + modellingAll phasesSchema

Phase 4 · Session 41

Data modelling and anti-patterns

Choose between columns, arrays, JSONB and child tables, let constraints enforce your rules, and recognise (and repair) the classic schema mistakes.

Topics

What a schema is for

A schema is a set of promises that the database keeps for you. Every rule written as a constraint is a bug that cannot happen, whoever writes the data: your app, an import script, a colleague in psql. A rule that lives only in application code will be broken by the first writer that does not run that code.

Normalisation in plain words

  • One fact in one place. A customer's city lives in customers, not copied onto every order. Copies drift apart (Session 39 Q14, and Q14 below).
  • One value per field. No lists in a text column ('3,5,7'), no phone1, phone2, phone3. A repeating group becomes a child table (or an array, Session 37).
  • Every column describes the whole key. In order_items (order_id, product_id), the quantity belongs to the line, while the product name belongs to the product and lives in products.
  • Denormalise on purpose only: a copy kept for speed, with a plan for keeping it correct (a trigger, a materialized view or a nightly rebuild).

order_items.unit_price looks like a copy of products.price, but it is not: it is the price at the time of the order, a historical fact. Know the difference between history (keep it) and duplication (avoid it).

Column, array, JSONB or child table?

Need                                                    Choose
------------------------------------------------------  -------------------------------------------------
filtered, joined, summed, constrained                   a column, with the right type and constraints
a short list of simple values, read with the row        an array (product_details.tags)
attributes that differ per kind of row, read as a whole JSONB (product_details.specs), plus real columns
                                                        for the keys you filter and join on
items with their own attributes or foreign keys         a child table (order_items)
a value that changes over time, with history            a child table with a validity range (price_history)

Constraints are documentation that cannot lie

NOT NULL                          the value must exist
CHECK (qty >= 0)                  a rule on one row
PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE              no two rows share these values
UNIQUE INDEX … WHERE active       unique among some rows only (partial unique index)
UNIQUE INDEX ON t (lower(email))  unique ignoring case (Session 40)
REFERENCES … ON DELETE …          the referenced row exists; NO ACTION / RESTRICT / CASCADE / SET NULL
EXCLUDE USING gist (…)            no two rows overlap (date ranges, bookings)
GENERATED ALWAYS AS (…) STORED    computed from other columns, never out of date
SELECT conrelid::regclass AS table_name, conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE contype = 'c' AND connamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
ORDER BY 1, 2;
table_nameconnamedefinition
ordersorders_status_checkCHECK ((status = ANY (ARRAY['pending'::text, 'shipped'::text, 'delivered'::text, 'cancelled'::text])))
order_itemsorder_items_quantity_checkCHECK ((quantity > 0))
reviewsreviews_rating_checkCHECK (((rating >= 1) AND (rating <= 5)))
inventoryinventory_qty_checkCHECK ((qty >= 0))
accountsaccounts_balance_checkCHECK ((balance >= (0)::numeric))
jobsjobs_status_checkCHECK ((status = ANY (ARRAY['queued'::text, 'running'::text, 'done'::text, 'failed'::text])))
table_bookingstable_bookings_party_size_checkCHECK ((party_size > 0))

(7 rows)

Adding a constraint to a table that already holds bad rows fails. ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID enforces it for new and changed rows straight away; you then fix the old rows and run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. Phase 6 uses the same trick for changes without downtime.

Anti-patterns you will meet

Anti-pattern                 Symptom                                     Fix
---------------------------  ------------------------------------------  ------------------------------
EAV (entity-attribute-value)  all values text, no types, no constraints,  real columns, or JSONB
                              a typo silently creates a new attribute
Comma-separated lists         LIKE '%,5,%' searches, no foreign key        child table or array
Repeated columns (phone1..3)  "please add phone4", NULLs everywhere       child table
Stored totals                 total <> sum(lines) after the first bug     compute, or sync on purpose
float for money               0.1 + 0.2 <> 0.3                            numeric
timestamp without time zone   "which time zone was that in?"              timestamptz (Session 15)
One table for all kinds       most columns NULL in every row              separate tables, or columns + JSONB
SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8              AS float_sum,
       0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8  AS float_equal,
       0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric = 0.3          AS numeric_equal;
float_sumfloat_equalnumeric_equal
0.30000000000000004ft

(1 row)

The EAV table in this database

product_attributes stores one row per product and attribute, with every value as text. It looks flexible ("add any attribute without a migration"). Here is what that flexibility allowed:

SELECT attr, count(*) AS products, array_agg(DISTINCT value ORDER BY value) AS distinct_values
FROM product_attributes
GROUP BY attr
ORDER BY attr;
attrproductsdistinct_values
color7{black,Black,blue,silver}
colour1{black}
warranty6{1,2,"2 years"}
weight_kg8{0.09,0.25,0.9,1.2,1.6,2.5,4.2,light}

(4 rows)

A typo (colour) created a new attribute. Black and black are different colours. light is a weight and 2 years a warranty. None of this can happen with typed columns: color text CHECK (color = lower(color)), weight_kg numeric, warranty_years int. If the attributes really differ per product, JSONB with CHECK constraints (or a validated JSON shape) is still better than EAV, because a product is one row, not many.

Time ranges: price_history

A daterange such as [2025-01-01,2025-02-01) includes its first day and excludes its last ([ vs )), so consecutive periods meet without overlapping. An empty upper bound means "until further notice". Useful operators: @> (contains a date), && (overlaps), lower() / upper(), upper_inf() (open-ended).

SELECT product_id, price, valid_during
FROM price_history
WHERE valid_during @> DATE '2025-01-15'
  AND product_id IN (1, 6, 12)
ORDER BY product_id;
product_idpricevalid_during
1118000.00[2025-01-01,2025-02-01)
618000.00[2024-06-01,2025-03-01)

(2 rows)

Product 12 has no row: its history has a gap in January 2025. Product 3 has the opposite problem: two rows overlap.

With the btree_gist extension (CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist;), the constraint EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, valid_during WITH &&) makes overlapping prices for the same product impossible. Without it you can only find overlaps after the fact (Q6).

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s41.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

GROUP BY product_id
ORDER BY product_id;

  11. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: add the constraint attr_known CHECK (attr IN ('color', 'weight_kg', 'warranty')) to product_attributes. It would fail on the existing typo, so add it NOT VALID, fix the typo, then VALIDATE it. Return conname and convalidated.

    BEGIN;
ALTER TABLE product_attributes
  ADD CONSTRAINT attr_known CHECK (attr IN ('color', 'weight_kg', 'warranty')) NOT VALID;

UPDATE product_attributes SET attr = 'color' WHERE attr = 'colour';

ALTER TABLE product_attributes VALIDATE CONSTRAINT attr_known;

SELECT conname, convalidated FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'attr_known';
ROLLBACK;
    connameconvalidated
    attr_knownt

    (1 row)

    From the moment it is added, a NOT VALID constraint already rejects new bad rows; only the old rows are not checked yet. VALIDATE then checks them without blocking writes for long (Phase 6).

  12. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: promote the event type out of the JSON. Add a stored generated column event_type to events computed from payload ->> 'type', give it a CHECK that it is one of the four known types, and index it. Then return event_type and events (count), ordered by event_type.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
ALTER TABLE events
  ADD COLUMN event_type text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (payload ->> 'type') STORED
  CHECK (event_type IN ('search', 'add_to_cart', 'checkout', 'app_error'));
CREATE INDEX events_event_type ON events (event_type);

SELECT event_type, count(*) AS events FROM events GROUP BY event_type ORDER BY event_type;
ROLLBACK;
    event_typeevents
    add_to_cart6
    app_error3
    checkout7
    search8

    (4 rows)

    The key you filter on most becomes a real column: typed, constrained, indexable, and impossible to get out of sync with the JSON, because Postgres computes it. Inserting an event with an unknown type now fails.

  13. Fix the repeated-columns anti-pattern. A legacy table arrives as (customer_id, phone1, phone2, phone3): (1, '98200 11111', NULL, '022 4000 1111'), (2, '98450 22222', '98450 33333', NULL), (3, NULL, NULL, NULL), (4, '99000 44444', NULL, NULL). Turn it into rows of a child table: customer_id, position, phone, skipping empty slots, ordered by customer_id, position.

    Expected: 5 rows

    Answer
    WITH legacy(customer_id, phone1, phone2, phone3) AS (
  VALUES (1, '98200 11111', NULL, '022 4000 1111'),
         (2, '98450 22222', '98450 33333', NULL),
         (3, NULL, NULL, NULL),
         (4, '99000 44444', NULL, NULL)
)
SELECT l.customer_id, p.position, p.phone
FROM legacy l
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES (1, l.phone1), (2, l.phone2), (3, l.phone3)) AS p(position, phone)
WHERE p.phone IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY l.customer_id, p.position;
    customer_idpositionphone
    1198200 11111
    13022 4000 1111
    2198450 22222
    2298450 33333
    4199000 44444

    (5 rows)

    A LATERAL VALUES list unpivots columns into rows. In the child table customer_phones (customer_id, phone), a fourth phone is just another row, and "find the customer with this phone" is one indexed lookup instead of three ORs.

  14. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: show how stored totals drift. Snapshot every order's total into a temp table order_totals. Then correct the price of the laptop in order 9 (product 2) to 85,000 in order_items. Return the orders whose stored total no longer matches the computed one: order_id, stored_total, actual_total.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE order_totals AS
SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS total
FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id;

UPDATE order_items SET unit_price = 85000 WHERE order_id = 9 AND product_id = 2;

SELECT t.order_id, t.total AS stored_total, a.actual_total
FROM order_totals t
JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * unit_price) AS actual_total
      FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) a ON a.order_id = t.order_id
WHERE t.total <> a.actual_total;
ROLLBACK;
    order_idstored_totalactual_total
    989000.0090000.00

    (1 row)

    The copy was right when it was made and wrong one statement later, and nothing warned anyone. Options, from simplest: compute totals when you read them (a view); refresh a materialized view on a schedule (Phase 6); keep the copy in sync with a trigger (Phase 7). Never "remember to update it in the app".

  15. Challenge: Normalise a legacy order import. Rows (ref, email, items): ('L-1001', 'aarav@mail.test', 'Wireless Mouse x2; USB-C Hub x1'), ('L-1002', 'DIYA@mail.test', 'laptop air 13 x1'), ('L-1003', 'kabir@mail.test', 'Desk Lamp x0; Chef Knife xtwo'), ('L-1004', 'nobody@mail.test', 'Hover Board x1'). Split items on ;, parse each into a product name and a quantity (name xN), match customers by email and products by name (both case-insensitively), and return one row per item: ref, line_no, customer_id, product_id, qty, problems (comma-separated: unknown customer, unknown product, bad qty; empty when fine). Ordered by ref, line_no.

    Expected: 6 rows

    Answer
    WITH legacy(ref, email, items) AS (
  VALUES ('L-1001', 'aarav@mail.test',  'Wireless Mouse x2; USB-C Hub x1'),
         ('L-1002', 'DIYA@mail.test',   'laptop air 13 x1'),
         ('L-1003', 'kabir@mail.test',  'Desk Lamp x0; Chef Knife xtwo'),
         ('L-1004', 'nobody@mail.test', 'Hover Board x1')
),
items AS (
  SELECT l.ref, l.email, i.line_no, regexp_match(trim(i.item), '^(.*?)\s*x(\S+)$') AS m
  FROM legacy l
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(string_to_array(l.items, ';')) WITH ORDINALITY AS i(item, line_no)
),
parsed AS (
  SELECT ref, email, line_no, m[1] AS product_name,
         CASE WHEN m[2] ~ '^\d+$' AND m[2]::int > 0 THEN m[2]::int END AS qty
  FROM items
),
cust AS (
  SELECT lower(email) AS email, min(customer_id) AS customer_id FROM customers GROUP BY lower(email)
)
SELECT p.ref, p.line_no, c.customer_id, pr.product_id, p.qty,
       concat_ws(', ',
         CASE WHEN c.customer_id IS NULL  THEN 'unknown customer' END,
         CASE WHEN pr.product_id IS NULL THEN 'unknown product' END,
         CASE WHEN p.qty IS NULL          THEN 'bad qty' END) AS problems
FROM parsed p
LEFT JOIN cust c      ON c.email = lower(p.email)
LEFT JOIN products pr ON lower(pr.name) = lower(p.product_name)
ORDER BY p.ref, p.line_no;
    refline_nocustomer_idproduct_idqtyproblems
    L-10011132
    L-10012151
    L-10021221
    L-10031312∅bad qty
    L-10032310∅bad qty
    L-10041∅∅1unknown customer, unknown product

    (6 rows)

    6 item rows: 3 clean, 3 with problems (L-1004 has two). Without the cust CTE, L-1002 would match customers 2 and 18 and come out twice: the duplicate customer from Session 1 strikes again. This is a real migration in miniature: split → parse → match → report, before a single row is written.

← Phase 4: JSONB, arrays + modellingAll phasesSchema

Phase 4 · Session 42

Review: arrays, JSONB, upsert and modelling

Pull Sessions 37–41 back out of memory, mixed with windows, recursion and sessions from Phase 3.

Topics

How to run this review

  • First 20 minutes: redo every question in mistakes.md from Sessions 37–41, cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below. They are mixed on purpose, and several also need Phase 3 tools.
  • Then the challenge: one JSON document per product, built from six sources without a single fan-out.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 37–41

Problem                                   Tool
----------------------------------------  -----------------------------------------------------------
Is x in the array / all of / any of       'x' = ANY (a)  ·  a @> ARRAY[…]  ·  a && ARRAY[…]
Array to rows (with position) and back    unnest(a) WITH ORDINALITY  ·  array_agg / ARRAY(SELECT …)
Number of elements                        cardinality(a)   (array_length is NULL for {})
JSON value as text / at a path            ->> 'key'  ·  #>> '{a,b}'   (cast before comparing numbers)
Filter that can use a GIN index           @> '{"k": v}'  ·  ? 'key'
JSON array to rows                        jsonb_array_elements / jsonb_to_recordset
Missing key vs JSON null                  ? 'key'  ·  jsonb_typeof(x) = 'null'
Change a document                         jsonb_set (nested) · || (shallow merge) · - 'key'
Build JSON                                jsonb_build_object · jsonb_agg · jsonb_object_agg · to_jsonb
Insert or update                          INSERT … ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET … WHERE …
Sync with deletes                         MERGE … WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND <scope> THEN DELETE
Value at a point in time                  JOIN … ON range @> date
Add a rule to dirty data                  ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID → fix → VALIDATE CONSTRAINT

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s42.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Kitchen products (by tag) that cost less than 10,000: name, price, ordered by price.

FROM products p
JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE 'kitchen' = ANY (d.tags) AND p.price < 10000
ORDER BY p.price;

WHERE d.specs ? 'ports'

  4. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK, in one statement: set Pune's stock of product 2 to 5 and create Delhi's first stock of product 2 (qty 1), both stamped 2026-02-15 10:00 India time. Return warehouse, product_id, qty, ordered by warehouse.

    Expected: 2 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
WITH up AS (
  INSERT INTO inventory (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at)
  VALUES ('Pune', 2, 5, '2026-02-15 10:00+05:30'), ('Delhi', 2, 1, '2026-02-15 10:00+05:30')
  ON CONFLICT (warehouse, product_id)
  DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
  RETURNING warehouse, product_id, qty
)
SELECT * FROM up ORDER BY warehouse;
ROLLBACK;

  10. For every checkout line item: was the product added to the cart by the same customer before the checkout? event_id, order_id, product_id, carted (boolean), ordered by event_id, product_id.

  13. Sessions in the app events (a new session after 30 minutes of silence): customer_id, session_no, types (array in time order) and ended_in_checkout. Ordered by customer_id, session_no.

    Expected: 9 rows

    Answer
    WITH g AS (
  SELECT customer_id, event_id, created_at, payload ->> 'type' AS type,
         created_at - lag(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, event_id) AS gap
  FROM events
),
s AS (
  SELECT *, sum(CASE WHEN gap IS NULL OR gap > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
              OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, event_id) AS session_no
  FROM g
)
SELECT customer_id, session_no,
       array_agg(type ORDER BY created_at, event_id) AS types,
       (array_agg(type ORDER BY created_at DESC, event_id DESC))[1] = 'checkout' AS ended_in_checkout
FROM s
GROUP BY customer_id, session_no
ORDER BY customer_id, session_no;

  14. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create temp table customer_stats (customer_id primary key, orders int, last_order date) from orders placed up to 31 Dec 2025. Then MERGE in the stats computed from all orders: update rows that changed, insert new customers. Return action, customer_id, orders, last_order for the rows that changed, ordered by customer_id.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE customer_stats (customer_id int PRIMARY KEY, orders int NOT NULL, last_order date NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO customer_stats
SELECT customer_id, count(*), max(order_date) FROM orders
WHERE order_date <= DATE '2025-12-31'
GROUP BY customer_id;

WITH m AS (
  MERGE INTO customer_stats t
  USING (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders, max(order_date) AS last_order
         FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) s
  ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
  WHEN MATCHED AND (t.orders, t.last_order) IS DISTINCT FROM (s.orders, s.last_order) THEN
    UPDATE SET orders = s.orders, last_order = s.last_order
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT VALUES (s.customer_id, s.orders, s.last_order)
  RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.*
)
SELECT * FROM m ORDER BY customer_id;
ROLLBACK;
    actioncustomer_idorderslast_order
    UPDATE242026-02-14
    UPDATE332026-02-01
    UPDATE532026-01-08
    UPDATE1422026-01-15

    (4 rows)

    Four customers ordered in 2026 and all of them already had stats, so: 4 updates, no inserts. Comparing row values with IS DISTINCT FROM is the compact way to say "anything changed".

  15. Challenge: Product 360: one JSON document per product with details, built from six sources. Keys: id, name, price, brand, tags (lower-cased, de-duplicated, sorted), list_price (current, from price_history; null if none), units_sold (delivered orders; 0 if none), avg_rating (1 decimal; null if no reviews), stock (object warehouse → qty; {} if none). Columns: product_id, doc, ordered by product_id.

    Expected: 13 rows

    Answer
    WITH sold AS (
  SELECT oi.product_id, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
rating AS (
  SELECT product_id, round(avg(rating), 1) AS avg_rating FROM reviews GROUP BY product_id
),
stock AS (
  SELECT product_id, jsonb_object_agg(warehouse, qty) AS stock FROM inventory GROUP BY product_id
),
list AS (
  SELECT product_id, price FROM price_history WHERE upper_inf(valid_during)
)
SELECT d.product_id,
       jsonb_build_object(
         'id',         p.product_id,
         'name',       p.name,
         'price',      p.price,
         'brand',      d.specs ->> 'brand',
         'tags',       to_jsonb(ARRAY(SELECT DISTINCT lower(t) FROM unnest(d.tags) AS t ORDER BY 1)),
         'list_price', l.price,
         'units_sold', COALESCE(s.units, 0),
         'avg_rating', r.avg_rating,
         'stock',      COALESCE(st.stock, '{}'::jsonb)
       ) AS doc
FROM product_details d
JOIN products p   ON p.product_id = d.product_id
LEFT JOIN sold s   ON s.product_id = d.product_id
LEFT JOIN rating r ON r.product_id = d.product_id
LEFT JOIN stock st ON st.product_id = d.product_id
LEFT JOIN list l   ON l.product_id = d.product_id
ORDER BY d.product_id;
    product_iddoc

    (13 rows, first 12 shown)

    Each CTE has at most one row per product, so the LEFT JOINs cannot multiply anything. That is the rule from Session 7, applied to a JSON API. Product 3 would appear twice if price_history had two open-ended rows for it; it does not, but the overlap from Session 41 shows how close that is.

Phase 4 · Session 43

Exit test + Apply: JSONB and modelling

Prove you can work with arrays, JSONB, upserts and constraints: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct.

Topics

Exit test rules

  • Cold: no notes, no earlier sessions, no answers until you are done.
  • Time box: 90 minutes for all 14 questions.
  • Score honestly: a question counts only if the output matches the expected rows exactly.
  • Pass = 11 of 14 or more. Pass → Phase 5 (indexes and EXPLAIN). Fail → redo every missed question, re-read its session, and retake the test later.

What the test checks

Q1, Q2        arrays: search, unnest, clean values      (S37)
Q3, Q4, Q9    JSONB: values, casts, expanding, lead         (S38, S26)
Q5, Q6, Q13   JSONB: change and build documents         (S39)
Q7, Q10, Q12  upsert and MERGE                          (S40)
Q8, Q11, Q14  ranges, EAV, constraints                  (S41)

Apply project: model Visitly

Write psql/projects/p4-visitly-schema.sql: the core schema of your Visitly restaurant-booking app, using what this phase taught. It must contain:

  • restaurants and menu_items: real columns for what you filter on (price, category, is_available), a TEXT[] for dietary tags (with a CHECK that they are lower-case), JSONB for item options (sizes, add-ons).
  • menu_prices with a daterange per price and an exclusion constraint so a dish never has two prices on the same day (CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist).
  • bookings with a tstzrange and an exclusion constraint: one table cannot be booked twice for overlapping times.
  • Every foreign key with a deliberate ON DELETE choice, and a comment saying why.
  • An idempotent menu import: INSERT … ON CONFLICT from a staging table, safe to rerun.
  • One query that returns a restaurant page as a single JSON document (restaurant, menu grouped by category, today's prices).

Load it into a fresh database, insert a few rows that should be rejected (overlapping bookings, upper-case tags, a second price on the same day) and check that each one fails with the error you expect. A constraint you have not seen fail is a constraint you have not tested. Phase 9 reviews this schema like a senior engineer would.

Return action, product_id, qty, ordered by product_id.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer

WITH m AS (
  MERGE INTO inventory t
  USING (VALUES (1, 5), (2, 3), (3, 41), (4, 12), (5, 25), (6, 8), (9, 6), (10, 15), (11, 4), (13, 1))
        AS s(product_id, qty)
  ON t.warehouse = 'Pune' AND t.product_id = s.product_id
  WHEN MATCHED AND t.qty <> s.qty THEN
    UPDATE SET qty = s.qty, updated_at = TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-02-15 18:00+05:30'
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT VALUES ('Pune', s.product_id, s.qty, TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-02-15 18:00+05:30')
  WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.warehouse = 'Pune' THEN
    DELETE
  RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.product_id, t.qty
)
SELECT * FROM m ORDER BY product_id;
ROLLBACK;

  12. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: load stock_feed into inventory with one INSERT … ON CONFLICT (latest row per key, known products only, qty ≥ 0; update only when newer and changed). Then return each warehouse's total units: warehouse, units, ordered by warehouse.

    Expected: 2 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
INSERT INTO inventory (warehouse, product_id, qty, updated_at)
SELECT warehouse, product_id, qty, received_at
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (warehouse, product_id) *
  FROM stock_feed
  ORDER BY warehouse, product_id, received_at DESC, feed_id DESC
) latest
WHERE qty >= 0
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.product_id = latest.product_id)
ON CONFLICT (warehouse, product_id)
DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE EXCLUDED.updated_at > inventory.updated_at AND EXCLUDED.qty <> inventory.qty;

SELECT warehouse, sum(qty) AS units FROM inventory GROUP BY warehouse ORDER BY warehouse;
ROLLBACK;

SELECT jsonb_build_object(
         'id', c.customer_id,
         'name', c.full_name,

                                                         'status', status, 'total', total)
                                     ORDER BY order_date) FROM t),

WHERE c.customer_id = 2;

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer

ALTER TABLE product_details
  ADD CONSTRAINT tags_lower CHECK (tags::text = lower(tags::text)) NOT VALID;

UPDATE product_details
SET tags = ARRAY(SELECT lower(t) FROM unnest(tags) WITH ORDINALITY AS x(t, n) ORDER BY n)
WHERE tags::text <> lower(tags::text);

ALTER TABLE product_details VALIDATE CONSTRAINT tags_lower;

SELECT conname, convalidated FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'tags_lower';
ROLLBACK;

  15. Challenge: A product-search API. For the search word wireless and a maximum price of 20,000: return one JSON array of matching products (tag match ignoring case, or name containing the word ignoring case; not discontinued; price within the limit). Each element: id, name, price, brand, battery_hours (a JSON number, even when stored as a string; null if absent), in_stock (true if any warehouse has qty > 0), avg_rating (1 decimal or null). Sort by avg_rating descending (nulls last), then price. Also return how many products matched. Columns: results, matches.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    WITH candidates AS (
  SELECT p.product_id, p.name, p.price, d.specs
  FROM products p
  JOIN product_details d ON d.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE NOT p.discontinued
    AND p.price <= 20000
    AND (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(d.tags) AS t(tag) WHERE lower(t.tag) = 'wireless')
         OR p.name ILIKE '%wireless%')
),
rating AS (
  SELECT product_id, round(avg(rating), 1) AS avg_rating FROM reviews GROUP BY product_id
),
stock AS (
  SELECT product_id, bool_or(qty > 0) AS in_stock FROM inventory GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT jsonb_agg(
         jsonb_build_object(
           'id',            c.product_id,
           'name',          c.name,
           'price',         c.price,
           'brand',         c.specs ->> 'brand',
           'battery_hours', (c.specs ->> 'battery_hours')::numeric,
           'in_stock',      COALESCE(s.in_stock, false),
           'avg_rating',    r.avg_rating)
         ORDER BY r.avg_rating DESC NULLS LAST, c.price) AS results,
       count(*) AS matches
FROM candidates c
LEFT JOIN rating r ON r.product_id = c.product_id
LEFT JOIN stock s  ON s.product_id = c.product_id;
    resultsmatches
    [{"id": 3, "name": "Wireless Mouse", "brand": "Clicko", "price": 1500.00, "in_stock": true, "avg_rating": 4.0, "battery_hours": null}, {"id": 7, "name": "Bluetooth Speaker", "brand": "Sonora", "price": 7000.00, "in_stock": true, "avg_rating": 3.5, "battery_hours": 12}, {"id": 6, "name": "Noise-Cancel Headphones", "brand": "Sonora", "price": 18000.00, "in_stock": true, "avg_rating": 3.5, "battery_hours": 30}]3

    (1 row)

    3 matches: Wireless Mouse (4.0), then Bluetooth Speaker and Noise-Cancel Headphones (both 3.5, cheaper first). Earbuds Lite matches the tag but is discontinued. Reading battery_hours with ->> and a cast turns both 30 and "6" into numbers, so the API is consistent even though the stored data is not.

Phase 5 · Session 44

Index anatomy + a big dataset

Load 320,000 rows, see how tables and B-tree indexes are stored, and watch one index turn a full table scan into a dozen page reads.

Topics

Phase 5 setup: a big dataset

Indexes only matter when tables are big: all 36 orders of the shop fit on a single page. Load big.sql once, into the same practice database (it takes a few seconds). Every Phase 5 session uses it.

psql -U postgres -d practice -f docs/data/big.sql

-- then reconnect: the file changes two settings for new connections
psql -U postgres -d practice
  • big_customers (20,000), big_orders (200,000) and big_events (100,000 JSONB events).
  • Only the primary keys are indexed. big_orders.customer_id has a foreign key but no index. Every other index is yours to create.
  • The rows are generated by formulas, not random(), and the statistics are complete, so the plans on your machine should match the ones shown here.
  • Two settings are switched off for this database: parallel query and JIT compilation. They make plans harder to read while learning; Session 53 explains them and turns them back on.

Questions that create an index do it inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK, so every question starts from the same database. Postgres can roll back CREATE INDEX (most databases cannot). To keep an index, end with COMMIT instead.

How a table is stored

A table (the heap) is a file of 8 kB pages. Each page holds as many rows as fit, in no particular order; usually the order they were inserted. Every row has an address, its ctid = (page number, item number on that page).

SELECT relname, relpages, reltuples::bigint AS reltuples, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS size
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname IN ('big_customers', 'big_orders', 'big_events')
ORDER BY relname;
relnamerelpagesreltuplessize
big_customers218200001744 kB
big_events158410000012 MB
big_orders183420000014 MB

(3 rows)

SELECT ctid, order_id, customer_id, status
FROM big_orders
WHERE order_id IN (1, 2, 109, 110, 200000)
ORDER BY order_id;
ctidorder_idcustomer_idstatus
(0,1)17920delivered
(0,2)215839delivered
(0,109)1093172delivered
(1,1)11011091delivered
(1833,77)20000042pending

(5 rows)

About 109 orders fit on one page: order 110 is the first row of page 1. relpages and reltuples are kept up to date by VACUUM and ANALYZE, and they are what the planner uses to estimate costs.

Seq Scan: read every page

Without a usable index, the only way to find customer 7's orders is to read every page and test every row:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 7)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 199990
  Buffers: shared hit=1834
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=12
  • actual rows=10: ten orders found.
  • Rows Removed by Filter: 199990: 199,990 rows were read and thrown away.
  • Buffers: shared hit=1834: every page of the table was touched. hit means found in Postgres's memory cache, read means fetched from disk. On your machine you may see a mix of both; what matters is hit + read.

B-tree: a sorted copy with a table of contents

                        root:  [ …   |  6000  |  12000  |  … ]
                       /              |               \
      branch: [ 1 … 2999 ]     branch: [ … ]        branch: [ … ]
          /         \
  leaf: [ 1 → (512,3)  1 → (1700,8)  2 → (40,1) … ]  ⇄  leaf: [ … ]  ⇄  leaf: [ … ]

  key → ctid of the row in the table
  • Leaf pages hold every key in sorted order, each with the ctid of its row. Leaves are linked to their neighbours, so a range (BETWEEN, >=) means "find the start, then walk right".
  • Branch pages and the root only route the search. A page holds hundreds of keys, so even millions of rows need just 3 or 4 levels: a lookup reads about 3 index pages, then the table pages of the matching rows.
  • Equal keys sit next to each other. Since Postgres 13, duplicates are stored once with a list of ctids (deduplication), which keeps indexes on repetitive columns small.
  • An index is a copy of some columns, sorted differently. It costs disk space, and every INSERT, DELETE and UPDATE of an indexed column has to maintain it.

Creating an index

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
ROLLBACK;
Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 7)
  Heap Blocks: exact=10
  Buffers: shared hit=10 read=2
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_id_idx (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 7)
        Index Searches: 1
        Buffers: shared read=2
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=4 read=1
  • Bitmap Index Scan: walk the index for customer_id = 7 and collect the ctids of the matches (actual rows=10).
  • Bitmap Heap Scan: visit those table pages in physical order, each page once (Heap Blocks: exact=10), and recheck the condition.
  • About a dozen pages instead of 1,834. That is the whole point of an index.

The access paths you will meet in plans: Seq Scan (read everything), Index Scan (follow each index entry to its row; best for very few rows, or when the index order is needed), Bitmap Index + Heap Scan (many rows: collect first, then visit each page once), Index Only Scan (the index alone holds the answer; no table visit).

Foreign keys do not get an index automatically: big_orders.customer_id references big_customers, but only the primary keys are indexed. Indexing foreign-key columns is usually the first fix on any schema (Session 11).

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s44.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  3. On average, how many orders fit on one page of big_orders? Return rows_per_page with 1 decimal, from pg_class.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    SELECT round((reltuples / relpages)::numeric, 1) AS rows_per_page
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname = 'big_orders';
    rows_per_page
    109.1

    (1 row)

    About 109. A row of big_orders is roughly 75 bytes including its header; a page is 8,192 bytes.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer

CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
ROLLBACK;
    Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders (actual rows=5010.00 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 42)
  Heap Blocks: exact=1834
  Buffers: shared hit=1834 read=6
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_id_idx (actual rows=5010.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
        Index Searches: 1
        Buffers: shared read=6
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=5 read=1

    Heap Blocks: exact=1834: every page of the table. Customer 42 placed every 40th order, so its 5,010 rows are spread over all pages. The index found them quickly, but the table pages still had to be read. An index pays off when the matching rows are few or close together, not merely when the condition is selective-looking.

  11. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index big_orders(created_at) and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for the orders created in the first hour of 2025 (India time). Which plan, and how many rows?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders
WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01 01:00';
ROLLBACK;
    Index Scan using big_orders_created_at_idx on big_orders (actual rows=12.00 loops=1)
  Index Cond: ((created_at >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-01-01 01:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))
  Index Searches: 1

  12. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create the customer_id index and compare sizes: relname, pages, size for big_orders, big_orders_pkey and the new index, largest first. Why is the new index less than half the size of the primary-key index, when both have 200,000 entries?

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
SELECT relname, pg_relation_size(oid) / 8192 AS pages, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS size
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname IN ('big_orders', 'big_orders_pkey', 'big_orders_customer_id_idx')
ORDER BY pages DESC;
ROLLBACK;
    relnamepagessize
    big_orders183414 MB
    big_orders_pkey5514408 kB
    big_orders_customer_id_idx2311848 kB

    (3 rows)

    Deduplication (Postgres 13+): customer_id repeats about 10 times per customer, so each value is stored once with a list of ctids. order_id is unique, so every entry is stored in full. Both indexes are far smaller than the table, because they copy only one column.

  13. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: by mistake, two people created the same index: big_orders_created_at_idx and orders_by_time, both on big_orders(created_at). Write a query on pg_index that finds duplicate indexes (same table, same columns, same expressions, same WHERE): table_name, indexes (array).

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
CREATE INDEX orders_by_time ON big_orders (created_at);

SELECT indrelid::regclass AS table_name,
       array_agg(indexrelid::regclass::text ORDER BY indexrelid::regclass::text) AS indexes
FROM pg_index
GROUP BY indrelid, indkey::text, indexprs::text, indpred::text
HAVING count(*) > 1;
ROLLBACK;
    table_nameindexes
    big_orders{big_orders_created_at_idx,orders_by_time}

    (1 row)

    A duplicate index doubles the write cost and the disk space for zero benefit, and Postgres does not warn you. This query is worth keeping in your toolbox (Session 53 adds "indexes that are never used").

  14. Look up order 123,456 by primary key with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF). How many pages in total did the lookup touch?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE order_id = 123456;
    Index Scan using big_orders_pkey on big_orders (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (order_id = 123456)
  Index Searches: 1
  Buffers: shared hit=4
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=6

    Four pages: the root and one more level of the index, a leaf page, and the one table page that holds the row. Compare with 1,834 for a sequential scan. This is why a primary-key lookup costs the same on 200 thousand or 200 million rows: the tree only gets one level deeper.

  15. Challenge: Explain Q9 with data. For customers 7, 42 and 12345: orders, pages (the number of distinct table pages their orders live on) and rows_per_page (orders ÷ pages, 1 decimal). Ordered by customer_id.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    SELECT customer_id,
       count(*) AS orders,
       count(DISTINCT (ctid::text::point)[0]) AS pages,
       round(count(*)::numeric / count(DISTINCT (ctid::text::point)[0]), 1) AS rows_per_page
FROM big_orders
WHERE customer_id IN (7, 42, 12345)
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
    customer_idorderspagesrows_per_page
    710101.0
    42501018342.7
    1234510101.0

    (3 rows)

    Customers 7 and 12345: 10 orders on 10 different pages. Customer 42: 5,010 orders on all 1,834 pages, under 3 per page. The cost of an index lookup is roughly "index pages + table pages it must visit", so the second number decides whether an index beats a Seq Scan. Postgres estimates it from the column's correlation with the physical order (Session 52). The ctid → point cast is a handy trick for this kind of investigation.

← Phase 5: Indexes + EXPLAINAll phasesSchema

Phase 5 · Session 45

Indexes for WHERE clauses

Write conditions an index can serve, choose the column order of composite indexes, and know which conditions no B-tree can help.

Topics

Selectivity: when is an index worth it?

The planner uses an index when it expects to fetch few rows (or rows that sit close together). There is no fixed percentage; it compares estimated costs. Reading the whole table in order is cheap per page, while jumping around through an index is expensive per row, so for most of the table a Seq Scan wins.

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_status_idx ON big_orders (status);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE status = 'pending';
ROLLBACK;
Index Scan using big_orders_status_idx on big_orders
  Index Cond: (status = 'pending'::text)

1,000 pending orders out of 200,000: the index is used. For status = 'delivered' (191,090 rows) the same index is ignored (Q7). An index on a column with few distinct values is only useful for the rare values.

Sargable conditions: leave the column alone

An index on a column can serve conditions of the form column <operator> value: =, <, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, and LIKE 'prefix%' with the right operator class. Wrap the column in a function or a cast, and the index on the bare column is useless: the index stores created_at, not created_at::date. A condition an index can use is called sargable (from "search argument able").

Not sargable                                    Sargable rewrite
----------------------------------------------  -----------------------------------------------------------
created_at::date = '2025-03-01'                 created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-03-02'
date_trunc('month', created_at) = '2025-03-01'  created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-04-01'
extract(year FROM created_at) = 2025            created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01'
total * 1.18 > 59000                            total > 59000 / 1.18
order_id = 42.0       (numeric: casts order_id)  order_id = 42
lower(email) = 'x'                              an expression index on lower(email)  (below)
BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE created_at::date = '2025-03-01';
ROLLBACK;
Aggregate
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders
        Filter: ((created_at)::date = '2025-03-01'::date)
BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-03-02';
ROLLBACK;
Aggregate
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_created_at_idx on big_orders
        Index Cond: ((created_at >= '2025-03-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-03-02 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))

Same question, same index; only the second one can use it. The half-open range [start, next start) from Session 16 is exactly the sargable form.

Expression indexes

When the function is the point (case-insensitive email login), index the expression itself: CREATE INDEX … ON big_customers (lower(email)). Postgres stores the computed value, so WHERE lower(email) = … becomes a plain lookup. The query must use exactly the same expression as the index.

Composite indexes: column order matters

An index on (customer_id, created_at) is sorted by customer_id, and by created_at within each customer, like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name.

  • It serves any condition on a leftmost prefix: customer_id = 42, or customer_id = 42 AND created_at in a range.
  • It cannot efficiently serve created_at alone, just as a phone book sorted by surname cannot find everyone called Diya.
  • Rule: equality columns first, the range column last. After a range on one column, the later columns can only be checked entry by entry inside that range.
BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_created_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-04-01';
ROLLBACK;
Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders (actual rows=224.00 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: ((customer_id = 42) AND (created_at >= '2025-03-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-04-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))
  Heap Blocks: exact=82
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_created_idx (actual rows=224.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((customer_id = 42) AND (created_at >= '2025-03-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-04-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))
        Index Searches: 1

One composite index usually beats two single-column indexes. Postgres can combine two indexes (BitmapAnd), but each one is read for its own condition alone. With separate indexes on customer_id and created_at, it reads all 8,928 March orders through the created_at index and throws away 8,704 of them (Q11).

Other conditions

  • IN (…) becomes = ANY (array): one index probe per value.
  • OR across different columns: a BitmapOr of two indexes. Both columns need an index, or the whole thing becomes a Seq Scan.
  • <> and NOT IN: no index (they match almost everything). If the remaining values are rare, list them with IN.
  • IS NULL / IS NOT NULL: B-trees store NULLs, so both can use an index.
  • LIKE 'abc%': only with the C collation or a text_pattern_ops index. LIKE '%abc' and '%abc%': never with a B-tree (trigram index, Session 47).

Collation decides whether a plain index helps LIKE 'prefix%'. Run SELECT datcollate FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database();. On Windows it is usually something like English_India.1252, not C, and then a plain index does not help LIKE. An index built with text_pattern_ops works under any collation, which is why the answers use it.

Write your answers in psql/s45.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

CREATE INDEX big_customers_email_pattern_idx ON big_customers (email text_pattern_ops);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_customers WHERE email LIKE 'user123%';
ROLLBACK;
-- SELECT datcollate FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database();
    Bitmap Heap Scan on big_customers
  Filter: (email ~~ 'user123%'::text)
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_customers_email_pattern_idx
        Index Cond: ((email ~>=~ 'user123'::text) AND (email ~<~ 'user124'::text))

    The prefix becomes a range on the index: email ~>=~ 'user123' AND email ~<~ 'user124' (the ~ operators compare byte by byte, ignoring collation). With a non-C collation, a plain index cannot do this; text_pattern_ops can. It serves equality too, but not ORDER BY under your collation.

  15. Challenge: The support team searches customers by email, ignoring case, either by full address or by prefix (the agent types the start). Create the one index that serves both lower(email) = 'user123@mail.test' and lower(email) LIKE 'user12%' under any collation. Show EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for the prefix search. How many customers match?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_customers_email_search_idx ON big_customers (lower(email) text_pattern_ops);

-- the exact search uses it too:
-- EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM big_customers WHERE lower(email) = 'user123@mail.test';

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_customers WHERE lower(email) LIKE 'user12%';
ROLLBACK;
    Bitmap Heap Scan on big_customers (actual rows=1111.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (lower(email) ~~ 'user12%'::text)
  Heap Blocks: exact=15
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_customers_email_search_idx (actual rows=1111.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((lower(email) ~>=~ 'user12'::text) AND (lower(email) ~<~ 'user13'::text))
        Index Searches: 1

    1,111 customers (user12, user120–129, user1200–1299, user12000–12999), mixed-case ones included. An expression index can carry an operator class, so one index covers both search patterns. In real life you would also store emails lower-cased and add a unique index on lower(email) (Session 40).

Phase 5 · Session 46

Reading EXPLAIN

Read every number in a plan (costs, estimates, actual rows, loops, buffers, memory) and find the node where a slow query goes wrong.

Topics

The four ways to ask

EXPLAIN query                              the plan and the planner's estimates; does NOT run the query
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) query                    runs it, adds what really happened (actual rows, time, loops)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) query           + pages touched per node (Postgres 18 shows them even without BUFFERS)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF,  what this site uses: only the shape and the actual rows,
         TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) query    so the output is the same on every machine

Typing that option list gets old. In psql, define it once: \set ea 'EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)' (put it in your .psqlrc), then write :ea SELECT …;.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the statement. EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE … deletes the rows. Wrap data-changing statements in BEGIN; … ROLLBACK;.

Costs, estimated rows and width

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..4334.00 rows=10 width=47)
  Filter: (customer_id = 7)
  • cost=0.00..4334.00: startup cost (work before the first row can be returned) and total cost (to return all rows). The unit is arbitrary: "one page read in sequence" = 1.
  • rows=10: how many rows the planner expects this node to return. Everything else in the plan is chosen based on these estimates.
  • width=47: the expected average size of a returned row, in bytes.

A Seq Scan's cost is simple arithmetic, which shows what the planner "thinks" a plan costs:

pages × seq_page_cost  +  rows × cpu_tuple_cost  +  rows × cpu_operator_cost × (operators in the filter)
 1834 × 1.0            +  200000 × 0.01           +  200000 × 0.0025 × 1
= 1834 + 2000 + 500 = 4334

An index scan costs random_page_cost (default 4) per table page it jumps to, because random reads were slow on spinning disks. Session 53 lowers it for SSDs.

Actual numbers: ANALYZE

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..4334.00 rows=10 width=47) (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 7)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 199990
  • (actual rows=10.00 loops=1): what really happened. Compare it with the estimate rows=10. Here they agree; when they differ by 10× or more, the planner chose its plan for a different query than the one that ran.
  • loops: how many times the node was executed. actual rows is the average per loop: the real total is rows × loops. Postgres 18 prints the average with two decimals; older versions rounded it, so an average of 0.45 showed up as rows=0.
  • Index Searches (Postgres 18): how many times the index was descended from the root. Normally 1 per loop.
  • With TIMING on (the default) you also get actual time=startup..total in milliseconds, per loop. SUMMARY adds "Planning Time" and "Execution Time" at the bottom.

Reading order

A plan is a tree. The most indented nodes run first and feed their parent; the top node returns the result. Read it inside-out (bottom-up), and for each node ask: how many rows came in, how many went out, and how good was the estimate?

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.city, sum(o.total) AS revenue
FROM big_orders o
JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered' AND o.created_at >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;
Limit (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
  ->  Sort (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
        Sort Key: (sum(o.total)) DESC
        Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 25kB
        ->  HashAggregate (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
              Group Key: c.city
              Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 32kB
              ->  Hash Join (actual rows=88844.00 loops=1)
                    Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
                    ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o (actual rows=88844.00 loops=1)
                          Filter: ((created_at >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (status = 'delivered'::text))
                          Rows Removed by Filter: 111156
                    ->  Hash (actual rows=20000.00 loops=1)
                          Buckets: 32768  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1135kB
                          ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c (actual rows=20000.00 loops=1)
  • The two Seq Scans run first: 20,000 customers go into a Hash; 88,844 delivered 2025 orders survive the Filter (Rows Removed by Filter: 111156).
  • Hash Join: each order finds its customer; 88,844 rows out.
  • HashAggregate: one entry per city (10 rows). Batches: 1 means it fitted in memory.
  • Sort, then Limit: 5 rows. Note the Sort is on 10 rows, so it is cheap; the expensive part is reading 200,000 orders.

Node catalogue

Seq Scan / Index Scan / Index Only Scan / Bitmap Heap + Bitmap Index Scan   how rows are read (Session 44)
Filter + "Rows Removed by Filter"   condition checked AFTER reading the row (no index helped)
Index Cond                          condition used to navigate the index
Recheck Cond                        bitmap scans re-test rows on each page they visit
Nested Loop / Hash Join / Merge Join (+ Semi, Anti, Left, Right, Full)    joins (Session 11, Session 48)
Hash                                builds the in-memory hash table for a Hash Join
Memoize                             cache in front of a nested loop's inner side
Sort ("Sort Method")                quicksort in memory, top-N heapsort, or external merge on disk
HashAggregate / GroupAggregate      GROUP BY via a hash table / via sorted input
Limit                               stops its child early
WindowAgg, Unique, Append, SubPlan, InitPlan, CTE Scan, Materialize, Gather

For long plans, paste the text into explain.dalibo.com or explain.depesz.com: they draw the tree and highlight the slowest nodes and the worst estimates. Do not paste plans that contain private data.

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s46.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Compute the cost of a plain Seq Scan on big_orders yourself, from pg_class and the two settings: pages × seq_page_cost + rows × cpu_tuple_cost. Then compare it with EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big_orders.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    SELECT relpages * current_setting('seq_page_cost')::numeric
     + reltuples::numeric * current_setting('cpu_tuple_cost')::numeric AS seq_scan_cost
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname = 'big_orders';
    seq_scan_cost
    3834.00

    (1 row)

    3834. EXPLAIN says cost=0.00..3834.00. The planner's costs are formulas over table statistics and settings, nothing mysterious.

  2. Show EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE total > 1000. Why is the total cost exactly 500 more than in Q1?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE total > 1000;
    Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..4334.00 rows=196393 width=47)
  Filter: (total > '1000'::numeric)

    The filter evaluates one operator (>) on each of 200,000 rows: 200,000 × 0.0025 = 500. The estimate rows=196393 comes from the histogram of total (Session 52).

  3. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for the orders of customer 7. Compare the estimated rows with the actual rows.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
    Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..4334.00 rows=10 width=47) (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 7)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 199990

    Estimated 10, actual 10. The planner knows there are about 19,500 distinct customer_ids in 200,000 rows, so it expects about 10 per customer.

  4. Show EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big_orders ORDER BY total. Why is the Sort's startup cost almost as high as its total cost?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big_orders ORDER BY total;
    Sort  (cost=27596.64..28096.64 rows=200000 width=47)
  Sort Key: total
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..3834.00 rows=200000 width=47)

    A sort cannot return its first row before it has read and sorted every input row. Startup ≈ total is the sign of a "blocking" node; Seq Scan and Index Scan start returning rows immediately (startup 0 or close to it).

  5. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for SELECT * FROM big_orders LIMIT 5. How many rows did the Seq Scan actually read?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders LIMIT 5;
    Limit (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)

    Only 5. Limit stops its child as soon as it has enough rows, so a Seq Scan under a Limit can be very cheap. Put a Sort in between (ORDER BY) and everything has to be read first.

  6. Safely look at the plan of DELETE FROM big_orders WHERE order_id <= 10 with ANALYZE (BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF).

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
DELETE FROM big_orders WHERE order_id <= 10;
ROLLBACK;
    Delete on big_orders (actual rows=0.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using big_orders_pkey on big_orders (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (order_id <= 10)
        Index Searches: 1

    The child Index Scan found 10 rows and the Delete node removed them (actual rows=0 on Delete only means it returned nothing; no RETURNING). ROLLBACK brings them back. Without BEGIN … ROLLBACK the rows would be gone.

  7. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index customer_id, then run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for customer 42's orders above 49,000. Which condition used the index, and which was checked afterwards?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND total > 49000;
ROLLBACK;
    Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders (actual rows=98.00 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 42)
  Filter: (total > '49000'::numeric)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 4912
  Heap Blocks: exact=1834
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_id_idx (actual rows=5010.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
        Index Searches: 1

    customer_id = 42 is the Index Cond (5,010 rows found); total > 49000 is a Filter applied to each fetched row (Rows Removed by Filter: 4912, 98 kept). Fetching 5,010 rows to keep 98 is the hint that an index on (customer_id, total) would serve this query better.

  8. Compare the width of SELECT order_id FROM big_orders with SELECT * (plain EXPLAIN). Why does it matter?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN SELECT order_id FROM big_orders;
    Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..3834.00 rows=200000 width=4)

    4 bytes instead of 47. Narrow rows mean smaller sorts and hash tables (less memory, fewer spills to disk) and less data sent to the client. SELECT * in application code costs more than it looks.

  9. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index customer_id and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for customers 1–5 joined to their orders (full_name, order_id, total). How many orders did the inner side return in total?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer

CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id, o.total
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id <= 5;
ROLLBACK;
    Nested Loop (actual rows=40.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id <= 5)
        Index Searches: 1
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders o (actual rows=8.00 loops=5)
        Recheck Cond: (c.customer_id = customer_id)
        Heap Blocks: exact=40
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_id_idx (actual rows=8.00 loops=5)
              Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
              Index Searches: 5

    The inner Bitmap Heap Scan says actual rows=8.00 loops=5: 8 per loop on average, 40 in total, matching the Nested Loop's 40. Reading "rows=8" as the total is the most common EXPLAIN mistake.

FROM big_orders o
JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered' AND o.created_at >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;

  ->  Sort (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
        Sort Key: (sum(o.total)) DESC

              Group Key: c.city

    Seq Scan big_customers → Hash; Seq Scan big_orders (filter) → Hash Join → HashAggregate → Sort → Limit. The HashAggregate turns 88,844 rows into 10. Everything above it is cheap, so tuning this query means making the bottom part (reading orders) cheaper, not the sort.

  11. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE created_at::date = '2025-03-01'. Where does the estimate come from?

        Filter: ((created_at)::date = '2025-03-01'::date)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 199712

With the default 4 MB it is Batches: 1. Batches above 1 on a hot query is a reason to raise work_mem for that query (Session 53).

  13. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for SELECT * FROM big_orders ORDER BY total. Which sort method was used, and why?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer

SELECT * FROM big_orders ORDER BY total;

  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)

    external merge Disk: …kB: 200,000 rows of 47 bytes do not fit in work_mem (4 MB), so Postgres sorted chunks, wrote them to disk and merged them. In memory it would say quicksort Memory: …kB. Session 50 shows how an index avoids the sort entirely.

    Answer

  Buffers: shared hit=1834
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
        Buffers: shared hit=1834

    1,834 pages: the whole table. Run it twice in a fresh session: the first time you may see read= (from disk or the OS cache), the second time hit= (Postgres's own cache). Timings change a lot between the two runs, but the page count does not, which makes BUFFERS more reliable than time for comparing two versions of a query.

  15. Challenge: A report is slow: per customer in Dubai (city 'Dubai', country 'UAE'), the number of orders placed in March 2025. Run it with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF). (1) Find the node whose estimate is most wrong, and by what factor. (2) Add the index that fixes the access path for big_orders and show the new plan. Return the final plan.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
-- 1) before: look at the Seq Scan on big_customers
-- EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) <query below>

-- 2) the fix for big_orders
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_created_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, created_at);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, count(*) AS march_orders
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.city = 'Dubai' AND c.country = 'UAE'
  AND o.created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND o.created_at < '2025-04-01'
GROUP BY c.customer_id;
ROLLBACK;
    GroupAggregate  (cost=557.66..557.73 rows=4 width=12) (actual rows=179.00 loops=1)
  Group Key: c.customer_id
  ->  Sort  (cost=557.66..557.67 rows=4 width=4) (actual rows=179.00 loops=1)
        Sort Key: c.customer_id
        Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 25kB
        ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.42..557.62 rows=4 width=4) (actual rows=179.00 loops=1)
              ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c  (cost=0.00..518.00 rows=8 width=4) (actual rows=400.00 loops=1)
                    Filter: ((city = 'Dubai'::text) AND (country = 'UAE'::text))
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 19600
              ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_customer_created_idx on big_orders o  (cost=0.42..4.94 rows=1 width=4) (actual rows=0.45 loops=400)
                    Index Cond: ((customer_id = c.customer_id) AND (created_at >= '2025-03-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-04-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))
                    Heap Fetches: 0
                    Index Searches: 400

    (1) The scan of big_customers expects rows=8 but gets actual rows=400: 50× too low. The planner multiplies the selectivity of city = 'Dubai' (2%) by that of country = 'UAE' (2%) as if they were independent, but every Dubai customer is in the UAE. Session 52 fixes this with CREATE STATISTICS. (2) With (customer_id, created_at), each of the 400 customers is one Index Only Scan into its March range: actual rows=0.45 loops=400: 179 rows ÷ 400 loops. (Before Postgres 18 this printed as rows=0, which looked like 'found nothing'.) Before the index, all 200,000 orders were read.
