Phase 5 · Session 47

Index types and special indexes

Use partial, covering, GIN, trigram and BRIN indexes and exclusion constraints, and pick the right one for a query pattern.

Topics

Beyond the plain B-tree

Type      Answers                                                       Typical use
--------  ------------------------------------------------------------  ------------------------------------
B-tree    = < > BETWEEN IN, IS NULL, LIKE 'prefix%', ORDER BY            almost everything (the default)
Hash      = only                                                        rarely worth it over a B-tree
GIN       "contains": arrays @> &&, JSONB @> ?, full text, trigrams       many values per row
GiST      overlaps / nearest: ranges, geometry, exclusion constraints    bookings, maps, trigram similarity
BRIN      min/max per block range                                       huge append-only tables (time order)

B-tree variations:  partial (WHERE …) · expression (Session 45) · multicolumn (Session 45)
                    covering (INCLUDE …) · UNIQUE

Partial indexes: index only the rows you search

A WHERE clause on CREATE INDEX indexes only the matching rows. The work queue of 1,000 pending orders does not need an index over 200,000 rows. A query can use a partial index only if its own WHERE implies the index's condition.

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_pending_created_idx ON big_orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx      ON big_orders (created_at);
SELECT relname, pg_relation_size(oid) / 8192 AS pages
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname IN ('big_orders_pending_created_idx', 'big_orders_created_at_idx');
ROLLBACK;
relnamepages
big_orders_pending_created_idx5
big_orders_created_at_idx551

(2 rows)

Classic uses: job queues (WHERE processed_at IS NULL), soft deletes (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), and partial UNIQUE indexes such as "one active subscription per user".

Covering indexes and Index Only Scans

An Index Only Scan answers from the index alone when (1) every column the query needs is in the index and (2) the page is marked all-visible in the visibility map (VACUUM maintains it; otherwise you see Heap Fetches). INCLUDE adds extra columns to the leaf entries without making them part of the sort key:

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_total_idx ON big_orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT sum(total) FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
ROLLBACK;
Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_customer_total_idx on big_orders (actual rows=5010.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
        Heap Fetches: 0
        Index Searches: 1

Compare Session 44 Q9: the same 5,010 rows cost 1,834 table pages through a plain index. With total in the index, the table is never visited.

Heap Fetches far above 0 on a busy table means the visibility map is behind (VACUUM has not caught up), and the "index only" scan is visiting the table after all. Phase 8 explains why.

GIN: indexes for "contains"

A GIN (generalised inverted index) maps every element (an array item, a JSON key and value, a trigram) to the rows that contain it, like the index at the back of a book. It is fast for @>, ? and &&, and slower to update than a B-tree.

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_events_payload_idx ON big_events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_events WHERE payload @> '{"type": "app_error", "code": "NETWORK"}';
ROLLBACK;
Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on big_events (actual rows=333.00 loops=1)
        Recheck Cond: (payload @> '{"code": "NETWORK", "type": "app_error"}'::jsonb)
        Heap Blocks: exact=333
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_events_payload_idx (actual rows=333.00 loops=1)
              Index Cond: (payload @> '{"code": "NETWORK", "type": "app_error"}'::jsonb)
              Index Searches: 1
  • jsonb_ops (the default) supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&. jsonb_path_ops supports only @> (and JSON path @? / @@), but is smaller and faster.
  • No GIN index helps payload ->> 'type' = 'app_error'. Write it as containment, or build a B-tree expression index on (payload ->> 'type') (Q14).

Trigram indexes: LIKE anywhere in the string

The pg_trgm extension splits text into 3-character pieces ("use", "ser", "er9", …). A GIN trigram index finds candidate rows for LIKE '%abc%', ILIKE and similarity searches; the candidates are then rechecked. The extension ships with Postgres; CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm enables it in a database.

BEGIN;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX big_customers_email_trgm_idx ON big_customers USING gin (email gin_trgm_ops);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_customers WHERE email LIKE '%9999%';
ROLLBACK;
Bitmap Heap Scan on big_customers (actual rows=2.00 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: (email ~~ '%9999%'::text)
  Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 36
  Heap Blocks: exact=20
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_customers_email_trgm_idx (actual rows=38.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (email ~~ '%9999%'::text)
        Index Searches: 1

BRIN: a tiny index for data in physical order

A BRIN (block range index) stores only the minimum and maximum value for each range of 128 table pages. If a column follows the physical order of the table (created_at in an append-only table), "which ranges might contain 1 March?" rules out almost the whole table, using an index of a few kilobytes. If the column is not in physical order, every range contains every value and BRIN is useless (Q11).

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_brin ON big_orders USING brin (created_at);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-03-02';
ROLLBACK;
Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders (actual rows=288.00 loops=1)
        Recheck Cond: ((created_at >= '2025-03-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-03-02 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))
        Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 13664
        Heap Blocks: lossy=128
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_created_brin (actual rows=1280.00 loops=1)
              Index Cond: ((created_at >= '2025-03-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-03-02 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))
              Index Searches: 1

lossy=128: BRIN can only say "somewhere in these 128 pages", so all rows in them are rechecked (13,664 thrown away to find 288). Still about 14× fewer pages than a Seq Scan, from an index of 3 pages.

Exclusion constraints (GiST)

A UNIQUE constraint says "no two rows have equal values". An exclusion constraint generalises it: "no two rows for which all these operators are true". With the btree_gist extension, EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, valid_during WITH &&) means "no two prices for the same product with overlapping periods". The same pattern prevents double-booked tables in your Visitly app: (table_id WITH =, during WITH &&).

  13. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK, on the practice table price_history: enable btree_gist, fix product 3's overlap (end its first period on 2025-02-15), then add the exclusion constraint price_history_no_overlap. Return conname and contype.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

UPDATE price_history
SET valid_during = daterange('2024-06-01', '2025-02-15')
WHERE product_id = 3 AND lower(valid_during) = DATE '2024-06-01';

ALTER TABLE price_history
  ADD CONSTRAINT price_history_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, valid_during WITH &&);

SELECT conname, contype FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'price_history_no_overlap';
ROLLBACK;
    connamecontype
    price_history_no_overlapx

    (1 row)

    contype x = exclusion. Without the fix the ALTER fails: "conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint". btree_gist is needed because GiST does not support = on integers by itself. From now on Postgres refuses any overlapping price, which Session 41 could only detect after the fact.

    Limit → Index Only Scan, Heap Fetches: 0, no Sort: the index has the right order (created_at), all the selected columns (INCLUDE), and only the rows that matter (WHERE). 8 pages instead of 1,166 for the full version, and it is never touched by the 199,000 non-pending orders. A partial covering index is the best tool for queue-like queries.

← Phase 5: Indexes + EXPLAINAll phasesSchema

Phase 5 · Session 48

Join performance

Predict which join algorithm Postgres will choose on real data sizes, give it the indexes it needs, and rewrite joins that cannot be fast.

Topics

The three join algorithms at scale

Session 11 met Nested Loop, Hash Join and Merge Join on 36 rows, where any of them is instant. With 200,000 orders the choice matters. The planner picks from the estimated row counts:

few rows on the outer side + an index on the inner join key    → Nested Loop (a few pages per outer row)
many rows on both sides, no useful order                       → Hash Join   (one pass over each input)
both inputs already sorted (indexes), or ORDER BY the join key  → Merge Join  (zip two sorted lists)

Most bad join plans come from a bad estimate, not from a missing feature: if the planner expects 8 rows where 400 arrive, it picks a nested loop that runs 400 times (Q13).

Index the inner join key

A nested loop is only fast if every lookup on the inner side uses an index on the join column, usually a foreign-key column (Session 11). With an index on created_at, "the 10 newest orders with customer names" reads 10 orders and does 10 customer lookups:

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT o.order_id, o.created_at, c.full_name
FROM big_orders o
JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
ROLLBACK;
Limit (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  ->  Nested Loop (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan Backward using big_orders_created_at_idx on big_orders o (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
              Index Searches: 1
        ->  Memoize (actual rows=1.00 loops=10)
              Cache Key: o.customer_id
              Cache Mode: logical
              Hits: 0  Misses: 10  Evictions: 0  Overflows: 0  Memory Usage: 2kB
              ->  Index Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c (actual rows=1.00 loops=10)
                    Index Cond: (customer_id = o.customer_id)
                    Index Searches: 10

Limit stops the nested loop after 10 rows. Without the created_at index (Q1), Postgres must join all 200,000 orders and sort them to find the newest 10. Index Scan Backward: a B-tree can be read in both directions, so one index serves ASC and DESC.

Hash joins: memory and the build side

  • The Hash node is built from the input with fewer rows after its filters; the other input streams past it.
  • The hash table must fit in work_mem; otherwise it is split into batches on disk (Batches above 1, Session 46 Q12).
  • Hash Right Join / Hash Right Anti Join mean the inputs were swapped so the smaller one could be hashed (Session 11).

Merge joins and order

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
ROLLBACK;
Merge Join
  Merge Cond: (c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c
  ->  Index Scan using big_orders_customer_id_idx on big_orders o

Both indexes return rows already sorted by customer_id, so the merge join needs no Sort node, and its output is already in the ORDER BY order.

Join on the column, not on an expression of it

The sargability rule from Session 45 applies to join conditions too. Joining events to orders with o.order_id::text = e.payload ->> 'order_id' casts the indexed column, so the primary key cannot be used. Cast the other side instead: o.order_id = (e.payload ->> 'order_id')::int (Q10, Q11).

Make the join smaller

If the join only adds labels (the customer's city), aggregate first and join the small result. Postgres does not do this rewrite for you:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.city, sum(x.orders) AS orders
FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders FROM big_orders GROUP BY customer_id) x
JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = x.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
HashAggregate (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  Group Key: c.city
  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 32kB
  ->  Hash Join (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
        Hash Cond: (c.customer_id = x.customer_id)
        ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c (actual rows=20000.00 loops=1)
        ->  Hash (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
              Buckets: 32768  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1094kB
              ->  Subquery Scan on x (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
                    ->  HashAggregate (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
                          Group Key: big_orders.customer_id
                          Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1305kB
                          ->  Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)

The join now handles 19,500 rows instead of 200,000. Same result as joining first and grouping by city.

Anti joins, semi joins and NOT IN

  • NOT EXISTS becomes an Anti Join and stops at the first match. EXISTS becomes a Semi Join, or a join against a de-duplicated list (Q8).
  • NOT IN (subquery) becomes a hashed SubPlan if the subquery's result fits in work_mem. If it does not, it becomes a plain SubPlan that re-reads the subquery for every outer row: 20,000 × 200,000 comparisons here. Add the NULL trap from Session 4, and the rule is simple: use NOT EXISTS.

Top-N per group: LATERAL + an index

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_created_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, x.order_id, x.created_at
FROM big_customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.created_at
  FROM big_orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
  LIMIT 3
) x
WHERE c.customer_id <= 5;
ROLLBACK;
Nested Loop (actual rows=12.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id <= 5)
        Heap Fetches: 0
        Index Searches: 1
  ->  Limit (actual rows=2.40 loops=5)
        ->  Index Scan Backward using big_orders_customer_created_idx on big_orders o (actual rows=2.40 loops=5)
              Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
              Index Searches: 5

For each of the 5 customers: jump to the end of its section of the index and read at most 3 entries. Session 24 did this with row_number(), which has to number every row; LATERAL + index touches only the rows it returns.

JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
    HashAggregate
  Group Key: c.city
  ->  Hash Join
        Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
        ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o
        ->  Hash
              ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c

    A Hash Join: every order is needed, so one pass over each table beats 200,000 index lookups. An index would not help this query.

  4. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index customer_id and show the plan (COSTS OFF) for the orders (full_name, order_id, total) of customers 1 to 5.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id, o.total
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id <= 5;
ROLLBACK;
    Nested Loop
  ->  Index Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c
        Index Cond: (customer_id <= 5)
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders o
        Recheck Cond: (c.customer_id = customer_id)
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_id_idx
              Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)

    A Nested Loop: 5 customers from the primary key, then one index lookup each on big_orders.customer_id. Few outer rows + an inner index.

  5. Same index: show the plan (COSTS OFF) for all customers joined to their orders, ordered by customer_id.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
ROLLBACK;
    Merge Join
  Merge Cond: (c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c
  ->  Index Scan using big_orders_customer_id_idx on big_orders o

    A Merge Join over two index scans. The output order comes for free, so there is no Sort, even for 200,000 rows.

  6. How many customers have never ordered? Use NOT EXISTS.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    SELECT count(*) AS never_ordered
FROM big_customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM big_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
    never_ordered
    500

    (1 row)

    500. The plan is a Hash Right Anti Join: the 20,000 customers are hashed, the orders stream through, and customers that never get a match come out.

  7. Show the plan (COSTS OFF) of the same question written with NOT IN.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*)
FROM big_customers c
WHERE c.customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM big_orders);
    Aggregate
  ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c
        Filter: (NOT (ANY (customer_id = (hashed SubPlan 1).col1)))
        SubPlan 1
          ->  Seq Scan on big_orders

    A hashed SubPlan: the 200,000 customer_ids just fit in work_mem. On a bigger table, or with less memory, it becomes a plain SubPlan that scans big_orders once per customer. Do not run that version with EXPLAIN ANALYZE: it is the slowest query in this course.

  8. How many customers have at least one order above 49,900? Use EXISTS, and look at the plan.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    SELECT count(*) AS big_spenders
FROM big_customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM big_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.total > 49900);
    big_spenders
    389

    (1 row)

    389. The plan has no "Semi Join": Postgres collects the distinct customer_ids of the qualifying orders (HashAggregate) and looks each one up in the primary key. Turning a semi join into "de-duplicate, then plain join" is one of the planner's standard tricks.

  9. Rewrite "orders per city" so that the orders are grouped per customer before the join. Run it with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF). How many rows does the join process now?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.city, sum(x.orders) AS orders
FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders FROM big_orders GROUP BY customer_id) x
JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = x.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
    HashAggregate (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  Group Key: c.city
  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 32kB
  ->  Hash Join (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
        Hash Cond: (c.customer_id = x.customer_id)
        ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c (actual rows=20000.00 loops=1)
        ->  Hash (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
              Buckets: 32768  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1094kB
              ->  Subquery Scan on x (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
                    ->  HashAggregate (actual rows=19500.00 loops=1)
                          Group Key: big_orders.customer_id
                          Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1305kB
                          ->  Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)

    19,500 rows (one per customer who ordered) instead of 200,000. The aggregation itself still reads every order, so the gain is in the join and its memory. The bigger the fan-out, the bigger the win.

  10. Count the checkout events among event_id ≤ 1000 that match an order, joining with o.order_id::text = e.payload ->> 'order_id'. Show the plan (COSTS OFF).

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*)
FROM big_events e
JOIN big_orders o ON o.order_id::text = e.payload ->> 'order_id'
WHERE e.payload @> '{"type": "checkout"}' AND e.event_id <= 1000;
    Aggregate
  ->  Hash Join
        Hash Cond: ((o.order_id)::text = (e.payload ->> 'order_id'::text))
        ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o
        ->  Hash
              ->  Index Scan using big_events_pkey on big_events e
                    Index Cond: (event_id <= 1000)
                    Filter: (payload @> '{"type": "checkout"}'::jsonb)

    A Hash Join with a Seq Scan on big_orders: casting order_id to text hides it from its primary key, so all 200,000 orders are read and hashed for about 40 checkout events.

  11. Fix Q10 by casting the other side, and show the new plan.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*)
FROM big_events e
JOIN big_orders o ON o.order_id = (e.payload ->> 'order_id')::int
WHERE e.payload @> '{"type": "checkout"}' AND e.event_id <= 1000;
    Aggregate
  ->  Nested Loop
        ->  Index Scan using big_events_pkey on big_events e
              Index Cond: (event_id <= 1000)
              Filter: (payload @> '{"type": "checkout"}'::jsonb)
        ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_pkey on big_orders o
              Index Cond: (order_id = ((e.payload ->> 'order_id'::text))::integer)

    A Nested Loop with an Index Only Scan on big_orders_pkey for each event. Same join, same result; the only change is which side gets the cast. Keep indexed columns bare, in joins as in WHERE.

  12. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create the index (customer_id, created_at) and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for the 3 newest orders of each of the customers 1 to 5, with LATERAL.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_created_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, x.order_id, x.created_at
FROM big_customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.created_at
  FROM big_orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
  LIMIT 3
) x
WHERE c.customer_id <= 5;
ROLLBACK;
    Nested Loop (actual rows=12.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_customers_pkey on big_customers c (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id <= 5)
        Heap Fetches: 0
        Index Searches: 1
  ->  Limit (actual rows=2.40 loops=5)
        ->  Index Scan Backward using big_orders_customer_created_idx on big_orders o (actual rows=2.40 loops=5)
              Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
              Index Searches: 5

    The Limit runs 5 times (loops=5), each over an Index Scan Backward that reads at most 3 entries. 12 rows in total: some of these customers have only 2 orders.

  13. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index customer_id and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for every order of the customers with city 'Dubai' and country 'UAE'. Is the nested loop a good choice here?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id, o.total
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.city = 'Dubai' AND c.country = 'UAE';
ROLLBACK;
    Nested Loop (actual rows=4000.00 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c (actual rows=400.00 loops=1)
        Filter: ((city = 'Dubai'::text) AND (country = 'UAE'::text))
        Rows Removed by Filter: 19600
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders o (actual rows=10.00 loops=400)
        Recheck Cond: (c.customer_id = customer_id)
        Heap Blocks: exact=4000
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_id_idx (actual rows=10.00 loops=400)
              Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
              Index Searches: 400

    No. The planner expected 8 Dubai customers (Session 46 challenge), so 8 index lookups looked cheap. Really it ran 400 lookups and visited 4,000 table pages, more than reading the whole table (1,834). A wrong estimate picked the wrong algorithm. Session 52 fixes the estimate, and Postgres then switches to a Hash Join by itself.

  14. Show EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for March 2025 orders joined to their customers (order_id, full_name). Which input does Postgres put into the hash table, and why that one?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT o.order_id, c.full_name
FROM big_orders o
JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND o.created_at < '2025-04-01';
    Hash Join (actual rows=8928.00 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o (actual rows=8928.00 loops=1)
        Filter: ((created_at >= '2025-03-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2025-04-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))
        Rows Removed by Filter: 191072
  ->  Hash (actual rows=20000.00 loops=1)
        Buckets: 32768  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1220kB
        ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c (actual rows=20000.00 loops=1)

    big_customers (20,000 rows) is hashed and the 8,928 March orders probe it. That looks backwards (8,928 < 20,000), but the cost also depends on row width and on where the filter runs: the orders' filter is applied while scanning, and hashing the narrow customers table was estimated to be cheaper. When in doubt, the plan tells you what the planner thought; do not guess.

  15. Challenge: For each of the 400 customers in Dubai: customer_id, full_name and their newest order's created_at and total. Write it twice: (a) DISTINCT ON over a join (Session 10) and (b) LATERAL … LIMIT 1 with an index that makes each lookup an Index Only Scan. Compare the pages read with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF), and return the plan of (b).

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
-- (a) for comparison: reads all of big_orders (about 2,050 pages)
-- EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
-- SELECT DISTINCT ON (c.customer_id) c.customer_id, c.full_name, o.created_at, o.total
-- FROM big_customers c JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
-- WHERE c.city = 'Dubai'
-- ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.created_at DESC;

CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_latest_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, x.created_at, x.total
FROM big_customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT o.created_at, o.total
  FROM big_orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
  LIMIT 1
) x
WHERE c.city = 'Dubai';
ROLLBACK;
    Nested Loop (actual rows=400.00 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=1012 read=407
  ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c (actual rows=400.00 loops=1)
        Filter: (city = 'Dubai'::text)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 19600
        Buffers: shared hit=218
  ->  Limit (actual rows=1.00 loops=400)
        Buffers: shared hit=794 read=407
        ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_customer_latest_idx on big_orders o (actual rows=1.00 loops=400)
              Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
              Heap Fetches: 0
              Index Searches: 400
              Buffers: shared hit=794 read=407
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=5 read=1

    (a) hashes the 400 customers, reads all 200,000 orders, sorts 4,000 and keeps 400: about 2,050 pages. (b) does 400 index probes of about 3 pages each, about 1,420 pages, with no table access (Heap Fetches: 0) and no sort. More importantly, (a) grows with the size of big_orders and (b) does not: with 20 million orders, (a) reads 100× more and (b) about the same. Per-group lookups through an index are how "latest X per Y" stays fast at any size.

← Phase 5: Indexes + EXPLAINAll phasesSchema

Phase 5 · Session 49

Review: indexes, plans and joins

Pull Sessions 44–48 back out of memory, mixed with window functions, anti joins and JSONB on the big tables.

Topics

How to run this review

  • First 20 minutes: redo every question in mistakes.md from Sessions 44–48, cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below. For each plan question, predict the plan before you run EXPLAIN, and write your prediction down. Being wrong is the useful part.
  • Then the challenge: make a whole customer dashboard come from index-only scans.

Checklist for a slow query

1. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) it. Read inside-out.
2. Find where the rows (or pages) explode: a Seq Scan with a huge "Rows Removed by Filter",
   a nested loop with high loops, a Sort or Hash that spills to disk.
3. Compare estimated and actual rows on every node. 10× off? Fix the estimate first (Session 52).
4. Is the condition sargable? Function or cast on the column, wrong type, leading wildcard?
5. Which index would let Postgres read only what it returns?
   equality columns first, range/ORDER BY column next, INCLUDE what the SELECT needs,
   WHERE for the subset you always query.
6. Can the query do less? Aggregate before joining, LATERAL + LIMIT per group, NOT EXISTS.
7. Re-run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Compare pages, not just milliseconds.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 44–48

Seq Scan cost             pages × 1 + rows × 0.01 (+ rows × 0.0025 per filter operator)
Read the plan             inside-out; actual rows are PER LOOP; compare rows= with actual rows=
Index Cond vs Filter      navigated vs checked afterwards ("Rows Removed by Filter")
Bitmap vs Index Scan      many rows / scattered → bitmap; few rows / order needed → index scan
Index Only Scan           all needed columns in the index (INCLUDE) + all-visible pages
Composite index           equality first, range last; leftmost prefix only
Not sargable              f(column), column::type, LIKE '%x', <>, wrong literal type
Special indexes           partial (WHERE), expression, GIN (@>, ?, trigram), BRIN (ordered data)
Joins                     few outer rows + inner index → Nested Loop; all rows → Hash; sorted → Merge

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s49.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Compute the cost of a Seq Scan on big_customers from pg_class, and check it against EXPLAIN.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    SELECT relpages * current_setting('seq_page_cost')::numeric
     + reltuples::numeric * current_setting('cpu_tuple_cost')::numeric AS seq_scan_cost
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname = 'big_customers';
    seq_scan_cost
    418.00

    (1 row)

    218 + 20,000 × 0.01 = 418, the same as EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big_customers.

  2. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index created_at, then show the plan for counting the orders of 2025 written with extract(year FROM created_at) = 2025.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE extract(year FROM created_at) = 2025;
ROLLBACK;
    Aggregate
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders
        Filter: (EXTRACT(year FROM created_at) = '2025'::numeric)

    A Seq Scan: a function on the column.

  3. Rewrite Q2 so the index can be used, and show the plan.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01';
ROLLBACK;
    Aggregate
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_created_at_idx on big_orders
        Index Cond: ((created_at >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone) AND (created_at < '2026-01-01 00:00:00+05:30'::timestamp with time zone))

    An Index Only Scan over almost half the table. It is still cheap: the index is much smaller than the table and is read in order.

  4. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for customer 42's orders, without any extra index. Compare estimated and actual rows.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
    Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..4334.00 rows=5010 width=47) (actual rows=5010.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 42)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 194990

    Estimated 5,010, actual 5,010: exact. For an ordinary customer the planner estimates about 10 (S46 Q3). It knows customer 42 is special because 42 is in the column's list of most common values with its exact frequency (Session 52).

  5. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: with a GIN index (jsonb_path_ops) on big_events.payload, show the plan for counting searches for 'desk'.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_events_payload_idx ON big_events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_events WHERE payload @> '{"type": "search", "query": "desk"}';
ROLLBACK;
    Aggregate
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on big_events
        Recheck Cond: (payload @> '{"type": "search", "query": "desk"}'::jsonb)
        ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_events_payload_idx
              Index Cond: (payload @> '{"type": "search", "query": "desk"}'::jsonb)

    Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index.

  6. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index coupon and show the plan (COSTS OFF) for counting the orders that used any coupon.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_coupon_idx ON big_orders (coupon);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE coupon IS NOT NULL;
ROLLBACK;
    Aggregate
  ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_coupon_idx on big_orders
        Index Cond: (coupon IS NOT NULL)

    IS NOT NULL can use a B-tree (NULLs are stored in it too). count(*) needs no other column, so it is an index-only plan. A partial index WHERE coupon IS NOT NULL would contain only the 4,588 orders that used one.

  7. How many customers have 'Kabir Kh' somewhere in their name, in any letter case? Write a query that a trigram index could serve.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    SELECT count(*) FROM big_customers WHERE full_name ILIKE '%kabir kh%';
    count
    167

    (1 row)

    167. A B-tree cannot serve ILIKE '%…%'; a GIN trigram index (Session 47) can.

  8. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create indexes on big_orders(customer_id) and big_orders(created_at), then list every index of big_orders with its size, largest first: indexname, size.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
SELECT indexname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass)) AS size
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'big_orders'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass) DESC;
ROLLBACK;
    indexnamesize
    big_orders_pkey4408 kB
    big_orders_created_at_idx4408 kB
    big_orders_customer_id_idx1848 kB

    (3 rows)

    Three indexes. The two unique-ish ones (order_id, created_at) are about 4.4 MB each; customer_id is smaller thanks to deduplication (Session 44). Together they are already about three quarters of the table's size.

  9. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create the index (customer_id, status) and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for customer 42's cancelled orders. Are both conditions in the Index Cond?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_status_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, status);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'cancelled';
ROLLBACK;
    Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders (actual rows=985.00 loops=1)
  Recheck Cond: ((customer_id = 42) AND (status = 'cancelled'::text))
  Heap Blocks: exact=985
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_status_idx (actual rows=985.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((customer_id = 42) AND (status = 'cancelled'::text))
        Index Searches: 1

    Yes: two equalities, so the index jumps straight to (42, cancelled). With two equality columns the order inside the index matters less for this query; choose it by which other queries can use a leftmost prefix.

  10. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create a partial index on (customer_id) WHERE status = 'cancelled' and the full (customer_id, status) index from Q9, and compare their sizes in pages.

    Expected: 2 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_cancelled_customer_idx ON big_orders (customer_id) WHERE status = 'cancelled';
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_status_idx   ON big_orders (customer_id, status);
SELECT relname, pg_relation_size(oid) / 8192 AS pages
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname IN ('big_orders_cancelled_customer_idx', 'big_orders_customer_status_idx')
ORDER BY pages;
ROLLBACK;
    relnamepages
    big_orders_cancelled_customer_idx9
    big_orders_customer_status_idx260

    (2 rows)

    The partial index is tiny (only 5,910 cancelled orders); the full one indexes all 200,000. If the app only ever asks for one status, the partial index is the better buy.

  11. The 2 newest orders of each of the customers 1 to 5, using row_number(). Return customer_id, order_id, created_at, ordered by customer_id, created_at descending. Put the customer filter where it lets Postgres avoid numbering all 200,000 orders.

    Expected: 8 rows

    Answer
    SELECT customer_id, order_id, created_at
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, created_at,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM big_orders
  WHERE customer_id <= 5
) t
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC;
    customer_idorder_idcreated_at
    21976792025-11-17 09:10:27+05:30
    21776792025-09-08 22:32:07+05:30
    31953582025-11-09 07:47:34+05:30
    31753582025-08-31 21:09:14+05:30
    41930372025-11-01 06:24:41+05:30
    41730372025-08-23 19:41:21+05:30
    51907162025-10-24 04:56:48+05:30
    51707162025-08-15 18:18:28+05:30

    (8 rows)

    8 rows: customer 1 has never ordered (every order the formula would give customer 1 went to the hot customer 42 instead). Filtering inside means only these customers' orders are numbered. Postgres can also push a filter on the PARTITION BY column through the window, but writing it inside makes the intent and the plan obvious.

  12. Delivered revenue per month in 2025 with a running total (Session 25 on the big table): month, revenue, running_total, ordered by month.

    Expected: 11 rows

Write it as one query for customer 42, and create the one index that makes every part an Index Only Scan. Return the plan from EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF).

  'spent',  (SELECT sum(total) FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 42),
  'latest', (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('order_id', order_id, 'created_at', created_at, 'total', total)
                              ORDER BY created_at DESC)
             FROM (SELECT order_id, created_at, total
                   FROM big_orders

                Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)

                Index Searches: 1
  InitPlan 2

                Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
                Heap Fetches: 0
                Index Searches: 1
  InitPlan 3

                ->  Index Only Scan using big_orders_dashboard_idx on big_orders big_orders_2 (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
                      Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
                      Heap Fetches: 0
                      Index Searches: 1

    Three InitPlans, each an Index Only Scan on the same index with Heap Fetches: 0. The sort order (created_at DESC) serves the "latest 5" with no Sort node; INCLUDE serves sum(total) and the JSON fields. Without it this is three passes over the table, or 3 × 1,834 pages for customer 42. One well-designed index per screen of your app is a good target.

Phase 5 · Session 50

Sorting and grouping

Know what ORDER BY, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, min/max and window functions cost, and let indexes deliver rows already in order.

Topics

What a sort costs

A Sort node must read all of its input before it can return the first row (Session 46: startup ≈ total). How it sorts depends on memory (work_mem, 4 MB by default):

quicksort        everything fits in work_mem
top-N heapsort   ORDER BY … LIMIT n: keeps only the best n rows in memory, whatever the input size
external merge   does not fit: sorted chunks are written to temporary files and merged ("Disk: …kB")
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 10;
Limit (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
  ->  Sort (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
        Sort Key: total DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 26kB
        ->  Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)

Cheap in memory, but every one of the 200,000 rows still had to be read and compared. Only an index on total could avoid reading them all.

Let an index deliver the order

A B-tree returns rows in key order, forwards or backwards. If the ORDER BY matches an index, there is no Sort node at all, and a LIMIT can stop after n rows.

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_created_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
ROLLBACK;
Limit
  ->  Index Scan Backward using big_orders_customer_created_idx on big_orders
        Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
Index (a, b) delivers, with no Sort:
  ORDER BY a            ORDER BY a, b            ORDER BY a DESC, b DESC   (read backwards)
  WHERE a = 5 ORDER BY b                  WHERE a = 5 ORDER BY b DESC
It does NOT deliver:
  ORDER BY b            ORDER BY a, b DESC  (mixed directions: needs an index on (a, b DESC))

Incremental sort

When an index provides only the first sort key, Postgres (13+) can sort just within each group of equal leading keys. With a LIMIT it stops after the first groups:

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_orders ORDER BY customer_id, created_at LIMIT 20;
ROLLBACK;
Limit (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
  ->  Incremental Sort (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
        Sort Key: customer_id, created_at
        Presorted Key: customer_id
        Full-sort Groups: 1  Sort Method: quicksort  Average Memory: 26kB  Peak Memory: 26kB
        ->  Index Scan using big_orders_customer_id_idx on big_orders (actual rows=21.00 loops=1)
              Index Searches: 1

21 rows read through the index, sorted in tiny groups, done. A full sort would have read all 200,000.

Grouping: hash or sorted

HashAggregate   builds a hash table with one entry per group; input in any order.
                Memory grows with the number of GROUPS; beyond work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier
                it spills to disk in batches.
GroupAggregate  needs input sorted by the group key (from an index or a Sort node);
                streams through it with almost no memory and can return groups early.

DISTINCT is planned the same way (HashAggregate or Unique over sorted input). count(DISTINCT x) is the exception: it always sorts or de-duplicates inside the Aggregate node, which EXPLAIN does not show, and it never uses a hash table. The rewrite SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT x …) can.

min and max

With an index on the column, max(created_at) reads one index entry from the end: Postgres rewrites it as ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1. Without the index it reads the whole table.

work_mem is the limit per sort or hash operation, per query, per connection. 100 connections × 3 sorts × 64 MB could use 19 GB. Raise it for one heavy query with SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB' inside its transaction, not for the whole server (Session 53).

Questions

Phase 5 · Session 51

Pagination

Replace OFFSET with keyset pagination that costs the same on page 1 and page 10,000, and handle ties, previous pages and total counts.

Topics

OFFSET pagination and why it gets slow

LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 still produces 100,020 rows and throws away the first 100,000. Page 1 is fast, page 5,001 is slow, and the database repeats that work on every request. If rows are inserted between two requests, the pages shift: a user sees a row twice, or never.

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_order_idx ON big_orders (created_at, order_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT order_id, created_at, total
FROM big_orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
ROLLBACK;
Limit (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan Backward using big_orders_created_order_idx on big_orders (actual rows=100020.00 loops=1)
        Index Searches: 1

Keyset (seek) pagination

Remember where the previous page ended (the sort key of its last row) and ask for the rows that come after it:

SELECT … FROM big_orders
WHERE (created_at, order_id) < (:last_created_at, :last_order_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 20;
BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_order_idx ON big_orders (created_at, order_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT order_id, created_at, total
FROM big_orders
WHERE (created_at, order_id) < ('2025-11-25 09:04:13+05:30', 199981)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 20;
ROLLBACK;
Limit (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan Backward using big_orders_created_order_idx on big_orders (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (ROW(created_at, order_id) < ROW('2025-11-25 09:04:13+05:30'::timestamp with time zone, 199981))
        Index Searches: 1
  • The index jumps to the cursor and reads 20 entries, on page 2 or on page 50,000.
  • The sort order must be unique. Add the primary key as the last ORDER BY column (the tiebreaker). Otherwise rows with equal sort keys can be skipped or repeated at page boundaries (Q11).
  • A row comparison (a, b) < (x, y) means a < x OR (a = x AND b < y): exactly "comes before in this order". Postgres turns it into a single index range. It only works when all columns sort in the same direction.
  • Inserts no longer shift pages: the cursor points at a value, not at a position.
  • You cannot jump to "page 37". You get next and previous, which is all that infinite scroll, "load more" buttons and API cursors need. You can also jump to a value: "orders before 1 July" (Q13).

Previous page

Flip the comparison and the sort direction, take 20 rows, and reverse them in an outer query (Q9).

Total counts

"Page 3 of 10,000" needs count(*), which reads every matching row (or index entry) on every request. The options:

  • Do not show a total. Most feeds do not.
  • Show an estimate: reltuples from pg_class, or the rows= of EXPLAIN for a filtered query.
  • Cap it: count at most 10,001 rows and show "10,000+".
SELECT count(*) AS counted
FROM (SELECT 1 FROM big_orders WHERE status = 'delivered' LIMIT 10001) t;
counted
10001

(1 row)

For an API, hand the client an opaque cursor: the last row's sort key encoded as a string (Q14), which it sends back to get the next page. Never expose OFFSET in a public API over a big table: it is a denial-of-service waiting to happen.

  11. The tiebreaker trap, concretely. Paging by total (highest first) with 10 per page and no tiebreaker: what total does the 10th order have, and how many orders share it?

    Expected: 1 row

FROM big_orders
WHERE total = (SELECT total FROM big_orders ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 9)
GROUP BY total;
    totalorders_with_this_total
    49997.714

    (1 row)

    49,997.71 is shared by 4 orders: 2 fall on page 1 and 2 on page 2, and without a tiebreaker which ones is not defined. With OFFSET a user can see one order twice and miss another; with keyset on total alone (total < 49997.71) the other two would be skipped entirely. Sort by total DESC, order_id DESC.

  14. Build an API cursor: from the last row of page 1 (order 199,981), produce an opaque string containing its created_at and order_id as JSON, base64-encoded. Then decode it back to (created_at, order_id) in the same query.

    Expected: 1 row

    WITH last_row AS (
  SELECT created_at, order_id FROM big_orders WHERE order_id = 199981
),
cursor AS (
  SELECT encode(convert_to(jsonb_build_object('t', created_at, 'id', order_id)::text, 'UTF8'), 'base64') AS c
  FROM last_row
)
SELECT c AS cursor,
       (convert_from(decode(c, 'base64'), 'UTF8')::jsonb ->> 't')::timestamptz AS created_at,
       (convert_from(decode(c, 'base64'), 'UTF8')::jsonb ->> 'id')::int       AS order_id
FROM cursor;

  15. Challenge: Paginate big_customers by signup date (oldest first), 20 per page, with keyset pagination. The cursor for page 3 is the 40th customer in that order. (1) Choose the ORDER BY and the index. (2) Get page 3 with a keyset query; for the exercise, compute the cursor with a CTE using OFFSET 39. (3) Check that it returns exactly the same 20 customers as OFFSET 40 LIMIT 20. Return page 3: customer_id, signup_date.

    Expected: 20 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_customers_signup_idx ON big_customers (signup_date, customer_id);

WITH cursor AS (
  SELECT signup_date, customer_id
  FROM big_customers
  ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id
  OFFSET 39 LIMIT 1
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.signup_date
FROM big_customers c, cursor k
WHERE (c.signup_date, c.customer_id) > (k.signup_date, k.customer_id)
ORDER BY c.signup_date, c.customer_id
LIMIT 20;

-- check: (the keyset page) EXCEPT (SELECT customer_id, signup_date FROM big_customers
--         ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id OFFSET 40 LIMIT 20)  → 0 rows
ROLLBACK;

Two questions for any paginated screen: what makes the order unique, and which index serves "WHERE (keys) > cursor ORDER BY keys"?

Phase 5 · Session 52

Query rewriting and statistics

Read the statistics the planner uses, fix estimates that are wrong (stale data, correlated columns, generic plans), and rewrite queries the planner cannot optimise.

Topics

Where estimates come from

ANALYZE (run by autovacuum, by you, or by VACUUM ANALYZE) reads a sample of each table and stores per-column statistics. The planner turns them into row estimates; the estimates decide the plan. The pg_stats view shows them:

SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals::text AS mcv, most_common_freqs::text AS mcv_freqs, correlation
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'big_orders' AND attname IN ('status', 'coupon')
ORDER BY attname;
attnamenull_fracn_distinctmcvmcv_freqscorrelation
coupon0.977062{SAVE10,FEST20}{0.02,0.00294}0.77704215
status04{delivered,cancelled,shipped,pending}{0.95545,0.02955,0.01,0.005}0.9443575

(2 rows)

null_frac          fraction of NULLs                         coupon: 97.7% NULL
n_distinct         number of distinct values (negative = fraction of rows: -1 means unique)
most_common_vals   the most frequent values, with their exact frequencies (MCV list)
histogram_bounds   for the other values: boundaries that split them into equal-sized buckets
correlation        how well the physical row order follows the column's order (-1 … 1)
  • status = 'pending': in the MCV list with frequency 0.005, so the estimate is 200,000 × 0.005 = 1,000.
  • customer_id = 7: not frequent enough to stand out, so the estimate is the average share per value: 200,000 ÷ 19,500 ≈ 10. Customer 42 is in the MCV list, so it gets its exact 5,010 (Session 49 Q4).
  • total > 49000: the share of the histogram buckets above 49,000.
  • Several conditions: their selectivities are multiplied, as if the columns were independent. That is the big weakness (below).

The statistics target

The sample size is 300 × the statistics target (default 100: 30,000 rows), and the MCV list and histogram hold up to "target" entries. For a skewed column, raise it: ALTER TABLE big_orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 500; ANALYZE big_orders;. big.sql sets 1,000 on order_id so that ANALYZE reads all 200,000 rows, which makes the statistics identical on every machine.

Correlated columns: CREATE STATISTICS

Every Dubai customer is in the UAE, but the planner multiplies 2% (city) × 2% (country) and expects 8 of 20,000 rows instead of 400 (Session 46). Extended statistics teach it that one column determines the other:

BEGIN;
CREATE STATISTICS big_customers_city_country (dependencies) ON city, country FROM big_customers;
ANALYZE big_customers;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM big_customers WHERE city = 'Dubai' AND country = 'UAE';
ROLLBACK;
Seq Scan on big_customers  (cost=0.00..518.00 rows=400 width=51) (actual rows=400.00 loops=1)
  Filter: ((city = 'Dubai'::text) AND (country = 'UAE'::text))
  Rows Removed by Filter: 19600
  • dependencies: "city determines country" (functional dependency). Good for equality on both columns.
  • ndistinct: the number of distinct (city, country) combinations, used for GROUP BY estimates.
  • mcv: the most common combinations with their frequencies, the most precise option.
  • Nothing happens until the next ANALYZE: CREATE STATISTICS only defines what to collect.

Stale statistics

Statistics describe the table as it was at the last ANALYZE. After a bulk load or a big UPDATE, estimates can be wildly wrong until autovacuum runs ANALYZE again (Q10). Run ANALYZE table yourself right after bulk changes, especially before the next big query.

Generic plans for prepared statements

Applications send parameterised queries (WHERE status = $1). For the first 5 executions Postgres plans with the real value (a custom plan). After that it may switch to one generic plan for all values, if that does not look more expensive on average. For skewed columns, one plan cannot fit every value:

BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_status_idx ON big_orders (status);
PREPARE orders_by_status(text) AS SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE status = $1;
SET LOCAL plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE orders_by_status('delivered');
DEALLOCATE orders_by_status;
ROLLBACK;
Index Scan using big_orders_status_idx on big_orders
  Index Cond: (status = $1)

The generic plan uses the index for every value, including delivered (95% of the table), where the custom plan would read the table sequentially (Q12). If a parameterised query is fast in psql and slow from the application, generic plans are a prime suspect. plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan fixes it for that session or role.

Rewrites the planner cannot do for you

Pattern                                     Rewrite
------------------------------------------  ------------------------------------------------------------
OR across two joined tables                 UNION of two selective queries                          (Q13)
scalar subquery per row in the SELECT list  JOIN + GROUP BY, or LATERAL                             (Q14)
CTE that blocks a filter (MATERIALIZED)     plain CTE (inlined), or move the filter inside           (Q8)
function / cast on an indexed column        sargable condition or expression index           (Session 45)
NOT IN (subquery)                           NOT EXISTS                                        (Session 48)
DISTINCT to undo a join fan-out             EXISTS (semi join)                                (Session 48)
join, then aggregate                        aggregate, then join                              (Session 48)

Before rewriting, check the estimates. Many "the planner is stupid" moments are really "the planner was given wrong numbers". Fix the statistics first; rewrite only what statistics cannot fix.

Write your answers in psql/s52.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  7. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index big_orders(customer_id), create the city/country statistics, ANALYZE, and show the plan (COSTS OFF) for all orders of Dubai/UAE customers. Compare it with Session 48 Q13.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
CREATE STATISTICS big_customers_city_country (dependencies) ON city, country FROM big_customers;
ANALYZE big_customers;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id, o.total
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.city = 'Dubai' AND c.country = 'UAE';

    Hash Join
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders o
  ->  Hash
        ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c
              Filter: ((city = 'Dubai'::text) AND (country = 'UAE'::text))

    A Hash Join: with 400 customers expected instead of 8, 400 index lookups (4,000 table pages) no longer look cheap, so Postgres reads big_orders once (1,834 pages). Better statistics, better plan, and no query change.

SELECT * FROM o WHERE order_id = 5;

  Filter: (order_id = 5)
  CTE o
    ->  Seq Scan on big_orders

    A CTE Scan over a Seq Scan of all 200,000 orders, filtered afterwards. Without MATERIALIZED the CTE is inlined, the filter reaches the table, and it is a primary-key lookup (Session 19, now on a table where it matters).

SELECT order_id + 200000, customer_id, created_at + INTERVAL '700 days', 'returned', total, shipping_city, coupon
FROM big_orders WHERE order_id <= 50000;

-- before: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE status = 'returned';
--         estimated rows=1, actual 50000

ANALYZE big_orders;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE status = 'returned';
ROLLBACK;
    Aggregate  (cost=5535.00..5535.01 rows=1 width=8) (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders  (cost=0.00..5410.00 rows=50000 width=0) (actual rows=50000.00 loops=1)
        Filter: (status = 'returned'::text)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 200000

    Before ANALYZE: estimated 1 row, actual 50,000. The statistics have never seen 'returned', so the planner assumes it is extremely rare. A query joining these rows would have been planned for 1 row. After ANALYZE: 50,000 estimated. Bulk load → ANALYZE.

  11. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index status, PREPARE orders_by_status(text) AS SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE status = $1, and show the custom plans (EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE …) for 'pending' and for 'delivered'. Return the 'delivered' one.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_status_idx ON big_orders (status);
PREPARE orders_by_status(text) AS SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE status = $1;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE orders_by_status('pending');     -- Index Scan
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE orders_by_status('delivered');
DEALLOCATE orders_by_status;
ROLLBACK;
    Seq Scan on big_orders
  Filter: (status = 'delivered'::text)

    Custom plans: an Index Scan for 'pending' (1,000 rows) and a Seq Scan for 'delivered' (191,090 rows). Each value gets the plan that suits it. Note: DEALLOCATE is needed because prepared statements belong to the session, not the transaction: ROLLBACK does not remove them.

  12. Same prepared statement, but with SET LOCAL plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan: show the plan for 'delivered'. Why is this a problem?

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_status_idx ON big_orders (status);
PREPARE orders_by_status(text) AS SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE status = $1;
SET LOCAL plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE orders_by_status('delivered');
DEALLOCATE orders_by_status;
ROLLBACK;
    Index Scan using big_orders_status_idx on big_orders
  Index Cond: (status = $1)

    One generic plan for all values, an Index Scan with status = $1, used even for 'delivered', where it means 191,090 index lookups instead of one sequential pass. Postgres switches to a generic plan by itself after 5 executions if it does not look worse on average; with skewed data the average hides the bad case. Watch for this with ORMs and connection poolers that prepare statements.

  13. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index big_orders(customer_id), big_orders(coupon) and big_customers(email). The orders of the customer with email 'user123@mail.test' OR with coupon 'FEST20': rewrite the OR-over-a-join as a UNION, and show EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF) for the rewrite.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX big_orders_coupon_idx ON big_orders (coupon);
CREATE INDEX big_customers_email_idx ON big_customers (email);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT o.order_id
FROM big_orders o JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.email = 'user123@mail.test'
UNION
SELECT o.order_id
FROM big_orders o
WHERE o.coupon = 'FEST20';
ROLLBACK;
    HashAggregate (actual rows=598.00 loops=1)
  Group Key: o.order_id
  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 57kB
  Buffers: shared hit=600 read=5
  ->  Append (actual rows=598.00 loops=1)
        Buffers: shared hit=600 read=5
        ->  Nested Loop (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
              Buffers: shared hit=12 read=3
              ->  Index Scan using big_customers_email_idx on big_customers c (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
                    Index Cond: (email = 'user123@mail.test'::text)
                    Index Searches: 1
                    Buffers: shared hit=1 read=2
              ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on big_orders o (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
                    Recheck Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
                    Heap Blocks: exact=10
                    Buffers: shared hit=11 read=1
                    ->  Bitmap Index Scan on big_orders_customer_id_idx (actual rows=10.00 loops=1)
                          Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
                          Index Searches: 1
                          Buffers: shared hit=1 read=1
        ->  Index Scan using big_orders_coupon_idx on big_orders o_1 (actual rows=588.00 loops=1)
              Index Cond: (coupon = 'FEST20'::text)
              Index Searches: 1
              Buffers: shared hit=588 read=2
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=29 read=6

    598 orders from about 600 pages: the first branch is an index lookup of one customer plus their 10 orders, the second an index scan of 588 coupon orders. The OR version can only test the condition after joining every order to its customer (Seq Scans, about 2,050 pages), because neither half of the OR is a condition on one table alone. UNION (not UNION ALL) removes an order that matches both branches.

  14. Show the plan (plain EXPLAIN, COSTS OFF; do not ANALYZE it) of a per-row scalar subquery: every Dubai customer with (SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id), with no index on big_orders.customer_id. Then write the join version and return its result: customer_id, orders, ordered by customer_id.

    Expected: 400 rows

    Answer
    -- EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT c.customer_id,
--   (SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS orders
-- FROM big_customers c WHERE c.city = 'Dubai';
-- → SubPlan 1: a Seq Scan of big_orders for EACH of the 400 customers

SELECT c.customer_id, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM big_customers c
LEFT JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.city = 'Dubai'
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
    customer_idorders
    710
    5710
    10710
    15710
    20710
    25710
    30710
    35710
    40710
    45710
    50710
    55710

    (400 rows, first 12 shown)

    The SubPlan runs once per customer: without an index, 400 full scans of big_orders (400 × 1,834 pages). The join version reads big_orders once. With an index on customer_id the SubPlan becomes 400 cheap lookups and is fine, so the real fix is "never a per-row subquery without an index".

  15. Challenge: A report runs: "orders per customer for customers in Dubai, UAE, who have at least one order above 45,000". It is slow and its plan is built on wrong estimates. Fix it in three steps inside one transaction: (1) correct the estimate (statistics), (2) add the index the join needs, (3) write the filter as EXISTS. Return customer_id and orders for those customers, ordered by orders descending, then customer_id.

    Expected: 320 rows

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE STATISTICS big_customers_city_country (dependencies) ON city, country FROM big_customers;
ANALYZE big_customers;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);

-- check the plan first: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) <query below>

SELECT c.customer_id, count(*) AS orders
FROM big_customers c
JOIN big_orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.city = 'Dubai' AND c.country = 'UAE'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM big_orders x
              WHERE x.customer_id = c.customer_id AND x.total > 45000)
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.customer_id;
ROLLBACK;
    customer_idorders
    5710
    10710
    20710
    25710
    35710
    40710
    50710
    55710
    65710
    70710
    75710
    80710

    (320 rows, first 12 shown)

    Statistics first, because a wrong estimate makes every other decision wrong. Then the index, so the EXISTS check is a cheap lookup per customer. Then EXISTS instead of joining the big orders and de-duplicating with DISTINCT. In real life you would keep the statistics and the index (COMMIT), and check with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) after each step to see which one mattered. 320 of the 400 Dubai customers qualify.

Phase 5 · Session 53

Monitoring and settings

Find the queries and indexes that matter with the statistics views and pg_stat_statements, and know which settings change plans and which protect the server.

Topics

Queries first, settings second

Sessions 44–52 fixed individual queries: indexes, rewrites, statistics. Settings work differently. They change how the planner prices every plan and how much memory each operation may use. A setting can help all queries a little, or one query a lot (SET LOCAL). It cannot fix a missing index.

Reading and changing settings

SELECT name, setting, unit, context
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('work_mem', 'random_page_cost', 'effective_cache_size', 'shared_buffers',
               'maintenance_work_mem', 'max_parallel_workers_per_gather', 'jit')
ORDER BY name;
namesettingunitcontext
effective_cache_size5242888kBuser
jitoff∅user
maintenance_work_mem65536kBuser
max_parallel_workers_per_gather0∅user
random_page_cost4∅user
shared_buffers163848kBpostmaster
work_mem4096kBuser

(7 rows)

  • setting is in unit: shared_buffers 16384 × 8kB = 128 MB; work_mem 4096 kB = 4 MB.
  • context says how a change takes effect: user (any session can SET it), sighup (reload the server config), postmaster (restart). shared_buffers needs a restart.
SET work_mem = '64MB';                         this session
SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB';                   this transaction only (the safest way to tune one query)
ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem = '64MB';    every new session of that role
ALTER DATABASE practice SET jit = off;         every new session in that database
ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '16MB';            whole server (written to postgresql.auto.conf),
SELECT pg_reload_conf();                       then reload
SHOW work_mem;                                 current value

Settings that change plans

random_page_cost        4      price of a random page read (a sequential read = 1). On SSDs and cloud disks
                               random reads are nearly as cheap: 1.1 is the usual setting. Makes index plans win more often.
effective_cache_size    4GB    how much data the planner may assume is cached (Postgres + OS). Bigger → index scans
                               look cheaper. Set it to about 50–75% of RAM; it allocates nothing.
work_mem                4MB    memory per sort / hash before spilling; also changes plan choices (Session 50 Q9)
max_parallel_workers_per_gather  2 (0 in this course)   worker processes per parallel plan node
default_statistics_target        100   sample and MCV size for ANALYZE (Session 52)
BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_total_idx ON big_orders (total);
SET LOCAL random_page_cost = 1.1;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE total > 30000;
ROLLBACK;
Index Scan using big_orders_total_idx on big_orders
  Index Cond: (total > '30000'::numeric)

With the default (4) the same query is a Seq Scan (Q5). Neither is "right" in general: the correct value describes your hardware. Change it, then measure both plans with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on realistic data.

Settings that protect the server

  • statement_timeout: cancel any statement running longer than this. Set it per role for web apps (for example 30s), so a runaway query cannot hold connections forever.
  • idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: end sessions that opened a transaction and went quiet; they block VACUUM and hold locks (Phase 6).
  • lock_timeout: give up waiting for a lock instead of queueing forever (Phase 6, migrations).
  • log_min_duration_statement: log every statement slower than this, for example 500ms. Your first source of slow queries.
  • maintenance_work_mem: memory for CREATE INDEX and VACUUM. Raising it speeds up building indexes on big tables.
  • shared_buffers: Postgres's own page cache. 25% of RAM is the common starting point; needs a restart.

Parallel query and JIT

For big scans, Postgres can split a Seq Scan, a join or an aggregate across worker processes: the plan shows Gather → Parallel Seq Scan (and Partial / Finalize Aggregate). JIT compiles expressions to machine code for long analytical queries, but the compilation itself takes tens of milliseconds, which hurts short queries. big.sql switched both off so the plans in this course stay simple. Turn them back on with ALTER DATABASE practice RESET max_parallel_workers_per_gather; ALTER DATABASE practice RESET jit; and reconnect (Q12).

Monitoring: the statistics views

pg_stat_user_tables     per table: seq_scan, idx_scan, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
pg_stat_user_indexes    per index: idx_scan (0 = never used since the last stats reset)
pg_statio_user_tables   per table: heap_blks_hit vs heap_blks_read (cache hit ratio)
pg_stat_activity        every connection right now: state, query, how long, waiting on what
pg_stat_statements      every distinct query since reset: calls, total and mean time, rows, buffers

The monitoring questions are marked "Run this one on your own Postgres": what they show depends on everything that has run on your server, so there is no expected output to compare with. Run them after the other sessions' work has given the counters something to count.

pg_stat_statements: the most useful performance tool

It groups every query by its shape (constants replaced by $1, $2, …) and records how often it ran and how long it took. Sort by total_exec_time: a 5 ms query that runs 1 million times a day matters more than a 10-second report that runs once. Setup (once): add shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements' to postgresql.conf, restart, then CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements; in the database (Q13).

Logging slow queries with their plans

auto_explain logs the plan of every statement slower than a threshold, so you can see why a query was slow in production after the fact: LOAD 'auto_explain'; SET auto_explain.log_min_duration = '500ms'; SET auto_explain.log_analyze = on; (or in postgresql.conf for all sessions).

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s53.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

    Aggregate
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders
Settings: max_parallel_workers_per_gather = '0', jit = 'off'

    A "Settings:" line lists every planner-related setting that differs from the built-in default, here the two from big.sql. Paste plans with SETTINGS when you ask someone for help: half of "why is my plan different?" is a setting.

  4. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: create indexes on big_orders(customer_id) and (created_at), then show the total size of big_orders, the table alone, and all its indexes.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX big_orders_created_at_idx ON big_orders (created_at);
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('big_orders')) AS total,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('big_orders'))       AS table_only,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('big_orders'))        AS indexes;
ROLLBACK;
    totaltable_onlyindexes
    25 MB14 MB10 MB

    (1 row)

    Three indexes already take about 10 MB next to a 14 MB table. pg_total_relation_size includes indexes and TOAST; pg_relation_size is the table file alone. On real systems indexes are often bigger than the tables, which is why unused ones (Q8) are worth finding.

  5. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index big_orders(total) and show the plan (COSTS OFF) for orders above 30,000 with the default random_page_cost.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_total_idx ON big_orders (total);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE total > 30000;
ROLLBACK;
    Seq Scan on big_orders
  Filter: (total > '30000'::numeric)

    A Seq Scan: about 40% of the rows, and at 4 units per random page read, visiting them through the index looks more expensive than reading the table.

  6. Same transaction, but with SET LOCAL random_page_cost = 1.1 first.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_total_idx ON big_orders (total);
SET LOCAL random_page_cost = 1.1;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE total > 30000;
ROLLBACK;
    Index Scan using big_orders_total_idx on big_orders
  Index Cond: (total > '30000'::numeric)

    An Index Scan: once random reads are priced like SSD reads, the index wins. Same data, same index; only the price list changed. That is why random_page_cost is the first setting to fix on SSD servers, and why plans differ between a laptop and production.

  7. On your own Postgres, after working through Sessions 44–52: show seq_scan, idx_scan, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup and last_autoanalyze for the three big tables.

    Run this one on your own Postgres: the site cannot check it

    Answer
    SELECT relname, seq_scan, idx_scan, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname LIKE 'big\_%'
ORDER BY seq_scan DESC;

    A table with many seq_scans and many rows is a candidate for a missing index: find the queries behind it with pg_stat_statements (Q13). n_dead_tup is the garbage VACUUM still has to clean up (Phase 8). Counters accumulate since the last pg_stat_reset().

  8. On your own Postgres: list the indexes that have never been used since the statistics were reset, with their size, excluding primary keys and unique indexes. (Create and COMMIT an index first to have something to find.)

    Run this one on your own Postgres: the site cannot check it

    Answer
    SELECT s.relname AS table_name, s.indexrelname AS index_name,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0
  AND NOT i.indisunique
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

    Each unused index costs disk space and write time for nothing. Before dropping one, check that the statistics have been collecting long enough to include monthly jobs, and on replicas too (each server counts its own scans). Unique indexes stay, because they enforce a rule even if no query reads them.

  9. Inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK: index big_orders(customer_id) and show the plan (COSTS OFF) for all orders of customers in Dubai (city only), first with the default random_page_cost and then with 1.1. Return the second plan.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX big_orders_customer_id_idx ON big_orders (customer_id);
-- default (4): Hash Join over a Seq Scan of big_orders
SET LOCAL random_page_cost = 1.1;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT o.order_id, o.total, c.full_name
FROM big_orders o
JOIN big_customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.city = 'Dubai';
ROLLBACK;
    Nested Loop
  ->  Seq Scan on big_customers c
        Filter: (city = 'Dubai'::text)
  ->  Index Scan using big_orders_customer_id_idx on big_orders o
        Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)

    A Nested Loop with 400 index lookups instead of a Hash Join. Session 48 Q13 called the nested loop the wrong choice, but that was on a disk where random reads cost 4×. On an SSD, 400 small lookups can beat reading 1,834 pages. The "right" plan depends on the hardware the cost settings describe.
