  12. On your own Postgres: turn parallel query back on for the practice database, reconnect, and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on SELECT status, count(*) FROM big_orders GROUP BY status. Which new nodes appear?

    Run this one on your own Postgres: the site cannot check it

    Answer
    ALTER DATABASE practice RESET max_parallel_workers_per_gather;
ALTER DATABASE practice RESET jit;
-- reconnect: \c practice
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
SELECT status, count(*) FROM big_orders GROUP BY status;

    Finalize GroupAggregate / HashAggregate → Gather Merge or Gather (Workers Planned: 2, Workers Launched: 2) → Partial HashAggregate → Parallel Seq Scan: each worker scans part of the table and aggregates it, and the leader combines the partial results. Compare the Execution Time with the serial plan. Then decide whether to keep it on (usually yes on multi-core servers) and run big.sql again if you want the course plans back.

  13. On your own Postgres: set up pg_stat_statements, run a few of this phase's queries, and list the top 5 statements by total execution time with calls, mean time and rows.

    Run this one on your own Postgres: the site cannot check it

    Answer
    -- once: in postgresql.conf  shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'  then restart Postgres
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

SELECT calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)  AS mean_ms,
       rows,
       left(query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;

    This answers "what should I optimise?" with data: the top of this list is where time goes. Constants appear as $1, $2, so a query run with 1,000 different customer ids is one row. SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset(); starts a fresh measurement, for example before and after a fix.

  14. On your own Postgres: make a runaway query fail fast. In one transaction set a 100 ms statement_timeout and run an expensive query (a cross join of big_customers with itself, counted). What happens? Then find long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions with pg_stat_activity.

    Run this one on your own Postgres: the site cannot check it

    Answer
    BEGIN;
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '100ms';
SELECT count(*) FROM big_customers a CROSS JOIN big_customers b;   -- 400 million rows
ROLLBACK;

SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS in_transaction_for, left(query, 60) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle' OR state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start;

    ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout after 100 ms: the server protected itself. pg_stat_activity shows every connection; an old idle in transaction session is a classic production problem (it blocks VACUUM and can hold locks). pg_cancel_backend(pid) cancels its query, pg_terminate_backend(pid) ends the session.

  15. Challenge: A nightly report must sort all 200,000 orders by total (the full list goes to a file). With the default work_mem it spills to disk. Without changing any server or role setting, make only this query sort in memory, and prove it: show EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF), and confirm with SHOW that work_mem is back to normal after the transaction.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
SET LOCAL work_mem = '32MB';
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT order_id, total FROM big_orders ORDER BY total;
ROLLBACK;
-- after the transaction:  SHOW work_mem;   → 4MB
    Sort (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
  Sort Key: total
  Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 12395kB
  ->  Seq Scan on big_orders (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)

    Sort Method: quicksort Memory: … instead of an external merge on disk. Note that selecting only order_id and total (not *) makes the rows narrower, so the sort needs less memory too (Session 46 Q8). SET LOCAL ends with the transaction (COMMIT or ROLLBACK), so the next query of the same connection is back at 4MB. With a connection pool this matters: a plain SET would leak to whoever gets that connection next.

Phase 5 · Session 54

Exit test + Apply: Performance

Prove you can read plans, design indexes and fix slow queries on real data sizes: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct.

Topics

Exit test rules

  • Cold: no notes, no earlier sessions, no answers until you are done.
  • Time box: 90 minutes for all 14 questions.
  • Score honestly: a plan question counts if your plan has the same shape (the same access paths and join types) as the answer; a result question counts only if the rows match exactly.
  • Pass = 11 of 14 or more. Pass → Phase 6 (transactions and locking). Fail → redo every missed question, re-read its session, and retake the test later.

What the test checks

Q1          storage and plan costs                    (S44, S46)
Q2, Q3      sargable conditions, composite order      (S45)
Q4          estimates vs actual rows                  (S46, S52)
Q5, Q6, Q7  partial, covering and GIN indexes         (S47)
Q8, Q12     join performance                          (S48)
Q9          keyset pagination                         (S51)
Q10         sorts avoided by an index                 (S50)
Q11         statistics                                (S52)
Q13         trigram search                            (S47)
Q14         settings                                  (S53)

Apply project: a performance audit

Write psql/projects/p5-performance.md about a real database: your Visitly app if you have it running locally, otherwise the practice database with big.sql.

  • Enable pg_stat_statements, use the app (or run the Phase 5 queries) for a while, and list the 5 statements with the highest total time.
  • For each: the plan before (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)), what you changed (index, rewrite, statistics) and why, and the plan after. Compare pages (Buffers), not only milliseconds.
  • List every index with its size and idx_scan from pg_stat_user_indexes. Drop (or justify) any index that is never used.
  • Check random_page_cost, work_mem, statement_timeout and log_min_duration_statement, and write down the value you would use in production and why.
  • Finish with a one-paragraph summary: total pages read by the top 5 queries before vs after.

This document is a portfolio piece: "I found the slowest queries with pg_stat_statements, cut their page reads by X% with these three indexes, and removed two unused ones" is exactly the story senior engineers tell in interviews.

Design one index so that page 2 of customer 42's delivered orders (cursor: created_at 2025-11-01 00:00 India time, order_id 190000) has every condition in the Index Cond, no Sort node and reads exactly 20 index entries. Show EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF).

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer

CREATE INDEX big_orders_search_idx ON big_orders (customer_id, status, created_at, order_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT order_id, created_at, total
FROM big_orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND status = 'delivered'
  AND (created_at, order_id) < ('2025-11-01 00:00+05:30', 190000)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 20;
ROLLBACK;
    Limit (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan Backward using big_orders_search_idx on big_orders (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)

        Index Searches: 1

    Equality columns first (customer_id, status), then exactly the ORDER BY columns including the tiebreaker. The scan jumps to (42, delivered, cursor) and reads backwards: 20 entries, no Sort, the same cost on page 2 or page 200. This one design rule (equality → sort keys → tiebreaker) covers most list screens in real apps.

Phase 6 · Session 55

Transactions and savepoints

Group changes into all-or-nothing units, recover from errors inside a transaction with savepoints, and know what a rollback does and does not undo.

Topics

Why transactions

Moving 1,000 from Aarav's wallet to Kabir's is two UPDATEs. If the server crashes, or the second UPDATE fails, between the two, money has disappeared. A transaction makes several statements one unit: either all of them take effect, or none do. This is the A (atomicity) in ACID; the others are Consistency (constraints hold at commit), Isolation (Session 57) and Durability (once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash).

This phase uses three new tables: accounts (four wallets, 9,200 in total, with CHECK (balance >= 0)), jobs (a work queue) and table_bookings (restaurant tables). Reload practice.sql first.

practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE account_id = 1;
UPDATE 1
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE account_id = 3;
UPDATE 1
practice=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
practice=# SELECT account_id, owner, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id;
 account_id | owner  | balance
------------+--------+---------
          1 | Aarav  | 4000.00
          2 | Diya   | 3000.00
          3 | Kabir  | 1000.00
          4 | Ananya | 1200.00
(4 rows)
  • Outside BEGIN … COMMIT, every statement is its own transaction (autocommit). A single statement is always atomic: an UPDATE of 10,000 rows that fails on the last row changes nothing.
  • The prompt shows the state: practice=# no transaction, practice=*# inside one, practice=!# inside a failed one.
  • Until COMMIT, other sessions do not see your changes (Session 57). ROLLBACK throws them all away.

An error aborts the whole transaction

practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 2;
UPDATE 1
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE account_id = 4;
ERROR:  new row for relation "accounts" violates check constraint "accounts_balance_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (4, Ananya, -800.00).
practice=!# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE account_id = 1;
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
practice=!# COMMIT;
ROLLBACK
practice=# SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (2, 4) ORDER BY account_id;
 account_id | balance
------------+---------
          2 | 3000.00
          4 | 1200.00
(2 rows)

After an error, Postgres refuses every further statement until the transaction ends, and COMMIT on a failed transaction quietly answers ROLLBACK. Application code that ignores the reply to COMMIT believes it saved data it did not save. Even the first, successful UPDATE (+100 for Diya) is gone.

Savepoints: undo part of a transaction

practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# INSERT INTO table_bookings VALUES (6, 2, '2026-02-20 20:00+05:30', 'Saanvi', 2);
INSERT 0 1
practice=*# SAVEPOINT before_second;
SAVEPOINT
practice=*# INSERT INTO table_bookings VALUES (7, 1, '2026-02-20 19:00+05:30', 'Vivaan', 2);
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "table_bookings_table_no_slot_key"
DETAIL:  Key (table_no, slot)=(1, 2026-02-20 19:00:00+05:30) already exists.
practice=!# ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_second;
ROLLBACK
practice=*# INSERT INTO table_bookings VALUES (7, 3, '2026-02-20 19:00+05:30', 'Vivaan', 2);
INSERT 0 1
practice=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
practice=# SELECT booking_id, table_no, guest FROM table_bookings WHERE booking_id >= 6 ORDER BY booking_id;
 booking_id | table_no | guest
------------+----------+--------
          6 |        2 | Saanvi
          7 |        3 | Vivaan
(2 rows)
  • SAVEPOINT name marks a point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes everything after it, including an error, and the transaction can continue. The savepoint stays defined; RELEASE SAVEPOINT name forgets it.
  • psql can do this for you: \set ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK interactive (Session 1) wraps every statement you type in an invisible savepoint, so a typo does not ruin a long manual transaction.
  • Savepoints are not free: each one is a subtransaction. Thousands of them in one transaction slow Postgres down (Phase 8). Use them around risky steps, not around every row.

What ROLLBACK does not undo

  • Sequences: nextval() is never rolled back, so identity and serial columns get gaps (Session 40).
  • Anything outside the database: an email you sent or an HTTP call you made from the application before the rollback.
  • Almost all DDL is transactional in Postgres: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX roll back like data. Exceptions: CREATE DATABASE, VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction at all.

Time inside a transaction

now() (= transaction_timestamp()) is frozen at the start of the transaction, so every row written by one transaction gets the same timestamp. clock_timestamp() is the real wall clock and changes during a statement. statement_timestamp() is the start of the current statement.

When constraints are checked

Normally every constraint is checked as each row is changed (UNIQUE: at the end of the statement only if the constraint is DEFERRABLE). A constraint declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, or switched with SET CONSTRAINTS … DEFERRED, is checked at COMMIT instead. That lets a transaction pass through a temporarily invalid state, such as swapping two unique values or inserting rows that reference each other.

Keep transactions short. A transaction holds its locks until it ends (Session 58), and an open transaction stops VACUUM from cleaning up after it (Phase 8). Never wait for user input, an HTTP call or a sleep inside one.

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s55.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

COMMIT;
SELECT account_id, balance, sum(balance) OVER () AS total FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id;
    practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE account_id = 2;
UPDATE 1
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE account_id = 3;
UPDATE 1
practice=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

  2. Try to move 6,000 from Aarav (balance 5,000) to Kabir in a transaction. Debit first. What happens, and what is left afterwards?

    practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 6000 WHERE account_id = 1;
ERROR:  new row for relation "accounts" violates check constraint "accounts_balance_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (1, Aarav, -1000.00).

ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

------------+---------
          1 | 5000.00
          3 |    0.00
(2 rows)

    The debit violates CHECK (balance >= 0), the transaction is aborted, the credit is refused and ROLLBACK ends it. Nothing changed. A constraint in the database is the last line of defence when application code forgets to check the balance.

  3. Inside a transaction, cause an error (divide by zero), then try to read the accounts. What does Postgres answer, and how do you get out?

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
SELECT 1 / 0;
SELECT count(*) FROM accounts;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT count(*) FROM accounts;
    practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# SELECT 1 / 0;
ERROR:  division by zero
practice=!# SELECT count(*) FROM accounts;
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
practice=!# ROLLBACK;
ROLLBACK
practice=# SELECT count(*) FROM accounts;
 count
-------
     4
(1 row)

    "current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block". Only ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT) gets you out. Some databases continue after an error; Postgres deliberately does not, so a half-failed unit of work cannot be committed by accident.

  4. In one transaction, queue three jobs (ids 11, 12, 13, kind send_email, run_after now()). The second insert accidentally reuses id 11. Use a savepoint so that the first and third jobs still get saved, then count the queued jobs.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (11, 'send_email', now());
SAVEPOINT s1;

  5. Show that now() is frozen inside a transaction while clock_timestamp() moves: start a transaction, store now() in a temp table, sleep 0.2 seconds, then compare.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE t AS SELECT now() AS started;
SELECT pg_sleep(0.2);
SELECT now() = started AS now_unchanged, clock_timestamp() > started AS clock_moved FROM t;
COMMIT;
    practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# CREATE TEMP TABLE t AS SELECT now() AS started;
SELECT 1
practice=*# SELECT pg_sleep(0.2);
 pg_sleep
----------

(1 row)
practice=*# SELECT now() = started AS now_unchanged, clock_timestamp() > started AS clock_moved FROM t;
 now_unchanged | clock_moved
---------------+-------------
 t             | t
(1 row)
practice=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

    t and t. Every row inserted by one transaction gets the same now(), which is usually what you want for created_at. For measuring durations inside a transaction, use clock_timestamp().

  6. Show that DDL is transactional: in a transaction, create a table promo_codes, insert a row, roll back, then try to read it.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE promo_codes (code text PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO promo_codes VALUES ('FEST20');
ROLLBACK;
SELECT * FROM promo_codes;
    practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# CREATE TABLE promo_codes (code text PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE
practice=*# INSERT INTO promo_codes VALUES ('FEST20');
INSERT 0 1
practice=*# ROLLBACK;
ROLLBACK
practice=# SELECT * FROM promo_codes;
ERROR:  relation "promo_codes" does not exist

    "relation promo_codes does not exist": the CREATE TABLE was rolled back with the data. That is why Postgres migrations can run inside one transaction and leave nothing half-applied when a step fails (Session 61). MySQL and Oracle commit DDL implicitly.

  7. Show that a sequence is not rolled back: create a sequence demo_seq, take a value inside a transaction that you roll back, then take another value.

    Answer

BEGIN;
SELECT nextval('demo_seq');
ROLLBACK;
SELECT nextval('demo_seq');
    practice=# CREATE SEQUENCE demo_seq;
CREATE SEQUENCE
practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# SELECT nextval('demo_seq');
 nextval
---------
       1
(1 row)
practice=*# ROLLBACK;
ROLLBACK
practice=# SELECT nextval('demo_seq');
 nextval
---------
       2
(1 row)

    The second call returns 2. Sequences never go back, so that many concurrent transactions can take numbers without waiting for each other. Ids therefore have gaps; never use them to count rows or as invoice numbers that must be gapless.

  9. Swap the positions of two queue entries. Create table queue_slots (job_id int primary key, pos int UNIQUE) and table queue_slots_d (same, but the UNIQUE is DEFERRABLE), each with rows (4, 1) and (5, 2). Run UPDATE … SET pos = 3 - pos on both.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer

CREATE TABLE queue_slots_d (job_id int PRIMARY KEY, pos int UNIQUE DEFERRABLE);
INSERT INTO queue_slots   VALUES (4, 1), (5, 2);
INSERT INTO queue_slots_d VALUES (4, 1), (5, 2);
UPDATE queue_slots   SET pos = 3 - pos;
UPDATE queue_slots_d SET pos = 3 - pos;

CREATE TABLE

CREATE TABLE
practice=# INSERT INTO queue_slots   VALUES (4, 1), (5, 2);
INSERT 0 2
practice=# INSERT INTO queue_slots_d VALUES (4, 1), (5, 2);
INSERT 0 2
practice=# UPDATE queue_slots   SET pos = 3 - pos;
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "queue_slots_pos_key"
DETAIL:  Key (pos)=(2) already exists.
practice=# UPDATE queue_slots_d SET pos = 3 - pos;
UPDATE 2
practice=# SELECT * FROM queue_slots_d ORDER BY pos;
 job_id | pos
--------+-----
      5 |   1
      4 |   2
(2 rows)

    The plain UNIQUE fails: Postgres checks it row by row, and after the first row is changed two rows briefly have pos 2. A DEFERRABLE unique constraint is checked at the end of the statement (and with SET CONSTRAINTS … DEFERRED, at COMMIT), when the swap is complete. A Postgres quirk worth knowing; the SQL standard says statement-end for all.

  11. Transfer 2,000 from Ananya (balance 1,200) to Kabir in one statement that moves nothing, without any error, when the balance is too low. Return the credited rows.

    Expected: 0 rows

    Answer
    WITH debit AS (
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000
  WHERE account_id = 4 AND balance >= 2000
  RETURNING account_id
)
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 2000
WHERE account_id = 3 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM debit)
RETURNING account_id, balance;
    account_idbalance

    (0 rows)

    0 rows: the debit found no row with enough money, so the credit had nothing to depend on. The application checks "rows returned = 1" instead of catching an exception. Both strategies are fine; the CHECK constraint stays as the safety net either way.

---------

  13. The silent-commit trap: in a transaction, queue job 11, then try to queue job 4 (it exists), then COMMIT. What does COMMIT answer, and is job 11 there?

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (11, 'send_email', now());
INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (4, 'send_email', now());
COMMIT;
SELECT count(*) FROM jobs WHERE job_id = 11;
    practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (11, 'send_email', now());
INSERT 0 1
practice=*# INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (4, 'send_email', now());
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "jobs_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (job_id)=(4) already exists.
practice=!# COMMIT;
ROLLBACK
practice=# SELECT count(*) FROM jobs WHERE job_id = 11;
 count
-------
     0
(1 row)

    COMMIT answers ROLLBACK and job 11 is not there. Drivers report this differently: some raise an error, some just return the "ROLLBACK" tag. Always check that the commit really committed, and treat any error inside a transaction as "the whole transaction is gone".

  15. Challenge: Build an audited transfer. Create table transfers (transfer_id int generated always as identity primary key, from_id int, to_id int, amount numeric(12,2) check (amount > 0), at timestamptz default now()). In one transaction move 1,500 from Aarav to Ananya: insert the transfer row, debit, credit, and before committing check in the same transaction that the total is still 9,200. Then show the transfer row and the two balances.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE transfers (transfer_id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, from_id int NOT NULL, to_id int NOT NULL, amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0), at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (1, 4, 1500);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1500 WHERE account_id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1500 WHERE account_id = 4;
SELECT sum(balance) AS total FROM accounts;
COMMIT;
SELECT t.transfer_id, t.amount, f.balance AS from_balance, d.balance AS to_balance
FROM transfers t
JOIN accounts f ON f.account_id = t.from_id
JOIN accounts d ON d.account_id = t.to_id;
    practice=# CREATE TABLE transfers (transfer_id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, from_id int NOT NULL, to_id int NOT NULL, amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0), at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
CREATE TABLE
practice=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
practice=*# INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (1, 4, 1500);
INSERT 0 1
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1500 WHERE account_id = 1;
UPDATE 1
practice=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1500 WHERE account_id = 4;
UPDATE 1
practice=*# SELECT sum(balance) AS total FROM accounts;
  total
---------
 9200.00
(1 row)
practice=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
practice=# SELECT t.transfer_id, t.amount, f.balance AS from_balance, d.balance AS to_balance
           FROM transfers t
           JOIN accounts f ON f.account_id = t.from_id
           JOIN accounts d ON d.account_id = t.to_id;
 transfer_id | amount  | from_balance | to_balance
-------------+---------+--------------+------------
           1 | 1500.00 |      3500.00 |    2700.00
(1 row)

    The ledger row and the two balance changes commit together or not at all, so the audit log can never disagree with the balances. Inside the transaction you see your own uncommitted changes (total still 9,200); other sessions see nothing until COMMIT. In Phase 7 this becomes a function, and the invariant becomes a check the database runs for you.

← Phase 6: Transactions + lockingAll phasesSchema

Phase 6 · Session 56

Review: performance and transactions

Pull Sessions 50–55 back out of memory: sorting, pagination, statistics, settings and transactions, mixed on the big tables.

Topics

How to run this review

  • You need both practice.sql (reloaded for Phase 6) and big.sql loaded.
  • First 20 minutes: redo every question in mistakes.md from Sessions 50–55, cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below. Predict each plan before you run EXPLAIN, and predict each transcript before you run it.
  • Then the challenge: archive old orders in safe, restartable batches.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 50–55

ORDER BY … LIMIT n        index on the ORDER BY columns → no Sort; otherwise top-N heapsort
Sort Method               quicksort (memory) · top-N heapsort · external merge (disk: raise work_mem with SET LOCAL)
Keyset pagination         WHERE (a, b) < (:a, :b) ORDER BY a DESC, b DESC LIMIT n   + index (…, a, b)
Estimates                 pg_stats: MCV list, histogram, n_distinct; CREATE STATISTICS for correlated columns
Generic plans             prepared statements with skewed data: plan_cache_mode
Settings                  random_page_cost (SSD 1.1), work_mem (per sort/hash), effective_cache_size
Transactions              BEGIN … COMMIT; an error aborts all; COMMIT of a failed transaction = ROLLBACK
Savepoints                SAVEPOINT s … ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s (undo part, continue)
Not rolled back           sequences (gaps), anything outside the database

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s56.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

Each batch is one statement, so a crash between batches loses nothing and duplicates nothing: the next run simply continues (it is idempotent, S40). Small batches keep locks short and let autovacuum keep up (S61). ← Phase 6: Transactions + lockingAll phasesSchema

Phase 6 · Session 57

Isolation levels and anomalies

Know exactly what one transaction can see of another at each isolation level, recognise lost updates and write skew, and handle serialization failures with retries.

Topics

Two terminals

Everything in this session needs two psql windows on the practice database, called A and B. Run the statements in the order shown. In the transcripts, B's output is indented, and ⏳ marks a statement that waits for the other terminal.

READ COMMITTED: the default

Each statement sees the data committed before that statement started. Two SELECTs in the same transaction can therefore see different values:

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)
            B=# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
            UPDATE 1
A=*# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 5100.00
(1 row)
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

This is a non-repeatable read. Postgres never shows you uncommitted data (a dirty read), not even at READ UNCOMMITTED, which Postgres treats as READ COMMITTED.

REPEATABLE READ: one snapshot for the whole transaction

A=# BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)
            B=# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
            UPDATE 1
A=*# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
A=# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 5100.00
(1 row)

The snapshot is taken at the first statement, not at BEGIN. Every later read in the transaction sees the database as of that moment: no non-repeatable reads, and (in Postgres, stronger than the standard requires) no phantoms either. Perfect for reports that run several queries and must add up.

Level            dirty read   non-repeatable read   phantom   lost update   write skew
---------------  -----------  --------------------  --------  ------------  ----------
READ COMMITTED   no           possible              possible  possible*     possible
REPEATABLE READ  no           no                    no        error 40001   possible
SERIALIZABLE     no           no                    no        error 40001   error 40001

* with read-then-write in the application; UPDATE … SET x = x - 1 is safe (below)

The lost update

The classic bug: the application reads a value, computes a new one, and writes it back. Two of these at once and one change is lost:

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 5000.00
(1 row)
            B=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            B=*# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
             balance
            ---------
             5000.00
            (1 row)
-- both apps compute 5000 - 100 = 4900 and 5000 - 200 = 4800
A=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = 4900 WHERE account_id = 1;
UPDATE 1
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            B=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = 4800 WHERE account_id = 1;
            UPDATE 1
            B=*# COMMIT;
            COMMIT
A=# SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 1;
 balance
---------
 4800.00
(1 row)

Two withdrawals of 100 and 200 should leave 4,700. The result is 4,800: A's withdrawal vanished. Fixes, from simplest: let the database do the arithmetic (SET balance = balance - 100, Q4), lock the row when reading it (SELECT … FOR UPDATE, Session 58), or use REPEATABLE READ and retry on conflict (Q5).

How READ COMMITTED handles concurrent UPDATEs

When an UPDATE in READ COMMITTED finds a row that another transaction is changing, it waits for that transaction to finish, then re-reads the new version of the row, re-checks its WHERE clause, and applies its change to the new version. That is why balance = balance - 100 never loses an update, and why a WHERE condition can stop matching while you wait (Q6).

Write skew and SERIALIZABLE

Two doctors are on call, and the rule is "at least one must stay on call". Each checks the rule, sees two on duty, and goes off duty. Neither transaction changed a row the other changed, so REPEATABLE READ sees no conflict, and the rule is broken. SERIALIZABLE tracks what each transaction read and aborts one of them:

A=# BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE on_duty;
 count
-------
     2
(1 row)
            B=# BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
            BEGIN
            B=*# SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE on_duty;
             count
            -------
                 2
            (1 row)
A=*# UPDATE on_call SET on_duty = false WHERE doctor = 'Asha';
UPDATE 1
            B=*# UPDATE on_call SET on_duty = false WHERE doctor = 'Rahul';
            UPDATE 1
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            B=*# COMMIT;
            ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
            DETAIL:  Reason code: …
            HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.
A=# SELECT * FROM on_call ORDER BY doctor;
 doctor | on_duty
--------+---------
 Asha   | f
 Rahul  | t
(2 rows)
  • SERIALIZABLE guarantees that the result is the same as if the transactions had run one after the other, in some order. You write each transaction as if it ran alone.
  • The price: any transaction may fail with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure), sometimes at COMMIT. The application must retry the whole transaction from the start. Not retrying is the most common bug with SERIALIZABLE.
  • REPEATABLE READ can fail with 40001 too ("could not serialize access due to concurrent update") when it tries to change a row that changed after its snapshot.
  • Deadlocks (40P01, Session 58) also need a retry. Write one retry loop for both.
retry loop (any language)

  for attempt in 1..5:
      BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
      … all reads and writes …
      COMMIT
      success → stop
      error 40001 or 40P01 → ROLLBACK, wait a little (random backoff), try again
      any other error → ROLLBACK, give up

Choosing: READ COMMITTED + atomic UPDATEs + row locks covers most OLTP code. REPEATABLE READ for reports and exports that must be consistent across queries. SERIALIZABLE when correctness depends on reading several rows and the rules are too complex for constraints and locks (and you have the retry loop). SET default_transaction_isolation changes the default per role or database.

(2 rows)

    The EXISTS alone is not enough at READ COMMITTED: each UPDATE only locks the row it changes, and both EXISTS subqueries could read the old state at the same moment (the write skew again, just faster). The fix is to serialise the decision on something both transactions must lock: here all on-call rows (FOR UPDATE), so B waits, then its EXISTS sees that Asha is off duty and updates 0 rows. With many rows, lock one "parent" row instead (the shift, the ward) or use an advisory lock (Session 59). Rules about "at least / at most N rows" are exactly the ones that need a lock or SERIALIZABLE.

Phase 6 · Session 58

Row locks and job queues

Lock exactly the rows you need with FOR UPDATE and its variants, build a job queue that many workers can share, and find, avoid and survive lock waits and deadlocks.

Topics

Row locks

Every UPDATE and DELETE locks the rows it changes until the transaction ends; a second writer of the same row waits (Session 57). A SELECT can take the same locks before changing anything, to reserve rows for a decision:

Lock                       taken by                                  blocks
-------------------------  ----------------------------------------  -------------------------------------------
FOR UPDATE                 DELETE, UPDATE of a key column, SELECT …  every other lock below
FOR NO KEY UPDATE          UPDATE of non-key columns                 FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE
FOR SHARE                  SELECT … FOR SHARE                        FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE
FOR KEY SHARE              foreign-key checks (inserting a child)    FOR UPDATE only

Plain SELECT takes no row lock and is never blocked by row locks (MVCC).
A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT job_id, status FROM jobs WHERE job_id = 4 FOR UPDATE;
 job_id | status
--------+--------
      4 | queued
(1 row)
            B=# SELECT job_id, status FROM jobs WHERE job_id = 4;
             job_id | status
            --------+--------
                  4 | queued
            (1 row)
            B=# SELECT job_id, status FROM jobs WHERE job_id = 4 FOR UPDATE;
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
A=*# UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running' WHERE job_id = 4;
UPDATE 1
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
             job_id | status
            --------+---------
                  4 | running
            (1 row)

B's plain SELECT ran at once; its FOR UPDATE waited, and when A committed it returned the new row (running). Three ways not to wait: NOWAIT (error immediately), SKIP LOCKED (pretend the locked rows are not there), SET lock_timeout = '2s' (error after waiting that long).

A job queue with SKIP LOCKED

The jobs table is a work queue. Each worker repeatedly claims the oldest due job that nobody else is working on. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED makes concurrent workers take different jobs instead of queueing behind each other:

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# UPDATE jobs
     SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-A', locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
     WHERE job_id = (
       SELECT job_id FROM jobs
       WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
       ORDER BY run_after, job_id
       FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
       LIMIT 1
     )
     RETURNING job_id, kind;
 job_id |    kind
--------+------------
      4 | send_email
(1 row)
            B=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            B=*# UPDATE jobs
                 SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-B', locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
                 WHERE job_id = (
                   SELECT job_id FROM jobs
                   WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
                   ORDER BY run_after, job_id
                   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
                   LIMIT 1
                 )
                 RETURNING job_id, kind;
             job_id |     kind
            --------+---------------
                  5 | export_report
            (1 row)
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            B=*# COMMIT;
            COMMIT
A=# SELECT job_id, status, locked_by, attempts FROM jobs WHERE status = 'running' ORDER BY job_id;
 job_id | status  | locked_by | attempts
--------+---------+-----------+----------
      4 | running | worker-A  |        1
      5 | running | worker-B  |        1
      9 | running | worker-2  |        1
(3 rows)
  • The subquery finds and locks one row, skipping rows locked by other workers; the UPDATE marks it as taken; RETURNING hands it to the worker. One statement, no race.
  • Here each worker commits the claim right away (status = running is the "lease"), does the work outside the transaction, then sets status = done. If it dies, the job stays "running": a reaper requeues jobs whose locked_at is too old (Q8).
  • The alternative is to keep the transaction open while working: if the worker dies, its connection drops and the lock disappears, so no reaper is needed. But long transactions hurt VACUUM and hold connections; prefer the lease for jobs that take more than a second or two.
  • Index the queue for the claim query: CREATE INDEX ON jobs (run_after, job_id) WHERE status = 'queued' (a partial index, Session 47).

Deadlocks

A deadlock is two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds. Postgres checks for one after deadlock_timeout (1 second) and cancels one of the two with SQLSTATE 40P01; the other continues:

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
            B=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
A=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
UPDATE 1
            B=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 2;
            UPDATE 1
A=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 2;
⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
            B=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
⏳ … A's statement finishes:
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process <pid> waits for ShareLock on transaction <xid>; blocked by process <pid>.
Process <pid> waits for ShareLock on transaction <xid>; blocked by process <pid>.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            UPDATE 1
A=!# COMMIT;
ROLLBACK
            B=*# COMMIT;
            COMMIT
  • Avoid them by taking locks in one global order: lock both accounts with … ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE first (Session 57 Q13), or always update the lower id first.
  • Keep transactions short so locks are held briefly.
  • Survive the rest: deadlocks can still happen (for example through foreign keys and triggers), so the retry loop from Session 57 handles 40P01 like 40001.

Who is blocking whom

pg_stat_activity shows every session and what it waits for; pg_blocking_pids(pid) returns the sessions blocking it. In production, the blocker is often an idle transaction that someone forgot to commit (state = 'idle in transaction'). pg_cancel_backend(pid) cancels its current query; pg_terminate_backend(pid) ends the session and rolls back its transaction.

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE account_id = 4;
UPDATE 1
            B=# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE account_id = 4;
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
                        C=# SELECT application_name AS who, wait_event_type, cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) AS blocked_by, left(query, 45) AS query
                            FROM pg_stat_activity
                            WHERE datname = current_database() AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()
                            ORDER BY application_name;
                            who     | wait_event_type | blocked_by |                     query
                        ------------+-----------------+------------+-----------------------------------------------
                         terminal A | Client          |          0 | UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHE
                         terminal B | Lock            |          1 | UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1 WHE
                        (2 rows)
A=*# ROLLBACK;
ROLLBACK
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            UPDATE 1

Foreign keys lock too. Inserting an order for customer 3 takes FOR KEY SHARE on customer 3, so deleting customer 3 (or changing its key) waits for that transaction, while updating the customer's name does not (Q10, Q11).

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s58.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  6. The worker finished job 4 successfully. Mark it done, but only if it is still this worker's job (it may have been requeued by the reaper and taken by someone else meanwhile). Return the row count via RETURNING.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    WITH claimed AS (
  UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-1', locked_at = now()
  WHERE job_id = 4 RETURNING job_id
)
SELECT 1 FROM claimed;  -- setup: worker-1 holds job 4

UPDATE jobs SET status = 'done', locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL
WHERE job_id = 4 AND locked_by = 'worker-1' AND status = 'running'
RETURNING job_id, status;

    4done

    One row: the worker still owned the job. If the reaper had handed it to worker-2, the WHERE would match nothing and worker-1 would know its result is stale. Checking ownership in the WHERE clause is a "fencing" condition, cheap insurance for leases.

Phase 6 · Session 59

Race-free creation and advisory locks

Create rows exactly once under concurrency (constraints, ON CONFLICT, exclusion constraints, idempotency keys), and serialise work that has no row to lock with advisory locks.

Topics

Check-then-insert is a race

"If the email is not subscribed yet, insert it": two requests at the same moment both check, both see nothing, both insert. Row locks cannot help, because there is no row yet to lock. Without a constraint you get a duplicate:

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT count(*) FROM subscribers WHERE email = 'aarav@mail.test';
 count
-------
     0
(1 row)
            B=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            B=*# SELECT count(*) FROM subscribers WHERE email = 'aarav@mail.test';
             count
            -------
                 0
            (1 row)
A=*# INSERT INTO subscribers VALUES ('aarav@mail.test', 'free');
INSERT 0 1
            B=*# INSERT INTO subscribers VALUES ('aarav@mail.test', 'pro');
            INSERT 0 1
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            B=*# COMMIT;
            COMMIT
A=# SELECT * FROM subscribers;
      email      | plan
-----------------+------
 aarav@mail.test | free
 aarav@mail.test | pro
(2 rows)

Even SERIALIZABLE only turns this into an error to retry. The robust fix is to let a unique index decide. The index is the one place where two inserts of the same key are forced to meet: the second waits for the first transaction, and then either fails (the first committed) or proceeds (the first rolled back).

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# INSERT INTO subscribers (email, plan) VALUES ('aarav@mail.test', 'free');
INSERT 0 1
            B=# INSERT INTO subscribers (email, plan) VALUES ('aarav@mail.test', 'pro');
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "subscribers_email_key"
            DETAIL:  Key (email)=(aarav@mail.test) already exists.

ON CONFLICT: insert-or-ignore, insert-or-update, get-or-create

INSERT … ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING                        insert once; a duplicate is skipped silently
INSERT … ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET plan = EXCLUDED.plan  insert, or update the existing row (upsert)
INSERT … ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email RETURNING id
                                                                get-or-create: always returns the id

ON CONFLICT is atomic even under concurrency: it uses the same unique index, waits for an in-progress insert of the same key, and then takes the right branch. It never fails with a duplicate-key error for its conflict target (Session 40).

Rules that are not equality: exclusion constraints

"A room cannot be booked twice for overlapping times" is a uniqueness rule on ranges. An exclusion constraint (Session 47) enforces it under concurrency exactly like UNIQUE does: the second overlapping insert waits, then fails.

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# INSERT INTO room_bookings VALUES (1, '[2026-02-20 19:00+05:30, 2026-02-20 21:00+05:30)', 'Aarav');
INSERT 0 1
            B=# INSERT INTO room_bookings VALUES (1, '[2026-02-20 20:00+05:30, 2026-02-20 22:00+05:30)', 'Diya');
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            ERROR:  conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "room_bookings_room_during_excl"
            DETAIL:  Key (room, during)=(1, ["2026-02-20 20:00:00+05:30","2026-02-20 22:00:00+05:30")) conflicts with existing key (room, during)=(1, ["2026-02-20 19:00:00+05:30","2026-02-20 21:00:00+05:30")).

Idempotency keys

A payment request times out on the client, which retries. Did the first one go through? An idempotency key chosen by the client (a UUID per logical request) makes the retry safe: the server records each key with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the work, and a retry with the same key does nothing (Q9). Stripe, payment gateways and most good APIs work this way.

Advisory locks: locks on an idea

Sometimes there is no row to lock: "only one export of this customer's data at a time", "only one instance of the nightly job". An advisory lock is a lock on a number you choose; Postgres enforces nothing except that two sessions cannot hold the same number at once.

pg_advisory_xact_lock(key)        wait for the lock; released at COMMIT / ROLLBACK      ← prefer this
pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(key)    true if taken, false immediately if someone has it
pg_advisory_lock(key)             session-level: held until pg_advisory_unlock(key) or disconnect
pg_try_advisory_lock(key)         session-level, non-blocking

key: a bigint, or two ints. From text: hashtext('export:customer:3') (collisions are possible but rare).
A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('export:customer:3'));
 pg_advisory_xact_lock
-----------------------

(1 row)
            B=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            B=*# SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('export:customer:3')) AS got_it;
             got_it
            --------
             f
            (1 row)
            B=*# SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('export:customer:5')) AS got_it;
             got_it
            --------
             t
            (1 row)
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            B=*# COMMIT;
            COMMIT

Session-level advisory locks survive COMMIT. With a connection pooler (PgBouncer in transaction mode), the next transaction on that connection may belong to another user, and it inherits your lock. Use the _xact_ versions unless you really need a lock across transactions.

Order of preference: a constraint (UNIQUE, exclusion, CHECK, foreign key) when the rule can be written as one; ON CONFLICT for create-once; row locks when the rule is about existing rows; advisory locks when there is nothing to lock; SERIALIZABLE when the rule is too complex for all of these.

Phase 6 · Session 60

Views and materialized views

Name and reuse queries with views, write through simple views safely, and serve expensive reports from materialized views refreshed without blocking readers.

Topics

A view is a stored query

A view stores a SELECT under a name. It holds no data: every query on the view runs the underlying query. The planner inlines it, so WHERE customer_id = 1 on the view is pushed into the query, and a view costs nothing compared with writing the query out.

CREATE VIEW customer_revenue AS
SELECT o.customer_id, count(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY o.customer_id;

SELECT * FROM customer_revenue ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 3;
customer_idordersrevenue
82150500.00
13139200.00
101126500.00

(3 rows)

  • Use views to give a name to business logic ("delivered revenue") so every report computes it the same way.
  • A view is also an interface: applications can read the view while you change the tables underneath, as long as the view keeps returning the same columns (Session 61).
  • Views are not a performance tool. A slow query is exactly as slow behind a view.

Writing through a view

A view over one table, without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, LIMIT or window functions, is automatically updatable: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the view change the table. WITH CHECK OPTION rejects changes that would make the row fall out of the view, for example a "pending orders" view that must not be used to ship an order.

CREATE VIEW pending_orders AS
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending'
  WITH CHECK OPTION;

UPDATE pending_orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE order_id = 27;
-- ERROR:  new row violates check option for view "pending_orders"

Views and schema changes

  • Postgres records which columns a view uses. DROP COLUMN or DROP TABLE of something a view uses fails (unless CASCADE, which drops the view too).
  • CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW can only add new columns at the end; renaming, removing or retyping a column needs DROP VIEW + CREATE VIEW (in one transaction).
  • SELECT * in a view is expanded when the view is created: columns added to the table later do not appear in the view.

Materialized views: stored results

A materialized view runs its query once and stores the result like a table. Reading it is as fast as reading a small table, and it can have indexes. The data is a snapshot: it changes only when you run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue AS
SELECT date_trunc('month', o.order_date)::date AS month, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY 1;

SELECT * FROM monthly_revenue ORDER BY month LIMIT 4;
monthrevenue
2025-01-01156000.00
2025-02-0139400.00
2025-03-01121500.00
2025-04-01132700.00

(4 rows)

Refreshing without blocking readers

A plain REFRESH rebuilds the view and holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock while it does: every reader waits until it commits.

B=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
B=*# REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue;
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
            A=# SELECT count(*) FROM monthly_revenue;
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
B=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … A's statement finishes:
             count
            -------
                10
            (1 row)

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY computes the new result next to the old one and applies only the differences. Readers keep reading the old data while it runs. It needs a unique index on the materialized view (to match old rows with new ones) and is slower than a plain refresh when most rows change.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON monthly_revenue (month);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_revenue;

Schedule refreshes with pg_cron (Phase 7) or your application's scheduler, and record when the data was refreshed, so dashboards can show "as of 10:00". If the data must always be current, a materialized view is the wrong tool: use a normal view (and indexes), or a summary table kept up to date in the same transaction as the source changes (Phase 7: triggers).

← Phase 6: Transactions + lockingAll phasesSchema

Phase 6 · Session 61

Zero-downtime migrations

Change the schema of a busy database without blocking the application: know which DDL takes which lock, avoid the lock queue, and use NOT VALID, CONCURRENTLY and expand/contract.

Topics

DDL takes table locks

Every statement takes a table-level lock besides any row locks. Most are harmless (SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE, writes take ROW EXCLUSIVE), but most ALTER TABLE forms take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which conflicts with everything, even SELECT.

Lock                     taken by (examples)                                    conflicts with
-----------------------  -----------------------------------------------------  -------------------------------
ACCESS SHARE             SELECT                                                 ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
ROW EXCLUSIVE            INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE                          SHARE and stronger
SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE   VACUUM, ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY,            itself and stronger
                         VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY            (reads and writes go on)
SHARE                    CREATE INDEX (not concurrently)                        all writes
EXCLUSIVE                REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY                 everything except SELECT
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE         most ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL,         everything, even SELECT
                         REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW

An ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock held for a millisecond is fine. The danger is how long the statement waits for it, and how long it holds it once it has it.

The lock queue: how a fast ALTER takes the site down

Locks are granted in order. An ALTER that waits for a long-running transaction also makes everyone who arrives after it wait, including plain SELECTs that would not conflict with the long transaction at all:

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT count(*) FROM orders;
 count
-------
    36
(1 row)
-- A is a slow report (or a forgotten open transaction). Now the migration starts:
            B=# ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
-- and an ordinary request from the application:
                        C=# SELECT order_id, status FROM orders WHERE order_id = 1;
                        ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            ALTER TABLE
                        ⏳ … C's statement finishes:
                         order_id |  status
                        ----------+-----------
                                1 | delivered
                        (1 row)

C's one-row SELECT waited behind B, which waited behind A. On a busy site every request piles up behind the ALTER, connections run out, and the application is down although the ALTER itself needs a millisecond. The fix: never wait long for a DDL lock. Set lock_timeout for the migration and retry if it gives up:

A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT count(*) FROM orders;
 count
-------
    36
(1 row)
            B=# SET lock_timeout = '1s';
            SET
            B=# ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
                        C=# SELECT order_id, status FROM orders WHERE order_id = 1;
                         order_id |  status
                        ----------+-----------
                                1 | delivered
                        (1 row)
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

Fast and slow ALTERs

Instant (catalog only)                         Rewrites or scans the whole table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
---------------------------------------------  ----------------------------------------------------------
ADD COLUMN (no default, or a constant default) ADD COLUMN with a volatile default (clock_timestamp(), random())
DROP COLUMN (space reclaimed later)            ALTER COLUMN TYPE that changes the storage (int → bigint)
RENAME TABLE / COLUMN                          SET NOT NULL (a full scan, unless a valid CHECK proves it)
varchar(50) → varchar(100) or text             text → varchar(n) (every value must be checked)
                                               ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK / FOREIGN KEY (full scan)
ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID                     CREATE INDEX (blocks writes for the whole build)
DROP / CREATE VIEW                             VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER

You can see whether a statement rewrote a table: the table's relfilenode (its data file) changes on a rewrite (Q4, Q5).

The safe recipes

  • Indexes: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without blocking writes (it takes longer and cannot run inside a transaction block; if it fails it leaves an INVALID index to drop and retry).
  • Constraints: ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID (instant, checks new rows only), then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (scans, but under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so reads and writes continue). Works for CHECK and FOREIGN KEY.
  • NOT NULL: add CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, validate it, then SET NOT NULL uses the valid check and skips the scan; drop the check afterwards (challenge).
  • Renames and type changes: expand/contract. Add the new column, write to both, backfill in batches, switch reads, stop writing the old one, drop it. Each step is a separate, quick, deployable change.
  • Backfills: in batches of a few thousand rows, each its own transaction, so locks are short and VACUUM can keep up (Q10).
  • Every migration: SET lock_timeout = '2s' (and a retry), and one change per transaction where possible.

Most migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase, Rails, Django, Prisma) wrap each migration in a transaction. That is great for atomicity (Session 55), but CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY must run outside it: every tool has a way to mark a migration as "no transaction". Check what yours does before production does it for you.

  4. Does adding a column with a constant default rewrite the table? Compare orders' relfilenode before and after ADD COLUMN source text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web'.

    (1 row)

    Same file (t), and all 36 rows report "web". Since Postgres 11 a constant default is stored once in the catalog and returned for old rows on read: instant, even on a billion rows.

  5. Now a volatile default: ADD COLUMN imported_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(). Does the file change?

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    CREATE TEMP TABLE before AS SELECT (SELECT relfilenode FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders') AS f;
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN imported_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp();
SELECT (SELECT relfilenode FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders') = (SELECT f FROM before) AS same_file;
    same_file
    f

    (1 row)

    f: a new file. Every row needs its own value, so Postgres rewrote the whole table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. On a big table: add the column without a default (instant), set the default for new rows, and backfill old rows in batches.

  6. Which type changes rewrite the table? customers.full_name is text. Change it to varchar(200), then widen it to varchar(300), then back to text, and record after each step whether customers got a new data file.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    CREATE TEMP TABLE f0 AS SELECT (SELECT relfilenode FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'customers') AS f;
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN full_name TYPE varchar(200);
CREATE TEMP TABLE f1 AS SELECT (SELECT relfilenode FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'customers') AS f;
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN full_name TYPE varchar(300);
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN full_name TYPE text;
SELECT (SELECT f FROM f1) = (SELECT f FROM f0)          AS same_after_text_to_varchar,
       (SELECT relfilenode FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'customers') = (SELECT f FROM f1) AS same_after_widening;
    same_after_text_to_varcharsame_after_widening
    ft

    (1 row)

    f, then t. text → varchar(200) must check every existing value against the new limit, and Postgres does that by rewriting the table. Widening a varchar, or going back to text, is only a catalog change, since the stored bytes are identical. int → bigint rewrites too (the bytes change), along with its indexes and the foreign keys that reference it: give new tables bigint ids from the start. Always test a type change on a copy and look at relfilenode before running it in production.

  7. Add a CHECK that order totals in order_items are positive (unit_price > 0) without scanning the table under a blocking lock: add it NOT VALID, check pg_constraint, validate, check again.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    ALTER TABLE order_items ADD CONSTRAINT unit_price_positive CHECK (unit_price > 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE order_items VALIDATE CONSTRAINT unit_price_positive;
SELECT conname, convalidated FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'unit_price_positive';
    connameconvalidated
    unit_price_positivet

    (1 row)

    convalidated t after VALIDATE. The ADD is instant (it only checks new rows from now on); VALIDATE scans the existing rows under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so the application keeps reading and writing during the scan. Session 41 used the same pair to clean data first.

  8. The payments table has no foreign key to orders (Phase 1). Add one without blocking writes, knowing that some existing payments point to missing orders. What happens at VALIDATE?

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer

INSERT INTO payments VALUES (33, 5000, 10, 'upi', now());
ALTER TABLE payments VALIDATE CONSTRAINT payments_order_fk;

ALTER TABLE
practice=# INSERT INTO payments VALUES (33, 5000, 10, 'upi', now());
ERROR:  insert or update on table "payments" violates foreign key constraint "payments_order_fk"
DETAIL:  Key (order_id)=(5000) is not present in table "orders".
practice=# ALTER TABLE payments VALIDATE CONSTRAINT payments_order_fk;
ERROR:  insert or update on table "payments" violates foreign key constraint "payments_order_fk"
DETAIL:  Key (order_id)=(9999) is not present in table "orders".

    The NOT VALID constraint is enforced at once: the new payment for order 5000 is rejected. VALIDATE then fails on the old orphans (orders 40 and 9999): clean them up (or move them to a quarantine table), and validate again. Until then the constraint protects all new data, which is already most of the value.

  9. Show that a plain CREATE INDEX blocks writers while CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not. A has an open transaction that updated an order; B creates an index on orders(customer_id) concurrently; C inserts an order meanwhile.

    Two terminals: compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE order_id = 36;
UPDATE 1
            B=# CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
                        C=# INSERT INTO orders VALUES (37, 1, '2026-02-15', 'pending', 'Mumbai');
                        INSERT 0 1
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            CREATE INDEX

    C's INSERT completes immediately although B is still waiting: CONCURRENTLY holds only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which allows writes. B finishes once A's transaction is over (it must wait for every transaction that could have started before the index existed). With a plain CREATE INDEX, C would have queued behind B: the lock queue again.

ALTER TABLE

           WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE city_code IS NULL AND shipping_city IS NOT NULL ORDER BY order_id LIMIT 10);

--------------+--------

(1 row)

    UPDATE 10, 10, 10, 5, 0: done. One order is left without a code because its shipping_city is NULL (order 24): decide what it should be before you make the column NOT NULL. In real life the batch is run by a script in a loop with a short pause, each batch its own transaction, so row locks last milliseconds and autovacuum keeps up. With millions of rows, batch by primary-key range (order_id BETWEEN x AND x + 9999) to avoid re-scanning for NULLs.

  11. Rename orders.shipping_city to ship_to_city without breaking the running application, which still reads shipping_city. Run the first expand steps in SQL: add ship_to_city, backfill it from shipping_city, and check that every row is in sync. The remaining steps are application deploys: describe them.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ship_to_city text;
UPDATE orders SET ship_to_city = shipping_city WHERE ship_to_city IS DISTINCT FROM shipping_city;
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE ship_to_city IS NOT DISTINCT FROM shipping_city) AS in_sync, count(*) AS orders FROM orders;
    practice=# ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ship_to_city text;
ALTER TABLE
practice=# UPDATE orders SET ship_to_city = shipping_city WHERE ship_to_city IS DISTINCT FROM shipping_city;
UPDATE 35
practice=# SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE ship_to_city IS NOT DISTINCT FROM shipping_city) AS in_sync, count(*) AS orders FROM orders;
 in_sync | orders
---------+--------
      36 |     36
(1 row)

    All 36 in sync. A plain RENAME is instant, but every running application server that still says shipping_city starts failing at that moment, and you cannot deploy all servers in the same millisecond. Expand/contract: (1) add ship_to_city; (2) deploy code that writes both columns; (3) backfill; (4) deploy code that reads ship_to_city; (5) deploy code that stops writing shipping_city; (6) drop shipping_city. Six boring steps, zero errors. (A trigger can do step 2 inside the database, Phase 7.)

  12. A migration script with protection: set lock_timeout to 1 second, start a transaction and add a column to orders, while another session (A) holds a long transaction that read orders. What happens, and what state is the table in afterwards?

    Two terminals: compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# SELECT count(*) FROM orders;
 count
-------
    36
(1 row)
            B=# SET lock_timeout = '1s';
            SET
            B=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            B=*# ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN priority int;
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
            B=!# ROLLBACK;
            ROLLBACK
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            B=# SELECT count(*) AS priority_columns FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'orders' AND column_name = 'priority';
             priority_columns
            ------------------
                            0
            (1 row)

    The ALTER gives up after 1 second; the transaction rolls back and the table is untouched (0 columns): nothing half-applied, nobody blocked for more than a second. The deploy script retries a few times with a pause; if it keeps failing, someone looks at what holds the lock (Session 58 Q12). Never "fix" this by removing lock_timeout.

  13. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can fail and leave an invalid index behind. Make it fail on purpose: create a UNIQUE index concurrently on orders(customer_id) (customers have several orders), then look at pg_index.indisvalid.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_one_per_customer ON orders (customer_id);
SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index_name, indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'orders'::regclass ORDER BY 1;
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_one_per_customer;
    practice=# CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_one_per_customer ON orders (customer_id);
ERROR:  could not create unique index "orders_one_per_customer"
DETAIL:  Key (customer_id)=(2) is duplicated.
practice=# SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index_name, indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'orders'::regclass ORDER BY 1;
       index_name        | indisvalid
-------------------------+------------
 orders_pkey             | t
 orders_one_per_customer | f
(2 rows)
practice=# DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_one_per_customer;
DROP INDEX

    The build fails on a duplicate key, but the index stays in the catalog with indisvalid = f. It is not used for queries, yet every write still maintains it. After any failed concurrent build, drop the invalid index (DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY) and retry. A monitoring query for NOT indisvalid catches the ones nobody noticed.

  14. Challenge: Make orders.shipping_city NOT NULL on a busy table. Order 24 has no shipping city; set it to 'Unknown'. Then add the NOT NULL without a long blocking scan: a CHECK (shipping_city IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, VALIDATE it, SET NOT NULL (which uses the valid check and skips the scan), and drop the now redundant check. Show attnotnull at the end.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    UPDATE orders SET shipping_city = 'Unknown' WHERE shipping_city IS NULL;
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT shipping_city_not_null CHECK (shipping_city IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT shipping_city_not_null;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN shipping_city SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT shipping_city_not_null;
SELECT attname, attnotnull FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND attname = 'shipping_city';
    practice=# UPDATE orders SET shipping_city = 'Unknown' WHERE shipping_city IS NULL;
UPDATE 1
practice=# ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT shipping_city_not_null CHECK (shipping_city IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE
practice=# ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT shipping_city_not_null;
ALTER TABLE
practice=# ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN shipping_city SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE
practice=# ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT shipping_city_not_null;
ALTER TABLE
practice=# SELECT attname, attnotnull FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND attname = 'shipping_city';
    attname    | attnotnull
---------------+------------
 shipping_city | t
(1 row)

    attnotnull = t. The only long step, VALIDATE, runs under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (reads and writes continue); SET NOT NULL sees the validated CHECK and skips its own full-table scan, so its ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock lasts milliseconds. In a real migration each statement is its own transaction with lock_timeout set, and the backfill (step 1) runs in batches. Postgres 18 can also add NOT NULL itself as NOT VALID (ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT NULL shipping_city NOT VALID); the CHECK recipe works on every version.

Phase 6 · Session 62

Exit test + Apply: Concurrency

Prove you can keep data correct when many sessions work at once: 14 questions written cold, no notes, at least 11 of 14 correct.

Topics

Exit test rules

  • Cold: no notes, no earlier sessions, no answers until you are done.
  • Time box: 90 minutes. Most questions need two psql windows (A and B); run the steps in the order the question gives.
  • Predict first: before running a two-terminal question, write down what each terminal will print (including who waits and who gets an error). A question counts only if your prediction and your output match the answer.
  • Pass = 11 of 14 or more. Pass → Phase 7 (functions, triggers and security). Fail → redo every missed question, re-read its session, and retake the test later.
  • Reload practice.sql before you start.

What the test checks

Q1, Q2, Q7      transactions, savepoints, ON CONFLICT          (S55, S59)
Q3, Q4, Q9, Q10 isolation levels and anomalies                (S57)
Q5, Q6, Q11     row locks, job queues, deadlocks               (S58)
Q12             advisory locks                                 (S59)
Q8, Q13         DDL locks and safe migrations                  (S61)
Q14             materialized views                             (S60)

Apply project: a concurrency-safe job system

Write psql/projects/p6-concurrency.sql and a short p6-concurrency.md:

  • A jobs table with the partial index that serves the claim query, and the claim, finish (with fencing), fail (attempts limit) and reaper statements from Session 58.
  • Open three psql windows as three workers and process all queued jobs with your statements. Paste the transcript into the .md and explain why no job ran twice.
  • Add an idempotency_key to job creation (Session 59) so that a client retrying "create job" cannot create it twice.
  • Write the migration that adds a priority column and changes the claim index to (priority DESC, run_after), as a zero-downtime script: lock_timeout, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY (Session 61).
  • For your Visitly app: list every place where two users can act on the same thing at once (the same table, the same slot, the same coupon), and which tool from this phase protects each one.

The last step is the one interviewers ask about: "what happens if two users book the last table at the same time?" Being able to answer with the exact constraint or lock, and show the transcript, is what this phase was for.

Write your answers in psql/s62.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  15. Challenge: Visitly rooms: private dining rooms are booked by time range. Create room_bookings with an exclusion constraint so a room can never be double-booked. Then A books room 1 from 19:00 to 21:00 (open transaction) while B tries 20:00–22:00 on room 1, and C books 20:00–22:00 on room 2. Show who waits, who fails, and the final bookings.

    Two terminals: compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# INSERT INTO room_bookings VALUES (1, '[2026-02-20 19:00+05:30, 2026-02-20 21:00+05:30)', 'Aarav');
INSERT 0 1
            B=# INSERT INTO room_bookings VALUES (1, '[2026-02-20 20:00+05:30, 2026-02-20 22:00+05:30)', 'Diya');
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
                        C=# INSERT INTO room_bookings VALUES (2, '[2026-02-20 20:00+05:30, 2026-02-20 22:00+05:30)', 'Kabir');
                        INSERT 0 1
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            ERROR:  conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "room_bookings_room_during_excl"
            DETAIL:  Key (room, during)=(1, ["2026-02-20 20:00:00+05:30","2026-02-20 22:00:00+05:30")) conflicts with existing key (room, during)=(1, ["2026-02-20 19:00:00+05:30","2026-02-20 21:00:00+05:30")).
A=# SELECT room, guest FROM room_bookings ORDER BY room;
 room | guest
------+-------
    1 | Aarav
    2 | Kabir
(2 rows)

    B waits for A (its range overlaps A's uncommitted booking on the same room) and fails when A commits; C, on another room, is not affected at all. The exclusion constraint is both the rule and the lock: no application code, no SERIALIZABLE, no race. This is the answer to "what if two users book the same room at once?"

Phase 6 · Session 63

Review: isolation, locks and migrations

Pull Sessions 57–62 back out of memory, mixed with earlier phases, before moving on to functions and triggers.

Topics

How to run this review

  • Reload practice.sql. First 20 minutes: redo every question you got wrong in the exit test (Session 62), cold.
  • Then the 14 questions below. For every two-terminal question, write down your prediction first: which statement waits, which one fails, what each SELECT returns.
  • Then the challenge: one booking flow that combines everything.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 57–62

Problem                                  Tool
---------------------------------------  -------------------------------------------------------------
read-modify-write loses updates          UPDATE … SET x = x + 1   or   SELECT … FOR UPDATE first
report must be consistent across queries BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY
rule over several rows (write skew)      lock a parent row FOR UPDATE, or SERIALIZABLE + retry (40001)
many workers, one queue                  … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1, lease + fencing + reaper
do not wait                              NOWAIT · lock_timeout · pg_try_advisory_xact_lock
deadlocks (40P01)                        lock in one global order; retry
create exactly once                      UNIQUE / exclusion constraint + INSERT … ON CONFLICT
retries of the same request              idempotency key in the same transaction
one at a time per X, no row to lock      pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('x:' || id))
expensive report, read often             materialized view + unique index + REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY
schema change on a busy table            lock_timeout, NOT VALID + VALIDATE, CONCURRENTLY, expand/contract
