← Phase 7: Functions, triggers + RLSAll phasesSchema

Phase 7 · Session 64

SQL functions 1

Package a query or a formula as a named SQL function with parameters and defaults, use it anywhere an expression is allowed, and manage functions safely (replace, overload, drop).

Topics

Why functions

Phase 6 ended with business rules spread over several statements. A function gives a rule one name and one definition, so every report, view and application computes "order total" or "price with tax" the same way, and you change it in one place. A function runs inside the server, next to the data: one round trip instead of several.

A SQL function

CREATE FUNCTION order_total(p_order_id int) RETURNS numeric
LANGUAGE sql
RETURN (SELECT COALESCE(sum(quantity * unit_price), 0) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = p_order_id);

SELECT order_total(9) AS order_9, order_total(30) AS order_30;
order_9order_30
89000.000

(1 row)

  • RETURNS numeric: the type of the result. LANGUAGE sql: the body is plain SQL (PL/pgSQL comes in Session 66).
  • RETURN expression (Postgres 14+) is the SQL-standard body: Postgres parses it at CREATE time, checks that the tables and columns exist, and records dependencies, so you cannot drop a column the function uses (Q9).
  • The older form puts the body in a string: AS $$ SELECT … $$. It is only checked when called, and has no dependencies. Both are common; prefer the standard body for SQL functions.
  • Name parameters so they cannot be confused with columns: p_order_id, not order_id.
  • A function call is an expression: use it in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, CHECK constraints, DEFAULTs and indexes (if immutable, Session 65).

Defaults and named arguments

CREATE FUNCTION price_with_tax(amount numeric, rate numeric DEFAULT 0.18) RETURNS numeric
LANGUAGE sql
RETURN round(amount * (1 + rate), 2);

SELECT price_with_tax(1000)              AS gst_18,
       price_with_tax(1000, 0.05)        AS gst_5,
       price_with_tax(amount => 1000, rate => 0.12) AS named;
gst_18gst_5named
1180.001050.001120.00

(1 row)

Changing and removing functions

  • CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION changes the body, but not the name, argument types or return type. To change those: DROP and CREATE (in one transaction).
  • Overloading: functions with the same name and different argument types are different functions. DROP FUNCTION f then needs the argument types: DROP FUNCTION f(int).
  • Every function lives in a schema (here public) and belongs to a role. Who may call it is Session 72.
\df order_total          list functions in psql
\sf order_total          show the source
\ef order_total          edit it in your editor

A function that runs a query, called once per row of a big table, runs that query once per row (Session 52's SubPlan problem, hidden behind a nice name). Use functions for logic and for single rows; for "every order with its total", a JOIN + GROUP BY is still the answer (Q11).

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s64.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Create order_total(p_order_id int) from the lesson and return the totals of orders 1, 2 and 30 (order 30 has no items).

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION order_total(p_order_id int) RETURNS numeric
LANGUAGE sql
RETURN (SELECT COALESCE(sum(quantity * unit_price), 0) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = p_order_id);

SELECT o AS order_id, order_total(o) AS total FROM unnest(ARRAY[1, 2, 30]) AS o;
    order_idtotal
    1119500.00
    223000.00
    300

    (3 rows)

    119,500, 23,000 and 0. Without COALESCE, order 30 would return NULL, and NULL + anything is NULL in every report that adds totals.

  2. Use order_total in a WHERE clause: delivered orders whose total is above 100,000, with their totals.

Phase 7 · Session 65

SQL functions 2: volatility and set-returning functions

Declare how a function behaves (IMMUTABLE, STABLE, VOLATILE, STRICT) so the planner can use indexes and inline it, and write functions that return whole result sets.

Topics

Volatility: a promise to the planner

IMMUTABLE   same arguments → same result, forever. No table reads, no settings.   lower(), abs(), 2 * x
            Required for expression indexes and generated columns. May be computed once at plan time.
STABLE      same result within one statement. May read tables and settings.          now(), current_setting(), lookups
            Can be used to search an index: evaluated once, then compared.
VOLATILE    may change on every call, or has side effects. The default!              random(), clock_timestamp(), nextval(), INSERT
            Called again for every row; never used as an index search value.

Postgres believes what you declare. Too pessimistic (the default VOLATILE for a pure formula) and you lose indexes and inlining; too optimistic (IMMUTABLE for something that reads a table or depends on the time zone) and you get wrong results, for example an index built with old values.

BEGIN;
CREATE FUNCTION email_key(p text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE
RETURN lower(trim(p));
CREATE INDEX customers_email_key ON customers (email_key(email));
SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE email_key(email) = 'diya@mail.test';
ROLLBACK;
Index Scan using customers_email_key on customers
  Index Cond: (lower(TRIM(BOTH FROM email)) = 'diya@mail.test'::text)

The index is used, and the Index Cond shows lower(TRIM(…)), not email_key(…): a simple SQL function like this one is inlined, so Postgres indexes the expression itself. A function that cannot be inlined (one that reads a table, or is written in PL/pgSQL) must be declared IMMUTABLE before it can be indexed, and must really be immutable (Q1). (On 20 rows the planner would scan the table anyway, which is why seq scans are switched off for the demonstration.)

STRICT and other attributes

  • STRICT (= RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT): if any argument is NULL, the function is not run and returns NULL. Saves writing NULL checks.
  • PARALLEL SAFE: may run in a parallel worker (Session 53). Mark pure functions so; the default is UNSAFE.
  • COST n and ROWS n: hints for the planner about how expensive a call is and how many rows a set-returning function returns (default 1000).
  • SECURITY DEFINER: runs with the owner's privileges (Session 72).

Set-returning functions

A function can return many rows: RETURNS TABLE (col type, …) or RETURNS SETOF some_table. Call it in FROM like a table; with LATERAL, once per row of another table. You already know some: generate_series, unnest, jsonb_array_elements.

CREATE FUNCTION customer_orders(p_customer_id int)
RETURNS TABLE (order_id int, order_date date, status text)
LANGUAGE sql STABLE
AS $$ SELECT order_id, order_date, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = p_customer_id $$;

SELECT * FROM customer_orders(1) ORDER BY order_date;
order_idorder_datestatus
12025-01-05delivered
32025-01-20delivered
132025-04-18delivered
272025-10-03pending

(4 rows)

Inlining: a function that is really a view

A simple SQL function (one SELECT, not VOLATILE, not STRICT, not SECURITY DEFINER) is inlined: the planner pastes its body into the query, so filters and joins work through it as through a view. A VOLATILE one is a black box: a Function Scan that returns all its rows (estimated as 1,000) before anything else can happen.

BEGIN;
CREATE FUNCTION customer_orders(p_customer_id int)
RETURNS TABLE (order_id int, order_date date, status text)
LANGUAGE sql STABLE
AS $$ SELECT order_id, order_date, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = p_customer_id $$;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM customer_orders(1) WHERE status = 'delivered';
ROLLBACK;
Seq Scan on orders
  Filter: ((customer_id = 1) AND (status = 'delivered'::text))

Rule of thumb: mark every function with the strongest volatility that is true. Pure formulas: IMMUTABLE (and PARALLEL SAFE). Functions that read tables or now(): STABLE. Functions that change data, or call random() / clock_timestamp() / nextval(): VOLATILE.

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s65.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Write city_zone(p_city text) that looks up the shipping zone in shipping_zones (default volatility), and try to index orders by city_zone(shipping_city). Then declare it IMMUTABLE and try again. Is the second attempt a good idea?

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION city_zone(p_city text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql
RETURN (SELECT zone FROM shipping_zones WHERE city = p_city);
CREATE INDEX orders_zone ON orders (city_zone(shipping_city));
ALTER FUNCTION city_zone(text) IMMUTABLE;
CREATE INDEX orders_zone ON orders (city_zone(shipping_city));
    practice=# CREATE FUNCTION city_zone(p_city text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql
           RETURN (SELECT zone FROM shipping_zones WHERE city = p_city);
CREATE FUNCTION
practice=# CREATE INDEX orders_zone ON orders (city_zone(shipping_city));
ERROR:  functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE
practice=# ALTER FUNCTION city_zone(text) IMMUTABLE;
ALTER FUNCTION
practice=# CREATE INDEX orders_zone ON orders (city_zone(shipping_city));
CREATE INDEX

    First: "functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE". After ALTER FUNCTION … IMMUTABLE the index builds, but it is a lie: the function reads shipping_zones, so when someone moves Pune to another zone, the index keeps the old zone and queries through it return wrong rows. Never mark a table lookup IMMUTABLE; store the zone in a column (or a generated column from an honest IMMUTABLE expression) instead.

  2. Show which volatility Postgres's own now(), lower(), random() and clock_timestamp() have.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    SELECT oid::regprocedure AS function, provolatile
FROM pg_proc
WHERE oid IN ('now()'::regprocedure, 'lower(text)'::regprocedure,
              'random()'::regprocedure, 'clock_timestamp()'::regprocedure)
ORDER BY 1::text;
    functionprovolatile
    lower(text)i
    now()s
    random()v
    clock_timestamp()v

    (4 rows)

    clock_timestamp v, lower i, now s, random v. ('lower(text)'::regprocedure picks one exact function: lower is overloaded for ranges too.) now() is STABLE because it is fixed within a transaction (Session 55); clock_timestamp() changes during a statement, so it is VOLATILE.

    BEGIN;
CREATE FUNCTION customer_orders(p_customer_id int)

  8. How many rows does the planner expect from a set-returning function it cannot inline? Show EXPLAIN (no options) for the VOLATILE customer_orders(1), then set ROWS 5 on it and explain again.

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE FUNCTION customer_orders(p_customer_id int)
RETURNS TABLE (order_id int, order_date date, status text)
LANGUAGE sql VOLATILE
AS $$ SELECT order_id, order_date, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = p_customer_id $$;

  9. STABLE vs VOLATILE in a WHERE clause. With an index on orders(order_date) and seq scans off, compare the plans for order_date >= cutoff(), where cutoff() returns the newest order date minus 45 days, when it is STABLE and when it is VOLATILE.

    Compare your plan with the answer

    Answer
    BEGIN;
CREATE INDEX orders_order_date_idx ON orders (order_date);
CREATE FUNCTION cutoff_s() RETURNS date LANGUAGE sql STABLE   RETURN (SELECT max(order_date) - 45 FROM orders);
CREATE FUNCTION cutoff_v() RETURNS date LANGUAGE sql VOLATILE RETURN (SELECT max(order_date) - 45 FROM orders);
SET LOCAL enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE order_date >= cutoff_s();   -- Index Scan
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE order_date >= cutoff_v();
ROLLBACK;
    Seq Scan on orders
  Disabled: true
  Filter: (order_date >= cutoff_v())

    STABLE: an Index (Only) Scan with cutoff_s() in the Index Cond, evaluated once. VOLATILE: a Seq Scan (marked Disabled, because there was no other way), calling cutoff_v() for every row. A forgotten STABLE on a lookup function silently turns index scans into full scans.

Phase 7 · Session 66

PL/pgSQL basics

Write procedural code inside the database (variables, IF, loops, SELECT INTO, RETURN QUERY), and know when a loop should really be one SQL statement.

Topics

When SQL is not enough

SQL functions are one query. Business logic often needs steps and decisions: "lock both accounts, check the balance, and either refuse with a reason or move the money". PL/pgSQL is Postgres's built-in procedural language: SQL statements plus variables, IF, loops and error handling, running inside the server.

CREATE FUNCTION name(params) RETURNS type
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  v_total numeric := 0;          -- variables, with optional initial value
  v_order orders%ROWTYPE;        -- a whole row of a table
  v_city  customers.city%TYPE;   -- the same type as a column
BEGIN
  SELECT … INTO v_total FROM …;  -- one row into variables (FOUND says whether a row came back)
  IF … THEN … ELSIF … ELSE … END IF;
  FOR r IN SELECT … LOOP … END LOOP;
  RETURN v_total;
END;
$$;

A DO block runs anonymous PL/pgSQL once, without creating a function. RAISE NOTICE prints a message (psql shows it as NOTICE); % placeholders are filled from the arguments:

practice=# DO $$
           DECLARE
             v_pending int;
           BEGIN
             SELECT count(*) INTO v_pending FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
             RAISE NOTICE 'There are % pending orders', v_pending;
             IF v_pending > 5 THEN
               RAISE NOTICE 'Too many: check the warehouse';
             END IF;
           END;
           $$;
NOTICE:  There are 7 pending orders
NOTICE:  Too many: check the warehouse
DO

A real function: transfer with checks

CREATE FUNCTION transfer(p_from int, p_to int, p_amount numeric) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  v_balance numeric;
BEGIN
  IF p_amount <= 0 THEN
    RETURN 'amount must be positive';
  END IF;
  -- lock both rows in id order (Session 58), read the source balance
  PERFORM 1 FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (p_from, p_to) ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE;
  SELECT balance INTO v_balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = p_from;
  IF NOT FOUND OR NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts WHERE account_id = p_to) THEN
    RETURN 'unknown account';
  ELSIF v_balance < p_amount THEN
    RETURN 'insufficient funds';
  END IF;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - p_amount WHERE account_id = p_from;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + p_amount WHERE account_id = p_to;
  RETURN 'ok';
END;
$$;

SELECT transfer(1, 3, 1000) AS first, transfer(3, 1, 5000) AS second, transfer(1, 99, 10) AS third;
firstsecondthird
okinsufficient fundsunknown account

(1 row)

  • PERFORM runs a query and throws the result away (PL/pgSQL does not allow a bare SELECT without INTO).
  • FOUND is true after a SELECT INTO / UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT that affected at least one row.
  • The whole function runs in the caller's transaction: if the caller rolls back, the transfer is undone too.
  • Name variables v_… and parameters p_…. A variable called like a column makes queries ambiguous (Q12).

Returning rows

RETURNS TABLE (…) / SETOF …   and inside:
  RETURN QUERY SELECT …;      append all rows of a query
  RETURN NEXT;                 append the current values of the OUT columns (in a loop)
  RETURN;                      finish

Loops vs set-based SQL

A loop over 10,000 rows that runs an UPDATE per row does 10,000 statements. One UPDATE with a join does the same work in one statement, usually 10–100× faster. Use loops for orchestration (batches, steps, decisions per batch), and keep the row work in SQL.

PL/pgSQL caches the plan of each query inside a function after the first few calls, like a prepared statement (generic plans, Session 52). Usually good; occasionally a skewed parameter needs EXECUTE (Session 67) to be planned with the real value every time.

  2. Write a PL/pgSQL function status_label(p_status text) RETURNS text that turns pending/shipped/delivered/cancelled into "Waiting", "On the way", "Delivered", "Cancelled" and anything else into "Unknown", using CASE. Show the label for each status in orders with its count.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION status_label(p_status text) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$
BEGIN
  CASE p_status
    WHEN 'pending'   THEN RETURN 'Waiting';
    WHEN 'shipped'   THEN RETURN 'On the way';
    WHEN 'delivered' THEN RETURN 'Delivered';
    WHEN 'cancelled' THEN RETURN 'Cancelled';
    ELSE RETURN 'Unknown';
  END CASE;
END;
$$;

SELECT status_label(status) AS label, count(*) FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
    labelcount
    Delivered21
    Waiting7
    On the way4
    Cancelled4

    (4 rows)

    4 labels. A CASE statement (with END CASE) is control flow; the SQL CASE expression would have done the same as a SQL function. Use PL/pgSQL when you need steps, not for a single expression.

  3. Write loyalty_tier(p_customer_id int) RETURNS text: delivered revenue ≥ 100,000 → Gold, ≥ 20,000 → Silver, > 0 → Bronze, otherwise New. Show the tier of customers 1 to 6.

    Expected: 6 rows

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION loyalty_tier(p_customer_id int) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  v_revenue numeric;
BEGIN
  SELECT COALESCE(sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) INTO v_revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.customer_id = p_customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered';

  IF v_revenue >= 100000 THEN RETURN 'Gold';
  ELSIF v_revenue >= 20000 THEN RETURN 'Silver';
  ELSIF v_revenue > 0 THEN RETURN 'Bronze';
  ELSE RETURN 'New';
  END IF;
END;
$$;

SELECT customer_id, loyalty_tier(customer_id) AS tier FROM customers WHERE customer_id <= 6 ORDER BY customer_id;

    1Gold
    2Gold
    3Bronze
    4Bronze
    5Silver
    6Bronze

    (6 rows)

    Gold, Gold, Bronze, Bronze, Silver, Bronze. Customer 6 has 19,800 of delivered revenue: 200 short of Silver. Thresholds like this belong in one function (or a tiers table, like discount_tiers) so that the boundary is the same everywhere. The IF chain stops at the first true condition: order the thresholds from highest to lowest.

  7. Use %ROWTYPE: write order_line(p_order_id int) RETURNS text that loads the order row and returns "Order 9 · delivered · 2025-03-15 · Bengaluru".

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION order_line(p_order_id int) RETURNS text
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  v orders%ROWTYPE;
BEGIN
  SELECT * INTO v FROM orders WHERE order_id = p_order_id;
  IF NOT FOUND THEN
    RETURN NULL;
  END IF;
  RETURN format('Order %s · %s · %s · %s', v.order_id, v.status, v.order_date, COALESCE(v.shipping_city, '?'));
END;
$$;

    %ROWTYPE follows the table: add a column and the variable has it too. format() with %s is the safe way to build text (and the only safe way to build SQL, Session 67).

  8. A loop: how many years until 10,000 grows to at least 20,000 at 7% a year? Write years_to_double(p_rate numeric) with a WHILE loop.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION years_to_double(p_rate numeric) RETURNS int
LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  v_amount numeric := 10000;
  v_years  int := 0;
BEGIN
  WHILE v_amount < 20000 LOOP
    v_amount := v_amount * (1 + p_rate);
    v_years := v_years + 1;
  END LOOP;
  RETURN v_years;
END;
$$;

SELECT years_to_double(0.07) AS at_7, years_to_double(0.10) AS at_10;
    at_7at_10
    118

    (1 row)

    11 and 8 years. A loop is natural for this; a loop over table rows usually is not (Q9). With rate 0 it would never end: real code guards against that (IF p_rate <= 0 THEN RETURN NULL).

  11. Write order_lines(p_order_id int) RETURNS TABLE (product text, line_total numeric, running_total numeric) using a FOR loop and RETURN NEXT, in product name order. Show order 9. Then write the same with a window function in one SELECT.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION order_lines(p_order_id int)
RETURNS TABLE (product text, line_total numeric, running_total numeric)
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  r record;
BEGIN
  running_total := 0;
  FOR r IN SELECT p.name, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS amount
           FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
           WHERE oi.order_id = p_order_id ORDER BY p.name LOOP
    product := r.name;
    line_total := r.amount;
    running_total := running_total + r.amount;
    RETURN NEXT;
  END LOOP;
END;
$$;

ERROR:  column reference "customer_id" is ambiguous
DETAIL:  It could refer to either a PL/pgSQL variable or a table column.

    "column reference customer_id is ambiguous": PL/pgSQL refuses to guess whether you meant the parameter or the column (the default plpgsql.variable_conflict = error). Even qualifying one side is not enough here. Fix it by naming the parameter p_customer_id. SQL functions resolve such names differently (the column wins), which is worse: no error, just wrong results.

  13. EXIT and CONTINUE: find the first day of February 2025 on which no order was placed, with a FOR loop over the days.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION first_quiet_day(p_from date, p_to date) RETURNS date
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  d date;
BEGIN
  FOR d IN SELECT g::date FROM generate_series(p_from, p_to, INTERVAL '1 day') AS g LOOP
    CONTINUE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE order_date = d);
    RETURN d;
  END LOOP;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

SELECT first_quiet_day('2025-02-01', '2025-02-28') AS quiet, first_quiet_day('2025-02-03', '2025-02-03') AS none;
    quietnone
    2025-02-01∅

    (1 row)

    2025-02-01, and NULL for a range where every day had an order. The set-based answer is a spine + NOT EXISTS + min() (Session 17): one query. Loops read naturally, but always ask whether one query can say it.

  14. Write account_report() RETURNS TABLE (owner text, balance numeric, share text) that returns every account with its share of the total as a percentage string like "54.3%", computing the total once before the loop.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION account_report() RETURNS TABLE (owner text, balance numeric, share text)
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  v_total numeric;
  r accounts%ROWTYPE;
BEGIN
  SELECT sum(a.balance) INTO v_total FROM accounts a;
  FOR r IN SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id LOOP
    owner := r.owner;
    balance := r.balance;
    share := round(100 * r.balance / NULLIF(v_total, 0), 1) || '%';
    RETURN NEXT;
  END LOOP;
END;
$$;

    Diya3000.0032.6%
    Kabir0.000.0%
    Ananya1200.0013.0%

    (4 rows)

    Aarav 54.3%, Diya 32.6%, Kabir 0.0%, Ananya 13.0%. Again a window function would do it in one query (balance / sum(balance) OVER ()); here the point is the pattern: compute once, loop, emit rows.

Phase 7 · Session 67

PL/pgSQL errors and dynamic SQL

Raise meaningful errors with codes, details and hints, catch and handle specific errors, and build SQL at run time without opening the door to SQL injection.

Topics

Raising errors

A function that returns "insufficient funds" as text (Session 66) can be ignored by a careless caller. An exception cannot: it aborts the statement and the transaction (Session 55), and the caller receives a SQLSTATE code it can act on.

RAISE EXCEPTION 'insufficient funds in account %', p_from
  USING ERRCODE = 'P1001',            -- your own 5-character code, or a name like 'check_violation'
        DETAIL  = 'balance 0.00, requested 500',
        HINT    = 'Transfer a smaller amount.';

RAISE NOTICE / WARNING / INFO …     messages that do not stop anything
ASSERT condition, 'message';         a check for "this cannot happen" (can be switched off)
practice=# CREATE FUNCTION transfer(p_from int, p_to int, p_amount numeric) RETURNS void
           LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
           DECLARE
             v_balance numeric;
           BEGIN
             IF p_amount <= 0 THEN
               RAISE EXCEPTION 'amount must be positive, got %', p_amount USING ERRCODE = 'invalid_parameter_value';
             END IF;
             PERFORM 1 FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (p_from, p_to) ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE;
             SELECT balance INTO v_balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = p_from;
             IF NOT FOUND THEN
               RAISE EXCEPTION 'account % does not exist', p_from USING ERRCODE = 'no_data_found';
             END IF;
             IF v_balance < p_amount THEN
               RAISE EXCEPTION 'insufficient funds in account %', p_from
                 USING ERRCODE = 'P1001',
                       DETAIL = format('balance %s, requested %s', v_balance, p_amount),
                       HINT = 'Transfer a smaller amount.';
             END IF;
             UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - p_amount WHERE account_id = p_from;
             UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + p_amount WHERE account_id = p_to;
           END;
           $$;
CREATE FUNCTION
practice=# SELECT transfer(3, 1, 500);
ERROR:  insufficient funds in account 3
DETAIL:  balance 0.00, requested 500
HINT:  Transfer a smaller amount.

Pick codes deliberately. Built-in names (unique_violation 23505, check_violation 23514, no_data_found P0002, invalid_parameter_value 22023) tell any client what kind of problem it was. For business rules, use your own codes (letters + digits, not starting with 0, 1 or 2, which are taken), document them, and let the application map them to messages.

Catching errors

BEGIN
  … statements …
EXCEPTION
  WHEN unique_violation THEN                  -- by condition name
    …
  WHEN SQLSTATE 'P1001' THEN                  -- by code
    …
  WHEN OTHERS THEN                            -- anything else (use with care)
    GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS v_state = RETURNED_SQLSTATE, v_msg = MESSAGE_TEXT;
    RAISE;                                    -- re-raise the same error
END;
  • When an error is caught, everything the block did is rolled back (the block is a savepoint, Session 55); the function continues after the EXCEPTION section.
  • Each BEGIN … EXCEPTION block costs a subtransaction. Fine around a risky step; slow around every row of a 100,000-row loop.
  • Catch only what you can handle. Catching WHEN OTHERS and carrying on silently hides bugs; log and re-raise instead.

Dynamic SQL

EXECUTE runs a SQL string built at run time: a table name passed as a parameter, an optional filter, DDL for a new partition. The string is a program; never paste user input into it. Use format() for identifiers and USING for values:

EXECUTE format('SELECT count(*) FROM %I WHERE %I = $1', p_table, p_column)
  INTO v_count
  USING p_value;

%I   identifier, quoted if needed:  orders, "Order Items"
%L   literal, quoted and escaped:   'O''Brien'      (prefer USING for values)
%s   plain text: never for anything that came from a user

String concatenation is SQL injection: '… WHERE full_name = ''' || p_name || '''' with p_name = x' OR '1'='1 becomes a query that matches every row (Q7). The same mistake in an application (building SQL strings from request parameters) is still one of the most common security holes on the web.

  9. A generic, safe filter: count_where(p_table text, p_column text, p_value text) RETURNS bigint that counts rows where a column equals a value. Use %I for the names and USING for the value; compare as text. Count pending orders and Pune customers.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION count_where(p_table text, p_column text, p_value text) RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  v bigint;
BEGIN
  EXECUTE format('SELECT count(*) FROM %I WHERE %I::text = $1', p_table, p_column) INTO v USING p_value;
  RETURN v;
END;
$$;

SELECT count_where('orders', 'status', 'pending') AS pending_orders,
       count_where('customers', 'city', 'Pune') AS pune_customers;
    pending_orderspune_customers
    73

    (1 row)

    7 and 3. Identifiers through %I, values through USING: the two rules that make dynamic SQL safe. (The ::text cast makes it generic, but it also stops any index on that column from being used: generic code has a price.)

  IF p_amount <= 0 THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'amount must be positive, got %', p_amount USING ERRCODE = 'invalid_parameter_value';
  END IF;
  PERFORM 1 FROM accounts WHERE account_id IN (p_from, p_to) ORDER BY account_id FOR UPDATE;
  SELECT balance INTO v_balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = p_from;
  IF NOT FOUND THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'account % does not exist', p_from USING ERRCODE = 'no_data_found';
  END IF;
  IF v_balance < p_amount THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'insufficient funds in account %', p_from
      USING ERRCODE = 'P1001',
            DETAIL = format('balance %s, requested %s', v_balance, p_amount),
            HINT = 'Transfer a smaller amount.';
  END IF;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - p_amount WHERE account_id = p_from;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + p_amount WHERE account_id = p_to;
END;
$$;

    CREATE FUNCTION transfer(p_from int, p_to int, p_amount numeric) RETURNS void
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$

  v_found int;

BEGIN

Challenge: A safe sortable product list for an API: sorted_products(p_sort text, p_desc boolean) RETURNS TABLE (name text, price numeric) where p_sort may only be name or price (anything else raises invalid_parameter_value with a HINT listing the allowed values). Build the ORDER BY with format(). Call it sorted by price descending, and once with p_sort = 'price; DROP TABLE products'.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION sorted_products(p_sort text, p_desc boolean DEFAULT false)
RETURNS TABLE (name text, price numeric)
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
BEGIN
  IF p_sort NOT IN ('name', 'price') THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'cannot sort by %', p_sort
      USING ERRCODE = 'invalid_parameter_value', HINT = 'Allowed: name, price.';
  END IF;
  RETURN QUERY EXECUTE format('SELECT p.name, p.price FROM products p ORDER BY %I %s, p.product_id',
                              p_sort, CASE WHEN p_desc THEN 'DESC' ELSE 'ASC' END);
END;
$$;
SELECT * FROM sorted_products('price', true) LIMIT 3;
SELECT * FROM sorted_products('price; DROP TABLE products');

               RAISE EXCEPTION 'cannot sort by %', p_sort
                 USING ERRCODE = 'invalid_parameter_value', HINT = 'Allowed: name, price.';
             END IF;
             RETURN QUERY EXECUTE format('SELECT p.name, p.price FROM products p ORDER BY %I %s, p.product_id',

Three layers: a whitelist (the only real defence for ORDER BY, which cannot take a $1), %I quoting as a second net, and the direction chosen from a boolean, never from text. The tiebreaker (product_id) keeps the order stable for pagination (Session 51).

Phase 7 · Session 68

Procedures

Write procedures that commit as they go, run large batch jobs in small transactions, and know exactly where transaction control is and is not allowed.

Topics

Function or procedure?

                     FUNCTION                       PROCEDURE
called with          SELECT f(…), inside any query  CALL p(…), on its own
returns              a value, a row or a set        nothing (or INOUT / OUT parameters)
COMMIT / ROLLBACK    never                          yes, when called outside BEGIN … COMMIT
use for              calculations, lookups, rules   batch jobs, maintenance, multi-step work

A function always runs inside the caller's transaction: everything it does commits or rolls back together. A procedure can end the transaction it runs in and start a new one: COMMIT inside the body saves the work so far, and the next statement automatically runs in a fresh transaction.

practice=# CREATE PROCEDURE enqueue_job(p_kind text, p_payload jsonb DEFAULT '{}')
           LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
           BEGIN
             INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, payload, run_after)
             SELECT max(job_id) + 1, p_kind, p_payload, now() FROM jobs;
           END;
           $$;
CREATE PROCEDURE
practice=# CALL enqueue_job('send_email', '{"to": "tara@mail.test", "template": "welcome"}');
CALL
practice=# SELECT job_id, kind, status FROM jobs WHERE job_id = 11;
 job_id |    kind    | status
--------+------------+--------
     11 | send_email | queued
(1 row)

Big jobs in small transactions

Moving 100,000 old rows in one DELETE holds row locks on all of them for the whole run, blocks VACUUM from cleaning up, builds a huge amount of WAL at once, and if it fails after 40 minutes, all of it rolls back. In batches, each transaction is short and each finished batch stays done:

LOOP
  move up to 1,000 rows
  EXIT WHEN nothing was moved
  COMMIT;              -- saved; locks released; other sessions carry on
END LOOP;

Where COMMIT is not allowed

  • When the CALL is inside an explicit transaction (BEGIN; CALL p(); …): the procedure cannot commit the caller's transaction. Error: invalid transaction termination.
  • Inside a BEGIN … EXCEPTION block (it is a subtransaction). Put the EXCEPTION block inside the loop and the COMMIT outside it (Q8).
  • In a procedure with a SET clause or SECURITY DEFINER, and when the procedure is called from a function (SELECT f() → CALL p()).
  • Drivers often wrap everything in a transaction by default; run a committing procedure with autocommit on.

A procedure that commits is no longer all-or-nothing. If it fails in batch 7, batches 1–6 are saved. That is the point, but the job must be safe to run again (it picks up what is left), and nothing else may depend on "all or none" happening.

  3. Create big_orders_archive and the batch procedure archive_cancelled() from the lesson, then archive cancelled orders created before 2025.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE big_orders_archive (LIKE big_orders);
CREATE PROCEDURE archive_cancelled(p_before timestamptz, p_batch int DEFAULT 1000)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  n bigint;
  total bigint := 0;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    WITH moved AS (
      DELETE FROM big_orders
      WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM big_orders
                         WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND created_at < p_before
                         ORDER BY order_id LIMIT p_batch)
      RETURNING *
    )
    INSERT INTO big_orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
    GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT;
    EXIT WHEN n = 0;
    total := total + n;
    COMMIT;                                   -- this batch is saved, its locks are released
    RAISE NOTICE 'batch of %, % archived so far', n, total;
  END LOOP;
END;
$$;
CALL archive_cancelled('2025-01-01');
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders_archive) AS archived,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS still_cancelled;

practice=# CREATE PROCEDURE archive_cancelled(p_before timestamptz, p_batch int DEFAULT 1000)
           LANGUAGE plpgsql SET work_mem = '64MB' AS $$
           DECLARE
             n bigint;
             total bigint := 0;
           BEGIN
             LOOP
               WITH moved AS (
                 DELETE FROM big_orders
                 WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM big_orders
                                    WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND created_at < p_before
                                    ORDER BY order_id LIMIT p_batch)
                 RETURNING *
               )
               INSERT INTO big_orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
               GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT;
               EXIT WHEN n = 0;
               total := total + n;
               COMMIT;                                   -- this batch is saved, its locks are released
               RAISE NOTICE 'batch of %, % archived so far', n, total;
             END LOOP;
           END;
           $$;

ERROR:  invalid transaction termination

    "invalid transaction termination" again. To change a setting for a committing procedure, use SET LOCAL inside each transaction, or SET for the session before the CALL. The same rule applies to SECURITY DEFINER (Session 72).

  8. Process each due job in its own transaction: write process_due_jobs() that loops over queued jobs with run_after <= now(), marks each one done, but treats resize_image as a failure (raise inside an inner BEGIN … EXCEPTION block; in the handler add 1 to attempts and fail the job at 3 attempts). COMMIT after each job. Show all jobs that were due.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE PROCEDURE process_due_jobs()
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  j record;
BEGIN
  FOR j IN SELECT job_id, kind FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY job_id LOOP
    BEGIN
      IF j.kind = 'resize_image' THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'image service down';
      END IF;
      UPDATE jobs SET status = 'done', attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE job_id = j.job_id;
    EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
      UPDATE jobs SET attempts = attempts + 1,
                      status = CASE WHEN attempts + 1 >= 3 THEN 'failed' ELSE 'queued' END
      WHERE job_id = j.job_id;
      RAISE NOTICE 'job % failed: %', j.job_id, SQLERRM;
    END;
    COMMIT;
  END LOOP;
END;
$$;
CALL process_due_jobs();
SELECT job_id, kind, status, attempts FROM jobs WHERE job_id IN (4, 5, 6, 7, 10) ORDER BY job_id;

  9. Prove that COMMIT starts a new transaction: in a DO block, save now() in v1, sleep 0.05 s, save now() in v2, COMMIT, save now() in v3. Print whether v1 = v2 and whether v1 = v3.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    DO $$
DECLARE
  v1 timestamptz; v2 timestamptz; v3 timestamptz;
BEGIN
  v1 := now();
  PERFORM pg_sleep(0.05);
  v2 := now();
  COMMIT;
  v3 := now();
  RAISE NOTICE 'same transaction: %, after commit: %', v1 = v2, v1 = v3;
END;
$$;
    practice=# DO $$
           DECLARE
             v1 timestamptz; v2 timestamptz; v3 timestamptz;
           BEGIN
             v1 := now();
             PERFORM pg_sleep(0.05);
             v2 := now();
             COMMIT;
             v3 := now();
             RAISE NOTICE 'same transaction: %, after commit: %', v1 = v2, v1 = v3;
           END;
           $$;
NOTICE:  same transaction: t, after commit: f
DO

    true, then false. Within a transaction now() never moves; after COMMIT the procedure is in a new transaction with a new start time. A long batch procedure that stamps rows with now() therefore gets a different time per batch. Use clock_timestamp() for the real time, or pass one fixed timestamp as a parameter.

Challenge: A resumable job with a progress table: create archive_progress (job text PRIMARY KEY, last_id int, rows_moved bigint) and archive_resumable(p_max_batches int) that walks big_orders by order_id (keyset, batches of 1,000 ids), archives cancelled orders before 2025 in each id range, and saves its position with each COMMIT. Call it with 50 batches (as if it were stopped), look at the progress, then call it again with 1000 batches to finish.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE big_orders_archive (LIKE big_orders);
CREATE TABLE archive_progress (job text PRIMARY KEY, last_id int NOT NULL, rows_moved bigint NOT NULL);
CREATE PROCEDURE archive_resumable(p_max_batches int)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  v_last int;
  v_max int;
  n bigint;
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO archive_progress VALUES ('cancelled_2024', 0, 0) ON CONFLICT (job) DO NOTHING;
  SELECT last_id INTO v_last FROM archive_progress WHERE job = 'cancelled_2024';
  SELECT max(order_id) INTO v_max FROM big_orders;
  FOR i IN 1..p_max_batches LOOP
    EXIT WHEN v_last >= v_max;
    WITH moved AS (
      DELETE FROM big_orders
      WHERE order_id > v_last AND order_id <= v_last + 1000
        AND status = 'cancelled' AND created_at < '2025-01-01'
      RETURNING *
    )
    INSERT INTO big_orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
    GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT;
    v_last := v_last + 1000;
    UPDATE archive_progress SET last_id = v_last, rows_moved = rows_moved + n WHERE job = 'cancelled_2024';
    COMMIT;
  END LOOP;
END;
$$;
CALL archive_resumable(50);
SELECT * FROM archive_progress;
CALL archive_resumable(1000);
SELECT p.last_id, p.rows_moved, (SELECT count(*) FROM big_orders_archive) AS archived FROM archive_progress p;

Phase 7 · Session 69

Triggers

Run code automatically when rows change: fill in and clean values, enforce rules, keep an audit trail, and know when a trigger is the wrong tool.

Topics

Two parts

A trigger function (RETURNS trigger, no arguments) holds the code. CREATE TRIGGER attaches it to a table and says when it runs. One function can serve many tables.

CREATE TRIGGER customers_email
  BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF email ON customers   -- when: BEFORE / AFTER, which events, which columns
  FOR EACH ROW                                   -- once per row (or FOR EACH STATEMENT)
  WHEN (NEW.email IS NOT NULL)                   -- optional filter, checked before calling the function
  EXECUTE FUNCTION normalize_email();

What the function sees

  • NEW: the row being written (INSERT, UPDATE). OLD: the row before (UPDATE, DELETE).
  • TG_OP (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE), TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_WHEN, TG_LEVEL.
  • BEFORE ROW: may change NEW, and its return value matters: return NEW (or OLD for DELETE) to go ahead, return NULL to silently skip this row.
  • AFTER ROW: the row is written; the return value is ignored. Use it for side effects: audit rows, queue entries, summaries.
  • Statement-level: runs once per statement, even if 0 rows changed; with REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS … it can read all changed rows at once.
  • Several triggers on the same event run in alphabetical order of their names.
practice=# CREATE FUNCTION normalize_email() RETURNS trigger
           LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
           BEGIN
             NEW.email := lower(trim(NEW.email));
             RETURN NEW;
           END;
           $$;
CREATE FUNCTION
practice=# CREATE TRIGGER customers_email BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF email ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION normalize_email();
CREATE TRIGGER
practice=# INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, full_name, email, city, signup_date)
           VALUES (21, 'Tara Iyer', '  Tara.Iyer@Mail.TEST ', 'Pune', '2026-02-20');
INSERT 0 1
practice=# SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 21;
 customer_id |        email
-------------+---------------------
          21 | tara.iyer@mail.test
(1 row)

Triggers are invisible. Someone reading UPDATE accounts … does not see the three triggers it fires. Use them for things that must happen whatever code writes the row (audit, timestamps, invariants); keep business workflows in functions and the application. And they run once per row: a 1,000,000-row UPDATE runs a row trigger 1,000,000 times.

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s69.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Add updated_at timestamptz to products and a BEFORE UPDATE trigger that sets it to now(). Change the price of product 2 and show its updated_at compared with now().

    Expected: 2 rows

    Answer
    ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN updated_at timestamptz;

CREATE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := now();
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER products_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON products
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

UPDATE products SET price = 82000 WHERE product_id = 2;

SELECT product_id, price, updated_at = now() AS stamped_now
FROM products WHERE product_id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY product_id;
    product_idpricestamped_now
    1120000.00∅
    282000.00t

    (2 rows)

    Product 2 is stamped (true); product 1 was not updated, so its updated_at is NULL. The trigger sets the column whatever the UPDATE says: even SET updated_at = '2000-01-01' is overwritten. set_updated_at() is generic: attach it to every table that has an updated_at column.

  3. Validate in a trigger: bookings must start on the hour and be for at most 8 people. Write a BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE trigger on table_bookings that raises a clear error otherwise, and try a booking at 19:30 and one for 10 people.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION check_booking() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF date_trunc('hour', NEW.slot) <> NEW.slot THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'bookings start on the hour, got %', NEW.slot USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation';
  END IF;
  IF NEW.party_size > 8 THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'party of % is too large (max 8)', NEW.party_size USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation';
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER table_bookings_check BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON table_bookings FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION check_booking();
INSERT INTO table_bookings VALUES (6, 4, '2026-02-20 19:30+05:30', 'Vivaan', 2);
INSERT INTO table_bookings VALUES (7, 4, '2026-02-20 19:00+05:30', 'Neel', 10);

             END IF;

               RAISE EXCEPTION 'party of % is too large (max 8)', NEW.party_size USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation';

    Both are rejected. Honestly, both rules fit in CHECK constraints (CHECK (party_size <= 8), CHECK (date_trunc('hour', slot) = slot)), which are simpler and faster, and visible in \d. Use a trigger for a rule only when it needs other rows or other tables, which CHECK cannot read.

  4. An audit trail: create audit_log and the generic audit() function, attach it AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE on accounts, then: move 100 from Aarav to Diya, add account 5 (Ishaan, 0), delete account 4. Show the log.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  audit_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  table_name text NOT NULL,
  op         text NOT NULL,
  old_row    jsonb,
  new_row    jsonb,
  changed_by text NOT NULL DEFAULT current_user,
  changed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE FUNCTION audit() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO audit_log (table_name, op, old_row, new_row)
  VALUES (TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_OP, to_jsonb(OLD), to_jsonb(NEW));   -- OLD is NULL on INSERT, NEW on DELETE
  RETURN NULL;                                                     -- ignored for AFTER triggers
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER accounts_audit AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON accounts FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit();
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 2;
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (5, 'Ishaan', 0);
DELETE FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 4;
SELECT audit_id, op, old_row->>'owner' AS owner, old_row->>'balance' AS old_balance, new_row->>'balance' AS new_balance
FROM audit_log ORDER BY audit_id;

        1 | UPDATE | Aarav  | 5000.00     | 4900.00
        2 | UPDATE | Diya   | 3000.00     | 3100.00
        3 | INSERT | ∅      | ∅           | 0.00
        4 | DELETE | Ananya | 1200.00     | ∅
(4 rows)

    Four rows: two UPDATEs (5000 → 4900, 3000 → 3100), the INSERT (no old row) and the DELETE (no new row; Ananya's 1200 is preserved in old_row). jsonb makes one function and one log table work for every table. The log is written in the same transaction: if the change rolls back, so does its audit row.

  6. A BEFORE trigger that returns NULL: on jobs, skip (with a NOTICE) any DELETE of a running job. Then run DELETE FROM jobs WHERE status IN ('running', 'done').

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION keep_running_jobs() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.status = 'running' THEN
    RAISE NOTICE 'job % is running, not deleted', OLD.job_id;
    RETURN NULL;
  END IF;
  RETURN OLD;
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER jobs_keep_running BEFORE DELETE ON jobs FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION keep_running_jobs();
DELETE FROM jobs WHERE status IN ('running', 'done');
    practice=# CREATE FUNCTION keep_running_jobs() RETURNS trigger
           LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
           BEGIN
             IF OLD.status = 'running' THEN
               RAISE NOTICE 'job % is running, not deleted', OLD.job_id;
               RETURN NULL;
             END IF;
             RETURN OLD;
           END;
           $$;
CREATE FUNCTION
practice=# CREATE TRIGGER jobs_keep_running BEFORE DELETE ON jobs FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION keep_running_jobs();
CREATE TRIGGER
practice=# DELETE FROM jobs WHERE status IN ('running', 'done');
NOTICE:  job 9 is running, not deleted
DELETE 2

    "DELETE 2": three rows matched, job 9 was skipped. Without the NOTICE, nobody would know why the count is 2. This is the classic trigger bug: a BEFORE ROW function that forgets RETURN NEW returns NULL and silently throws away every insert. If a row must not be deleted, raising an error is usually clearer.

  8. Transition tables: an AFTER UPDATE … FOR EACH STATEMENT trigger on accounts that compares sum(balance) in the old and new rows and raises if money was created or lost. Move 100 from Aarav to Diya in one UPDATE, then in two UPDATEs.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION check_money() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  v_old numeric; v_new numeric;
BEGIN
  SELECT sum(balance) INTO v_old FROM old_rows;
  SELECT sum(balance) INTO v_new FROM new_rows;
  IF v_old IS DISTINCT FROM v_new THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'money was created or lost: % before, % after', v_old, v_new;
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER accounts_money AFTER UPDATE ON accounts
  REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS old_rows NEW TABLE AS new_rows
  FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION check_money();
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + CASE account_id WHEN 1 THEN -100 ELSE 100 END
WHERE account_id IN (1, 2);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
    practice=# CREATE FUNCTION check_money() RETURNS trigger
           LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
           DECLARE
             v_old numeric; v_new numeric;
           BEGIN
             SELECT sum(balance) INTO v_old FROM old_rows;
             SELECT sum(balance) INTO v_new FROM new_rows;
             IF v_old IS DISTINCT FROM v_new THEN
               RAISE EXCEPTION 'money was created or lost: % before, % after', v_old, v_new;
             END IF;
             RETURN NULL;
           END;
           $$;
CREATE FUNCTION
practice=# CREATE TRIGGER accounts_money AFTER UPDATE ON accounts
             REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS old_rows NEW TABLE AS new_rows
             FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION check_money();
CREATE TRIGGER
practice=# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + CASE account_id WHEN 1 THEN -100 ELSE 100 END
           WHERE account_id IN (1, 2);
UPDATE 2
practice=# UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
ERROR:  money was created or lost: 4900.00 before, 4800.00 after

    The single-statement transfer passes (8000 before and after for the two rows). The two-statement version fails at its first UPDATE: "4900.00 before, 4800.00 after". A statement trigger checks one statement; a rule that only holds at the end of the transaction needs a deferred constraint trigger (Session 71). Transition tables are also the fast way to audit big updates: one INSERT … SELECT per statement instead of one per row.

  9. Trigger order: on a fresh copy of customers' email rules, create a_check_email (rejects emails that are not lower case) and z_normalize_email (lower-cases them), both BEFORE INSERT. Insert Tara. Then fix the order without changing either function.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION normalize_email() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.email := lower(trim(NEW.email));
  RETURN NEW;
END;

CREATE FUNCTION check_email() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF NEW.email <> lower(NEW.email) THEN

  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

--------+---------+----------

(1 row)

    The first UPDATE fires the trigger, whose UPDATE fires it again, and so on until "stack depth limit exceeded"; everything rolls back. With the depth guard, the inner UPDATE does not fire it: status running, attempts 1. Better still: change NEW in a BEFORE trigger (NEW.attempts := OLD.attempts + 1), which needs no second UPDATE at all.

  11. Protect history: a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger on orders that rejects any change to a delivered order. Try to cancel order 1 (delivered) and to delete it; then cancel a pending order.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION freeze_delivered() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.status = 'delivered' THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'order % is delivered and cannot be changed (%)', OLD.order_id, TG_OP;
  END IF;
  RETURN COALESCE(NEW, OLD);
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER orders_freeze BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON orders FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION freeze_delivered();
UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE order_id = 1;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 1;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE order_id = (SELECT min(order_id) FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending');
    practice=# CREATE FUNCTION freeze_delivered() RETURNS trigger
           LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
           BEGIN
             IF OLD.status = 'delivered' THEN
               RAISE EXCEPTION 'order % is delivered and cannot be changed (%)', OLD.order_id, TG_OP;
             END IF;
             RETURN COALESCE(NEW, OLD);
           END;
           $$;
CREATE FUNCTION
practice=# CREATE TRIGGER orders_freeze BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON orders FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION freeze_delivered();
CREATE TRIGGER
practice=# UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE order_id = 1;
ERROR:  order 1 is delivered and cannot be changed (UPDATE)
practice=# DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 1;
ERROR:  order 1 is delivered and cannot be changed (DELETE)
practice=# UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE order_id = (SELECT min(order_id) FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending');
UPDATE 1

    Both changes to order 1 are rejected; the pending order is cancelled (UPDATE 1). COALESCE(NEW, OLD) returns the right row for UPDATE (NEW) and DELETE (NEW is NULL, so OLD). This rule needs the old value, which a CHECK constraint cannot see: a good use of a trigger.

  13. Challenge: Maintain price_history automatically: when a product's price changes, close its open range (upper bound = today) and open a new one from today with the new price. If the open range already starts today (a second change on the same day), just update its price. Change product 2's price twice and show its history (price, whether the range starts today, whether it is open).

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION track_price() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE price_history SET price = NEW.price
  WHERE product_id = NEW.product_id AND upper_inf(valid_during) AND lower(valid_during) = current_date;
  IF NOT FOUND THEN
    UPDATE price_history SET valid_during = daterange(lower(valid_during), current_date)
    WHERE product_id = NEW.product_id AND upper_inf(valid_during);
    INSERT INTO price_history VALUES (NEW.product_id, NEW.price, daterange(current_date, NULL));
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER products_price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW
  WHEN (OLD.price IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.price)
  EXECUTE FUNCTION track_price();
UPDATE products SET price = 82000 WHERE product_id = 2;
UPDATE products SET price = 80000 WHERE product_id = 2;
SELECT price, lower(valid_during) = current_date AS starts_today, upper_inf(valid_during) AS open
FROM price_history WHERE product_id = 2 ORDER BY lower(valid_during);

           FROM price_history WHERE product_id = 2 ORDER BY lower(valid_during);

----------+--------------+------
 85000.00 | f            | f

    Two rows: 85,000 (closed, ends today) and 80,000 (starts today, open). The 82,000 never appears: same-day changes overwrite, because a range [today, today) would be empty. Now no code path can change a price without leaving history, and the history never has gaps or overlaps (the exclusion constraint from Session 47 guarantees it).

Phase 7 · Session 70

Review: functions, procedures and triggers

Pull Sessions 64–69 back out of memory, mixed with earlier phases, before triggers part 2 and security.

Topics

How to run this review

  • Reload practice.sql. Close your notes from Sessions 64–69.
  • For every question, write down your prediction first: the result, the error, or the NOTICE you expect. Then run it.
  • Anything you got wrong goes on a card; redo those questions cold at the start of Session 71.

Cheat sheet: Sessions 64–69

Need                                         Tool
-------------------------------------------  ---------------------------------------------------------
a reusable calculation inside queries        SQL function, RETURN (…) or BEGIN ATOMIC (S64)
the planner may cache / index it             IMMUTABLE (never lie), STABLE for table reads (S65)
a function that returns rows                 RETURNS TABLE / SETOF, call in FROM (S65)
variables, IF, loops, error checks           PL/pgSQL, SELECT … INTO STRICT, FOUND (S66)
fail loudly with a code                      RAISE EXCEPTION … USING ERRCODE, DETAIL, HINT (S67)
recover from one failure                     BEGIN … EXCEPTION WHEN … END (a savepoint) (S67)
SQL text built at run time                   EXECUTE format('%I', name) … USING value (S67)
long batch job, commit as you go             PROCEDURE + COMMIT, CALL outside BEGIN (S68)
fill in / clean a value on every write       BEFORE ROW trigger, change NEW, RETURN NEW (S69)
side effects: audit, queue                   AFTER ROW trigger (S69)
check all changed rows of one statement      AFTER STATEMENT trigger + transition tables (S69)

Questions

Write your answers in psql/s70.sql and run them on the practice database. Open an answer only after you have tried.

  1. Write order_count(p_customer int) as a SQL function with a standard body, and use it to list customers 1–3 with their number of orders.

    Expected: 3 rows

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION order_count(p_customer int) RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE sql STABLE
RETURN (SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = p_customer);

SELECT customer_id, full_name, order_count(customer_id) AS orders
FROM customers WHERE customer_id <= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;
    customer_idfull_nameorders
    1Aarav Shah4
    2Diya Menon4
    3Kabir Khan3

    (3 rows)

    4, 4 and 3 (S64). STABLE because it reads a table. Called per row like this, it runs one query per customer: fine for 3 rows, a join or GROUP BY for 30,000 (S64, S52).

  2. Without running it first: what is the volatility of now(), random(), clock_timestamp() and upper(text)? Then check in pg_proc.

    Expected: 4 rows

    Answer
    SELECT oid::regprocedure AS function, provolatile
FROM pg_proc
WHERE oid IN ('now()'::regprocedure, 'random()'::regprocedure,
              'clock_timestamp()'::regprocedure, 'upper(text)'::regprocedure)
ORDER BY 1::text;
    functionprovolatile
    upper(text)i
    now()s
    random()v
    clock_timestamp()v

    (4 rows)

    now() s (fixed within a transaction), random() and clock_timestamp() v (a new value on every call), upper(text) i (same input, same output forever) (S65).

  3. Write orders_between(p_from date, p_to date) RETURNS TABLE (order_id int, order_date date, status text) and count the orders of Q1 2025 with it.

    Expected: 1 row

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION orders_between(p_from date, p_to date)
RETURNS TABLE (order_id int, order_date date, status text)
LANGUAGE sql STABLE
BEGIN ATOMIC
  SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, o.status FROM orders o
  WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN p_from AND p_to;
END;

SELECT count(*) FROM orders_between('2025-01-01', '2025-03-31');
    count
    10

    (1 row)

    10 (S65). Prefixing the columns with the alias (o.order_id) avoids a clash with the OUT columns of the same name.

    CREATE PROCEDURE requeue_running()
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  n bigint;
BEGIN
  UPDATE jobs SET status = 'queued', locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL WHERE status = 'running';
  GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT;
  COMMIT;
  RAISE NOTICE 'requeued % job(s)', n;
END;
$$;

Phase 7 · Session 71

Triggers 2: summaries, views, deferred checks and LISTEN/NOTIFY

Keep summary tables correct, make join views writable, check rules at COMMIT, react to DDL, and tell other programs about changes the moment they commit.

Topics

More kinds of triggers

INSTEAD OF … ON a_view FOR EACH ROW     run instead of the INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on a view
CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER …
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED          an AFTER ROW trigger that runs at COMMIT
CREATE EVENT TRIGGER … ON ddl_command_end  runs on CREATE / ALTER / DROP, not on rows

Summary tables

A count that a dashboard needs a thousand times a second can be kept in a small table and updated by a trigger. Always change it with an atomic statement (n = n + 1 or an upsert), never by reading the old value first (Session 57). The cost: every order for the same customer now updates the same summary row, so concurrent writers queue on that row lock (Q2).

LISTEN / NOTIFY

A session runs LISTEN jobs_ready;. Any other session runs NOTIFY jobs_ready, '42' (or SELECT pg_notify('jobs_ready', '42'), which takes the channel as a value). Every listener gets the message, but only when the sending transaction commits; a rollback sends nothing. Workers can sleep until there is work instead of polling every second.

B=# LISTEN jobs_ready;
LISTEN
            A=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            A=*# NOTIFY jobs_ready, 'job 11';
            NOTIFY
B=# SELECT 1 AS before_commit;
 before_commit
---------------
             1
(1 row)
            A=*# COMMIT;
            COMMIT
B=# SELECT 1 AS after_commit;
 after_commit
--------------
            1
(1 row)
Asynchronous notification "jobs_ready" with payload "job 11" received from server process with PID <pid>.

psql only shows a notification after the next command it runs, which is why B runs a SELECT. Real listeners (drivers like psycopg or node-postgres) receive them as events.

NOTIFY is not a queue. A listener that is disconnected when the message is sent never gets it, and payloads are limited to 8,000 bytes. Keep the real work in a table (jobs, outbox) and use NOTIFY only as a "wake up and look" signal.

  1. Create customer_order_counts with the count_orders() trigger (code below), then insert order 37 for customer 3, move it to customer 5, insert order 38 for customer 3 and delete it again. Compare the summary with a real count for customers 3 and 5.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE customer_order_counts (customer_id int PRIMARY KEY, n bigint NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO customer_order_counts SELECT customer_id, count(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

CREATE FUNCTION count_orders() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP IN ('INSERT', 'UPDATE') THEN
    INSERT INTO customer_order_counts VALUES (NEW.customer_id, 1)
    ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE SET n = customer_order_counts.n + 1;
  END IF;
  IF TG_OP IN ('DELETE', 'UPDATE') THEN
    UPDATE customer_order_counts SET n = n - 1 WHERE customer_id = OLD.customer_id;
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_count AFTER INSERT OR DELETE OR UPDATE OF customer_id ON orders

FROM customer_order_counts s

  2. The cost of a summary row: with the counting trigger in place, A and B each insert an order for customer 3 in their own transaction. What happens to B?

    Two terminals: compare your output with the answer

    Answer

    Setup, run first:

    CREATE TABLE customer_order_counts (customer_id int PRIMARY KEY, n bigint NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO customer_order_counts SELECT customer_id, count(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

CREATE FUNCTION count_orders() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP IN ('INSERT', 'UPDATE') THEN
    INSERT INTO customer_order_counts VALUES (NEW.customer_id, 1)
    ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE SET n = customer_order_counts.n + 1;
  END IF;
  IF TG_OP IN ('DELETE', 'UPDATE') THEN
    UPDATE customer_order_counts SET n = n - 1 WHERE customer_id = OLD.customer_id;
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_count AFTER INSERT OR DELETE OR UPDATE OF customer_id ON orders
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION count_orders();
    A=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
A=*# INSERT INTO orders VALUES (37, 3, '2026-02-20', 'pending', 'Pune');
INSERT 0 1
            B=# INSERT INTO orders VALUES (38, 3, '2026-02-20', 'pending', 'Pune');
            ⏳ blocked: waiting for a lock …
A=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
            ⏳ … B's statement finishes:
            INSERT 0 1
            B=# SELECT n FROM customer_order_counts WHERE customer_id = 3;
             n
            ---
             5
            (1 row)

    B is blocked until A commits: the orders do not conflict, but both triggers update the same summary row. Then B adds its 1 and the count is 5. Correct, but every write for the same customer is serialised. For hot counters, insert +1/−1 rows into a delta table and add them up periodically, or count on demand with an index.

  3. Make a join view writable: create order_view (order_id, status, customer name) over orders JOIN customers, try to UPDATE its status, then add an INSTEAD OF UPDATE trigger that changes orders.status and rejects name changes. Try again.

    Answer
    CREATE VIEW order_view AS
SELECT o.order_id, o.status, c.full_name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
UPDATE order_view SET status = 'shipped' WHERE order_id = 30;
CREATE FUNCTION order_view_update() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF NEW.full_name IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.full_name THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'change the name in customers, not through order_view';
  END IF;
  UPDATE orders SET status = NEW.status WHERE order_id = OLD.order_id;
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER order_view_update INSTEAD OF UPDATE ON order_view FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION order_view_update();
UPDATE order_view SET status = 'shipped' WHERE order_id = 30;
UPDATE order_view SET full_name = 'Someone Else' WHERE order_id = 30;
SELECT order_id, status FROM orders WHERE order_id = 30;

  4. A check at COMMIT: create the deferred constraint trigger accounts_total (code below) that requires the total to be 9,200. Run a two-statement transfer in a transaction, then a transaction that only debits.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer

LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF (SELECT sum(balance) FROM accounts) <> 9200 THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'money was created or lost: total is %', (SELECT sum(balance) FROM accounts);
  END IF;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER accounts_total AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON accounts
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION check_total();
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 2;
COMMIT;
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 1;
COMMIT;
SELECT sum(balance) FROM accounts;

  6. Log every schema change: create ddl_log, an event trigger function that records the command tag and object for each DDL command, and an event trigger on ddl_command_end. Then create a table, add a column, create an index, and show the log.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE ddl_log (logged_at timestamptz DEFAULT now(), username text DEFAULT current_user, command text, object text);
CREATE FUNCTION log_ddl() RETURNS event_trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  r record;
BEGIN
  FOR r IN SELECT * FROM pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands() LOOP
    INSERT INTO ddl_log (command, object) VALUES (r.command_tag, r.object_identity);
  END LOOP;
END;
$$;
CREATE EVENT TRIGGER log_ddl ON ddl_command_end EXECUTE FUNCTION log_ddl();
CREATE TABLE coupons (code text PRIMARY KEY, pct int);
ALTER TABLE coupons ADD COLUMN expires date;
CREATE INDEX ON coupons (expires);

  7. Block DROP TABLE: an event trigger on ddl_command_start, limited with WHEN TAG IN ('DROP TABLE'), that raises unless the setting app.allow_drop is 'on'. Try to drop jobs, then allow it for one transaction with SET LOCAL.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE FUNCTION no_drop_table() RETURNS event_trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF current_setting('app.allow_drop', true) IS DISTINCT FROM 'on' THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'DROP TABLE is blocked'
      USING HINT = 'SET LOCAL app.allow_drop = on inside the transaction if you really mean it.';
  END IF;
END;
$$;
CREATE EVENT TRIGGER no_drop_table ON ddl_command_start WHEN TAG IN ('DROP TABLE') EXECUTE FUNCTION no_drop_table();
DROP TABLE jobs;
BEGIN;
SET LOCAL app.allow_drop = on;
DROP TABLE jobs;
ROLLBACK;

  8. NOTIFY from a trigger, and rollback: attach the jobs_notify trigger (code below; it notifies for due jobs). B listens. A inserts job 11 and rolls back; then inserts job 12 and commits. What does B receive?

    Two terminals: compare your output with the answer

    Answer

    Setup, run first:

    CREATE FUNCTION notify_job() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  PERFORM pg_notify('jobs_ready', NEW.job_id::text);
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER jobs_notify AFTER INSERT ON jobs FOR EACH ROW
  WHEN (NEW.status = 'queued' AND NEW.run_after <= now())
  EXECUTE FUNCTION notify_job();
    B=# LISTEN jobs_ready;
LISTEN
            A=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            A=*# INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (11, 'send_email', now());
            INSERT 0 1
            A=*# ROLLBACK;
            ROLLBACK
B=# SELECT 1 AS after_rollback;
 after_rollback
----------------
              1
(1 row)
            A=# INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (12, 'send_email', now());
            INSERT 0 1
B=# SELECT 1 AS after_commit;
 after_commit
--------------
            1
(1 row)
Asynchronous notification "jobs_ready" with payload "12" received from server process with PID <pid>.

    Nothing after the rollback; "12" after the commit. A worker woken by the message will always find job 12 in the table, because the notification is sent only after the row is visible. That is what makes NOTIFY safe to send from inside a transaction.

            NOTIFY

            NOTIFY

----------

(1 row)
Asynchronous notification "ping" with payload "a" received from server process with PID <pid>.
Asynchronous notification "ping" with payload "b" received from server process with PID <pid>.

    Two: "a" once and "b". A trigger that notifies for each of 10,000 updated rows with the same payload sends one message; with job_id in the payload it sends 10,000. For bulk changes, notify from a statement-level trigger, or just send "something changed" and let the listener read the table.

  10. The outbox pattern: create the outbox table and the orders_outbox trigger (code below). Ship order 30, then deliver it. Then act as the relay: take up to 10 events with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, delete them, and return them (in a real system: publish them to a message broker, then commit).

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE outbox (
  event_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  event_type text NOT NULL,
  payload    jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE FUNCTION order_status_event() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload)
  VALUES ('order_' || NEW.status, jsonb_build_object('order_id', NEW.order_id, 'from', OLD.status, 'to', NEW.status));
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_outbox AFTER UPDATE OF status ON orders FOR EACH ROW
  WHEN (OLD.status IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.status)
  EXECUTE FUNCTION order_status_event();
UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE order_id = 30;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'delivered' WHERE order_id = 30;
DELETE FROM outbox
WHERE event_id IN (SELECT event_id FROM outbox ORDER BY event_id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING event_id, event_type, payload;
SELECT count(*) AS left_in_outbox FROM outbox;

----------+-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------

    Two events, order_shipped and order_delivered, in order; the outbox is then empty. The event is written in the same transaction as the change, so you never publish "shipped" for an update that rolled back, and never lose one for an update that committed. Sending to a broker directly from the app cannot promise both. SKIP LOCKED lets several relays run (Session 58).

  11. A bulk-friendly summary: replace the row-level counter with an AFTER INSERT statement-level trigger that reads a transition table and does one grouped upsert. Insert three orders (two for customer 3, one for customer 5) in one INSERT.

    Compare your output with the answer

    Answer
    CREATE TABLE customer_order_counts (customer_id int PRIMARY KEY, n bigint NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO customer_order_counts SELECT customer_id, count(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
CREATE FUNCTION count_new_orders() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO customer_order_counts
  SELECT customer_id, count(*) FROM new_rows GROUP BY customer_id
  ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE SET n = customer_order_counts.n + EXCLUDED.n;
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;
CREATE TRIGGER orders_count_bulk AFTER INSERT ON orders REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS new_rows
  FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION count_new_orders();

  (39, 5, '2026-02-20', 'pending', 'Delhi');

  12. Challenge: A worker that sleeps until there is work: with the jobs_notify trigger in place, B is a worker that LISTENs on jobs_ready. A queues two jobs in one transaction: job 11 due now and job 12 for tomorrow, and commits. B wakes on the notification and claims one due job with the claim statement from Session 58 (SKIP LOCKED). Which notifications does B get, and which job does it claim?

    Two terminals: compare your output with the answer

    Answer

    Setup, run first:

    CREATE FUNCTION notify_job() RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  PERFORM pg_notify('jobs_ready', NEW.job_id::text);
  RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER jobs_notify AFTER INSERT ON jobs FOR EACH ROW
  WHEN (NEW.status = 'queued' AND NEW.run_after <= now())
  EXECUTE FUNCTION notify_job();
    B=# LISTEN jobs_ready;
LISTEN
            A=# BEGIN;
            BEGIN
            A=*# INSERT INTO jobs (job_id, kind, run_after) VALUES (11, 'send_email', now()),
                                                               (12, 'send_email', now() + interval '1 day');
            INSERT 0 2
            A=*# COMMIT;
            COMMIT
B=# UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', locked_by = 'worker-B', locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
    WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' AND run_after <= now()
                    ORDER BY run_after, job_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
    RETURNING job_id, kind;
 job_id |    kind
--------+------------
      4 | send_email
(1 row)
Asynchronous notification "jobs_ready" with payload "11" received from server process with PID <pid>.

    One notification ("11"): the trigger's WHEN skipped job 12, which is not due. But B claims job 4, not 11: the oldest due job wins, and 4 to 10 were already waiting. That is the right design: the notification only says "look now", and the claim query decides what to take. Job 12 needs a timer anyway (a worker still polls, say, every 30 s for jobs that become due later); LISTEN just removes the delay for new work.

Phase 7 · Session 72

Roles, privileges and row-level security

Give each program and person exactly the access it needs, hide rows other users must not see, and write SECURITY DEFINER functions that cannot be abused.

Topics

Roles

A role is both a user and a group. A role with LOGIN can connect; a role without it is a group you grant privileges to. Members inherit the privileges of the groups they are in.

CREATE ROLE reporting NOLOGIN;                          a group
CREATE ROLE meera LOGIN PASSWORD '…' IN ROLE reporting;  a person in that group
GRANT SELECT ON orders, order_items TO reporting;
REVOKE SELECT ON orders FROM reporting;
SET ROLE meera;  …  RESET ROLE;                          act as meera to test (needs membership or superuser)

Who can do what

  • The owner of an object (who created it) can do everything with it, including GRANT. A superuser bypasses every check: never let an application connect as one.
  • Privileges per table: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER; SELECT and UPDATE can be limited to columns. Schemas need USAGE (and CREATE to create objects). Sequences need USAGE for nextval().
  • PUBLIC means every role. By default PUBLIC may EXECUTE every new function and use the public schema (since Postgres 15, not create objects in it).
  • GRANT … ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA covers the tables that exist now. For future tables: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES.

Row-level security (RLS)

ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY own_orders ON orders
  USING (customer_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.customer_id', true), '')::int)        -- which rows you can see / change
  WITH CHECK (customer_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.customer_id', true), '')::int);  -- which rows you may write

The app runs SET LOCAL app.customer_id = '3' at the start of each transaction.

With RLS on and no policy, a normal role sees nothing. Policies are added to every query as an invisible WHERE. The table owner, superusers and BYPASSRLS roles skip the policies (the owner stops skipping with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY).

SECURITY DEFINER

A normal function runs with the caller's privileges. A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with its owner's: a controlled door ("anyone may call cancel_my_order(), nobody may UPDATE orders"). Always give it a fixed search_path, and REVOKE EXECUTE FROM PUBLIC unless everyone should have the door.

CREATE FUNCTION … SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public, pg_temp AS …;
REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION … FROM PUBLIC;
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION … TO app_user;

Every question here uses SET ROLE inside your superuser session. Run RESET ROLE when a question is done (the answers do), or the next one runs as the wrong role. A transcript that ends with roles still existing is fine: drop them with DROP OWNED BY r; DROP ROLE r;.

    Tenant 1 sees 3 and cannot insert for tenant 2 (the USING expression doubles as WITH CHECK); tenant 2 sees 1; outside a transaction the setting is gone and app_user sees 0. The pieces: a separate owner (and FORCE as a seatbelt), a non-owner app role, SET LOCAL per transaction (a plain SET would leak to the next request on a pooled connection), fail-closed when unset (NULLIF turns the empty string that SET LOCAL leaves behind into NULL), and an index on tenant_id because the policy is in every query's WHERE.
